### [1] [Continuous Audio Thinking for Large Audio Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18273)
*Gyojin Han,Dong-Jae Lee,Changho Choi,Jongsuk Kim,Junmo Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CoAT introduces a continuous latent thinking workspace into audio language models, distilled from audio experts, enabling the model to preserve and leverage rich acoustic information (phonetics, prosody, emotion, etc.) without increasing autoregressive decoding cost, yielding consistent gains across multiple LALMs and benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large audio language models are trained to produce text-aligned responses, causing their hidden states to progressively lose acoustic information (phonetic detail, prosody, sound events, affect, pitch) that is crucial for nuanced audio understanding. This acoustic information loss limits the model's ability to leverage the full richness of audio inputs in downstream tasks.

Method: The authors propose Continuous Audio Thinking (CoAT), which inserts a continuous latent thinking workspace into the LALM architecture. This workspace is trained via distillation from external audio experts (e.g., models specialized in speech, emotion, music) to organize acoustic information before text generation. The thinking block operates in a single prefill step, incurring no extra autoregressive decoding overhead. The approach is applied to three LALMs: Qwen2-Audio, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, and Audio Flamingo 3.

Result: CoAT yields performance improvements across a broad benchmark suite covering audio reasoning, audio understanding, music classification, speech emotion recognition, and speech transcription. Analysis further shows that the auxiliary acoustic supervision propagates from the thinking positions into the model's textual responses, confirming effective information transfer.

Conclusion: CoAT provides an effective, cost-efficient method for preserving and utilizing rich acoustic information in audio language models through a continuous thinking workspace distilled from audio experts, significantly improving performance across diverse audio tasks without additional decoding cost.

Abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) have shown impressive capabilities on diverse audio understanding tasks, ranging from speech transcription to music analysis. However, because LALMs are typically trained to produce text-aligned responses, their hidden states are progressively shaped for text generation rather than for preserving acoustic information. As a result, the diverse acoustic content that audio carries, such as phonetic detail, prosody, sound events, affect, and pitch, is lost along the way and difficult to leverage in the response. We introduce Continuous Audio Thinking (CoAT), a framework that equips audio language models with a continuous latent workspace for organizing acoustic information prior to response generation, grounded by distillation from audio experts. Within the thinking space, the model can utilize the rich acoustic information provided by expert distillation when generating its response. Furthermore, the proposed continuous thinking block can be processed in a single prefill, so CoAT does not require additional autoregressive decoding cost over the baseline. Across three LALMs, Qwen2-Audio, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, and Audio Flamingo~3, performance gains on a broad benchmark suite spanning audio reasoning, audio understanding, music classification, speech emotion, and speech transcription demonstrate the effectiveness of CoAT. Further analysis confirms that the auxiliary supervision propagates from the thinking positions to the model's textual responses.

</details>


### [2] [Redact or Keep? A Fully Local AI Cascade for Educational Dialogue De-Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18372)
*Haocheng Zhang,Zhuqian Zhou,Kirk Vanacore,Bakhtawar Ahtisham,René F. Kizilcec*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A local cascade framework for educational transcript de-identification that combines a recall-first candidate proposer with a context-aware binary reviewer achieves 0.958 macro F1, outperforming both same-family LLM baselines (0.767) and commercial APIs (0.706), while running entirely on a single laptop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Educational dialogue transcripts contain PII entangled with curricular content (e.g., "Riemann" as a student name vs. a mathematical concept). Existing solutions force a tradeoff: commercial LLMs handle ambiguity but require sending sensitive data to third parties; local NER systems preserve data governance but over-redact domain terms. A solution that maintains both privacy and accuracy without external data transfer is needed.

Method: A two-stage fully local cascade framework: (1) A recall-first union proposer combines two lightweight encoders with deterministic rules to over-generate candidate PII spans. (2) A context-aware reviewer makes a binary Redact/Keep decision per candidate using surrounding dialogue and speaker role. Three reviewer configurations are evaluated against same-family LLM-only baselines and a commercial API.

Result: The strongest local configuration achieves 0.958 macro F1 on math tutoring transcripts from two large platforms, compared to 0.767 (same-family LLM-only) and 0.706 (commercial API). On a targeted ambiguity challenge set (curricular-personal name confusion), the same configuration degrades by only 0.03 F1 vs. 0.19–0.25 for smaller reviewers. All processing runs on a single laptop.

Conclusion: For educational de-identification, problem formulation (constrained privacy triage rather than open-ended NER) matters more than model scale. The cascade design resolves the governance-accuracy tradeoff, enabling high-performance PII redaction without external data exposure.

Abstract: Educational dialogue is a valuable but sensitive resource for research: the same transcripts that capture authentic learning often capture personally identifiable information (PII) entangled with curricular content, where "Riemann" may refer to a real student or to a mathematical concept. Existing approaches force a tradeoff between governance and accuracy. Commercial Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle this ambiguity but require sending student data to third parties, while local named entity recognition (NER) systems preserve governance but over-redact curricular terms. We propose a fully local cascade framework that reframes de-identification from open-ended entity recognition to constrained privacy triage. A recall-first union proposer combines two lightweight encoders with deterministic rules to over-generate candidate spans; a context-aware reviewer then makes a binary Redact/Keep decision for each candidate using surrounding dialogue and speaker role. We evaluate three reviewer configurations against same-family LLM-only baselines and a commercial API on math tutoring transcripts from two large platforms. The strongest local configuration reaches 0.958 macro F1, compared with 0.767 for a same-family LLM-only baseline and 0.706 for the commercial API, while running entirely on a single laptop. On a targeted challenge set of curricular-personal name ambiguity, the same configuration degrades by only 0.03 F1 versus 0.19 to 0.25 for smaller reviewers. These results suggest that for educational de-identification, problem formulation matters more than model scale.

</details>


### [3] [SproutRAG: Attention-Guided Tree Search with Progressive Embeddings for Long-Document RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18381)
*Amirhossein Abaskohi,Issam H. Laradji,Peter West,Giuseppe Carenini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SproutRAG is an attention-guided hierarchical RAG framework that organizes sentence-level chunks into a binary tree using learned inter-sentence attention, enabling multi-granularity retrieval without external LLM calls or lossy summarization, and achieves a 6.1% average improvement in information efficiency over the strongest baseline across four benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG systems face a trade-off between retrieval granularity and contextual coherence. Current solutions either rely on costly LLM-guided chunking, restrict context aggregation to a single granularity level, or introduce information loss through hierarchical summarization. A method is needed that can provide multi-granularity retrieval while preserving semantic coherence without these drawbacks.

Method: SproutRAG constructs a binary chunking tree from sentence-level chunks using learned inter-sentence attention, automatically discovering which attention heads and layers best capture semantic document structure. Larger, semantically coherent units are built progressively. At retrieval time, hierarchical beam search retrieves candidates across multiple granularities to capture multi-sentence relevance. The entire framework is trained end-to-end with a joint objective that simultaneously optimizes embeddings and tree structure.

Result: Experiments across four benchmarks (scientific, legal, and open-domain settings) show SproutRAG improves information efficiency (IE) by 6.1% on average over the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: SproutRAG demonstrates that learning document structure via inter-sentence attention, rather than relying on external LLMs or fixed heuristics, enables effective multi-granularity retrieval. The end-to-end training of both embeddings and tree structure yields consistent gains in information efficiency across diverse domains.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems must balance retrieval granularity with contextual coherence, a challenge that existing methods address through LLM-guided chunking, single-level context expansion, or hierarchical summarization. These approaches variously depend on costly LLM calls during indexing or retrieval, limit context aggregation to a single granularity level, or introduce information loss through summarization. We present SproutRAG, an attention-guided hierarchical RAG framework that addresses this trade-off by organizing sentence-level chunks into progressively larger but semantically coherent units, using learned inter-sentence attention to construct a binary chunking tree. Unlike prior approaches that rely on external LLMs, fixed context expansion, or lossy summarization, SproutRAG learns which attention heads and layers best capture semantic document structure, enabling multi-granularity retrieval without additional LLM calls or compressed summaries. At retrieval time, SproutRAG uses hierarchical beam search to retrieve candidates at multiple granularities, capturing multi-sentence relevance beyond flat retrieval. The framework is trained end-to-end with a joint objective that improves both embeddings and tree structure. Experiments across four benchmarks spanning scientific, legal, and open-domain settings demonstrate that SproutRAG improves information efficiency (IE) by 6.1% on average over the strongest baseline. Code is available on https://github.com/AmirAbaskohi/SproutRAG.

</details>


### [4] [Want Better Synthetic Data? Steer It: Activation Steering for Low-Resource Language Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18389)
*Jan Cegin,Daniil Gurgurov,Yusser Al Ghussin,Simon Ostermann*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Investigates activation steering (Language Steering and Quality Steering) as an alternative to few-shot prompting for synthetic data generation in low-resource languages, finding that steering on early layers improves data diversity and downstream classifier performance across 11 languages and 4 LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Few-shot prompting with target-language examples, while effective for synthetic data generation in low-resource languages, increases inference costs and may reduce output diversity through lexical anchoring. Activation steering offers a potential alternative that avoids these drawbacks.

Method: Two activation steering strategies are proposed: (1) Language Steering — targets linguistic identity of a language; (2) Quality Steering — captures well-formedness by contrasting human-written vs. backtranslated text representations. Evaluated across 4 open-source LLMs, multiple layers, and 11 typologically diverse languages by generating sentiment and topic classification data, then finetuning smaller classifiers. Steering is tested in both zero-shot and few-shot settings against non-steered baselines.

Result: Steering on early layers consistently improves diversity of generated data and often yields stronger downstream model performance, particularly for low-resource languages. Both zero-shot and few-shot steering settings outperform non-steered counterparts.

Conclusion: Activation steering is a viable, cost-effective alternative to few-shot prompting for low-resource synthetic data generation, offering gains in both diversity and downstream task performance without requiring target-language exemplars at inference time.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become an effective tool for synthetic data generation, including for low-resource languages, where generated data can improve downstream task performance. Current best-performing approaches typically rely on few-shot prompting with target-language examples, which increases inference costs and may reduce diversity through lexical anchoring. In this work, we investigate activation steering as an alternative for low-resource synthetic data generation. We study two steering strategies: Language Steering, which targets the linguistic identity of a language, and Quality Steering, which captures well-formedness by contrasting human-written and backtranslated text representations. We evaluate these methods across four open-source LLMs, multiple layers, and 11 typologically diverse languages by generating sentiment and topic classification data and finetuning smaller classifiers. Steering is applied in both zero-shot and few-shot prompting settings and compared against non-steered counterparts. Our results show that steering on early layers consistently improves the diversity of generated data while often yielding stronger downstream model performance, particularly for low-resource languages.

</details>


### [5] [MCompassRAG: Topic Metadata as a Semantic Compass for Paragraph-Level Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18508)
*Amirhossein Abaskohi,Raymond Li,Gaetano Cimino,Peter West,Giuseppe Carenini,Issam H. Laradji*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MCompassRAG addresses the chunking trade-off in RAG systems by enriching chunk embeddings with topic metadata and training a lightweight retriever via LLM-teacher distillation, enabling topic-aware retrieval that improves information efficiency by 8.24% while reducing latency by over 5× compared to the best efficient baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core motivation is the fundamental tension in RAG document chunking: fine-grained chunks improve retrieval precision but increase search space (latency/cost), while coarse-grained chunks reduce candidates but introduce semantic noise from mixed topics, degrading dense similarity reliability. This trade-off is particularly acute in deep research tasks requiring both speed and precision across large, heterogeneous corpora.

Method: MCompassRAG introduces a metadata-guided retrieval framework with three key components: (1) enrichment of chunk representations with topic-level metadata signals embedded in the same vector space, serving as a "semantic compass"; (2) training a lightweight retriever via LLM-teacher distillation, where the LLM provides supervision for selecting relevant evidence; (3) at inference time, the system performs topic-aware retrieval without requiring additional LLM calls, maintaining efficiency.

Result: Across six complex retrieval benchmarks, MCompassRAG achieves an average improvement of 8.24% in Information Efficiency (IE) while operating with over 5× lower latency compared to the strongest efficient RAG baselines.

Conclusion: MCompassRAG demonstrates that incorporating topic-level metadata into chunk embeddings, combined with distilled lightweight retrievers, effectively resolves the precision-vs-efficiency trade-off in RAG systems. The approach enables fast, precise retrieval without sacrificing either dimension, and the public release of code supports reproducibility and further research.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems depend critically on how documents are chunked and searched. Fine-grained chunks can improve retrieval precision but expand the search space, increasing latency and cost; larger chunks reduce the number of candidates but make dense similarity less reliable, as the representation for each chunk mixes multiple topics and introduces more semantic noise. This trade-off becomes especially limiting in deep research tasks, where retrieval must be both fast and precise across large, heterogeneous corpora. We introduce MCompassRAG, a metadata-guided retrieval framework that uses topic-level signals as a semantic compass for selecting relevant evidence. Instead of relying only on cosine similarity between queries and noisy chunk embeddings, MCompassRAG enriches chunk representations with topic metadata in the same embedding space and trains a lightweight retriever through LLM-teacher distillation. At inference time, MCompassRAG performs topic-aware retrieval without additional LLM calls, improving both efficiency and evidence quality. Across six complex retrieval benchmarks, MCompassRAG improves information efficiency (IE) by 8.24% on average with over 5 times lower latency than the strongest efficient RAG baselines. Code is available on https://github.com/AmirAbaskohi/MCompassRAG.

</details>


### [6] [JetFlow: Breaking the Scaling Ceiling of Speculative Decoding with Parallel Tree Drafting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18394)
*Lanxiang Hu,Zhaoxiang Feng,Yulun Wu,Haoran Yuan,Yujie Zhao,Yu-Yang Qian,Bojun Wang,Daxin Jiang,Yibo Zhu,Tajana Rosing,Hao Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: JetFlow combines one-forward drafting efficiency with branch-wise causal conditioning to overcome the scaling ceiling in speculative decoding, achieving up to 9.64× speedup on math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding faces a scaling ceiling where increasing draft budget fails to improve speed due to a causality-efficiency dilemma: autoregressive drafters produce high-quality path-conditioned candidates but suffer from drafting cost scaling with tree depth; bidirectional block-diffusion drafters are efficient but generate mutually inconsistent tokens that waste budget and reduce acceptance.

Method: JetFlow trains a causal parallel draft head over fused hidden states from a frozen target LLM. This draft head produces candidate trees whose scores align with the target model's autoregressive factorization, enabling efficient one-forward drafting while maintaining branch-wise causal conditioning for tree speculative decoding.

Result: JetFlow consistently outperforms bidirectional-head and tree-based SD baselines across math, coding, and chat benchmarks on dense and MoE Qwen3 models. On H100 GPUs, it achieves up to 9.64× speedup on MATH-500 and 4.58× on open-ended conversational workloads, with further gains via vLLM integration under realistic serving loads.

Conclusion: JetFlow breaks the speculative decoding scaling ceiling by reconciling drafting efficiency with causal coherence, enabling larger draft budgets to translate into longer accepted prefixes and higher end-to-end speedup.

Abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) by drafting multiple tokens and verifying them in parallel, but it faces a scaling limitation: increasing the draft budget improves speed only when acceptance remains high and drafting overhead stays low. This ceiling has been difficult to break because prior head-based SD methods face a causality-efficiency dilemma. Autoregressive drafters produce path-conditioned candidates that are effective for tree speculative decoding with higher acceptance length, but their drafting cost grows with tree depth. Bidirectional block-diffusion drafters generate all positions in one pass, but their branch-agnostic marginals can form individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent trees, wasting budget and reducing acceptance. We propose JetFlow, a head-based SD framework that combines one-forward drafting efficiency with branch-wise causal conditioning. JetFlow trains a causal parallel draft head over fused hidden states from the frozen target model, producing candidate trees whose scores align with the target model's autoregressive factorization. This enables JetFlow to convert larger draft budgets into longer accepted prefixes and higher end-to-end speedup. Across math, coding, and chat benchmarks on dense and MoE Qwen3 models, JetFlow consistently outperforms bidirectional-head and tree-based SD baselines. On H100 GPUs, JetFlow achieves up to 9.64x speedup on MATH-500 and 4.58x on open-ended conversational workloads, with further latency gains demonstrated through vLLM integration under realistic serving loads. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetFlow.

</details>


### [7] [TW-LegalBench: Measuring Taiwanese Legal Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18699)
*Fei-Yueh Chen,Chun Huang Lin,Chan Wei Hsu,Kuan Hsuan Yeh,Zih-Ching Chen,Kuan-Ming Chen,Patrick Chung-Chia Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TW-LegalBench evaluates 13 LLMs on Taiwanese legal tasks (16K+ MCQs, 117 essay questions, 14K+ judgment predictions). Top models pass the lawyer bar (11%) but fail judge/prosecutor exams (1–2%), and struggle with precise statute citation despite reasonable verdict prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM evaluation on jurisdiction-specific legal reasoning is underexplored. Existing benchmarks focus on English common-law or Simplified Chinese civil-law sources, leaving Taiwanese law — with its rich public official corpus — unaddressed.

Method: TW-LegalBench covers three task types: (1) 16,000+ multiple-choice questions from five years of official exams in 18 domains, evaluated by accuracy; (2) 117 open-ended essay questions with official rubrics, evaluated via a decomposed LLM-as-Judge framework keyed to rubric points; (3) 14,000+ legal judgment prediction instances spanning hundreds of crime categories, evaluated on sentencing accuracy and statute citation metrics. Thirteen LLMs are benchmarked.

Result: Top models exceed the passing threshold for qualified lawyers (11% pass rate) but fall short for judges and prosecutors (1–2% pass rate). Models show reasonable verdict-type accuracy and sentence prediction but struggle to cite exact legal articles, indicating reliable legal text generation remains challenging.

Conclusion: Despite near-human performance on qualification exams, LLMs still cannot reliably generate precise legal text, particularly in citing specific statutes. TW-LegalBench provides a critical resource for advancing jurisdiction-specific legal NLP.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, yet their performance on jurisdiction-specific legal reasoning remains underexplored. We present TW-LegalBench that utilizes Taiwanese legal system's rich official corpus open to the public to fill the gap in evaluating LLMs on Taiwanese law, among common-law benchmarks that focus on English sources and civil-law benchmarks focusing on sources of Simplified Chinese. TW-LegalBench comprises three task types: (1) over 16,000 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) across five years of official examinations in 18 professional domains; (2) 117 open-ended essay questions (OEQs) from examinations for legal professionals with official scoring rubrics; and (3) more than 14,000 legal judgment prediction (LJP) instances covering hundreds of crime categories. We evaluate 13 LLMs using accuracy for MCQs, a decomposed LLM-as-Judge framework based on the scoring rubric points for OEQs, and metrics for sentencing accuracy and statute citation for LJP. Our results reveal that top-performing models exceed the passing threshold for qualified lawyers (passing rate: 11%) but fall short of that for judges and prosecutors (passing rate: 1~2%). For LJP, while models demonstrate reasonable verdict type accuracy and sentence prediction capability, they struggle to cite exact legal articles. These findings highlight that reliable legal text generation remains challenging for LLMs, even though their performance on qualification examinations approaches human level.

</details>


### [8] [CoreMem: Riemannian Retrieval and Fisher-Guided Distillation for Long-Term Memory in Dialogue Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18406)
*Jiaqi Chen,Yongqin Zeng,Shaoshen Chen,Yijian Zhang,Hai-Tao Zheng,Chunxia Ma,XiuTeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CoreMem proposes an information-geometry-grounded memory architecture for personalized dialogue agents on edge devices (≤8 GB VRAM), replacing cosine similarity with Riemannian (Fisher-Rao metric) retrieval and heuristic compression with Fisher-guided discrete token distillation, achieving +4-5 pp gains on LOCOMO and LongMemEval-S benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized dialogue agents need long-term memory, but deploying them on consumer-grade edge devices (e.g., 8 GB VRAM) creates severe memory/compute bottlenecks. Existing solutions using isotropic cosine retrieval suffer from the hubness problem in high dimensions, and heuristic compression causes syntactic fragmentation. There is no unified theoretical framework addressing both retrieval and compression jointly.

Method: CoreMem is an edge-cloud memory architecture unified by information geometry: (1) Riemannian retrieval replaces cosine matching with a locally adaptive Fisher-Rao metric, penalizing hub memories via Mahalanobis distance with O(Ndr) Woodbury acceleration for real-time search; (2) Fisher-guided discrete token distillation (FDTD) performs hierarchical sentence-to-token compression using Fisher information traces to derive sensitivity scores, yielding a principled compression-KL tradeoff with explicit syntactic structure protection.

Result: On LOCOMO and LongMemEval-S benchmarks, CoreMem achieves significant accuracy improvements: +4.51 pp in Open-domain reasoning and +4.17 pp in Temporal reasoning. Profiling confirms operation within a strict 8 GB VRAM budget.

Conclusion: CoreMem successfully bridges resource-constrained edge devices with theoretically grounded lifelong memory agents, demonstrating that information geometry provides a principled unified foundation for both memory retrieval and compression in personalized dialogue systems.

Abstract: Personalized dialogue agents require continuous long-term memory to maintain coherent interactions across multiple sessions. However, deploying these capabilities on consumer-grade hardware (e.g., 8 GB VRAM edge devices) introduces severe memory and compute bottlenecks. Existing systems typically rely on isotropic cosine similarity for retrieval and heuristic rules for context compression. These approaches lack a unified theoretical foundation, frequently suffering from the hubness problem in high-dimensional retrieval and syntactic fragmentation during compression. To overcome these limitations, we propose CoreMem, a resource-efficient edge-cloud memory architecture fundamentally unified by information geometry. First, Riemannian retrieval replaces cosine matching with a locally adaptive Fisher-Rao metric, effectively penalizing hub memories via Mahalanobis distance with O(Ndr) Woodbury acceleration for real-time search. Second, Fisher-guided discrete token distillation (FDTD) introduces a hierarchical sentence-to-token compression mechanism. It derives sensitivity scores from Fisher information traces, providing a principled compression-KL tradeoff augmented with explicit structural syntax protection. Evaluated on the LOCOMO and LongMemEval-S benchmarks, CoreMem achieves strong accuracy improvements, yielding substantial gains in Open-domain (+4.51 pp) and Temporal (+4.17 pp) reasoning. Extensive profiling confirms that CoreMem operates seamlessly within a strict 8 GB VRAM budget, successfully bridging the gap between resource-constrained edge devices and the demand for theoretically grounded, lifelong memory agents.

</details>


### [9] [ScholarSum: Student-Teacher Abstractive Summarization via Knowledge Graph Reasoning and Reflective Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18850)
*Bohou Zhang,Xiaoyu Tao,Mingyue Cheng,Huijie Liu,Qi Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ScholarSum introduces a hierarchical graph-based framework for scientific summarization that mimics a student-teacher writing process, combining a hierarchical knowledge graph for global structure with iterative refinement to ensure both fluency and factual faithfulness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scientific summarization methods suffer from a fluency-faithfulness trade-off: extractive methods preserve facts but disrupt logical coherence through sentence splicing, while LLM-based generative methods produce fluent text but lack factual consistency. A method reconciling both is needed.

Method: ScholarSum constructs a hierarchical knowledge graph from the document by segmenting it into semantically coherent units with multi-layered community structure capturing global logic. A student model generates an initial draft guided by this structure, then a teacher-like reviewer iteratively examines the draft, identifies unsupported content, and triggers targeted evidence re-retrieval and rewriting until quality standards are met.

Result: Extensive experiments show that ScholarSum significantly outperforms previous baselines on both completeness and faithfulness metrics.

Conclusion: The hierarchical reflective graph-based framework with iterative student-teacher refinement effectively reconciles linguistic fluency with factual faithfulness in scientific summarization, advancing the state of the art.

Abstract: Abstractive summarization plays a crucial role in enabling efficient understanding of scientific literature, yet it inherently demands both linguistic fluency and factual faithfulness. Existing approaches often fail to reconcile these two requirements. Extractive methods rely on rigid sentence splicing that disrupts macro-level logical coherence, while large language model (LLM)-based generative approaches, despite mastering linguistic fluency, exhibit limited factual consistency. In this work, we propose ScholarSum, a hierarchical reflective graph-based framework that emulates a student-teacher writing process for fluent and faithful scientific summarization. ScholarSum first organizes the document into a hierarchical knowledge graph by segmenting it into semantically coherent units, whose multi-layered community structure captures global logic and macro-level themes. Guided by this global structure, the student generates an initial draft, which is subsequently refined through fine-grained evidence retrieval. To ensure factual consistency, a teacher-like reviewer then iteratively examines the draft, identifies unsupported content, and prompts targeted re-retrieval and rewriting until the summary meets rigorous quality standards. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScholarSum significantly outperforms previous baselines in terms of both completeness and faithfulness. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xiaoyu-Tao/ScholarSum.

</details>


### [10] [VISUALSKILL: Multimodal Skills for Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18448)
*Ziyan Jiang,Li An,Yujian Liu,Jiabao Ji,Qiucheng Wu,Jacob Andreas,Yang Zhang,Shiyu Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VISUALSKILL introduces hierarchical multimodal skill artifacts for GUI computer-use agents, preserving visual figures alongside text. Using a two-stage pipeline (authored docs + live UI exploration) and an MCP-based `load_topic` retrieval tool, a Claude Opus 4.6 agent gains +15.3 points over no-skill and +8.3 points over matched text-only skills on CUA-World and OSExpert-Eval benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing skill libraries for computer-use agents represent skills as text only, discarding the inherently visual nature of GUI interaction. This limits agent performance on long-horizon tasks and unseen software, where visual cues are critical for identifying UI elements and verifying workflow state.

Method: VISUALSKILL constructs hierarchical multimodal skills organized as a central index over per-topic files. Each skill is built via a two-stage pipeline: (1) incorporating authored documentation, and (2) live-application UI exploration. The agent accesses skills through a `load_topic` MCP tool that fetches relevant text and figures on demand, rather than verbalizing visual information away.

Result: On CUA-World and OSExpert-Eval, a Claude Code CLI agent with Claude Opus 4.6 and VISUALSKILL achieves an average score of 0.456, a +15.3 absolute point lift over the no-skill baseline (0.303). Against a matched text-only skill derived from the same source content, VISUALSKILL provides an additional +8.3 absolute point gain (0.373 vs. 0.456).

Conclusion: Retaining visual figures in skill artifacts, rather than converting them to text, yields statistically and practically significant improvements in CUA performance. The multimodal approach aids both UI element identification and post-action workflow state verification. Code is open-sourced.

Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) approach human-level performance on standardised benchmarks but still struggle on long-horizon tasks and unseen software. Existing skill libraries address this with reusable skills, but represent the skill artifact as text only, despite the visual nature of GUI interaction. We propose VISUALSKILL: a hierarchical multimodal skill, tailored to each target application and organised as a central index over per-topic files, which the agent consumes through a load_topic MCP tool that fetches the relevant topic's text and figures on demand. We construct each skill with a two-stage pipeline that combines authored documentation with live-application UI exploration. On two CUA benchmarks, CUA-World and OSExpert-Eval, a Claude Code CLI agent backed by Claude Opus 4.6 reaches an average score of 0.456 with VISUALSKILL, a +15.3 point absolute lift over the no-skill baseline (0.303). Against a matched text-only skill that is generated from the same source content and differs from VISUALSKILL only in modality, VISUALSKILL yields a further +8.3 point absolute gain over the matched text-only skill (0.373 vs. 0.456), providing direct evidence that retaining visual figures in the skill artifact, rather than verbalizing them away, helps the agent both identify UI elements and verify workflow state after each action. Our code is available at https://github.com/XMHZZ2018/VisualSkills.

</details>


### [11] [LLM Parameters for Math Across Languages: Shared or Separate?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18453)
*Behzad Shomali,Luisa Victor,Tim Selbach,Ali Hamza Bashir,David Berghaus,Joachim Koehler,Mehdi Ali,Markus Frey*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A mechanistic analysis of multilingual LLMs reveals that mathematical reasoning relies on partially overlapping parameters across languages, concentrated in intermediate layers. English activates the largest set of math-relevant parameters, while lower-resource languages show smaller sets, indicating neither fully shared nor fully language-specific mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models show significant cross-lingual variation in mathematical reasoning, but it is unknown whether this stems from language-specific parameters or a shared underlying mechanism expressed differently across languages. The authors aim to resolve this ambiguity through mechanistic interpretability.

Method: Cross-lingual mechanistic analysis — localizing and comparing model parameters that support mathematical reasoning across different languages using parameter-level probing and causal intervention techniques.

Result: Math-associated parameters show partial cross-lingual overlap, strongest in intermediate layers. English consistently yields the largest set of math-relevant parameters; lower-resource languages exhibit smaller relevant parameter sets, revealing systematic language-dependent differences.

Conclusion: Math-related behavior in multilingual LLMs is neither fully language-invariant nor fully language-specific. Instead, it exhibits partial cross-lingual parameter overlap with systematic, resource-driven disparities favoring high-resource languages like English.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit substantial cross-lingual variation in mathematical reasoning performance, but it remains unclear whether these differences reflect language-specific parameters or a shared mechanism that manifests differently by language. We present a cross-lingual mechanistic analysis of mathematical reasoning in LLMs, enabling us to localize and compare model parameters that support mathematical reasoning across languages. We find that the extracted math-associated parameters exhibit partial cross-lingual overlap, with the strongest overlap concentrated in intermediate model layers. We further observe that English consistently produces the largest set of math-relevant parameters, whereas lower-resource languages reveal smaller sets of relevant parameters. These results suggest that math-related behavior in multilingual LLMs is neither fully language-invariant nor fully language-specific, but instead exhibits partial cross-lingual parameter overlap with systematic language-dependent differences.

</details>


### [12] [Montreal Forced Aligner and the state of speech-to-text alignment in 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18466)
*Michael McAuliffe,Kaylynn Gunter,Michael Wagner,Morgan Sonderegger*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MFA 3.0 is a major update to the widely-used forced alignment tool, now supporting more languages, achieving state-of-the-art alignment accuracy (mean boundary errors under 15 ms) across English, Japanese, and Korean, with effective adaptation and cross-language remapping for unseen languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Documenting a decade of development since MFA 1.0 (2016), and rigorously benchmarking the new version against both classic and neural forced aligners to validate improvements in accuracy, language coverage, and adaptability.

Method: Expanded training on larger multilingual open-source datasets with harmonized IPA dictionaries; introduced model adaptation, cross-language phone remapping, pronunciation probability modeling, phonological rules, and support utilities; evaluated on four benchmark datasets across English, Japanese, and Korean.

Result: MFA 3.0 achieves state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance with mean boundary errors below 15 ms on all four benchmarks. Adaptation and cross-language remapping prove effective for out-of-distribution languages; pronunciation probability modeling and phonological rules yield gains in specific conditions.

Conclusion: MFA 3.0 represents a substantial advance in forced alignment, combining broad multilingual coverage with high accuracy, and its adaptation capabilities make it practical for languages beyond the original training distribution.

Abstract: The Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) was released in 2016 and has since become the most widely used tool for forced alignment in research and industry. In the decade since, MFA has undergone substantial development, including expanded coverage across more languages and dialects using larger open-source datasets, harmonized IPA dictionaries, model adaptation, cross-language phone remapping, and support utilities. This paper documents MFA 3.0's developments since version 1.0 and evaluates MFA's performance across English, Japanese, and Korean, benchmarked against classic and neural forced aligners. MFA 3.0 achieves state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance across all four benchmark datasets with mean boundary errors below 15 ms. Adaptation and cross-language remapping are effective for languages outside MFA's training distribution, and pronunciation probability modeling and phonological rules provide gains in specific conditions.

</details>


### [13] [Which Sections of a Research Paper Best Reveal Its Research Methods? Evidence from Library and Information Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19051)
*Qiuyu Fang,Jiayi Hao,Chengzhi Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a segment combination strategy for automatic multi-label classification of research methods by partitioning full-text articles based on physical position, finding that middle-to-late and final segments are most informative and that combining bibliographic metadata with cross-segment strategies improves classification performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatic classification of research methods relies on titles and abstracts, which contain limited methodological information. Full-text articles are richer but suffer from excessive length and information redundancy, making effective utilization challenging. A strategy is needed to selectively leverage full-text content for better method classification.

Method: The authors partition full-text content by physical position into segments, then evaluate classification performance of individual segments and their combinations across multiple models using an annotated corpus of 1,954 full-text articles from three LIS journals (JASIST, LISR, JDoc). They also test the integration of bibliographic metadata with cross-segment combination strategies.

Result: Methodological information is unevenly distributed within full-text papers: the middle-to-late and final segments exhibit greater discriminative power for research method classification. Integrating bibliographic metadata with cross-segment combination strategies effectively enhances classification performance.

Conclusion: A full-text segment combination strategy that prioritizes mid-to-late and concluding sections, supplemented by bibliographic metadata, offers a practical and effective approach for automatic multi-label classification of research methods, overcoming the limitations of abstract-only approaches.

Abstract: Research methods are essential carriers of knowledge contribution in academic papers. Automatic multi-label classification of research methods can support knowledge services such as method retrieval, review generation, and research intelligence analysis. While existing studies primarily rely on titles and abstracts, abstracts often provide only limited methodological information, whereas utilizing full-text content faces challenges related to excessive length and information redundancy. Therefore, this paper proposes a segment combination strategy by partitioning the full-text content according to its physical postion. Using an annotated corpus of 1,954 full-text articles from three representative journals in Library and Information Science (JASIST, LISR, and JDoc), we evaluate the classification performance of various segments and their combinations across multiple models. Experimental results indicate that methodological information is distributed unevenly within the full-text content, with the middle-to-late and final segments exhibiting greater discriminative power. Furthermore, integrating bibliographic metadata with cross-segment combination strategies effectively enhances classification performance.

</details>


### [14] [Possible or Definite? A Benchmark for Evaluating Diagnostic Uncertainty Preservation in Clinical Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18471)
*Hongbo Du,Zixin Lu,Jiaming Qu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs poorly preserve diagnostic uncertainty when summarizing/revising clinical text, often retaining uncertainty cues less than 50% of the time and struggling with nuanced adjacent-level distinctions — a failure mode missed by standard fluency/coherence metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diagnostic uncertainty expressions (e.g., "possible pneumonia") are clinically critical because they convey evidence strength and directly guide follow-up testing and treatment decisions. Existing LLM evaluations focus on fluency and coherence but neglect whether models correctly preserve these nuanced uncertainty cues, creating a potentially dangerous blind spot for clinical deployment.

Method: A two-step systematic evaluation: (1) Construction of a benchmark comprising 1,200 clinical documents annotated with 9,184 uncertainty labels spanning five levels of diagnostic certainty. (2) Evaluation of three LLMs on this benchmark to assess how faithfully they preserve original uncertainty expressions during summarization/revision tasks.

Result: (1) LLMs preserve original uncertainty cues poorly — often below 50% of the time. (2) LLMs particularly struggle with fine-grained distinctions between adjacent uncertainty levels, indicating a systematic failure in capturing graded clinical uncertainty rather than just coarse certain/uncertain binary distinctions.

Conclusion: The study reveals a critical failure mode not captured by standard evaluation metrics (fluency, coherence). This has direct implications for the safe deployment of LLMs in clinical workflows, where altered uncertainty expressions could change clinical meaning and lead to inappropriate follow-up decisions.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for clinical text tasks such as summarization and revision. While most studies evaluate the fluency and coherence of LLM-generated text, whether LLMs correctly preserve diagnostic uncertainty remains underexplored. In clinical practice, phrases such as ``possible pneumonia'' communicate the strength of available evidence and directly guide decisions about follow-up testing and treatment. Altering these uncertainty expressions can change the clinical meaning entirely. In this paper, we systematically evaluated this problem in two steps. First, we constructed a benchmark of 1,200 clinical documents with 9,184 uncertainty annotations across five levels. Second, we evaluated three LLMs on this benchmark. Our results show that (1) LLMs preserve the original uncertainty cues poorly, often less than half the time; (2) LLMs struggle with nuanced distinctions between adjacent levels. This work reveals a failure mode not captured by standard evaluation metrics and provides implications for the safe deployment of LLMs in clinical workflows.

</details>


### [15] [Leadership as Coordination Control: Behavioral Signatures and the Recovery-Advantage Boundary in Multi-Agent LLM Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19111)
*Haewoon Kwak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether process-level coordination control (operationalized as classical leadership styles) adds value in multi-agent LLM teams. Aligning with team science's contingency theory, it finds no single controller dominates; gains appear only when the round-0 majority is unreliable and the task is recoverable—precisely the conditions contingency theory predicts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Team science posits that leadership is contingent—beneficial only under specific conditions. The authors ask whether the same holds for multi-agent LLM teams: under what measurable conditions does process-level coordination control add value, and do those conditions match established contingency theory predictions?

Method: Three classical leadership styles (transactional, transformational, situational) are operationalized as explicit controllers over a shared action vocabulary (explore, revise, accept, synthesize). Using behavioral signatures (majority lock-in, exploration, recovery from incorrect round-0 consensus) and per-action ablations, the authors test these controllers across four task regimes and three open-weight model families. A matched controller with an arbitrary rule serves as a baseline. Four boundary probes test a recovery-advantage account.

Result: No controller dominates by accuracy, consistent with contingency theory. Transactional control matches a shared round-0 vote on all 12 (model, regime) combinations to within 1.3pp. Gains appear only where the round-0 majority is unreliable (llama-4-scout social; situational +8pp over flat). The recovery-advantage account holds: a controller beats plain interaction only where the round-0 majority is unreliable, the task is recoverable, and undirected interaction does not already repair it.

Conclusion: Process-level coordination control should be understood as a contingency to be measured and theory-mapped, not a leaderboard to be topped. The largely null accuracy result confirms contingency theory predictions, not controller failure. Leadership in LLM teams adds value only under specific, measurable conditions that map onto classical substitutes, path-goal redundancy, and situational readiness gaps.

Abstract: Team science holds that leadership is contingent: it helps only under specific conditions, and capable, autonomous teams may need none at all. We ask the analogous question for multi-agent LLM teams: under what measurable conditions does process-level coordination control add value, and do those conditions match what team science predicts? We use behavioral signatures (majority lock-in, exploration, recovery from an incorrect round-0 consensus) and per-action ablations, clean because each controller is an explicit action set, not a monolithic prompt. We operationalize three classical leadership styles (transactional, transformational, situational) as controllers over a shared action vocabulary (explore, revise, accept, synthesize). A matched controller with the same actions but an arbitrary rule recovers no better than majority voting, so the theory-derived rule, not the vocabulary, does the work. Across four task regimes and three open-weight model families, no controller dominates by accuracy, as the contingency view predicts: transactional control matches a shared round-0 vote on all 12 (model, regime) combinations to within 1.3pp, and gains appear only on the one combination where the round-0 majority is unreliable (llama-4-scout social; situational +8pp over flat). A recovery-advantage account, tested with four boundary probes, says a controller beats plain interaction only where the round-0 majority is unreliable, the task is recoverable, and undirected interaction does not already repair it. These regions map onto contingency theory (leadership substitutes, path-goal redundancy, the situational readiness gap), so a largely null accuracy result is what the theory predicts, not a failure of the controllers. We read process-level coordination control as a contingency to be measured and theory-mapped, not a leaderboard to be topped.

</details>


### [16] [PreUnlearn: Auditing Collateral Knowledge Damage Before Large Language Model Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18473)
*Bo Su,Ankit Shah,Thai Le*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates how machine unlearning in LLMs causes collateral damage beyond the targeted knowledge, finding a decay pattern where damage weakens with semantic distance but persists across domain boundaries. The authors propose forget-set auditing as a pre-unlearning prediction task to identify risky unlearning runs before execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The boundary between knowledge to forget and knowledge to retain in LLM unlearning is often unclear due to entangled representations. The authors aim to understand how unlearning effects propagate from the forget set to related and distant knowledge, and whether this collateral damage can be predicted before unlearning occurs.

Method: The authors adopt a data-centric perspective, measuring how unlearning effects propagate from the forget set to same-domain and distant-domain knowledge. They formulate forget-set auditing as a pre-unlearning prediction task, analyzing which data features — particularly interaction features between forget and evaluation sets — are most predictive of downstream collateral damage.

Result: A consistent decay pattern emerges: collateral damage is strongest near the forget set and weakens with semantic distance, but does not disappear at domain boundaries. Interaction features between the forget set and evaluation set provide the strongest predictive signals, indicating that collateral damage is partially reflected in data geometry before model updates.

Conclusion: Forget-set auditing can serve as an early warning tool for identifying risky unlearning runs and informing the design of more reliable unlearning procedures, helping practitioners anticipate collateral damage before committing to model updates.

Abstract: Machine unlearning for large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specified knowledge while preserving the rest of the model's capabilities. However, the boundary between knowledge to forget and knowledge to retain is often unclear, since related and even distant information may be entangled in the model. In this paper, we study LLM unlearning from a data-centric perspective and measure how unlearning effects propagate from the forget set to same-domain and distant-domain knowledge. We find a consistent decay pattern: collateral damage is strongest near the forget set, weakens with semantic distance, but does not disappear at domain boundaries. We further ask whether such damage can be audited before unlearning is executed. We formulate forget-set auditing as a pre-unlearning prediction task and analyze which data features are most predictive of downstream damage. Our results show that interaction features between the forget set and evaluation set provide the strongest signals, suggesting that collateral damage is partly reflected in data geometry before model updates occur. These findings position forget-set auditing as an early warning tool for identifying risky unlearning runs and designing more reliable unlearning procedures.

</details>


### [17] [Enhancing Decision-Making with Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Fictitious Play](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19308)
*Leyang Shen,Yang Zhang,Xiaoyan Zhao,Chun Kai Ling,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MAFP introduces a game-theoretic multi-agent paradigm where agents, representing stakeholder stances, iteratively best-respond to past decisions of others, converging toward equilibrium to resolve "stance entanglement" in interdependent decision-making tasks, outperforming baselines in tournament strength and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems excel at execution complexity via divide-and-conquer task decomposition, but fail on decision-making tasks where stakeholder decisions are mutually dependent and cannot be solved in isolation. The authors identify this as "stance entanglement," a distinct form of decision complexity that prior MAS paradigms do not address.

Method: The authors propose Multi-Agent Fictitious Play (MAFP), a paradigm that casts stakeholder stances as agents and frames decision-making as an equilibrium-seeking process. MAFP employs the game-theoretic principle of fictitious play: each agent iteratively updates its decision by best responding to the empirical mixture distribution of other agents' past decisions, progressively exposing and addressing weaknesses to improve decision quality and robustness.

Result: MAFP was evaluated on challenging decision-making tasks requiring strategy formation for competitive scenarios. It outperformed both single-round and multi-round baselines on two complementary metrics: tournament strength and robustness.

Conclusion: MAFP effectively addresses stance entanglement in LLM-based MAS, demonstrating that game-theoretic iterative best-response dynamics can substantially improve interdependent decision-making over existing paradigms.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated great potential in solving tasks with execution complexity, by distributing subtasks across cooperative agents. However, this divide-and-conquer paradigm falls short on decision-making tasks that are also prevalent in the real world. These tasks require simultaneous reasoning from the stances of all involved stakeholders whose decisions are mutually dependent and thus cannot be solved in isolation. We characterize this challenge as stance entanglement, a form of decision complexity distinct from execution complexity. To address it, we propose Multi-Agent Fictitious Play (MAFP), a novel MAS paradigm that represents stakeholder stances as agents and formulates decision-making as an equilibrium-seeking process. Built on the game-theoretic principle of fictitious play, MAFP iteratively updates each agent's decision by best responding to the empirical mixture of other agents' past decisions. This enables agents to expose and address one another's weaknesses, progressively improving decision quality and robustness. We evaluate MAFP on challenging decision-making tasks that test the capability of deciding strategies for competitive scenarios prior to acting. MAFP outperforms both single-round and multi-round baselines on two complementary metrics, tournament strength and robustness, demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing stance entanglement.

</details>


### [18] [Towards Scalable Customization and Deployment of Multi-Agent Systems for Enterprise Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18502)
*Paresh Dashore,Shreyas Kulkarni,Uttam Gurram,Nadia Bathaee,Kartik Balasubramaniam,Genta Indra Winata,Sambit Sahu,Shi-Xiong Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A two-stage framework for customizing and efficiently deploying LLM-based multi-agent systems: (1) Agentic Model Customization adapts compact models to specialized domains via continual pretraining, SFT, and preference optimization; (2) Inference Optimization uses speculative decoding and FP8 quantization to achieve 4.48× throughput speedup with minimal quality loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems is hindered by two key challenges: (1) the need for domain-specific customization to handle specialized enterprise tasks, and (2) high latency and inference costs in agentic workflows, which involve multiple sequential or parallel LLM calls that compound serving overhead.

Method: The framework operates in two stages. Stage 1 — Agentic Model Customization: applies continual pretraining on domain corpora, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated agentic task traces, and preference optimization (e.g., DPO/RLHF) to align a compact base model with specialized domain requirements while preserving general agentic reasoning abilities. Stage 2 — Inference Optimization: combines speculative decoding (using a lightweight draft model to accelerate autoregressive generation) with FP8 quantization and targeted calibration techniques to reduce memory footprint and latency, enabling cost-efficient serving.

Result: On enterprise workloads, the framework demonstrates rapid domain adaptation. The inference optimization stage achieves a 4.48× throughput speedup compared to unoptimized serving, while maintaining task performance and improving robustness on long-tail scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed unified framework effectively addresses both customization and deployment efficiency for production multi-agent systems, making LLM-based agents more practical for real-world enterprise use by combining model-level adaptation with inference-level optimization.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems demonstrate strong performance on complex reasoning and task execution, enabling broad enterprise applications. However, production deployment remains challenging due to domain-specific customization requirements and high latency and inference costs in agentic workflows. We propose a unified framework for customization and efficient deployment of multi-agent systems in real-world settings. The first stage, Agentic Model Customization, combines continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and preference optimization to adapt a compact model to specialized domains while retaining strong agentic capabilities. The second stage, Inference Optimization, integrates speculative decoding and FP8 quantization with targeted calibration to enable cost-efficient serving with minimal quality loss. Across enterprise workloads, our framework enables rapid domain adaptation and achieves a 4.48x speedup in throughput while maintaining performance and improving robustness on long-tail scenarios.

</details>


### [19] [Speech-Driven End-to-End Language Discrimination towards Chinese Dialects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18584)
*Fan Xu,Jian Luo,MingWen Wang,GuoDong Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes combining speech-driven MFCC features with word-level embeddings via a CNN for fine-grained Chinese dialect discrimination, outperforming text-only and state-of-the-art methods on two benchmark corpora.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional text-driven approaches yield poor results for discriminating among similar languages, varieties, and dialects. The authors hypothesize that speech-driven features can capture phonetic and prosodic cues that text alone cannot, particularly for Chinese dialects where distinctions often manifest in pronunciation rather than orthography.

Method: A three-component framework: (1) MFCC features are systematically evaluated with a CNN for dialect classification; (2) an end-to-end HMM-DNN speech recognition model with attention mechanism extracts discriminative dialect-specific words; (3) a CNN fuses word-level embeddings with MFCC-based acoustic features for final dialect discrimination.

Result: Evaluation on two benchmark Chinese dialect corpora demonstrates that the speech-driven approach outperforms text-only methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on fine-grained Chinese dialect discrimination.

Conclusion: Speech-driven features, particularly the fusion of MFCC acoustic features with attention-weighted word embeddings, provide a more effective paradigm than text-only approaches for fine-grained dialect discrimination in Chinese.

Abstract: Language discrimination among similar languages, varieties, and dialects is a challenging natural language processing task. The traditional text-driven focus leads to poor results. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of speech-driven features towards language discrimination among Chinese dialects. First, we systematically explore the appropriateness of speech-driven MFCC features towards CNN-based language discrimination. Then, we design an end-to-end speech recognition model based on HMM-DNN to predict Chinese dialect words. We adopt attention to extract the discriminative words related to different Chinese dialects. Finally, through a CNN, we combine the word-level embedding and the MFCC-based features. Evaluation of two benchmark Chinese dialect corpora shows the appropriateness and effectiveness of the proposed speech-driven approach to fine-grained Chinese dialect discrimination compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [20] [Dual Dimensionality for Local and Global Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18587)
*Zhiyuan Wang,Xuan Luo,Sirui Zeng,Xifeng Yan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Distance-Adaptive Representation (DAR), which assigns full-dimensional key/value representations to local tokens and reduced-dimensional representations to distant tokens in decoder-only Transformers. This matches full-dimensional baseline performance while challenging the uniform-dimensionality assumption, enabling KV cache reduction during inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In natural language, immediate next-word prediction is most strongly influenced by nearby tokens, while distant tokens serve primarily as long-range memory. The authors hypothesize that this creates asymmetric demands on representational capacity: local tokens need richer (higher-dimensional) representations for precise prediction, whereas distant tokens can function adequately with lower-dimensional representations. Existing Transformer architectures ignore this asymmetry, uniformly allocating the same dimensionality to all keys and values regardless of positional distance from the prediction target.

Method: DAR is implemented by preserving full-dimensional key/value representations for tokens within a local context window and assigning reduced-dimensional representations (e.g., 1/4 of original dimensionality) to tokens beyond that window. This is evaluated across multiple pretraining scales (70M to 410M parameters) and continued supervised fine-tuning on a 1B-scale model. The method is compared against both full-dimensional baselines and uniform dimensionality reduction across all positions.

Result: DAR closely matches the performance of full-dimensional baselines across all tested scales. In contrast, uniformly reducing dimensionality across all token positions leads to significantly worse performance, demonstrating that the distance-adaptive allocation—not merely dimensionality reduction—is the critical factor.

Conclusion: The results challenge the standard assumption that key and value dimensionality should be uniform across all token positions. Distance-adaptive representation offers a promising direction for designing attention architectures that intelligently allocate representational capacity, enabling KV cache compression during inference without sacrificing model quality.

Abstract: Decoder-only Transformers compute attention over the KV cache of preceding tokens. Keys (and Values) are typically represented with the same dimensionality, regardless of its distance from the prediction target. In natural language, however, the next word is most strongly influenced by the immediately preceding tokens. We hypothesize that local and distant tokens impose asymmetric demands on representational capacity: local tokens are more critical for predicting immediate outputs and thus require richer representations, whereas distant tokens primarily serve as long-range memory, for which lower-dimensional representations may suffice. We formalize this idea as Distance-Adaptive Representation (DAR), implemented in a controlled setting that preserves full-dimensional representations within a local context window while assigning reduced-dimensional representations (e.g. 1/4 of the original dimensionality) to tokens beyond that window. Across multiple pretraining scales (70M to 410M parameters), as well as continued supervised fine-tuning on a 1B-scale model, this approach closely matches the performance of full-dimensional baselines. In contrast, uniformly reducing dimensionality across all token positions leads to worse performance. These results challenge the common assumption that key and value dimensionality should be uniform across token positions. Our findings suggest a new direction for designing attention architectures that adaptively allocate representational capacity across sequences, enabling further reductions in KV cache during inference.

</details>


### [21] [Low-resource Language Discrimination Towards Chinese Dialects with Transfer learning and Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18597)
*Fan Xu,Yangjie Dan,Keyu Yan,Yong Ma,Mingwen Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A transfer learning and data augmentation framework (CDDTLDA) for Chinese dialects discrimination that pre-trains on a large dialect corpus, augments low-resource target data, fine-tunes via self-attention, and uses hidden representations for classification, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chinese dialects discrimination suffers from scarce annotation resources, making it a challenging NLP task. There is a need to overcome low-resource limitations for robust dialect identification.

Method: The authors propose CDDTLDA: (1) pre-train a source-side ASR model on a relatively larger Chinese dialects corpus; (2) apply data augmentation (speed, pitch, and noise disturbance) to the low-resource target-side dialect data; (3) fine-tune a target ASR model using transfer learning from the source model, incorporating a self-attention mechanism to capture common semantic features across source and target domains; (4) extract hidden semantic representations from the target ASR model to perform dialect discrimination.

Result: The proposed CDDTLDA framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two benchmark Chinese dialects corpora.

Conclusion: Transfer learning combined with simple data augmentation and self-attention is an effective strategy for low-resource Chinese dialects discrimination, achieving superior performance over existing approaches.

Abstract: Chinese dialects discrimination is a challenging natural language processing task due to scarce annotation resource. In this article, we develop a novel Chinese dialects discrimination framework with transfer learning and data augmentation (CDDTLDA) in order to overcome the shortage of resources. To be more specific, we first use a relatively larger Chinese dialects corpus to train a source-side automatic speech recognition (ASR) model. Then, we adopt a simple but effective data augmentation method (i.e., speed, pitch, and noise disturbance) to augment the target-side low-resource Chinese dialects, and fine-tune another target ASR model based on the previous source-side ASR model. Meanwhile, the potential common semantic features between source-side and target-side ASR models can be captured by using self-attention mechanism. Finally, we extract the hidden semantic representation in the target ASR model to conduct Chinese dialects discrimination. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two benchmark Chinese dialects corpora.

</details>


### [22] [Steerable Cultural Preference Optimization of Reward Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18606)
*Minsik Oh,Advit Deepak,Sophie Wu,Douwe Kiela,Ekaterina Shutova*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SCPO is a novel reward model training algorithm that balances diverse cultural preferences in LLM alignment, achieving up to 7-point gains for minority groups across 7 countries while being up to 280% more data-efficient than full-data finetuning, and mitigating excessive bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM alignment research predominantly predicts unified response preferences from annotators in certain regions, neglecting the need to serve diverse cultural sub-communities. There is a need for alignment models with a global outlook that accurately represent subcommunity preferences without excessive bias toward any group.

Method: The authors propose SCPO (Steerable Cultural Preference Optimization), a reward model training algorithm that incorporates diverse cultural preferences in a balanced manner. The method uses a weighting scheme to ensure minority preferences are adequately represented. It is evaluated on two datasets: PRISM and GlobalOpinionQA, spanning 7 countries.

Result: SCPO yields up to 7-point performance improvements for minority reward models over baselines. It is up to 280% more training data-efficient compared to full-data finetuning of reward models. Bias analysis confirms excessive bias toward dominant groups is mitigated through the proposed weighting method.

Conclusion: SCPO successfully advances culturally-aware LLM alignment by enabling reward models that fairly represent diverse subcommunity preferences, demonstrating both improved minority-group performance and bias reduction while maintaining high data efficiency.

Abstract: It is essential for large language model (LLM) technology to serve many different cultural sub-communities in a manner that is acceptable to each community. However, research on LLM alignment has so far predominantly focused on predicting a unified response preference of annotators from certain regions. This paper aims to advance the development of alignment models with a more global outlook, that are able to accurately represent the preferences of subcommunities and do not exhibit excessive bias towards any of them. We focus on the development of reward models for this purpose and present a novel reward model training algorithm (SCPO) that can incorporate diverse cultural preferences in a balanced manner. Our method results in performance increases of the minority reward model of up to 7 points over the baseline model across two datasets, PRISM and GlobalOpinionQA, and across 7 countries. SCPO is up to 280% more training data-efficient than full-data finetuning of reward models. In addition, we perform analysis of bias by separately evaluating on the preference of subcommunities and show that excessive bias is mitigated via our weighting method. Our code is available at https://github.com/minsik-ai/Steerable-Cultural-Preference

</details>


### [23] [Are LLMs Ready to Assist Physicians? PhysAssistBench for Interactive Doctor-Patient-EHR Assistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18613)
*Tianming Du,Peijie Yu,Sihan Shang,Danli Shi,My Linh Nguyen,Shengbo Gao,Guangyuan Li,Yinghong Yu,Yan Jiang,Qianlong Zhao,Behzad Bozorgtabar,Shaoxiong Ji,Jiazhen Pan,Daniel Rueckert,Jiancheng Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PhysAssistBench introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLMs in interactive doctor-patient-EHR coordination, using patient agents built from MIMIC-IV records. Leading LLMs prove unreliable in this integrated setting, revealing that clinical assistance requires simultaneous mastery of knowledge, communication, and system use — not isolated capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical LLM evaluations test isolated skills (clinical knowledge, EHR interaction, patient communication) in silos. Real physician assistance demands coordinating all three within a single interaction, where requests are underspecified, patient descriptions are ambiguous, and EHR systems require precise tool use. No existing benchmark captures this integrated, interactive challenge.

Method: The authors construct PhysAssistBench using MIMIC-IV real patient cases. A scalable pipeline creates "agentic patients" — interactive agents grounded in EHR records that convert static clinical data into multi-turn scenarios while preserving clinical factuality. The resulting bilingual evaluation set contains 1,296 turns, each manually reviewed and physician-validated.

Result: Experiments with leading LLMs demonstrate that current models remain unreliable in the physician-assistance setting. Models that perform well on isolated benchmarks fail when required to simultaneously coordinate clinical knowledge, patient communication, and EHR tool use.

Conclusion: Reliable clinical LLM assistance is bottlenecked not by any single capability but by the need for coordinated mastery across knowledge, communication, and systems. Future progress requires integrated evaluation and training paradigms rather than isolated capability improvements.

Abstract: The most plausible near-term role of medical LLMs is to assist rather than replace physicians, yet current evaluations often test isolated capabilities: clinical knowledge, EHR system interaction, or patient communication. Physician assistance instead requires coordinating these capabilities within the same interaction, where physicians issue underspecified requests, patients describe symptoms ambiguously, and EHR systems demand precise tool use. We introduce PhysAssistBench, a benchmark for interactive doctor-patient-EHR assistance. Built from real MIMIC-IV cases, PhysAssistBench uses a scalable pipeline to construct agentic patients: interactive, record-grounded agents that turn static EHR records into multi-turn clinical scenarios while preserving clinical factuality. PhysAssistBench provides a curated bilingual evaluation set of 1,296 manually reviewed and physician-validated turns. Experiments with leading LLMs show that current models remain unreliable in this setting, which exposes a key bottleneck for clinical LLMs: reliable assistance requires coordination across knowledge, communication, and systems, not isolated gains in any of them.

</details>


### [24] [BCL: Bayesian In-Context Learning Framework for Information Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18620)
*Haoliang Liu,Chengkun Cai,Xu Zhao,Han Zhu,Shizhou Huang,Xinglin Zhang,Tao Chen,Jenq-Neng Hwang,Zhang Huaping,Lei Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: BCL introduces a Bayesian optimization framework that uses particle filtering with Bayesian updates to systematically refine label representations for information extraction via in-context learning, generalizing across sequence labeling and relation classification tasks with consistent improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ICL-based IE methods suffer from inconsistent performance across different model scales and lack systematic optimization and generalizability. There is a need for a principled framework that can adaptively refine task representations.

Method: BCL employs a four-step particle filtering process: (1) Initialization of label representations as particles, (2) Observation of model outputs on examples, (3) Weight update via Bayesian updating to reweight particles based on alignment with ground truth, and (4) Resampling to focus on high-probability representations. This framework is designed to generalize across both sequence labeling and relation classification IE paradigms.

Result: Extensive experiments show that BCL delivers substantial and consistent improvements over existing ICL-based IE approaches.

Conclusion: BCL provides the first systematic, Bayesian-grounded optimization framework for ICL in IE, offering both strong empirical gains and cross-task generalizability, addressing key limitations of prior ad-hoc methods.

Abstract: Existing information extraction (IE) tasks increasingly adopt in-context learning (ICL) with large language models. However, current approaches either show inconsistent performance across model scales or lack systematic optimization and generalizability. Building on this, we propose BCL (Bayesian In-Context Learning Framework for Information Extraction), the first optimization framework that uses particle filtering with Bayesian updates to systematically refine label representations across IE tasks. Through four steps initialization, observation, weight update, and resampling, BCL generalizes to both sequence labeling and relation classification paradigms. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial and consistent improvements over existing approaches.

</details>


### [25] [PragReST: Self-Reinforcing Counterfactual Reasoning for Pragmatic Language Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18624)
*Jihyung Park,Minchao Huang,Leqi Liu,Elias Stengel-Eskin*

Main category: cs.CL
