Subsequent analysis on Qwen3-8B further suggests that cross-condition differences are concentrated more in attention heads than in layers, while better With-gloss generations coincide with stronger gloss anchoring.

</details>


### [48] [Enhancing Multilingual Reasoning via Steerable Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19002)
*Zhuoran Li,Rui Xu,Jian Yang,Junnan Liu,Zhijun Chen,Qianren Mao,Hongcheng Guo,Jiaheng Liu,Likang Xiao,Ming Li,Xiaojie Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ST-Merge proposes a steerable model merging framework using gated cross-attention to adaptively modulate the contribution of two source models (multilingual + reasoning), outperforming baselines on multilingual reasoning across 21 languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model merging methods apply a fixed, one-size-fits-all strategy that fails to account for input-dependent characteristics. Different inputs may require prioritizing one source model (e.g., multilingual vs. reasoning) over the other, and fixed merging leads to suboptimal performance due to unresolved conflicts between source models.

Method: The ST-Merge framework introduces a gated cross-attention mechanism that adaptively weights or filters the contributions of the two attended source models on a per-input basis. This steerable modulation allows the merged model to dynamically prioritize the multilingual or reasoning model depending on the input characteristics.

Result: Extensive experiments show ST-Merge consistently outperforms multiple strong baselines on four multilingual reasoning benchmarks spanning 21 different languages.

Conclusion: Input-adaptive, steerable model merging via gated cross-attention effectively resolves conflicts between source models and yields superior multilingual reasoning performance compared to static merging strategies.

Abstract: Model merging is an effective technique for composing the capabilities of a multilingual model and a reasoning model. It has achieved promising generalization in multilingual reasoning tasks by aligning feature spaces of different models. However, the merged single model often fails to address the conflicts between source models, leading to suboptimal performance. In other words, the one-size-fits-all merging strategy may not align with the characteristics of different inputs which may require prioritizing certain models over others. To this end, we propose a Steerable Model Merging (ST-Merge) framework to modulate the contribution of each source model. To realize this idea, we introduce a gated cross-attention mechanism to weight or filter the two attended source models in an adaptive manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ST-Merge consistently outperforms multiple strong baselines on four multilingual reasoning benchmarks across 21 different languages.

</details>


### [49] [Sumi: Open Uniform Diffusion Language Model from Scratch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19005)
*Mengyu Ye,Keito Kudo,Wataru Ikeda,Ryosuke Matsuda,Keisuke Sakaguchi,Jun Suzuki*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Sumi is the first 7B-parameter uniform diffusion language model pretrained from scratch on 1.5T tokens, providing a clean reference point for studying scaling behavior of UDLMs. It performs competitively with autoregressive models on knowledge, reasoning, and coding benchmarks but underperforms on commonsense tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No uniform diffusion language model (UDLM) has been pretrained from scratch at large scale (both parameter count and token budget). The community lacks a clean reference point for studying scaling behavior, generation dynamics, controllability, and trade-offs of UDLMs against established autoregressive and masked diffusion models.

Method: The authors pretrain Sumi, a 7B-parameter uniform diffusion language model from scratch on 1.5T tokens using a fully open recipe. They specify the complete data mixture over publicly available corpora and release all model weights, checkpoints, and training details.

Result: Sumi matches autoregressive models at comparable token budgets on knowledge, reasoning, and coding benchmarks. It underperforms on commonsense benchmarks, likely due to an education-heavy data mixture.

Conclusion: Sumi establishes the first large-scale, scratch-pretrained UDLM, offering the community a baseline for studying uniform diffusion at scale and stimulating further research into under-explored aspects of this model class.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Among these, uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) permit any token to be updated at any step, in principle enabling more flexible generation. However, no UDLM has yet been pretrained from scratch at both large parameter scale and large token budget. Both autoregressive modeling and masked diffusion modeling already have capable models at scale that the community can study and build on; uniform diffusion has none. A scratch-pretrained UDLM at scale would provide a clean reference point for studying scaling behavior, generation dynamics, controllability, and trade-offs against established autoregressive and masked diffusion models. To this end, we introduce Sumi ("ink" in Japanese), a fully open 7B uniform diffusion language model pretrained from scratch on 1.5T tokens. Sumi performs competitively with autoregressive models trained at comparable token budgets on knowledge, reasoning, and coding benchmarks, while under-performing on commonsense benchmarks, where our education-heavy data mixture is a likely contributor. We release our model weights, checkpoints, and full training recipe, including a complete specification of the data mixture over publicly available corpora. We hope this release enables the community to study native uniform diffusion at scale and catalyzes work on its as-yet poorly understood aspects.

</details>


### [50] [Dango: A Strictly L1-Only Large Language Model for Studying Second Language Acquisition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19170)
*Shiho Matta,Yin Jou Huang,Fei Cheng,Takashi Kodama,Hirokazu Kiyomaru,Yugo Murawaki*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Dango is a 1.8B-parameter Japanese L1 model fine-tuned on synthetic L2 lessons to simulate English acquisition. A key contribution is a filtering method that reduces unintended L2 contamination in the pretraining corpus. The model produces human-like L2 patterns, outperforming unfiltered and multilingual baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior SLA studies using language models have been limited to small or non-decoder architectures, which cannot generate open-ended text and are poor L2 simulators. Scaling up introduces a critical problem: L2 (English) contamination in the ostensibly monolingual L1 (Japanese) pretraining data, which undermines the validity of controlled acquisition experiments.

Method: The authors pretrain a 1.8B-parameter decoder-only model on Japanese text filtered to minimize English exposure while retaining realistic incidental L2 contact. They then fine-tune the model using L2-learning lessons generated by a large language model to simulate the second language acquisition process in a controlled manner.

Result: Dango exhibits human-like L2 (English) production patterns and outperforms both an unfiltered baseline (trained without the contamination-reduction step) and standard multilingual models, validating the effectiveness of the filtering approach for controlled SLA simulation.

Conclusion: Scaling up L1-to-L2 transfer models for SLA research is feasible but requires careful mitigation of L2 contamination in pretraining data. The proposed filtering method enables controlled, reproducible SLA experiments at a practical scale, and the release of model, data, and code supports future computational SLA research and learner-facing applications.

Abstract: We introduce Dango, a 1.8B-parameter large language model designed for controlled studies of L1-to-L2 (Japanese-to-English) transfer in second language acquisition (SLA). While previous studies have explored SLA in language models, they have predominantly relied on smaller or non-decoder models, limiting their ability to generate open-ended text and reducing their suitability as practical L2 simulators. We identify a key challenge when scaling models to this size: L2 contamination within the "monolingual" pretraining corpus used for L1 acquisition. To address this, we propose a filtering method to reduce premature exposure to English while preserving realistic, minimal exposure. We then fine-tune the model on LLM-generated L2-learning lessons to simulate the L2 acquisition process. Our evaluations confirm that Dango develops human-like L2 production patterns, outperforming both unfiltered and standard multilingual baselines. We release the model, data, and code to facilitate reproducible computational SLA research and learner-facing applications.

</details>


### [51] [Language Models as Interfaces, Not Oracles: A Hybrid LLM-ML System for Pediatric Appendicitis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19183)
*Soheyl Bateni,Maryam Abdolali*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ClaMPAPP is a hybrid clinical decision support system that uses an LLM to extract structured features from free-text clinical narratives, then feeds validated features into an XGBoost classifier for appendicitis diagnosis. It outperformed end-to-end LLM baselines on two pediatric cohorts, showing superior stability and fewer missed cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs offer accessibility for interpreting free-text clinical documentation but suffer from prompt sensitivity, order dependence, and hallucinated outputs, making them unreliable as direct diagnostic engines. Structured ML models are stable but require tabular inputs incompatible with narrative workflows. A hybrid approach is needed to combine the usability of natural language interfaces with the reliability of structured prediction.

Method: ClaMPAPP uses an LLM interface to extract schema-constrained clinical features from note-like narratives, applies deterministic plausibility checks on extracted features, and feeds validated features into an XGBoost classifier trained on clinical, laboratory, and ultrasound variables. Narratives were generated from structured EHRs via template rendering and constrained LLM rewriting, with sentence-order permutation to test positional robustness. The system was evaluated against end-to-end LLM baselines (open-source and proprietary) on two independent pediatric appendicitis cohorts from German hospitals.

Result: ClaMPAPP achieved the strongest overall diagnostic performance in both internal and external validation, with fewer missed appendicitis cases — the critical safety metric in acute triage. End-to-end LLMs exhibited unstable sensitivity-specificity trade-offs and greater performance degradation under narrative reordering.

Conclusion: The LLM-as-interface, ML-as-predictor design effectively decouples natural-language usability from predictive inference, yielding a more robust, auditable clinical decision support pathway than using LLMs as end-to-end diagnostic engines.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make clinical decision support more accessible by interpreting free-text documentation, but their direct use as diagnostic engines is limited by sensitivity to prompts, information order, and plausible but incorrect outputs. Structured machine-learning models offer more stable risk prediction, yet they require tabular inputs that are difficult to integrate with narrative clinical workflows. We present ClaMPAPP (Clinical Language-assisted Machine-learning Pipeline for Appendicitis), a hybrid system that uses an LLM as an interface rather than as the final decision-maker. ClaMPAPP extracts schema-constrained clinical features from note-like narratives, applies deterministic plausibility checks, and passes validated features to an XGBoost classifier trained on clinical, laboratory, and ultrasound variables. We evaluated ClaMPAPP on two independent pediatric appendicitis cohorts from German hospitals and compared it with end-to-end LLM baselines, including open-source and proprietary models. To preserve ground truth while testing free-text input, narratives were generated from structured electronic health records through template rendering and constrained LLM rewriting, with additional sentence-order permutation to assess positional robustness. ClaMPAPP achieved the strongest overall diagnostic performance in both internal and external validation while minimizing missed appendicitis cases, the key safety concern in acute triage. End-to-end LLMs showed unstable sensitivity-specificity trade-offs and greater degradation under narrative reordering. These results support an LLM-as-interface, ML-as-predictor design that separates natural-language usability from predictive inference and provides a more auditable pathway for clinical decision support.

</details>


### [52] [RECOM: A Validity Discrimination Tradeoff in Automatic Metrics for Open Ended Reddit Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19218)
*Pushwitha Krishnappa,Amit Das,Vinija Jain,Aman Chadha,Tathagata Mukherjee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RECOM introduces a contamination-free Reddit-based evaluation dataset to assess LLM evaluation metrics along two axes—validity (distinguishing real from random text) and discriminative power (ranking model quality)—revealing a fundamental tradeoff: cosine similarity excels at validity but fails discrimination, while BERTScore's apparent discrimination collapses when controlling for response length, and all metrics (including LLM judges) struggle to do both jobs well.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automatic evaluation metrics for LLM-generated text are implicitly expected to perform two distinct functions: (1) validity—separating genuine content alignment from superficial pattern matching, and (2) discriminative power—reliably distinguishing better systems from worse ones. On open-ended, opinion-driven tasks, these two goals are in tension, yet no prior work has systematically measured this tradeoff.

Method: The authors construct RECOM, a dataset of 15,000 r/AskReddit questions from September 2025 paired with authentic community replies, ensuring all data postdates every evaluated model's training cutoff (contamination-free). Five open-source LLMs (7–10B parameters) are scored against each reply using multiple automatic metrics. A random-derangement baseline (pairing questions with unrelated replies) serves as a noise floor. Metrics are evaluated on two axes: validity (separation between real and random via Cohen's d) and discriminative power (ability to rank the five models). Three independent LLM judges are also tested.

Result: No metric performs both validity and discrimination well. Cosine similarity achieves strong validity (Cohen's d ≈ 2) but negligible discriminative power (|d| < 0.1). BERTScore precision shows apparent discriminative power (raw |d| up to 0.63), but this collapses to |d| = 0.09 after controlling for response length, and its validity is weak (d ≈ 0.8). LLM judges reproduce the validity gap and also weakly separate the models. The validity–discrimination tradeoff is a property of metric design (representation choice), not model quality.

Conclusion: The validity–discrimination tradeoff is inherent to current evaluation metric design. The authors recommend that metrics be reported on both axes with an explicit random-baseline floor. RECOM is publicly released as a benchmark for future metric development.

Abstract: Automatic metrics are the default for evaluating LLM-generated text, yet a metric is quietly asked to do two jobs: tell genuine content alignment from surface coincidence (validity), and tell a better system from a worse one (discriminative power). On open-ended, opinion-driven question answering, the two are in tension. We introduce RECOM (Reddit Evaluation for Correspondence of Models), a contamination-free evaluation dataset of 15,000 r/AskReddit questions (September 2025), each paired with its authentic community replies, which postdate every evaluated model's training cutoff. Scoring five open-source LLMs (7--10B) against every reply each metric paired with a random-derangement noise floor we find that no metric does both jobs well. Cosine similarity separates real from random answers (Cohen's $d \approx 2$) but cannot rank the five models ($|d| < 0.1$); BERTScore precision appears to rank the models (raw $|d|$ up to 0.63), but once response length is controlled this collapses to $|d| = 0.09$ and its validity is weak ($d \approx 0.8$, versus cosine's $\approx 2$). Because every metric scores the same outputs, this validity--discrimination tradeoff is a property of the metrics, not the models, and we argue it stems from representation design. Three independent LLM judges reproduce the validity gap and likewise separate the five models only weakly. We recommend reporting metrics on both axes, with an explicit random-baseline floor. RECOM is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/recom-D4B0

</details>


### [53] [DreamReasoner-8B: Block-Size Curriculum Learning for Diffusion Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19257)
*Zirui Wu,Lin Zheng,Jiacheng Ye,Shansan Gong,Xueliang Zhao,Yansong Feng,Wei Bi,Lingpeng Kong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DreamReasoner-8B is an open-source block diffusion reasoning model that uses block-size curriculum learning to bridge the gap between fine-grained training and coarse-grained inference, achieving competitive reasoning performance with autoregressive models like Qwen3-8B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Block diffusion language models offer fast parallel decoding, but it is unknown whether they can be reliably scaled for long chain-of-thought reasoning. The authors identify a critical granularity gap: large training block sizes degrade reasoning quality, while small block sizes are effective but limit decoding efficiency.

Method: The authors develop DreamReasoner-8B and systematically study the effect of training and inference block sizes on long-CoT reasoning. They propose block-size curriculum learning, which progressively transitions training from small (fine-grained) to large (coarse-grained) block sizes, enabling strong reasoning that generalizes across diverse inference block sizes.

Result: DreamReasoner-8B achieves competitive results with leading open autoregressive models (e.g., Qwen3-8B) on mathematical and code reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating that diffusion language models can be practically scaled for reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: Block-size curriculum learning effectively resolves the training-inference granularity mismatch in block diffusion models, establishing a practical foundation for efficient, reasoning-capable diffusion language models that rival autoregressive approaches.

Abstract: Block diffusion language models accelerate decoding through parallel block-wise denoising, yet whether they can be reliably scaled for long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning remains unresolved. To this end, we develop DreamReasoner-8B, an open-source block diffusion reasoning model, and conduct a systematic study of how training and inference block sizes affect long-CoT reasoning. Our analysis reveals a stark performance disparity: training with large block sizes yields remarkably poor reasoning, whereas small block sizes preserve effective reasoning. To bridge this granularity gap, we propose block-size curriculum learning, which gradually transitions training from fine-grained to coarse-grained block sizes, thereby overcoming this limitation and enabling strong reasoning performance that generalizes across diverse inference block sizes. On mathematical and code reasoning benchmarks, DreamReasoner-8B achieves results competitive with leading open autoregressive models such as Qwen3-8B. This work establishes a practical foundation for efficient, reasoning-capable diffusion language models. We release our model at https://github.com/DreamLM/DreamReasoner.

</details>


### [54] [Trade-offs in Medical LLM Adaptation: An Empirical Study in French QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19266)
*Ikram Belmadani,Oumaima El Khettari,Carlos Ramisch,Frederic Bechet,Richard Dufour,Benoit Favre*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates domain adaptation strategies for LLMs using French medical QA as a case study, comparing continual pretraining (CPT), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and their combination. For MCQA, SFT alone is a strong, cost-effective choice; for OEQA, CPT improves lexical metrics while instruction tuning and CPT+SFT are preferred by LLM-based judges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The effectiveness of domain adaptation strategies for LLMs remains unclear despite growing interest in adapting models to specialized domains and languages. The authors aim to disentangle adaptation effects from base model choice through systematic comparison.

Method: The study compares CPT, SFT, and CPT+SFT across three model families, multiple sizes, and three initialization types on French medical QA. Evaluation covers both MCQA and OEQA using automatic metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge, with greedy and constrained decoding. Cross-lingual transfer from French to English benchmarks is also tested.

Result: For MCQA, CPT+SFT marginally outperforms SFT alone, but gains are small and rarely statistically significant, positioning SFT as a cost-effective default. For OEQA, CPT consistently improves overlap-based metrics, whereas SFT alone often degrades generation quality; instruction tuning and CPT+SFT are preferred by LLM-based evaluation. French adaptation transfers effectively to English benchmarks.

Conclusion: SFT alone is a practical default for MCQA under computational constraints. For OEQA, a combination of CPT and instruction-tuned SFT is recommended. The work provides actionable guidelines for domain adaptation strategy selection.

Abstract: The development of large language models (LLMs) has led to an increased focus on their adaptation to specialized domains and languages, yet the effectiveness of domain adaptation strategies remains unclear. We present a study of medical domain adaptation using French medical question-answering (QA) as a case study. We compare continual pretraining (CPT), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and their combination across three model families, multiple sizes, and three initialization types, explicitly disentangling adaptation effects from base model choice. We evaluate both multiple-choice (MCQA) and open-ended QA (OEQA) under greedy and constrained decoding using automatic metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation. For MCQA, CPT+SFT most often achieves the best scores, but gains over SFT are small and frequently not statistically significant, making SFT a strong and cost-effective default. For OEQA, CPT consistently improves overlap-based metrics, while SFT often degrades generation quality; instruction tuning and CPT+SFT are preferred by LLM-based evaluation. Cross-lingual experiments further show effective transfer from French adaptation to English benchmarks. Overall, we provide practical guidelines for selecting adaptation strategies under computational constraints.

</details>


### [55] [Freeing the Law with LOCUS: A Local Ordinance Corpus for the United States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19334)
*Denis Peskoff,Joe Barrow,Christopher Vu,Diag Davenport*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LOCUS is a large-scale corpus of U.S. local ordinances covering 9,239 cities/counties, with a harmonized subset for 2,309 counties, enabling machine-readable access to previously fragmented local laws. It includes ModernBERT-based classifiers for analyzing dimensions like opacity and paternalism at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Local ordinances govern critical everyday regulatory domains (zoning, housing, public health, etc.) but are largely absent from machine-readable legal corpora because they are fragmented across human-browsing-oriented vendor platforms. This gap impedes progress in legal AI, which increasingly depends on access to authoritative legal text at scale.

Method: The authors construct LOCUS by aggregating nearly all publicly available municipal and county ordinance codes (9,239 jurisdictions), using OCR to process diverse document formats. They create a county-harmonized access layer for the 2,309 largest U.S. counties. They then train ModernBERT-based classifiers and scorers to analyze local law along novel dimensions (e.g., opacity, paternalism).

Result: LOCUS provides the first comprehensive machine-readable corpus of U.S. local ordinances, with full coverage metadata for reproducibility. The county-harmonized layer covers counties representing a majority of the U.S. population. The trained ModernBERT models enable analysis of local law characteristics at unprecedented scale.

Conclusion: LOCUS fills a critical gap in legal AI infrastructure by making local law machine-accessible. The corpus and models are publicly released on Hugging Face to support reproducibility, downstream research, and incremental expansion of computational access to local law.

Abstract: Progress in legal AI increasingly depends on access to authoritative legal text at scale. Yet one of the most consequential layers of American law remains largely absent from existing machine-readable corpora: local ordinances. Local codes govern zoning, housing, business licensing, public health, noise, animal control, and many other domains of everyday regulation, but they are fragmented across vendor platforms designed for human browsing rather than bulk research access. We introduce LOCUS - the Local Ordinance Corpus for the United States - a comprehensive corpus and county-harmonized access layer for U.S. municipal and county ordinance codes. The raw corpus, available for release to researchers, represents nearly all publicly available municipal and county ordinance codes. The resulting raw corpus contains codes from 9,239 cities and counties. A smaller county-harmonized LOCUS access layer provides coverage for the largest 2,309 of 3,144 U.S. counties, accounting for a majority of the population. We use OCR to handle the myriad of document formats that have kept the law from being a public resource. We release the corpus with coverage metadata to support reproducibility, downstream legal AI research, and the incremental expansion of machine-readable access to local law. We train a collection of ModernBERT-based classifiers and scorers to facilitate analyzing U.S. local law among several dimensions, such as opacity and paternalism, that have not previously been studied at this scale. LOCUS-v1 and its derivative models are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/LocalLaws/LOCUS-v1

</details>


### [56] [Learning User Simulators with Turing Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19336)
*Yingshan Susan Wang,Cedegao E. Zhang,Linlu Qiu,Zexue He,Pengyuan Li,Alex Pentland,Roger P. Levy,Yoon Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes Turing-RL, a reinforcement learning method that trains user simulator LLMs by optimizing for indistinguishability from real users (via a Turing Test reward), rather than matching ground-truth responses. Experiments in conversational chat and Reddit show consistent outperformance over baselines on both human and LLM evaluation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing user simulator training methods rely on maximizing log probability or similarity rewards against a single ground-truth response. These approaches fail to capture the multi-modal nature of human responses—there are many plausible things a user could say in a given context. The authors argue that optimizing for indistinguishability (passing a Turing Test) is a more principled objective.

Method: Turing-RL uses a discriminative Turing reward: an LLM judge scores how indistinguishable a generated response is from the real user's, conditioned on the user's interaction history. The user simulator (also an LLM) is then fine-tuned via reinforcement learning using this reward signal, encouraging it to produce responses that cannot be reliably distinguished from authentic user behavior.

Result: Across two domains—conversational chat and Reddit forum discussions—Turing-RL consistently outperforms baseline methods (log-probability maximization and similarity-reward approaches) on both LLM-based and human evaluation metrics.

Conclusion: Optimizing for indistinguishability via a Turing Test–style RL objective is more effective for learning user simulators than traditional response-matching approaches, suggesting a promising direction for training interactive agent assistants and personalization systems.

Abstract: Learning to simulate human users in interactive settings could advance the training of agent assistants, evaluation of personalization systems, research in the social sciences, and more. Existing approaches generally do so by training a large language model (LLM) to match a single ground truth response, either by maximizing the log probability or by using a similarity reward. We instead propose {Turing-RL}: a Turing-Test-based reinforcement learning approach for training user simulator models. {Turing-RL} uses a discriminative Turing reward with an LLM judge to score how indistinguishable a generated response is from the real user's given the user's history, and the user simulator LLM learns to produce responses indistinguishable from what the user could have said with such rewards. Across two different domains--conversational chat and Reddit forum discussion--we find that {Turing-RL} consistently outperforms baseline methods on both LLM and human evaluation metrics. Our study suggests that optimizing for indistinguishability, rather than response matching, is effective for learning user simulators.

</details>

### [57] [NAVI-Orbital: First In-Orbit Demonstration of a Zero-Shot Vision-Language Model for Autonomous Earth Observation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18271)
*Juan Manuel Delfa Victoria,Taran Cyriac John,Andrew W. Herson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NAVI-Orbital demonstrates the first in-orbit deployment of a vision-language model (Gemma 3) on a LEO spacecraft, enabling onboard scene classification, textual description, and natural-language dialogue for semantic compression of Earth observation data, achieving 88.16% accuracy on the AID benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Earth Observation data generation rates exceed downlink bandwidth and ground-based human processing capacity, creating a bottleneck between data collection and actionable intelligence. The authors aim to invert the traditional "acquire-then-downlink-everything" paradigm by enabling onboard semantic compression through autonomous multi-modal inference directly on the spacecraft.

Method: The system deploys a vision-language model (Gemma 3) on satellite-class edge hardware with GPU-accelerated inference. It classifies captured scenes, generates textual descriptions of content and inter-feature relationships, and supports follow-up natural-language dialogue with operators. Tasking uses plain-English prompts instead of conventional command sequences. A graph-based state machine (LangGraph) orchestrates dedicated agents for detection and dialogue. No fine-tuning was applied for the flight instrument.

Result: Ground benchmarking: 88.16% accuracy on the 7,960-image AID dataset. Flatsat validation and live in-orbit captures (including uncorrected YAM-9 imagery) confirmed successful operation on previously unseen Earth imagery with hardware-accelerated onboard GPU inference.

Conclusion: Running foundation models on satellite-class edge computers is feasible and enables semantic compression of Earth observations in orbit, fundamentally inverting the conventional bandwidth-limited acquire-then-downlink data pipeline.

Abstract: As Earth Observation data generation outpaces downlink bandwidth and human-in-the-loop processing, a widening gap has emerged between onboard collection and actionable ground intelligence. This paper presents NAVI-Orbital, a software system deployed on a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) spacecraft. On April 16, 2026, NAVI-Orbital achieved what is, to the authors' knowledge, the first in-orbit demonstration of a vision-language model performing autonomous multi-modal inference entirely onboard. NAVI-Orbital uses a local vision-language model (Gemma 3) to classify each captured scene, produce a text description of its content and the relationships between its features, and respond to operator follow-up via natural-language dialogue. The system is re-tasked through plain-English prompts in place of conventional command sequences, and is orchestrated by a graph-based state machine (LangGraph) coordinating dedicated agents for detection and dialogue. Results across ground benchmarking (88.16% accuracy on the 7,960-image curated AID benchmark), Flatsat validation, and live in-orbit captures of newly acquired, previously unseen Earth imagery (including uncorrected YAM-9 imagery, processed onboard with hardware-accelerated GPU inference and no fine-tuning for the flight instrument) demonstrate the feasibility of running foundation models on satellite-class edge computers to invert the conventional acquire-then-downlink-everything bandwidth profile through semantic compression of Earth observations in-orbit.

</details>


### [58] [CaVe-VLM-CoT: An Interpretable Vision-Language Model Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18385)
*Sneha Rao,Shaina Raza,Dhanesh Ramachandram*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CaVe-VLM-CoT introduces a five-stage agentic-RAG framework with closed-loop verification that enforces step-level citation grounding in VLMs. When ungrounded claims are detected, structured feedback triggers re-retrieval, achieving 87.1% accuracy on ScienceQA and 55.2% on MMMU, alongside a new 23-metric evaluation suite anchored by CaVeScore.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs produce fluent but visually unfaithful outputs (hallucinations). Existing chain-of-thought and retrieval-augmented methods lack (1) step-level citation grounding enforcement and (2) mechanisms to route verification failures back to retrieval for correction. No existing framework jointly measures retrieval quality, step-wise citation faithfulness, and cross-modal grounding.

Method: A modular, reflection-based agentic-RAG framework with a five-stage closed-loop pipeline: (1) Extractor — identifies information needs; (2) Retriever — fetches relevant evidence; (3) Solver — generates reasoning with citations; (4) Citation Injector — embeds grounded citations; (5) Verifier — detects ungrounded claims and triggers structured feedback to the Extractor for targeted re-retrieval. Also introduces 23 component-wise metrics across all stages and CaVeScore, a composite metric weighting accuracy, citation precision/recall, attribution, and evidence grounding.

Result: Without any architectural or prompt modifications, CaVe-VLM-CoT achieves 87.1% accuracy and 56.6% CaVeScore on ScienceQA, and 55.2% accuracy and 35.7% CaVeScore on MMMU (across 30 subjects).

Conclusion: The closed-loop verification and re-retrieval mechanism effectively reduces hallucinations in VLM outputs by enforcing step-level citation grounding. The framework is plug-and-play, requiring no modifications to the underlying VLM. The proposed evaluation suite provides a standardized way to jointly assess retrieval quality, citation faithfulness, and cross-modal grounding.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) remain prone to hallucinations, producing fluent but visually unfaithful outputs. Existing chain-of-thought and retrieval-augmented methods only partially address this, as they neither enforce step-level citation grounding nor route verification failures back to retrieval for correction. We present CaVe-VLM-CoT, a modular reflection-based agentic-RAG framework that enforces evidence-grounded reasoning through a five-stage closed-loop pipeline: Extractor, Retriever, Solver, Citation Injector, and Verifier, in which detected ungrounded claims trigger structured feedback to the Extractor for targeted re-retrieval. Since no existing framework jointly measures retrieval quality, step-wise citation faithfulness, and cross-modal grounding, we propose a suite of 23 component-wise metrics across all stages, anchored by CaVeScore, a composite metric weighting accuracy, citation precision and recall, attribution, and evidence grounding. Without any architectural or prompt modifications, CaVe-VLM-CoT achieves 87.1\% accuracy and 56.6\% CaVeScore on ScienceQA , and 55.2\% accuracy and 35.7\% CaVeScore on MMMU (30 subjects).

</details>


### [59] [Searching for Synergy in Shared Workspace Human-AI Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18413)
*Nachiket Kotalwar,Rohini Das,Carolyn Rose*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Adding human collaborators to AI teams can backfire without proper coordination structures. This paper shows that shared group memory combined with human-in-the-loop approval gates improves performance in shared-workspace human-AI teams, especially in three-person configurations, by clarifying responsibility and routing expertise effectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents grow more capable, many real-world scientific and professional tasks still require human judgment and contextual expertise. The key open question is not just whether to include humans, but how to structure human-AI collaboration to avoid process loss — where additional collaborators become coordination overhead rather than assets.

Method: The authors use the Collaborative Gym environment with DiscoveryBench tasks to simulate shared-workspace human-AI teams across 1,482 sessions. They systematically examine team configurations with and without coordination scaffolding. The scaffolding intervention consists of (1) shared group memory and (2) simulated human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates, where designated simulated participants must approve selected actions before the team proceeds.

Result: Adding relevant collaborators without coordination structure can degrade performance due to process loss. The scaffolding (shared memory + HITL gates) yields higher mean performance, with the clearest gains in three-person teams. The benefits stem from clearer responsibility signals and stronger routing of expertise to appropriate team actions.

Conclusion: How human-AI teams coordinate and integrate expertise matters as much as the raw capability available to them. Effective coordination mechanisms — rather than simply adding more capable agents or humans — are essential for realizing the benefits of collaborative human-AI systems.

Abstract: Automated AI agents are increasingly capable, yet many scientific and professional tasks require human judgment and contextual expertise. We study shared-workspace human-AI teams, where AI agents and human collaborators must coordinate responsibilities before submitting a final answer. Using the Collaborative Gym environment with DiscoveryBench tasks, we examine when adding simulated human collaborators improves performance and when process loss turns additional collaborators into coordination overhead. Across 1,482 sessions, adding relevant collaborators can lower performance when teams lack structure to coordinate their contributions. We then evaluate scaffolding that combines shared group memory with simulated human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates, where selected actions require approval from a designated simulated participant. This scaffolding yields higher mean performance, most clearly in three-person teams, with clearer responsibility signals and stronger routing of expertise to team actions. Overall, how human-AI teams coordinate and integrate expertise matters as much as the capability available to them.

</details>


### [60] [CEO-Bench: Can Agents Play the Long Game?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18543)
*Haozhe Chen,Karthik Narasimhan,Zhuang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CEO-Bench is a benchmark that evaluates language model agents on their ability to operate a simulated startup for 500 days, requiring long-horizon planning, noisy information acquisition, adaptation to change, and multi-faceted coordination. Even the strongest models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5) barely exceed the initial $1M balance and fail to consistently turn a profit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current language model agents excel at isolated, short-horizon tasks (e.g., software engineering, customer service) but remain largely untested on the integrated, sustained, and adaptive decision-making required in real-world challenges. The authors aim to close this gap by testing agents on capabilities like long-horizon navigation under uncertainty, noisy information acquisition, world adaptation, and multi-part coordination — all simultaneously, as a human CEO would face.

Method: The authors introduce CEO-Bench, a simulated environment where an agent acts as CEO of a fictional startup for 500 days. The agent interacts via a programmable Python interface to manage pricing, marketing, budgeting, and other business operations. The environment provides noisy, interconnected business databases. Success requires the agent to analyze signals, formulate strategy, and coordinate decisions through code. Performance is measured by financial outcomes relative to the $1M starting balance.

Result: Only Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 finished above the $1M starting balance; neither consistently turned a profit. The strongest agents employed sophisticated strategies such as simulating customer cohorts to forecast cash flow and mining negotiation history to uncover hidden preferences. All other state-of-the-art models performed worse, underscoring the benchmark's difficulty.

Conclusion: CEO-Bench represents a first step toward measuring the intelligence required for sustained, adaptive progress over time. The poor performance of even frontier models highlights a significant capability gap in long-horizon, multi-faceted, real-world agentic tasks.

Abstract: Language model agents are becoming proficient executors at isolated, short-horizon tasks such as software engineering and customer service. Yet real-world challenges require a combination of sophisticated skills that remain largely untested in agents: (1) navigating long horizons amid uncertainty; (2) acquiring information in noisy environments; (3) adapting to a changing world; (4) orchestrating multiple moving parts toward a coherent goal. We introduce CEO-Bench, which evaluates these capabilities together by simulating a representative real-world task: operating a startup for 500 days. An agent manages pricing, marketing, budgeting, and many other aspects of a fictional company through a programmable Python interface, operating in the same environment and facing the same challenges as a human CEO. Success demands analyzing noisy, interconnected business databases, translating signals into sound strategy, and coordinating many decisions with programming. The strongest agents write sophisticated code that simulates customer cohorts to forecast future cash and mines negotiation history to uncover hidden customer preferences. Even so, most state-of-the-art models struggle in this environment. Only Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 finish above the $1M starting balance, and neither consistently turns a profit. CEO-Bench takes a first step toward measuring the intelligence required to drive sustained, adaptive progress over time.

</details>


### [61] [DeFAb: A Verifiable Benchmark for Defeasible Abduction in Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18557)
*Patrick Cooper,Alvaro Velasquez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeFAb is a benchmark for defeasible abduction that converts decades of knowledge bases into formally verifiable instances where hypotheses must satisfy polynomial-time checks for validity, conservativity, and minimality. Frontier LLMs achieve only 7.8–23.5% accuracy under rendering-robust evaluation versus 100% for a symbolic solver, revealing that current models lack disciplined defeasible reasoning capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current language models excel at fluent text generation but lack the logical rigor needed for defeasible abduction — the construction of hypotheses that explain anomalies by overriding defaults while preserving unrelated expectations. Existing benchmarks fail to measure whether models can perform disciplined theory revision rather than producing convincing but logically unsound prose. The authors aim to make logical rigor the instrument for measuring creativity and theoretical reasoning.

Method: The DeFAb pipeline pairs taxonomic hierarchies (OpenCyc, YAGO, Wikidata) with behavioral property graphs (ConceptNet, UMLS) to generate 372,648+ instances across 33.75M materialized rules from 18 sources. Every generated hypothesis must pass polynomial-time checks for valid derivation, conservativity, and minimality, establishing formally grounded gold standards. Three difficulty levels are produced. Evaluation includes rendering-robust testing (four surface renderings), chain-of-thought variance analysis, and matched contamination control. They also introduce DeFAb-Hard (235-instance Level 3 variant) and CONJURE (kernel-verified transformative-creativity variant using Lean 4/Mathlib). The verifier doubles as an exact reward for preference optimization (DPO, RLVR/GRPO).

Result: A rule-based symbolic solver resolves every instance in under 50 microseconds with 100% accuracy. Frontier models achieve at best 65% and drop to 7.8–23.5% under rendering-robust evaluation. Chain-of-thought variance (~36 pp) exceeds any inter-model gap. A matched contamination control isolates a +19.4 pp Level 3 gap. On DeFAb-Hard, the best model reaches 53.3% vs 100% symbolic. The CONJURE pilot finds zero novel concepts generated by LLMs.

Conclusion: Frontier language models do not reliably internalize defeasible reasoning. The dramatic accuracy drop under rendering-robust conditions and high chain-of-thought variance suggest surface-level pattern matching rather than genuine logical understanding. The DeFAb framework demonstrates that formal verifiability can serve as both an evaluation instrument and an exact reward signal for alignment, with implications for training models capable of disciplined theory construction.

Abstract: A rule-based logic solver resolves every instance in our benchmark in under 50 microseconds with 100% accuracy; the best frontier language model reaches 65% at best and drops to 23.5% under rendering-robust evaluation (worst case over four surface renderings). We introduce DeFAb (Defeasible Abduction Benchmark), a dataset and generation pipeline that converts four decades of publicly funded knowledge bases into formally grounded instances for defeasible abduction: constructing hypotheses that explain anomalies by overriding defaults while preserving unrelated expectations. Because every hypothesis must pass polynomial-time checks for valid derivation, conservativity, and minimality, DeFAb makes logical rigor the instrument for measuring creativity and theoretical reasoning, scoring the disciplined construction of theory revisions rather than fluent but theory-destroying prose. The pipeline pairs taxonomic hierarchies (OpenCyc, YAGO, Wikidata) with behavioral property graphs (ConceptNet, UMLS) to produce 372,648+ instances across 33.75M materialized rules from 18 sources, in three levels with polynomial-time verifiable gold standards. Four frontier models do not reliably internalize defeasible reasoning: rendering-robust Level 2 accuracy is 7.8-23.5%; chain-of-thought variance (~36 pp) exceeds any inter-model gap; and a matched contamination control isolates a +19.4 pp Level 3 gap. We further release DeFAb-Hard (a 235-instance Level 3 difficulty variant; best model 53.3% vs 100% symbolic) and CONJURE (a kernel-verified transformative-creativity variant of 560 Lean 4/Mathlib instances whose gold answers are definitions the proof kernel did not previously contain, judge-free verifier; a pilot finds zero novel concepts). The same verifier doubles as an exact reward for preference optimization (DPO, RLVR/GRPO). Released under MIT at https://huggingface.co/datasets/PatrickAllenCooper/DeFAb.

</details>


### [62] [Optimizing Lithium Production Decisions under Geological, Demand, and Pricing Uncertainties: A POMDP Framework for Multi-Objective Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18598)
*Anna C. Edmonds,Mansur M. Arief,Robert J. Moss,Mykel J. Kochenderfer,Jef Caers*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper frames lithium production decision-making as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) to optimize which mines to open, when to open them, and which extraction technology to use, under price and demand uncertainty. POMDP solvers outperform human-inspired heuristics across various pricing regimes by dynamically managing uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior optimization models for lithium mine production planning inadequately account for three key uncertainties: price volatility, demand fluctuations, and the choice among different extraction technologies (e.g., direct lithium extraction vs. hard rock mining). This gap limits the robustness of investment and operational strategies in real-world settings.

Method: The authors formulate the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and apply belief state planning methods to derive optimal policies. They evaluate performance across four pricing regimes — static, linear, exponential, and stochastic — and compare POMDP-based decisions against human-inspired heuristic baselines.

Result: POMDP solvers consistently outperform heuristic approaches by dynamically adapting to shifting price regimes through belief state planning and explicit uncertainty management. The framework achieves higher demand fulfillment and better-balanced economic and environmental outcomes across all tested pricing and deposit scenarios.

Conclusion: Incorporating pricing uncertainty, demand uncertainty, and technology choice into a POMDP framework yields more robust and adaptive lithium production strategies. The belief-state planning approach optimally sequences exploration, production, and technology selection, delivering superior long-term performance over heuristic methods.

Abstract: Decision making in lithium production is challenging, whether from an investor's perspective or a strategic production standpoint. Determining which mines to open and when to open them involves not only geological and price uncertainties, but also complexities around the choice of extraction method, from direct lithium extraction to hard rock mining. Prior work explored models of this problem and different methods to optimize mining decisions; these models did not account for uncertainty in pricing, uncertainty in demand, or different mining technologies to extract lithium. Incorporating different pricing models and extraction technology into these models enables more robust strategies for determining not only when and where to open a mine, but also which method of production to pursue. We frame the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and solve using belief state planning methods to get optimal decision making. In our study, we show that POMDP solvers outperform human inspired heuristics by dynamically adapting to shifting lithium price regimes (static, linear, exponential, and stochastic) through belief state planning and explicit uncertainty management. By optimally sequencing exploration, production, and technology choice, the framework achieves higher demand fulfillment and more balanced economic environmental outcomes over the projects lifetime in all different pricing and deposit scenarios.

</details>


### [63] [ForecastBench-Sim: A Simulated-World Forecasting Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18686)
*Jaeho Lee,Nick Merrill,Ezra Karger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ForecastBench-Sim is a simulated-world forecasting benchmark built on Freeciv game rollouts. It generates forecasting questions at arbitrary time horizons, supports paired intervention worlds for causal questions, and provides immediately resolvable tasks to study probabilistic reasoning under dynamic world states — complementing real-world benchmarks that are constrained by slow resolution, rare tail events, and unscorable counterfactuals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world forecasting benchmarks suffer from three key limitations: outcomes resolve slowly, tail events are rare, and counterfactual questions are difficult to score. These constraints hinder the study of probabilistic reasoning in AI systems. The authors aim to create a controlled, simulated environment that overcomes these limitations while retaining the complexity and dynamism of real-world forecasting.

Method: The benchmark is built on game rollouts from Freeciv, a turn-based strategy game similar to Civilization. Forecasters receive a fixed world report (a structured snapshot of the current game state) and answer questions about hidden future states. The simulation then continues, and forecasts are scored against ground-truth outcomes. The pipeline supports continuous and binary questions at arbitrary time horizons, and can generate paired intervention worlds for conditional or causal forecasting questions. The authors describe the full pipeline, question families, scoring protocol, and release artifacts, and validate it through model evaluations and an anonymized human pilot.

Result: The benchmark successfully produces diverse forecasting questions with immediate resolvability. It enables the study of rare/disruptive outcomes and causal reasoning through intervention worlds. Validation slices from model evaluations and a human pilot demonstrate the benchmark's utility and provide baseline performance metrics.

Conclusion: ForecastBench-Sim complements real-world forecasting benchmarks by providing a controlled, immediately resolvable sandbox for studying probabilistic reasoning under dynamic world states. It addresses key weaknesses of real-world benchmarks — slow resolution, rarity of tail events, and unscorable counterfactuals — while maintaining ecological validity through a complex strategy game environment.

Abstract: Forecasting benchmarks for general-purpose AI systems usually inherit the constraints of the real world: outcomes resolve slowly, tail events are rare, and counterfactual questions are difficult to score. We introduce ForecastBench-Sim, a simulated-world forecasting benchmark built on game rollouts from Freeciv, a turn-based strategy game modelled on the Civilization series. Forecasters receive a fixed world report (a structured snapshot of the current game state) and answer questions about hidden future states; the benchmark then continues the simulation and scores forecasts. Because the world is simulated, the same setup can generate continuous or binary forecasting questions at arbitrary time horizons, paired intervention worlds for conditional or causal questions, and resolved examples of rare or disruptive outcomes. We describe the benchmark pipeline, question families, scoring protocol, and release artifacts, and report validation slices from model evaluations and an anonymized human pilot. ForecastBench-Sim is intended to complement real-world forecasting benchmarks by providing controlled, immediately resolvable tasks for studying probabilistic reasoning under dynamic world states.

</details>


### [64] [What Must Generalist Agents Remember?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18746)
*Khurram Yamin,Namrata Deka,Maitreyi Swaroop,Albert Ting,Jeff Schneider,Bryan Wilder*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proves that generalist agents operating across multiple environments must store domain-disambiguating information in memory at observational bottlenecks, and that memory rich enough for value estimation can also approximately reconstruct local transition dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To formally characterize what information a generalist agent must retain in memory to act near-optimally across diverse environments and goals, addressing the fundamental tension between shared observations and incompatible optimal actions across domains.

Method: Formal analysis establishing a separation theorem: when two domains share an observational bottleneck but demand incompatible optimal actions, any uniformly near-optimal policy must produce distinct memory distributions at that bottleneck. The paper further proves that memory sufficient for value estimation across related goals enables approximate reconstruction of local transition dynamics.

Result: A separation theorem showing that near-optimal generalist agents cannot rely solely on current observations — they must preserve domain-relevant information in memory. Additionally, memory encoding value estimates for related goals supports approximate recovery of local transition dynamics.

Conclusion: Memory serves as the foundational substrate for three critical capabilities in generalist agents: domain disambiguation, transition-model reconstruction, and planning.

Abstract: This paper develops a formal account of what generalist agents must store in memory in order to act near-optimally across multiple environments and goals. It shows that when two domains share an observational bottleneck but require incompatible optimal actions, any uniformly near-optimal policy must induce distinct memory distributions at that bottleneck. The result yields a separation theorem: sufficiently successful agents cannot rely only on current state observations, but must preserve domain-relevant information in memory. The paper further shows that if an agent's memory contains enough information to estimate values for related goals, then that memory can be used to approximately reconstruct the agent's local transition dynamics. Together, these results characterize memory as the substrate that supports domain disambiguation, transition-model reconstruction, and planning for generalist agents.

</details>


### [65] [Decoupling Search from Reasoning: A Vendor-Agnostic Grounding Architecture for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18947)
*Emmanuel Aboah Boateng,Kyle MacDonald,Amardeep Kumar,Siddharth Kodwani,Sudeep Das*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Decoupled Search Grounding (DSG), a vendor-agnostic boundary that externalizes search grounding from LLMs into a controllable MCP-compatible gateway. DSG provides first-class controls over routing, caching, fallback, and context rendering, achieving near-native accuracy on multiple QA benchmarks while reducing search costs by 91–98% and latency by 68%, with a 99.4% warm-cache hit rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current production LLM agents rely on native search grounding where retrieval policy, provider choice, evidence injection, cost, latency, and generation behavior are tightly coupled within a single model-provider boundary. This coupling makes grounding opaque to inspect, hard to tune or reuse, and can trigger Search-Induced Verbosity (SIV) that violates strict output format contracts. The authors seek to decouple these concerns for better controllability, portability, and cost efficiency.

Method: DSG is designed as an MCP (Model Context Protocol)-compatible gateway sitting between the reasoning model and search backends. It surfaces provider routing, source-aware context rendering, configured fallback policies, retrieval-depth control, and exact-plus-semantic caching as externally configurable controls. The system is evaluated across five frontier models on SimpleQA, FreshQA, HotpotQA, and a production e-commerce Query Understanding (QIU) workload, comparing native search grounding against DSG on accuracy, search cost, latency, cache hit rates, and answer conciseness/contract compliance.

Result: On SimpleQA, DSG nearly matches native accuracy (86.1% vs. 87.7%) at 91% lower search cost and preserves concise answer contracts. Warm-cache hit rate reaches 99.4% with 68% latency reduction. Native search leads on recency-sensitive FreshQA. On the production e-commerce QIU workload, DSG matches or slightly exceeds native-search accuracy while cutting search cost by over 98%. The results demonstrate that grounding benefits from being treated as an optimizable interface boundary rather than a fixed model feature.

Conclusion: Real-time search grounding should be decoupled from the model as an independent, optimizable infrastructure layer. DSG demonstrates that externalizing grounding as a shared production layer with first-class controls yields dramatic cost savings, lower latency, and competitive accuracy, while avoiding Search-Induced Verbosity and enabling model interchangeability. This architectural shift makes grounding inspectable, tunable, reusable, and portable across models and tasks.

Abstract: Production LLM agents increasingly depend on real-time search, yet native search grounding bundles retrieval policy, provider choice, evidence injection, cost, latency, and generation behavior behind a single model-provider boundary. This coupling makes grounding hard to inspect, tune, reuse, or port, and can trigger Search-Induced Verbosity that breaks strict output contracts. We present Decoupled Search Grounding (DSG), a vendor-agnostic boundary that moves grounding outside the reasoning model through an MCP-compatible gateway, exposing provider routing, source-aware context rendering, configured fallback, retrieval-depth control, and exact plus semantic caching as first-class controls. Across five frontier models on SimpleQA, FreshQA, and HotpotQA, native search leads on recency-sensitive FreshQA, but DSG exposes a stronger frontier when control matters: on SimpleQA it nearly matches native accuracy (86.1% vs. 87.7%) at 91% lower search cost, preserves concise answer contracts, and reaches a 99.4% warm-cache hit rate with 68% lower latency. Deployed as a shared production grounding layer for large-scale agentic workloads with interchangeable models, DSG matches or slightly exceeds native-search accuracy on an e-commerce query-understanding (QIU) workload while cutting search cost by over 98%. Real-time grounding is best treated as an optimizable interface boundary, not a fixed model feature.

</details>


### [66] [R2D-RL: A RoboCup 2D Soccer Environment for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18786)
*Haobin Qin,Baofeng Zhang,Hidehisa Akiyama,Keisuke Fujii*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: R2D-RL bridges the RoboCup 2D Soccer Simulation platform with Python-based MARL workflows, enabling multi-agent reinforcement learning with discrete/hybrid action spaces, reward shaping, and parallel execution, with baselines on front-goal and 11-vs-11 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robot soccer presents a rich MARL challenge (partial observability, cooperative/adversarial dynamics, sparse rewards, long-horizon tactics), but the existing RCSS2D platform uses a competition-oriented server-client architecture incompatible with modern Python-based MARL frameworks. R2D-RL fills this gap by providing a seamless RL interface.

Method: R2D-RL connects RCSS2D and HELIOS-based player clients to a Python MARL interface via shared-memory communication and cycle-level synchronization. It supports full-field and scenario-based training, configurable opponents, Base discrete and Hybrid parameterized action spaces, action masks, EPV-based reward shaping, and parallel execution.

Result: The authors provide front-goal scenarios and an 11-vs-11 full-field benchmark along with baseline results, demonstrating the environment's utility for MARL research.

Conclusion: R2D-RL successfully bridges the gap between the RCSS2D simulation platform and modern MARL tooling, offering a standardized, flexible, and scalable environment for multi-agent reinforcement learning research in the robot soccer domain.

Abstract: Robot soccer is a challenging testbed for multi-agent reinforcement learning because it combines partial observability, cooperative and adversarial interaction, sparse rewards, and long-horizon tactical behavior. RoboCup 2D Soccer Simulation (RCSS2D) provides a mature robot-soccer platform, but its competition-oriented server-client architecture is difficult to use directly with modern Python-based MARL workflows. We introduce R2D-RL, a reinforcement learning environment that connects RCSS2D and HELIOS-based player clients to a Python MARL interface through shared-memory communication and cycle-level synchronization. R2D-RL supports full-field and scenario-based training with configurable opponents, Base discrete and Hybrid parameterized action spaces, action masks, expected possession value (EPV)-based reward shaping, and parallel execution. We provide front-goal scenarios and an 11-vs-11 full-field benchmark, together with baseline results.

</details>


### [67] [ProfiLLM: Utility-Aligned Agentic User Profiling for Industrial Ride-Hailing Dispatch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18803)
*Tengfei Lyu,Zirui Yuan,Xu Liu,Kai Wan,Zihao Lu,Li Ma,Hao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProfiLLM is an agentic LLM pipeline that extracts semantic user profiles from platform-scale behavioral logs for ride-hailing dispatch, using tool-augmented global knowledge mining and utility-aligned profile exploration with DPO fine-tuning, achieving significant GMV, completion rate, and cancel-rate improvements in production A/B tests at DiDi.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ride-hailing dispatch systems rely on structured numerical features but miss decisive, contextual behavioral signals (e.g., driver aversion to regions) that LLMs could extract as semantic profiles. Scaling LLM profiling to live millisecond-latency dispatch faces three constraints: (1) behavioral logs exceed LLM context windows by orders of magnitude, (2) most users are long-tail with sparse interactions, and (3) surface-fluent profiles do not guarantee downstream prediction utility.

Method: ProfiLLM consists of two modules: (1) Tool-Augmented Global Knowledge Mining — an LLM agent equipped with 27 analytical tools mines platform-scale data to produce reusable global knowledge, adaptive user clustering rules, and region-level supply-demand priors, circumventing per-user context limits; (2) Utility-Aligned Profile Exploration — generates multiple candidate profiles per cluster, evaluates them via a lightweight downstream utility proxy, iteratively refines the best candidates, and constructs preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) fine-tuning, ensuring profiles improve prediction utility rather than just surface fluency.

Result: On DiDi's production dispatcher, ProfiLLM achieved up to +6.14% relative AUC improvement in outcome prediction, up to +4.35% GMV gain in dispatch simulation, and consistent online A/B improvements over 14 days: +0.47% GMV, +0.33% Completion Rate, and -0.82% Cancel-Before-Accept rate.

Conclusion: LLM-generated semantic profiles, when utility-aligned and scaled via tool-augmented global knowledge mining, can be operationalized in production matching systems and deliver statistically and economically significant improvements in ride-hailing dispatch performance.

Abstract: Bringing Large Language Models (LLMs) into industrial ride-hailing dispatch as semantic feature extractors over platform-scale behavioral logs is a compelling but under-explored data systems problem. Production matching pipelines remain dominated by structured numerical features, yet decisive behavioral signals (e.g., a driver's habitual aversion to certain regions) are inherently contextual and naturally expressible as LLM-generated user profiles. However, scaling such profiling to a live, millisecond-latency dispatcher faces three intertwined constraints rarely addressed together: on a platform with millions of daily orders, logs exceed any LLM's context window by orders of magnitude; most users are long-tail, with too few interactions for per-user profiling; and surface-fluent profiles do not necessarily improve downstream prediction utility. We present ProfiLLM, an agentic LLM data pipeline that operationalizes utility-aligned user profiling for production matching systems through two modules. (1) Tool-Augmented Global Knowledge Mining equips an LLM agent with 27 analytical tools to mine platform-scale data, producing reusable global knowledge, adaptive user clustering rules, and region-level supply-demand priors. (2) Utility-Aligned Profile Exploration generates multiple candidate profiles per cluster, evaluates them via a lightweight downstream utility proxy, iteratively refines the best candidates and constructs preference pairs for DPO fine-tuning. Deployed on DiDi's production dispatcher, ProfiLLM achieves up to +6.14% relative AUC improvement in outcome prediction, up to +4.35% GMV gain in dispatching simulation, and consistent improvements in a 14-day online A/B test including +0.47% GMV, +0.33% Completion Rate, and -0.82% Cancel-Before-Accept rate.

</details>


### [68] [WorldLines: Benchmarking and Modeling Long-Horizon Stateful Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18847)
*Yehang Zhang,Jianchong Su,Haojian Huang,Yifan Chang,Tianhao Zhou,Xinli Xu,Yingjie Xu,Yinchuan Li,Zexi Li,Ying-Cong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorldLines is a project-driven benchmark for evaluating long-term memory in embodied household agents, using temporally extended traces with dialogues, actions, and state changes. The authors also propose ObsMem, an observer-grounded memory architecture that tracks visibility-aware memories and action-native state trails, revealing persistent challenges in partial observability and memory-to-plan translation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-term memory benchmarks focus on language-centric retrieval and QA, while embodied benchmarks emphasize short-horizon tasks without testing long-term memory use in dynamic, real-home environments. There is a gap in evaluating how embodied agents remember user routines, world states, and past interactions over extended periods.

Method: The authors introduce WorldLines, a benchmark that constructs temporally extended household traces containing dialogues, actions, execution feedback, and object/device state changes. These traces are converted into evidence-linked samples for two tasks: Memory QA and Embodied Task Planning. They also propose ObsMem, an observer-grounded memory framework that maintains visibility-aware memories and action-native state trails to enable state-aware decision-making under partial observability.

Result: Experiments reveal persistent challenges in handling partial observability, managing overwritten world states, and translating long-term memory into executable embodied plans. ObsMem demonstrates stronger performance as a reference architecture compared to baseline approaches in this benchmark setting.

Conclusion: Long-term memory for embodied agents remains a significant open challenge, particularly under partial observability and dynamic state changes. ObsMem provides a stronger architectural foundation, but substantial gaps remain in effectively leveraging long-term memory for embodied task planning.

Abstract: To assist humans over extended periods in real homes, embodied agents must remember user routines, world states, and past interactions. Existing long-term memory benchmarks mainly evaluate language-centric retrieval and question answering, while embodied benchmarks often focus on short-horizon task execution without testing long-term memory use in dynamic environments. We introduce WorldLines, a project-driven benchmark for long-horizon embodied household assistance. It constructs temporally extended household traces with dialogues, actions, execution feedback, object and device state changes, and converts them into evidence-linked samples for Memory QA and Embodied Task Planning. We further propose ObsMem, an observer-grounded memory framework that maintains visibility-aware memories and action-native state trails for state-aware decisions. Experiments reveal persistent challenges in partial observability, overwritten world states, and translating long-term memory into embodied plans, while ObsMem offers a stronger reference architecture for this setting.

</details>


### [69] [Externalizing Research Synthesis and Validation in AI Scientists through a Research Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18874)
*Zijian Wang,Hanqi Li,Ziyue Yang,Zijian Hu,Shenghan Zuo,Yunzhe Zhang,Da Ma,Danyu Luo,Chenrun Wang,Jing Peng,Tiancheng Huang,Sijia Guo,Huayang Wang,Zichen Zhu,Senyu Han,Yilu Cao,Kai Yu,Lu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Xcientist is a research harness that makes AI-driven scientific reasoning inspectable by externalizing synthesis and validation into contract-governed, artifact-based processes, preventing "claim drift" where runnable results no longer support their original claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI systems automating scientific workflows keep reasoning implicit within model inference, making the evidential chain from prior literature to final claims opaque. This creates a risk of "claim drift," where generated implementations and artifacts become decoupled from the mechanisms they are supposed to validate, undermining scientific accountability.

Method: Xcient$ist organizes research into persistent, inspectable artifacts — including literature evidence, idea states, implementation plans, ablation records, and repair traces — governed by explicit contracts. These contracts ensure that generated mechanisms remain grounded in evidence and can be executed, tested, and revised without losing their evidential basis. The system tracks full trajectories from problem formulation through mechanism design, validation, and bounded revision.

Result: Across three diverse domains — training-free memory systems, graph-structured traffic forecasting, and multi-scale physics-informed neural networks — Xcientist preserved traceable, attributable trajectories. The system successfully maintained alignment between runnable artifacts and claimed mechanisms, demonstrating that contract-governed processes can prevent claim drift.

Conclusion: AI scientists should be evaluated not solely on final artifacts but on whether their synthesis and validation processes remain attributable, inspectable, and scientifically accountable. Xcientist demonstrates that externalizing reasoning into structured, contract-governed artifacts is a viable path toward this goal.

Abstract: AI systems can increasingly automate scientific workflows, but the reasoning that links prior evidence, generated ideas, experiments and final claims often remains implicit inside model inference. Here we introduce Xcientist, a research harness that externalizes research synthesis and experimental validation into inspectable, contract-governed processes. Xcientist organizes literature evidence, idea states, implementation plans, ablation records and repair traces as persistent research artifacts, so that generated mechanisms can be grounded, executed, tested and revised without losing their evidential basis. We identify claim drift as a failure mode of automated research, where runnable artifacts no longer support the mechanism originally claimed. Across training-free memory systems, graph-structured traffic forecasting and multi-scale physics-informed neural networks, Xcientist preserves traceable trajectories from problem formulation to mechanism design, validation and bounded revision. These results suggest that AI scientists should be evaluated not only by their final artifacts, but by whether their synthesis and validation processes remain attributable, inspectable and scientifically accountable.

</details>


### [70] [Generative-Model Predictive Planning for Navigation in Partially Observable Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18888)
*Thomas Quilter,Yifan Zhu,Guorui Quan,Mingfei Sun,Samuel Kaski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BeliefDiffusion combines diffusion models for multimodal belief representation with Model Predictive Control for planning, enabling robust navigation in partially observable environments by imagining plausible world configurations and planning across them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing belief-based methods using neural networks fail to capture the inherent multimodality of belief spaces in partially observable environments with perceptual aliasing. Generative models offer a solution but typically require large datasets or expert demonstrations and lack explicit long-term planning mechanisms. There is a need for a framework that jointly handles multimodal belief representation and planning.

Method: BeliefDiffusion is a two-step framework: (1) Diffusion models are used to generate (imagine) multiple plausible environment configurations conditioned on the agent's observation history, explicitly capturing the multimodal belief distribution. (2) Model Predictive Control (MPC) plans efficient navigation strategies across this aggregated set of imagined configurations, enabling simultaneous belief modeling and forward planning.

Result: Extensive experiments in synthetic map environments show BeliefDiffusion significantly outperforms both model-free reinforcement learning baselines and other generative approaches in terms of navigation success rate and path efficiency.

Conclusion: Explicitly incorporating multimodal belief representations into planning leads to more robust navigation in partially observable settings, validating the synergistic combination of diffusion-based belief modeling and MPC.

Abstract: Navigation in partially observable environments presents a significant challenge for autonomous agents, requiring effective decision-making with limited sensory information in unknown environments. Belief-based methods, particularly those using neural networks to approximate the belief space, often fail to capture the inherent multimodality of belief spaces, especially in high-dimensional cases with perceptual aliasing. While generative models present a compelling alternative, they typically require substantial data or expert demonstrations and lack explicit mechanisms for long-term planning. In this paper, we introduce BeliefDiffusion, a novel framework that combines the benefits of both generation and planning. BeliefDiffusion leverages diffusion models to explicitly characterize multimodal belief distributions and utilizes Model Predictive Control (MPC) to simultaneously plan ahead. It consists of two steps: (1) Imagining plausible environment configurations based on observation history and (2) Planning efficient navigation strategies across an aggregated configurations. Through extensive experiments in synthetic map environments, we demonstrate that BeliefDiffusion significantly outperforms both model-free reinforcement learning baselines and other generative approaches in navigation success rate and path efficiency.
