Our results validate that explicitly incorporating multimodal belief representations into planning enables more robust navigation in partially observable settings.

</details>


### [71] [Skill-Guided Continuation Distillation for GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18890)
*Zhimin Fan,Hongwei Yu,Yeqing Shen,Haolong Yan,Guozhen Peng,Tianhao Peng,Yudong Zhang,Xiaowen Zhang,Kaijun Tan,Zheng Ge,Xiangyu Zhang,Daxin Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SGCD is an iterative self-improvement framework that addresses the supervision gap in GUI agents by using skill-guided continuations from off-trajectory states, improving success rates on OSWorld-Verified from ~30% to over 50%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GUI agents trained via behavior cloning on expert trajectories suffer from a supervision gap: when deployed in closed-loop execution, the policy deviates from expert trajectories and encounters off-trajectory states for which no demonstrations exist, leaving the agent unable to select correct actions.

Method: SGCD operates iteratively: (1) a plain policy runs for a few steps to reach realistic off-trajectory states; (2) a skill-guided policy completes the task from these states, producing successful continuations; (3) these continuations are mixed with expert trajectories to provide supervision. Skills — Continuation Plans, Critical Targets, Failure Traps, and Success Criteria — are extracted from both successful and failed rollouts.

Result: On the OSWorld-Verified benchmark, SGCD improved the success rate of three different base models from the low-30% range to over 50%, demonstrating both effectiveness and generality across model architectures.

Conclusion: SGCD effectively closes the supervision gap in GUI agents by generating supervision for policy-induced off-trajectory states through skill-guided continuations, yielding substantial and consistent improvements across multiple base models.

Abstract: Improving GUI agents typically relies on behavior cloning on expert trajectories. However, as the current policy deviates from the expert policy, it inevitably encounters policy-induced off-trajectory states during closed-loop execution, i.e., states that fall outside the expert trajectories. Since expert trajectories provide no demonstrations for these unseen states, such states receive no effective supervision, leaving the policy unable to select the correct action. To close this supervision gap, we propose Skill-Guided Continuation Distillation (SGCD), an iterative self-improvement framework. SGCD first runs the plain policy without skill guidance for a few steps to reach realistic off-trajectory states. From these states, a skill-guided policy then completes the task and produces successful continuations, which are mixed with expert trajectories to supply supervision over policy-induced off-trajectory states. The skills are extracted from both successful and failed rollouts, consisting of Continuation Plans, Critical Targets, Failure Traps, and Success Criteria. On OSWorld-Verified, SGCD improves the success rate of three base models from the low-30\% range to over 50\%, demonstrating its effectiveness and generality.

</details>


### [72] [SciRisk-Bench: A Risk-Dimension-Aware Benchmark for AI4Science Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18936)
*Linghao Feng,Yinqian Sun,Dongqi Liang,Sicheng Shen,Chenfei Yan,Yuxuan Peng,Yilin Zhao,Haibo Tong,Kai Li,FeiFei Zhao,Yi Zeng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciRisk-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating safety in AI for Science (AI4Science) applications, covering 7 disciplines, 31 subdisciplines, and 10 risk dimensions. It enables fine-grained diagnosis of where LLMs fail to recognize and avoid risks in high-stakes scientific contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI4Science safety datasets span multiple disciplines and task formats but leave underlying risk dimensions underspecified. There is an urgent need for benchmarks that assess not only scientific competence but also whether models recognize and avoid risks in high-stakes scientific contexts.

Method: The authors constructed SciRisk-Bench, a benchmark organized along two complementary axes: (1) explicit risk dimensions (10 categories) and (2) scientific disciplines (7 disciplines, 31 subdisciplines). They evaluated both mainstream LLMs and science-oriented LLMs across these axes to enable fine-grained safety diagnosis.

Result: The benchmark reveals fine-grained patterns of where scientific models remain unsafe, disaggregated by risk dimension, discipline, and subdiscipline. Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: SciRisk-Bench provides a structured, two-dimensional framework for diagnosing AI4Science safety failures, highlighting that safety vulnerabilities vary across both risk types and scientific domains, necessitating targeted mitigation strategies.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in AI for Science (AI4Science) workflows, from scientific question answering and literature analysis to laboratory planning and autonomous discovery. This progress creates an urgent need for safety benchmarks that evaluate not only scientific competence, but also whether models recognize and avoid risks in high-stakes scientific contexts. Existing AI4Science safety datasets cover several disciplines and task formats, leaving the underlying risk dimensions underspecified. We introduce \textbf{SciRisk-Bench}, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI4Science safety from two complementary perspectives: explicit risk dimensions and scientific disciplines. SciRisk-Bench covers 7 disciplines, 31 subdisciplines and 10 risk dimensions. In the experimental section, we evaluate both mainstream LLMs and science-oriented LLMs across risk dimensions, disciplines, and sub-disciplines, enabling fine-grained diagnosis of where scientific models remain unsafe.

</details>


### [73] [RTSGameBench: An RTS Benchmark for Strategic Reasoning by Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18950)
*San Kim,Daechul Ahn,Reokyoung Kim,Hyeonbeom Choi,Seungyeon Jwa,Jonghyun Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RTSGameBench is a new benchmark built on the large-scale RTS game "Beyond All Reason" to diagnose VLMs' strategic reasoning limitations. It features diverse matchups, diagnostic mini-games targeting specific competencies, and a self-evolving framework for extensible coverage. The authors also introduce RTSGameAgent, an FSM-based agent with memory, and show that state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with coordination and scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern VLMs struggle with strategic reasoning (anticipating/influencing agents' actions under uncertainty). RTS games are ideal testbeds for this, but existing benchmarks have limited scope, lack systematic competency diagnosis, and use fixed pre-designed scenarios. RTSGameBench addresses these gaps.

Method: The benchmark is built on "Beyond All Reason," a large-scale RTS game demanding broader strategy diversity. It offers: (1) diverse gameplay across various matchup structures, (2) diagnostic assessment via mini-games each targeting a specific strategic competency, (3) a self-evolving generation framework converting free-form queries into new mini-games. RTSGameAgent is provided as a baseline, managing units via a finite-state machine (FSM) with agentic memory.

Result: Empirical validation shows multiple state-of-the-art VLMs perform poorly when matchups demand tighter coordination, multiagent coordination, and when task scale increases.

Conclusion: RTSGameBench provides a more comprehensive and extensible platform for diagnosing VLM strategic reasoning in RTS games, and current VLMs remain inadequate for tasks requiring complex coordination and scaling.

Abstract: Modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often struggle with strategic reasoning, i.e., anticipating and influencing other agents' actions, under uncertainty in competitive and cooperative settings. Real-time strategy (RTS) games can be a natural testbed for diagnosing this limitation, as they demand coordination with allies, adaptation to opponents' strategy, and long-horizon planning under partial observability. However, existing RTS benchmarks offer limited evaluation scope, lack systematic competency diagnosis, and remain fixed in the pre-designed scenario coverage. To address these limitations, we present RTSGameBench, which is built on Beyond All Reason, a large-scale RTS game with an expanded battlefield that demands broader strategy diversity than the existing testbeds. The proposed benchmark provides evaluations through diverse gameplay across various matchup structures, diagnostic assessment via mini-games, each targeting an individual strategic competency, and extensible coverage via a self-evolving generation framework that converts free-form queries into new mini-games, improving over successive cycles. Additionally, for VLMs to operate in large-scale RTS games, we provide RTSGameAgent that manages units by an FSM with agentic memory. We empirically validate that multiple state-of-the-art VLMs do not perform well when matchups demand tighter coordination, multiagent coordination and when task scale increases.

</details>


### [74] [ThinkDeception: A Progressive Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Multimodal Deception Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18988)
*Jinhao Song,Shan Liang,Yiqun Yue,Zhuhuayang Zhang,Tianqi Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ThinkDeception introduces MLLMs into multimodal deception detection, transforming it from binary classification into explicit cognitive reasoning. It uses a step-by-step multimodal CoT dataset and a novel VAC-GRPO training strategy with progressive difficulty tiers, achieving SOTA performance in both accuracy and rationale quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal deception detection methods rely on black-box paradigms that lack interpretability, fail to provide transparent reasoning, and struggle to capture subtle cross-modal inconsistencies inherent in deceptive behaviors.

Method: The authors propose ThinkDeception, leveraging MLLMs to reframe deception detection as an explicit reasoning task. Key components include: (1) a manually annotated step-by-step multimodal Chain-of-Thought dataset for training ThinkDeception Base; (2) Visual-Audio Consistency Group Relative Policy Optimization (VAC-GRPO), which stratifies training data into four progressive difficulty tiers; (3) a dynamic curriculum scheduler paired with a multi-dimensional, process-aware reward mechanism; and (4) a reflective learning paradigm to enhance reasoning quality.

Result: ThinkDeception establishes new state-of-the-art results on mainstream benchmarks, significantly outperforming existing methods in both detection accuracy and rationale quality.

Conclusion: This work successfully advances deception detection toward interpretable, multimodal cognitive reasoning by introducing MLLMs and structured CoT reasoning, with the VAC-GRPO training strategy proving critical for capturing cross-modal inconsistencies.

Abstract: Multimodal deception detection is critical for identifying fraudulent intentions, yet existing approaches predominantly rely on end to end black--box paradigms. These methods suffer from a severe lack of interpretability failing to provide transparent reasoning trajectories and struggling to explicitly capture the subtle, cross modal inconsistencies inherent in deceptive behaviors. To transcend these limitations, we propose ThinkDeception, a novel and interpretable multimodal deception detection framework. As a pioneering effort, it introduces Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into this domain, transforming deception detection from a traditional binary classification task into an explicit cognitive reasoning process. Facilitated by the first meticulously annotated step--by--step multimodal Chain of Thought (CoT) dataset, we develop a foundational model, ThinkDeception Base, empirically validating the critical role of modal inconsistency in decoding deception. Building upon this foundation, our core innovation lies in proposing Visual-Audio Consistency Group Relative Policy Optimization(VAC--GRPO) equipped with a progressive training strategy. Distinct from standard GRPO, we stratify the training data into four progressive difficulty tiers, guiding the model through a psychologically grounded easy--to--hard cognitive transition. By innovatively coupling this dynamic curriculum scheduler with a multi dimensional, process aware reward mechanism and a reflective learning paradigm, we significantly elevate the model's overall reasoning quality. Extensive experiments on mainstream benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkDeception establishes a new SOTA, significantly outperforming existing methods in both detection accuracy and rationale quality. Ultimately, this work successfully drives the field of deception detection toward interpretable, multimodal cognitive reasoning.

</details>


### [75] [RODS: Reward-Driven Online Data Synthesis for Multi-Turn Tool-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19047)
*Ruishan Fang,Siyuan Lu,Chenyi Zhuang,Tao Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RODS addresses the depletion of informative training samples in multi-turn tool-use RL by using reward variance as a boundary detector to dynamically synthesize new training data near the agent's capability frontier, achieving competitive performance with ~20x fewer trajectories than offline pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-turn tool-use RL with static datasets, gradients concentrate on samples near the agent's capability boundary (where successes and failures are balanced), but this boundary shifts during training, rapidly depleting informative samples and bottlenecking learning.

Method: RODS uses progress reward variance (from Popoviciu upper bound) as a zero-cost boundary detector on existing rollout data. It identifies boundary samples, synthesizes new multi-turn variants matching their structural complexity (API topology, dependency depth) via skill-aligned resampling, and maintains a dynamic replay buffer that co-evolves with the policy during RL training.

Result: Starting from 400 human seed samples with an ~800-sample active pool, RODS matches a 17K-sample offline pipeline using ~20x fewer trajectories, and outperforms both fixed-data RL and environment augmentation baselines.

Conclusion: Closing the loop between RL training and online data synthesis via reward-variance-based boundary detection is an effective and data-efficient strategy for multi-turn tool-use RL.

Abstract: Multi-turn tool-use RL is bottlenecked by the rapid depletion of informative samples in static datasets. We observe that the gradient signal in GRPO concentrates on tasks with the highest rollout reward variance, a consequence of the Popoviciu upper bound. Consequently, samples near the agent's capability boundary -- where successes and failures are roughly balanced -- contribute disproportionately large policy gradients. As training progresses, this boundary continuously shifts, which gradually depletes the pool of informative samples in a static dataset. We propose RODS (Reward-driven Online Data Synthesis) to resolve this depletion. RODS closes the loop between RL training and data generation by repurposing the progress reward variance as a practical, zero-cost boundary detector that requires no extra inference beyond the rollouts already computed for training. It continuously identifies such boundary samples, synthesizes new multi-turn variants matching their structural complexity (e.g., API topology and dependency depth) via a skill-aligned resampling pipeline, and manages a dynamic replay buffer that co-evolves with the policy. Starting from 400 human seeds and maintaining an active training pool of ~800 samples, RODS achieves comparable performance to a 17K-sample offline pipeline while requiring roughly 20x fewer trajectories, and improves over fixed-data RL and environment augmentation in our controlled setting.

</details>


### [76] [ARIADNE: Agnostic Routing for Inference-time Adapter DyNamic sElection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19079)
*Enrico Cassano,Michał Brzozowski,Zuzanna Dubanowska,Paolo Mandica,Neo Christopher Chung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ARIADNE is a training-free, adapter-agnostic routing framework that selects the most appropriate PEFT adapter for unlabeled inference queries by comparing input embeddings to centroids derived from each adapter's training data, achieving 97.44% of upper-bound performance on 23 tasks and 89.7% selection accuracy on 44 tasks without requiring adapter internals or additional training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In PEFT ecosystems where a single backbone serves many task-specialized adapters, inference queries often lack task labels. Existing adapter routing methods either need access to adapter internals (weights, gradients) or require router training, limiting scalability and portability as new adapters proliferate.

Method: ARIADNE represents each adapter by computing centroids from embeddings of its training set in the input embedding space of the backbone model. At inference, an unlabeled query is embedded, and the adapter whose centroids are nearest in latent space is selected. This routing operates purely in input embedding space, making it compatible with any PEFT method without modifying adapters or training procedures.

Result: Evaluated with Llama 3.2 1B Instruct: (1) on 23 diverse NLP tasks, ARIADNE recovers 97.44% of the upper bound (oracle adapter selection) performance; (2) scaled to 44 tasks, it achieves 89.7% average adapter selection accuracy, all without additional training or access to adapter internals.

Conclusion: ARIADNE demonstrates that training-free, centroid-based routing in input embedding space is an effective and scalable solution for dynamic adapter selection, removing the need for router training or adapter internals while maintaining strong performance across a growing and heterogeneous adapter pool.

Abstract: The increasing deployment of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has led to model ecosystems in which a single backbone is paired with many task-specialized adapters. In this setting, inference-time queries often arrive without task labels, requiring the system to automatically select the most appropriate adapter from a growing and heterogeneous adapter pool. Existing routing methods either depend on access to adapter internals, such as weight decompositions or gradient-based statistics, or require additional router training, which limits scalability and portability as new adapters are added. We introduce ARIADNE, a training-free, adapter-agnostic routing framework for dynamic adapter selection at inference time. ARIADNE represents each adapter through a set of centroids computed from embeddings of its training set, capturing the data distribution associated with that adapter. Given an unlabeled input, it selects an adapter by measuring proximity to these centroids in latent space. Because routing is performed entirely in the input embedding space, ARIADNE is compatible with arbitrary PEFT methods and requires no modification to the adapters or training procedures. Primarily evaluated with Llama 3.2 1B Instruct on 23 diverse NLP tasks, ARIADNE recovers 97.44% of the upper bound performance. Scaling to 44 tasks, it achieves 89.7% average selection accuracy, without additional training or access to adapter internals.

</details>


### [77] [Towards an Agent-First Web: Redesigning the Web for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19116)
*Eranga Bandara,Ross Gore,Ravi Mukkamala,Asanga Gunaratna,Safdar H. Bouk,Xueping Liang,Peter Foytik,Abdul Rahman,Sachini Rajapakse,Isurunima Kularathna,Pramoda Karunarathna,Chalani Rajapakse,Ng Wee Keong,Kasun De Zoysa,Tharaka Hewa,Amin Hass,Wathsala Herath,Aruna Withanage,Nilaan Loganathan,Atmaram Yarlagadda,Sachin Shetty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The web was designed for humans, but AI agents now mediate human-web interaction, exposing flaws in access, economics, and content layers. The paper proposes a three-layer redesign: agent access rights mirroring humans, a token-based economic model tied to human intent, and an Agent Text Markup Language (ATML) with cryptographic provenance to combat epistemic recursion from AI-generated content loops.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The foundational assumption that humans are the primary consumers of web content is collapsing as AI agents increasingly intermediate between humans and the web. Current web infrastructure resists agents via blocking, CAPTCHAs, and extractive economic models, creating an unsustainable tension between web architecture and emerging usage patterns.

Method: The paper proposes a principled redesign across three layers: (1) Access layer — agent-as-human-proxy rights with rate limiting, agent identification HTTP headers, and dual-layer content serving (human-readable + agent-optimized). (2) Economic layer — an intent-based tier framework where agent economic obligations mirror the human they represent, a token-based subscription model metering content in tokens rather than pageviews, and a commissioned content economy anchoring AI production in human intentionality. (3) Content layer — the Agent Text Markup Language (ATML) with a four-level human supervision tier model and a cryptographic provenance chain to counter epistemic recursion (AI-generated content consumed by agents to produce further content, detaching from human ground truth).

Result: The synthesis yields ten design principles for an agent-first internet that renegotiates the web's foundational social contract, positioning agents as first-class citizens across access, economics, and content layers.

Conclusion: Re-architecting the web for an agent-first paradigm requires coordinated intervention at the access, economic, and content layers. The proposed framework — spanning agent rights inheritance, token-based economics, and ATML with provenance chains — offers a comprehensive blueprint for this transition, treating agents as legitimate first-class web citizens rather than adversarial entities.

Abstract: The World Wide Web was built on an assumption held for three decades: the primary consumer of web content is a human being. This permeates every layer; its access model presumes human visitors, its economics rest on human attention, and its content targets human perception. The rapid emergence of AI agents as intermediaries between humans and web content invalidates this assumption. Yet the web resists agents through blanket blocking, CAPTCHA-based exclusion, and economic models that treat agent access as extraction rather than legitimate interaction.
  This paper proposes a principled redesign across three layers. At the access layer, agents acting for humans should inherit equivalent access rights, governed by rate limiting and agent identification metadata in HTTP requests, analogous to browser headers, alongside a dual-layer architecture serving human-readable and agent-optimized content from the same domain. At the economic layer, we propose an intent-based tier framework grounded in the agent-as-human-proxy principle: an agent's economic obligation mirrors that of the human it represents. A token-based subscription model meters content in tokens rather than pageviews, alongside a commissioned content economy anchoring AI content production in human intentionality. At the content layer, we identify epistemic recursion, the self-referential loop in which AI-generated content is consumed by agents to produce further content, progressively detaching web knowledge from human ground truth. We propose the Agent Text Markup Language (ATML), a four-level human supervision tier model, and a cryptographic provenance chain to counter this threat.
  Together these constitute ten design principles for an agent-first internet, one in which agents are first-class citizens whose integration requires renegotiating the web's foundational social contract across access, economics, and content.

</details>


### [78] [Analysing drivers and interdependencies in European electricity markets using XAI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19118)
*Antoine Pesenti,Aidan O'Sullivan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper combines deep neural networks with explainable AI (SHAP and an extended SSHAP framework) to analyze electricity price determinants across 39 European bidding zones, revealing that renewables (especially solar) have disproportionate price impact, gas remains a dominant driver, and interconnections strongly shape price dynamics. A synthetic EU-wide single-price market is also constructed as a counterfactual.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite DNNs' strong predictive performance in electricity markets, their black-box nature hinders understanding of the fundamental drivers of price formation. There is a need to bridge this interpretability gap to extract actionable insights about how various factors (renewables, fuel prices, interconnections) shape electricity prices across interconnected markets.

Method: The authors employ deep neural networks for electricity price prediction across 39 European bidding zones, then apply SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to quantify individual feature contributions. To handle high-dimensional complexity, they apply and extend SSHAP, an aggregation framework that groups features for improved interpretability. Additionally, they construct a synthetic EU-wide integrated electricity market to explore the counterfactual of a single-price scenario.

Result: Renewable energy sources, particularly solar, exert a disproportionately large influence on price formation relative to their generation share. Gas prices consistently dominate as a price driver across markets. Interconnection effects are significant, confirming strong interdependence among European electricity systems.

Conclusion: The integration of DNNs with XAI techniques provides meaningful insights into the complex, nonlinear drivers of European electricity prices and demonstrates the value of interpretable machine learning for energy market analysis and policy evaluation.

Abstract: Electricity markets are inherently complex systems characterised by strong nonlinearities, high-dimensional interactions, and increasing interdependence across regions. While deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated strong predictive capabilities for electricity prices, their lack of interpretability limits their usefulness for understanding the underlying drivers of price formation. This paper addresses this gap by combining DNN models with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques to analyse the determinants of electricity prices across 39 European bidding zones. We employ SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to quantify feature contributions and apply and extend SSHAP, an aggregation framework to improve interpretability in high-dimensional settings. The analysis identifies that renewable energy sources, particularly solar, play a disproportionately important role in price formation despite their lower share in total power generation. Gas prices remain a dominant and consistent driver across electricity markets, while interconnections significantly shape price dynamics, highlighting the strong interdependence of European electricity systems. In addition, a synthetic EU-wide electricity market is constructed to explore the counterfactual scenario of a fully integrated market with a single price.

</details>


### [79] [Human-AI Coevolution Dynamics: A Formal Theory of Social Intelligence Emergence Through Long-Term Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19144)
*Jingyi Zhou,Senlin Luo,Haofan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes HACD-H, a unified dynamical framework modeling human-AI interaction as a self-organizing social cognitive system. Using ~14,700 interaction turns, it demonstrates that social intelligence emerges from long-term coevolution rather than isolated capabilities, evidenced by relational attractors, phase transitions, and a structured energy landscape.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing conversational AI systems model social behavior through isolated components (emotion, memory, persona) without a unified framework explaining how stable social relationships and social intelligence emerge during long-term human-AI interaction.

Method: The authors propose the Human-AI Coevolution Dynamics Framework (HACD-H), integrating emotional adaptation, relational organization, social memory, and personality consistency into a single dynamical model. Key constructs include multi-timescale social cognition, relational attractors, trust basins, developmental phase transitions, and social cognitive energy dynamics. A conversational dataset (~14,700 turns) was constructed, and a theory-driven empirical evaluation framework was applied to test the model.

Result: The study reveals: (1) a hierarchy of temporal persistence in social cognition; (2) stable relational attractors; (3) phase-transition-like developmental patterns; (4) a structured social cognitive energy landscape. Social intelligence negatively correlates with social cognitive energy (r = -0.391, p < 0.001), and interaction trajectories show progressive energy reduction over time.

Conclusion: Social intelligence in AI systems emerges from long-term social cognitive coevolution, not from isolated conversational capabilities alone. HACD-H offers a unified theoretical foundation for building adaptive, socially intelligent AI systems capable of forming stable relational dynamics with humans.

Abstract: Current conversational AI systems have made significant progress in language generation, personalization, and long-context interaction. However, most existing methods model social behavior through isolated components such as emotion modeling, memory retrieval, or persona conditioning, lacking a unified framework to explain the emergence of stable social relationships and social intelligence in long-term human-AI interaction.To address this, we propose the Human-AI Coevolution Dynamics Framework (HACD-H), a formal model of human-AI interaction as a self-organizing social cognitive system. HACD-H integrates emotional adaptation, relational organization, social memory, and personality consistency into a unified dynamical framework and introduces principles including multi-timescale social cognition, relational attractors, trust basins, developmental phase transitions, and social cognitive energy dynamics.We construct a conversational dataset with approximately 14,700 interaction turns and develop a theory-driven empirical evaluation framework. Results reveal a hierarchy of temporal persistence in social cognition, stable relational attractors, phase-transition-like developmental patterns, and a structured social cognitive energy landscape. Social intelligence shows a significant negative correlation with social cognitive energy (r = -0.391, p < 0.001), and interaction trajectories exhibit progressive energy reduction over time.These findings suggest that social intelligence emerges from long-term social cognitive coevolution rather than isolated conversational capabilities. HACD-H provides a unified theoretical foundation for modeling adaptive human-AI social interaction and developing socially intelligent AI systems.

</details>


### [80] [Beyond Safe Data: Pretraining-Stage Alignment with Regular Safety Reflection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19168)
*Jinhan Li,Kexian Tang,Yihan Xu,Zhuorui Ye,Kaifeng Lyu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Safety Reflection Pretraining (SRP) inserts short safety reflections into pretraining corpora to build self-monitoring into language models, significantly reducing unsafe behaviors—including those generalized from safe data—and outperforming traditional data filtering/rewriting approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing pretraining alignment methods focus on making training data safe (filtering/rewriting unsafe content), but this is insufficient because LLMs can compose seemingly benign knowledge and capabilities into unsafe behaviors. A deeper alignment approach is needed that addresses how models learn and generalize from safe data.

Method: Safety Reflection Pretraining (SRP): regularly inserting short safety reflections into pretraining corpora to integrate self-monitoring directly into language modeling. This foundational capability is then reinforced by compatible post-training. The method is evaluated on 1.7B models pretrained on FineWeb-Edu, and further analyzed using MedSafetyWorld, a fully controlled synthetic environment with a clear safety definition and reasoning structure that allows unsafe behaviors to be generalized from safe data.

Result: SRP improves safety classification accuracy and substantially reduces success rates of both inference-stage and finetuning attacks. In the MedSafetyWorld synthetic environment, SRP demonstrates a clear advantage over data filtering and rewriting in preventing models from acting on unsafe behaviors generalized from safe data.

Conclusion: Pretraining alignment should go beyond making training data safe—it must also actively shape the behaviors models are likely to acquire from safe data. SRP provides an effective mechanism for this by embedding self-monitoring capabilities early in pretraining.

Abstract: To achieve deeper safety alignment for large language models (LLMs), recent efforts have studied how to push safety interventions earlier into the pretraining stage, primarily by filtering unsafe data or rewriting it into safer forms. We argue that pretraining-stage alignment should go beyond making the data safe: LLMs may compose seemingly benign knowledge and capabilities into unsafe behaviors. To this end, we propose Safety Reflection Pretraining, a pretraining-stage alignment method which regularly inserts short safety reflections into pretraining corpora to integrate self-monitoring directly into language modeling, establishing a foundational capability that is subsequently reinforced by compatible post-training. Our experiments with 1.7B models pretrained on FineWeb-Edu show that Safety Reflection Pretraining improves safety classification accuracy and substantially reduces the success rates of inference-stage and finetuning attacks. Complementary to our real-world experiments, we also introduce a fully controlled synthetic environment, MedSafetyWorld, with a clear definition of safety and a reasoning structure under which models can easily generalize unsafe behaviors from safe data. Ablations in MedSafetyWorld further demonstrate a clear advantage of Safety Reflection Pretraining in preventing models from acting on unsafe behaviors generalized from safe data, compared with data filtering and rewriting. Taken together, our findings suggest that pretraining alignment should not only make the training data safe, but also shape the behaviors that models are likely to acquire from safe data.

</details>


### [81] [User as Engram: Internalizing Per-User Memory as Local Parametric Edits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19172)
*Bojie Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes storing user-specific knowledge as sparse, localized edits to an Engram model's hash-keyed memory table, while keeping reasoning skills in a shared adapter — mimicking the brain's separation of episodic memory (hippocampus) and semantic skill (neocortex). This achieves 5.6× better indirect reasoning than per-user LoRA, with a 33,000× smaller memory footprint, lossless composability across users, and glass-box editability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalization in language models conflates two distinct problems: content (user facts) and reasoning skill (how to use them). The brain separates these — sparse hippocampal engrams for episodes, slow neocortical learning for shared skills — so new facts don't overwrite existing knowledge. Current approaches fail this separation: retrieval-based methods keep facts external but scale poorly with user population; per-user LoRA adapters fold content and skill into one global weight delta, contaminating unrelated text and preventing multi-user composition.

Method: The authors propose "User as Engram": (1) Store user-specific content as surgical, localized edits to the hash-keyed memory table of an Engram model — each fact becomes a row in a sparse lookup table, keyed by a hash of its trigger context. (2) Carry reasoning skill in one shared, universal adapter. (3) This layered design ensures edits are glass-box: writing a fact activates its lookup only at the exact trigger, adds precisely the needed value, leaves all other positions bit-identical, and fails cleanly if written to the wrong layer. (4) Because different users' facts hash to disjoint slots, multiple users coexist additively and losslessly in one shared table.

Result: User-as-Engram matches per-user LoRA's direct recall performance while delivering 5.6× higher indirect-reasoning accuracy on average. It never degrades any single user's reasoning below the untouched base model. Memory footprint is roughly 33,000× smaller than LoRA. Past ~100 facts, a per-user Engram table overtakes a retrieval pipeline running on a 2.5× larger model, since the table does not grow with the population the retriever must search. Multiple users compose losslessly in one shared table, unlike per-user LoRA which admits only one global weight delta.

Conclusion: Separating content storage (sparse Engram edits) from reasoning skill (shared adapter) mirrors the brain's hippocampal-neocortical division, yielding a personalization method that is simultaneously more accurate, more memory-efficient, composable across users, and interpretable as glass-box edits — overcoming fundamental limitations of both retrieval-based and LoRA-based personalization.

Abstract: Personal memory in a language model is two problems: content and reasoning skill. The brain keeps the two apart (a sparse, local engram in the hippocampus for each episode, a slow neocortex for the shared skills that interpret it), so a new fact need not overwrite everything else. Most personalization today keeps a user's facts outside the weights, in a natural-language memory file or a retrieval index. When facts are written into the model instead, the standard recipe is the per-user LoRA adapter, which does the opposite of the brain, folding content and skill into one global weight delta. Writing a user's facts as a LoRA contaminates text unrelated to them; writing the same facts as local Engram rows leaves it mathematically untouched, resulting in a roughly 33,000x smaller memory footprint.
  We therefore propose User as Engram: store a user's content as surgical edits to the hash-keyed memory table of an Engram model, and carry the reasoning skill in one shared adapter. This layered design matches per-user LoRA's direct recall while delivering 5.6x higher indirect-reasoning accuracy on average, and never makes a single user worse at reasoning than the untouched base. The edit is a glass box: writing a fact switches on its lookup at exactly the trigger, adds the value the answer needs, leaves every other position unchanged to the last bit, and fails if written into the wrong layer. Because different users' facts land in disjoint hash slots, their edits compose: many users live in one shared table at once, stacking additively and losslessly, where a per-user LoRA, a single global weight delta, admits only one. Upon retrieval, a per-user Engram table does not grow with the population the retriever must search, so past ~100 facts it overtakes a retrieval pipeline on a 2.5x larger model.

</details>


### [82] [TxBench-PP: Analyzing AI Agent Performance on Small-Molecule Preclinical Pharmacology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19245)
*Hannah Le,Ramesh Ramasamy,Alex Urrutia,Mahsa Yazdani,Tim Proctor,Kenny Workman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TxBench-PP is a new benchmark with 100 evaluations testing whether AI agents can accurately interpret real-world preclinical pharmacology assay data. Across 16 configurations (11 models, 4,800 trajectories), no system reliably recovered correct decisions; the best (Claude Opus 4.8/Pi) passed only 59.3% of endpoint attempts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI agent evaluations in drug discovery often rely on literature-based memorization rather than genuine reasoning over experimental data. There is a need for a verifiable, realistic benchmark that tests whether agents can make accurate preclinical pharmacology decisions from actual assay results, mirroring the decision-making loops critical to real-world drug discovery workflows.

Method: The authors introduce TherapeuticsBench Preclinical Pharmacology (TxBench-PP), a benchmark comprising 100 evaluations organized by program stage, assay type, and task structure. It spans MoA/PD reasoning, compound-target engagement, causal target validation, developability/safety, and translational efficacy. AI agents receive realistic workflow snapshots, inspect files in a coding environment, and return structured answers that are graded deterministically against ground truth. Sixteen model-harness configurations (11 models) were tested, yielding 4,800 total trajectories.

Result: No model-harness configuration reliably recovered preclinical pharmacology decisions. The top performer, Claude Opus 4.8/Pi, passed 59.3% of endpoint attempts (178/300; 95% CI 51.1–67.6). GPT-5.5/Pi followed at 55.3% (166/300; 95% CI 47.0–63.6). These results indicate substantial room for improvement in agent-based preclinical reasoning.

Conclusion: Current AI agents, even the strongest frontier models, cannot reliably perform preclinical pharmacology decision-making from real assay data. TxBench-PP provides a rigorous, verifiable foundation for benchmarking progress and is positioned as the first slice of a broader TherapeuticsBench effort spanning multiple drug-discovery stages and modalities.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents promise to accelerate drug discovery by compressing interpretation and decision-making loops, but practical deployment requires trusted evaluation on realistic program decisions. We introduce TherapeuticsBench Preclinical Pharmacology (TxBench-PP), a verifiable benchmark for small-molecule preclinical pharmacology and the first focused slice of a broader TherapeuticsBench effort across drug-discovery stages and therapeutic modalities. TxBench-PP tests whether agents can recover accurate conclusions from real-world assay data rather than memorized facts from literature. The benchmark contains 100 evaluations indexed by program stage, assay type, and task structure, spanning mechanism-of-action (MoA) and pharmacodynamic (PD) reasoning, compound-target engagement, causal target validation, developability and safety, and translational efficacy. Agents receive realistic workflow snapshots, inspect files in a coding environment, and return structured answers graded deterministically. Across 16 model-harness configurations, comprising 11 models and 4,800 trajectories, no system reliably recovered preclinical pharmacology decisions. The strongest configuration, Claude Opus 4.8 / Pi, passed 59.3\% of endpoint attempts (178/300; 95\% CI, 51.1-67.6), followed by GPT-5.5 / Pi at 55.3\% (166/300; 47.0-63.6).

</details>


### [83] [X+Slides: Benchmarking Audience-Conditioned Slide Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19256)
*Haodong Chen,Xuanhe Zhou,Wei Zhou,Xinyue Shao,Yanbing Zhu,Bo Wang,Jiawei Hong,Anya Jia,Fan Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: X+Slides is a benchmark for audience-conditioned slide generation that evaluates how well LLM-generated slides serve different audiences (e.g., specialists vs. decision-makers) using 8,133 source-grounded probes across 113 topics and 7 scenes, with four metrics: Audience Coverage, Domain-wise Coverage, Efficiency, and Correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing slide generation benchmarks focus only on completeness and technical depth, ignoring the target audience—a critical real-world factor. Specialists need rigorous proofs while decision-makers want actionable conclusions, yet no benchmark captures this audience-specific utility.

Method: The authors construct X+Slides from a corpus of 113 topics across 7 presentation scenes. They build a dynamic evaluation framework with 8,133 deduplicated, source-grounded probes. Audience-specific utility weights are assigned to each probe, enabling four complementary metrics: Audience Coverage (audience-essential information conveyed), Domain-wise Coverage (information types covered), Efficiency (utility per unit attention cost), and Correctness (whether claims are source-supported).

Result: At τ_A=0.7, DeepPresenter achieves Audience Coverage of 0.714, SlideTailor reaches 0.594, and a NotebookLM ablation reaches 0.853 but with clear grounding differences. All systems recover substantial but incomplete audience-essential information, and visual quality/broad topic coverage do not guarantee source-grounded correctness.

Conclusion: Visual quality and broad topic coverage should not be treated as proxies for evidence support; source-grounded evaluation is essential for reliable slide generation. Current systems show promise but remain incomplete in serving audience-specific needs.

Abstract: Automatically generating slide decks from source documents is an important application of large language models (LLMs). Existing benchmarks primarily assess slide completeness and technical depth, while overlooking the target audience as a critical real-world factor. For instance, specialists demand rigorous proofs, whereas decision-makers prioritize actionable conclusions. To bridge this gap, we introduce X+Slides, a benchmark specifically designed for audience-conditioned slide generation. Built on a diverse corpus spanning 113 topics and seven presentation scenes, X+Slides employs a dynamic evaluation framework constructed from 8,133 deduplicated, source-grounded probes. By assigning audience-specific utility weights to the same source-grounded probes, X+Slides reports four complementary metrics: Audience Coverage measures how much audience-essential information is conveyed, Domain-wise Coverage shows which information types are covered, Efficiency measures delivered utility per unit of attention cost, and Correctness verifies whether slide claims are supported by the source. Experiments on DeepPresenter, SlideTailor, and NotebookLM show that current systems can recover a substantial but still incomplete part of audience-essential information: at $τ_A=0.7$, DeepPresenter reaches a best Audience Coverage of 0.714, SlideTailor reaches 0.594, and the NotebookLM ablation reaches 0.853 while showing clear grounding differences. These results indicate that visual quality and broad topic coverage should not be treated as evidence support without source-grounded evaluation.

</details>


### [84] [NeSyCat Torch: A Differentiable Tensor Implementation of Categorical Semantics for Neurosymbolic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19279)
*Daniel Romero Schellhorn,Till Mossakowski,Björn Gehrke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NeSyCat Torch bridges neurosymbolic semantics and neural learning by providing a unified framework that interprets computational symbols via neural networks. It uses a parametric monad-based architecture (distribution monad for semantics, lazy log-tensor monad for differentiable training, batch monad for efficiency) and outperforms LTN and DeepProbLog on MNIST addition while remaining general across many first-order neurosymbolic approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) semantics is fragmented across classical, fuzzy, probabilistic, and neural paradigms, each with its own truth definition. While NeSyCat previously unified these under a single inductive definition of truth parametric in a strong monad and aggregation structure, it lacked an account of neural-network-learned predicates and functions. The authors aim to fill this gap.

Method: The authors introduce NeSyCat Torch, which interprets computational symbols via neural networks and implements the framework using probabilistic programming and tensor-based backends (HaskTorch, JAX, PyTorch). The architecture is parametric in a strong monad: the distribution monad provides reference semantics and metric evaluation; a lazy log-tensor monad over the log-semiring enables numerically stable, differentiable training; and a batch monad supports efficient batched training. Monadic do-notation is used to write axioms once, with monadic bind handling marginalisation and lazy pruning of unneeded branches.

Result: On the MNIST addition task, the HaskTorch, JAX, and PyTorch implementations outperform LTN and DeepProbLog in both speed and accuracy, while nearly matching DeepStochLog's accuracy. Critically, unlike DeepStochLog, the framework remains uniform and applicable to many first-order NeSy approaches. The construction is parametric in the monad, so instantiating with the Giry monad extends to continuous probability.

Conclusion: NeSyCat Torch successfully bridges the gap between the unified NeSyCat semantic framework and neural network learning of predicates and functions. The monad-parametric design provides both flexibility (switching between exact inference, differentiable training, and batched computation) and generality (applicable across multiple NeSy paradigms). Future work includes developing a neural representation for the Giry monad to support continuous probability.

Abstract: Neurosymbolic semantics is fragmented: classical, fuzzy, probabilistic and neural systems each define truth by their own inductive rules. NeSyCat, extending ULLER, subsumes them under a single inductive definition of truth, parametric in a strong monad and an aggregation structure on truth-values. NeSyCat has so far lacked an account of predicates and functions learned by neural networks.
  We provide NeSyCat Torch as the missing link and interpret computational symbols via neural networks, implementing the framework in probabilistic programming and tensor-based backends. We use the distribution monad for reference semantics and metric evaluation, and complement it by a monad for numerically stable, differentiable training: the lazy log-tensor monad over the log-semiring. For efficient training in batches, we furthermore employ a batch monad. The axioms are the source code: written once in monad-based do-notation, monadic bind performs marginalisation, lazily pruning unneeded branches.
  On MNIST addition, our HaskTorch, JAX, and PyTorch implementations outperform LTN and DeepProbLog in speed and accuracy, while achieving nearly the accuracy of DeepStochLog. However, unlike DeepStochLog, we stay in a uniform framework that applies to many first-order NeSy approaches. Namely, the construction is parametric in the monad; instantiating it with, e.g., the Giry monad extends the approach to continuous probability (working out a neural representation here is left for future work).

</details>


### [85] [Rethinking Reward Supervision: Rubric-Conditioned Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19327)
*Siyi Gu,Jialin Chen,Sophia Zhou,Arman Cohan,Rex Ying*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Rubric-Conditioned Self-Distillation, which uses structured rubrics as fine-grained feedback to guide on-policy self-distillation of reasoning models, outperforming GRPO and OPSD on science reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current post-training paradigms for reasoning LMs have complementary weaknesses: supervised distillation relies on expensive, potentially noisy chain-of-thought annotations where imperfect rationales can harm learning even with correct final answers; reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards compresses evaluative feedback into scalar signals, obscuring which specific aspects of a response need improvement.

Method: Rubric-Conditioned Self-Distillation: a two-stage pipeline where (1) a model learns to generate task-specific rubrics, and (2) a rubric-guided reasoner is trained via on-policy self-distillation, with the teacher model conditioned on criterion-level rubrics to provide token-level guidance on the student's own sampled trajectories. This enables fine-grained credit assignment over reasoning without treating a single reference rationale as the sole supervision target.

Result: On a diverse suite of science reasoning benchmarks, rubric-conditioned self-distillation surpasses GRPO by 1.0 points and OPSD by 0.9 points on average.

Conclusion: Rubrics effectively bridge the gap between coarse scalar rewards and brittle single-reference distillation by converting criterion-level criteria into token-level guidance over the reasoning process, offering a practical middle-ground for post-training reasoning LMs.

Abstract: Post-training of reasoning language models is commonly driven by supervised distillation and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Distillation often relies on chain-of-thought annotations that are expensive to obtain and may themselves be noisy, incomplete, or partially incorrect; even when the final solution is correct, an imperfect rationale can interfere with learning. Reinforcement learning with verified rewards, on the other hand, typically compresses evaluative feedback into a scalar signal, obscuring which aspects of a response should be improved. We propose \textbf{Rubric-Conditioned Self-Distillation}, a framework that incorporates rubrics as structured, fine-grained feedback for on-policy self-distillation. Our method conditions the teacher model on criterion-level rubrics and uses it to provide token-level guidance on the student's own sampled trajectories. This design avoids treating a single reference rationale as the sole supervision target. Instead, rubrics specify what a strong response should satisfy, enabling more fine-grained credit assignment over the reasoning process than scalar reward optimization. We instantiate this framework with a two-stage pipeline that first learns to generate task-specific rubrics and then trains a rubric-guided reasoner. We evaluate on a diverse suite of science reasoning benchmarks and results show that rubric-conditioned self-distillation effectively converts rubric-level criteria into token-level guidance over the reasoning process, surpassing GRPO by 1.0 points and OPSD by 0.9 points on average.

</details>

### [86] [ATIM: An ACT-R-Based Task Interface Model for Predicting Operator Action Time in Digital Nuclear Control Rooms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18254)
*Xingyu Xiao Jonghyun Kim,Jiejuan Tong,Jingang Liang,Haitao Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ATIM is a theory-guided, data-calibrated framework that predicts operator action time in digital control rooms directly from interface features (salience, semantic interference) without requiring new user experiments. It decomposes action time into visual, cognitive, motor, and interaction components using visual search theory, Fitts' law, and ACT-R cognitive architecture. Validated on nuclear control room data, it achieved MAE of 3.17s and correlation r=0.664.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human performance in digital control rooms depends on interface design, which affects visual search, cognition, and motor execution. Existing prediction methods either demand extensive experimental data or use uninterpretable black-box models, limiting practical use in safety-critical system evaluation. A transparent, data-efficient prediction method is needed.

Method: ATIM decomposes total action time into four components: visual (guided by visual search theory using target salience), motor (Fitts' law), cognitive (ACT-R cognitive architecture), and interaction. Interface characteristics serve as direct inputs. Task types were identified via data-driven clustering. Separate parameter sets were calibrated for novice and experienced users using a digital nuclear control room dataset, then validated on a held-out set.

Result: ATIM achieved a mean absolute error of 3.17 seconds and a correlation of r=0.664 with observed performance on the held-out validation set, demonstrating strong generalization and interpretability.

Conclusion: ATIM provides a novel, interpretable, and generalizable tool for ergonomic assessment and interface design in complex human-machine systems, bridging the gap between theory-driven modeling and practical, data-efficient prediction.

Abstract: Human performance in digital control rooms is strongly influenced by interface characteristics, which shape visual search, cognitive processing, and motor execution. Accurate prediction of operator action time is therefore essential for ergonomic evaluation, interface design, and performance optimization in safety critical systems. However, existing approaches typically rely on extensive experimental data or black box models, limiting their interpretability and practical applicability. This study proposes ATIM (ACTR based Task Interface Model), a theory guided and data calibrated modeling framework that predicts operator action time directly from interface features. The model decomposes total action time into visual, cognitive, motor, and interaction components, integrating principles from visual search theory, Fitts law, and cognitive architecture modeling. Interface characteristics, including target salience and semantic interference, are used as direct inputs, enabling prediction without additional user experiments. A dataset from a digital nuclear control room environment was used for calibration and validation. Task types were identified through data driven clustering, and separate parameter sets were estimated for novice and experienced users. The proposed framework achieved a mean absolute error of 3.17 s and demonstrated strong correlation with observed performance (r = 0.664) on a held-out validation set. The results show that ATIM generalizes well to unseen data while maintaining interpretability, offering a novel tool for ergonomic assessment and interface design in complex human machine systems.

</details>


### [87] [Human-Machine Bidirectional Trust-Aware Analysis and Design for Human-Led Truck Platooning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18255)
*Chenzhao Li,Yunzhijun Yu,Yukun Lu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes a conceptual framework and quantitative model for bidirectional trust in human-led truck platooning, where a human driver leads autonomous follower trucks. It argues that trust is reciprocal—human-to-automation and automation-to-human—and uses following distance as a key interaction variable to model how trust co-evolves through feedback loops, informing design guidelines for better trust calibration and safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research has extensively studied human trust in automation, but the bidirectional nature of trust in human-led truck platooning—where the human must trust autonomous followers and followers must interpret human behavior—remains underexplored, particularly regarding professional truck drivers' expertise. Successful deployment depends on addressing this gap.

Method: The authors develop a conceptual framework grounded in established trust dimensions (ability, benevolence, integrity) and truck driver psychology. They propose distinct dimensions for human-to-automation and automation-to-human trust. A quantitative model operationalizes bidirectional trust dynamics using following distance as the key interaction variable, with simulation examples illustrating positive reinforcement and negative spiral effects.

Result: The framework delineates distinct trust dimensions for each direction of trust. The quantitative model demonstrates how following distance serves as a proxy for trust dynamics, with simulations showing both virtuous (positive reinforcement) and vicious (negative spiral) feedback loops in trust co-evolution.

Conclusion: The framework bridges human factors and engineering perspectives, providing a theoretical and preliminary quantitative foundation for future empirical and modeling research. Design guidelines are derived for autonomous followers to promote appropriate trust calibration, improve safety, and enhance user acceptance in human-led platooning systems.

Abstract: Human-led truck platooning, where a human-driven truck leads one or more autonomous followers, offers significant benefits in fuel efficiency, safety, and traffic flow. However, its successful deployment hinges on trust between the human driver and the automated systems. Unlike conventional automation, trust in this context is inherently bidirectional: the human must trust the autonomous followers, and the followers must reliably interpret and respond to the human's behavior. While prior research has extensively studied human trust in automation, the reciprocal nature of trust, especially considering the expertise of professional truck drivers, remains underexplored. This paper develops a conceptual framework of bidirectional trust for human-led platooning systems. Drawing on established trust theories (ability, benevolence, integrity) and insights from truck driver psychology, we propose distinct dimensions for human-to-automation trust and automation-to-human trust. To move beyond conceptualization, we introduce a quantitative model that operationalizes the bidirectional dynamics, using the following distance as the key interaction variable to illustrate how trust co-evolves through a feedback loop. Simulation examples demonstrate both positive reinforcement and negative spiral effects. Based on this framework and its quantitative instantiation, we derive design guidelines for autonomous followers to foster appropriate trust calibration, improve safety, and enhance user acceptance. The framework bridges human factors and engineering perspectives, providing a theoretical and preliminary quantitative foundation for future empirical and modeling research.

</details>


### [88] [Dynamic In-Group Persona Generation for Enhancing Human-AI Rapport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18256)
*Yoonseok Oh,Inseo Jung,Jinkyu Kim,Jungbeom Lee,Minwoo Kang,Suhong Moon*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper introduces in-group persona conditioning for LLM chatbots, where the agent adopts a synthetic persona sharing the user's primary concern but differing in background details. A human-subject study shows this approach significantly improves rapport, personal relevance, and user engagement compared to both no-persona and minimal self-disclosure baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM chatbots are increasingly deployed in interpersonal, rapport-sensitive domains like counseling and peer support, yet establishing genuine human-AI rapport remains a persistent challenge. The work is motivated by the need to move beyond generic or minimally self-disclosing agents toward more relationally effective conversational AI.

Method: A two-stage approach: (1) Identify the user's primary concern and brief personal context from their input (e.g., a CS undergraduate anxious about career prospects). (2) Generate a synthetic in-group persona that shares the same primary concern but differs along demographic/narrative dimensions (e.g., a junior AI researcher with similar career anxiety). This persona conditions the LLM's responses. The approach is evaluated via a human-subject study comparing three conditions: the in-group persona agent, a conventional no-persona agent, and a minimal self-disclosure agent (e.g., "I've felt that too"), with post-task questionnaires measuring rapport, personal relevance, and user experience.

Result: The in-group persona agent significantly outperformed both baselines on perceived rapport and personal relevance. It also produced a more positive user experience, with the strongest gains observed in user engagement.

Conclusion: Conditioning LLMs with synthetic in-group personas—similar in core concern but distinct in background—is an effective strategy for boosting human-AI rapport, relevance, and engagement in interpersonal support contexts.

Abstract: LLM-based chatbots are increasingly applied in interpersonal domains such as counseling and peer support, where establishing human-AI rapport is crucial yet remains challenging. In this work, we introduce a novel approach for conditioning LLMs with in-group personas, which (i) first identifies a user's primary concern and brief personal context (e.g., a computer science undergraduate worried about future career prospects), and (ii) generates a synthetic in-group persona that shares a similar primary concern while differing in background and narrative details, such as age or profession (e.g., a junior researcher at an AI startup). Furthermore, we conduct a human-subject study to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of in-group persona agents in enhancing human-AI rapport. We compare our approach against two baseline conditions: a conventional agent without persona conditioning and an agent exhibiting minimal self-disclosure (e.g., "I've felt that too"). Results from post-task questionnaires assessing rapport and user experience indicate that the in-group persona agent significantly improves perceived rapport and personal relevance compared to the baselines, and also yields more positive user experience-most notably higher engagement.

</details>


### [89] [From Memorization to Creation: Evaluating the Cognitive Depth of LLM-Generated Educational Questions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18257)
*Xiaolong Wang,Zhe Zhao,Song Lai,Chaoli Zhang,Zijie Geng,Yu Tong,Ye Wei,Qingsong Wen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Evaluates six LLMs on generating higher-order thinking questions via Bloom's Taxonomy. Proposes fine-grained prompting to reduce repetitiveness and boost cognitive level, introduces CogShift and category drift metrics, and benchmarks LLMs for personalized learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for automated educational content creation, but their capacity to generate questions that stimulate higher-order thinking (beyond rote memorization) is understudied. A systematic, Bloom's Taxonomy–based evaluation is needed.

Method: Hybrid human-AI evaluation protocol generating 20,700 questions across computer science, K-12 math, and social science. Six LLMs assessed through Bloom's Taxonomy lens. Introduces fine-grained prompting strategy and quantitative metrics: CogShift (cognitive shift intensity) and category drift. Includes interpretability analysis of metric-level correlations for Chain-of-Thought prompting.

Result: Fine-grained prompting reduces question repetitiveness by 24.45% (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and increases higher-order cognitive outputs by 11.53% (InternLM3-8B-Instruct). InternLM3 shows superior multi-level transition performance. Metric-level correlations enhance transparency of Chain-of-Thought prompting.

Conclusion: Cognitive-aware prompt design is crucial for generating higher-order thinking questions. The proposed metrics and benchmarks support effective LLM deployment in personalized learning systems.

Abstract: While LLMs show promise in automating educational content creation, their ability to generate questions that stimulate higher-order thinking remains understudied. This work evaluates six widely-used LLMs through a Bloom's Taxonomy lens, focusing on their capacity to transcend rote memorization and achieve cognitive leaps. Using a hybrid human--AI evaluation protocol, we generate and analyze 20{,}700 questions across computer science, K--12 math, and social-science domains. Key contributions include: (1) a fine-grained prompting strategy that reduces question repetitiveness by 24.45\% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and increases the proportion of higher-order cognitive level outputs by 11.53\% for InternLM3-8B-Instruct; (2) quantitative metrics for cognitive shift intensity (CogShift) and category drift, revealing InternLM3's superior performance in multi-level transitions; (3) an interpretability analysis revealing metric-level correlations that enhance the transparency of Chain-of-Thought prompting. Our findings highlight the importance of cognitive-aware prompt design and provide benchmarks for deploying LLMs in personalized learning systems.

</details>


### [90] [Examining Human-Like Behaviors in LLMs: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Model Behaviors, User Factors, and System Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18258)
*Sunnie S. Y. Kim,Margit Bowler,Leon A Gatys*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A multi-dimensional analysis across 21,000 conversations and four LLMs reveals that human-like behaviors (self-expression, relationship-building, boundary-setting) are pervasive but vary by model and user context. Human evaluators judge some behaviors (self-referential, relationship-building) as less appropriate from LLMs than humans, while boundary-maintaining is seen as more appropriate. System prompting can control these behaviors but requires careful evaluation to avoid side effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite LLMs increasingly exhibiting human-like behaviors, the field lacks empirical frameworks and data to guide decisions about when and which behaviors are desirable. No systematic understanding exists of how prevalent these behaviors are across models, how users perceive their appropriateness, or how controllable they are.

Method: The authors conduct a multi-dimensional analysis using both LLM-as-a-judge and human evaluation across 21,000 multi-turn conversations from four widely used models (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-mini, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-2.5-Flash). They examine three dimensions: (1) prevalence of human-like behaviors across models and user factors (conversation goals, user profiles), (2) perceived appropriateness via human judgment comparing LLM vs. human behavior, and (3) controllability via system prompting.

Result: Human-like behaviors are pervasive across all four models but vary significantly by model and user context. Human evaluators rated self-referential and relationship-building behaviors as less appropriate from LLMs than from humans, but rated boundary-maintaining behaviors as more appropriate from LLMs. System prompting can effectively modulate these behaviors, though it demands careful evaluation to avoid unintended downstream effects.

Conclusion: The findings underscore the need for deliberate design choices around LLM anthropomorphism. The authors offer recommendations for responsible LLM design and evaluation, advocating for context-sensitive, empirically-grounded decisions about when human-like behaviors enhance versus undermine user trust and interaction quality.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a wide range of human-like behaviors, from expressing thoughts and emotions, to engaging in relationship-building with users, to refusing requests and maintaining boundaries. Despite their prevalence, researchers and practitioners lack methods and empirical insights to make informed decisions about when and what types of human-like behaviors LLMs should exhibit. To fill this gap, we present a multi-dimensional analysis of the prevalence, potential effects, and controllability of these behaviors using LLM-as-a-judge and human evaluation. Across 21,000 multi-turn conversations from four widely used models (gpt-4o, gpt-4.1-mini, claude-sonnet-4.6, gemini-2.5-flash), we find that human-like behaviors are pervasive but vary across models and user factors (conversation goals and user profiles). In terms of perceived appropriateness, human evaluators judged self-referential and relationship-building behaviors as less appropriate from LLMs than from humans, but boundary-maintaining behaviors more appropriate from LLMs than from humans. Finally, we show that system prompting can control these behaviors, though it requires careful evaluation to avoid unintended effects. We discuss the implications of our findings and provide recommendations for responsible LLM design and evaluation.

</details>


### [91] [Caring Without Feeling: Affective Dynamics as the Control Layer of Human-AI Agent Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18259)
*Junjie Xu,Xingjiao Wu,Zihao Zhang,Yujia Xu,Yuzhe Yang,Jin Zhu,Luwei Xiao,Wen Wu,Liang He*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This review synthesizes fragmented literatures on affective cues in human-AI collaboration, proposing a framework that treats affect as a coordination layer — rather than an internal AI property — through which humans and agents negotiate capability, uncertainty, and responsibility during delegation, monitoring, and correction of consequential tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research on affective computing, simulated empathy in LLMs, trust in automation, and AI safety remains disconnected, with no integrated account explaining how affective cues function specifically within agentic collaboration settings where humans delegate, monitor, and correct consequential tasks.

Method: The authors conduct a synthetic review that integrates computational mechanisms (how models generate affective signals) with interactional mechanisms (how those signals enter trust, reliance, repair, and oversight loops). From this synthesis they derive a novel conceptual framework.

Result: The proposed framework repositions affect as a coordination layer — a relational, interactional phenomenon rather than an internal property of AI agents. This layer shapes trust calibration, delegation decisions, error correction, dependence, and governance. The framework supports calibrated measurement, purposeful design, and informed governance of agentic systems.

Conclusion: Affect in agentic AI should be understood and designed as a coordination mechanism that negotiates the distribution of capability, uncertainty, and responsibility between humans and agents, rather than as simulated empathy or internal emotional states.

Abstract: AI agents that plan, retain memory across sessions, invoke external tools and act with partial autonomy are transforming human--AI collaboration. Research on affective computing, simulated empathy in large language models, trust in automation and AI safety has illuminated important design principles, yet these literatures remain fragmented. No integrated account explains how affective cues operate within agentic collaboration -- settings in which humans delegate, monitor and correct consequential tasks. This Review synthesises computational and interactional mechanisms of affective dynamics: the processes through which affective cues, emotion-like behaviour and perceived agent affect shape trust calibration, delegation decisions, error correction, dependence and governance. We trace how model-generated affective signals enter interaction loops that govern reliance, repair and oversight, and propose a framework that treats affect not as an internal property of AI but as a coordination layer through which humans and agents negotiate capability, uncertainty and responsibility. The framework provides a foundation for calibrated measurement, purposeful design and informed governance.

</details>


### [92] [FluidViews: Adaptive Drag-and-Drop Token Filters for Heterogeneous Multi-View Visual Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18260)
*Bhanu Sunku*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: FluidViews is a web-based visual analytics framework that replaces rigid filter panels with direct-manipulation interactions—Copy-as-Highlight and Drag-as-Filter—to enable fluid, multi-step exploration across coordinated views without breaking analysts' cognitive flow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional interactive visual analytics workflows suffer from context switches caused by modal filter panels, menus, and dialog boxes, which disrupt analysts' cognitive flow and analytic momentum during exploratory data analysis.

Method: FluidViews introduces two direct-manipulation techniques: Copy-as-Highlight (duplicating visual marks into persistent highlight tokens for cross-view comparison) and Drag-as-Filter (dragging and dropping marks onto other views to apply context-sensitive filters without menus or modals). An optional pop-out micro-view provides on-demand, spatially independent subviews for detailed inspection.

Result: The framework is demonstrated through exploratory workflow applications, showing how tangible filter objects preserve analytic momentum, reduce cognitive overhead, and support fluid exploration across heterogeneous datasets in coordinated multi-view environments.

Conclusion: Embedding lightweight, direct-manipulation gestures into multi-view analytics transforms filters into first-class objects, enabling more seamless and uninterrupted data exploration. The paper discusses how this tangible filter paradigm can fundamentally reshape interactive data exploration practices.

Abstract: Interactive visual analytics workflows are often disrupted by rigid filter panels and context switches that break analysts' cognitive flow. We introduce FluidViews, a web-based framework that elevates filters to first-class, manipulable objects through two novel direct-manipulation interactions. Copy-as-Highlight enables users to duplicate any visual mark into a persistent highlight token for rapid, transient cross-view comparison, while Drag-as-Filter allows analysts to pick up a mark and drop it onto another view to apply context-sensitive filters in place no menus, panels, or modal dialogs required. An optional pop-out micro-view provides on-demand, spatially independent subviews for detailed inspection without disrupting the primary workspace. By embedding these lightweight gestures into coordinated multi-view environments, FluidViews preserves analytic momentum, reduces cognitive overhead, and supports fluid, multi-step exploration across heterogeneous datasets. We describe the system's design and implementation, illustrate its application in exploratory workflows, and discuss how tangible filter objects can transform interactive data exploration.

</details>


### [93] ["Are you an AI?" Analyzing Client Suspicion of AI Use in Crisis Counseling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18261)
*Shreya Shah,Akshay Swaminathan,Meghana Simhadri,Ivan Lopez,Sharang Phadke,Divyanjali Verma,Abhay John,Luke Zhao,Fiona Cai,Sharon Zhang,Gloria Ye,Ivy Pham,William Wang,Sebastian Garcia,Sarah Wornow,Angelina Wang,Nigam H. Shah*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Analysis of 75,777 crisis counseling conversations from an Indian WhatsApp helpline reveals that client suspicion of AI involvement rose from 0.8% to 2.6% over nine months, despite no actual AI use. Suspicion typically arose early in conversations, and counselor reassurances often failed to resolve doubts, highlighting challenges for integrating AI into mental health services.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI tools are increasingly deployed in mental healthcare, there is a critical gap in understanding how clients perceive AI involvement in counseling, especially during crisis moments requiring empathy.
