Public trust remains uncertain, and no prior work has systematically characterized how often clients suspect AI, what triggers those suspicions, and how counselors respond.

Method: The authors analyzed a corpus of 75,777 crisis counseling conversations from a human-staffed WhatsApp helpline in India. They characterized the frequency of client AI suspicion over time (June 2024–March 2025), identified when suspicion arose within conversation timelines, examined triggers of doubt, and evaluated the effectiveness of counselor responses, including explicit reassurances.

Result: Key findings: (1) AI suspicion increased from 0.8% to 2.6% of conversations over nine months, despite no actual AI involvement. (2) In suspicious conversations, 21.5% of clients explicitly stated a preference for human counselors. (3) Suspicion arose in the first half of messages 68.3% of the time. (4) When counselors offered direct reassurance, clients continued pressing or ended the conversation 17.6% of the time.

Conclusion: The rising prevalence of AI suspicion — even in purely human-delivered counseling — signals growing public awareness and wariness of AI in mental health contexts. The findings underscore the need for careful design of AI-augmented counseling workflows to preserve therapeutic trust, particularly since counselor reassurances are often insufficient to resolve client doubt.

Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools get increasingly deployed for mental healthcare, public trust in these systems remains uncertain. It is unclear how clients perceive AI involvement in counseling interactions, particularly in moments of crisis that require empathy and connection. To address this gap, we analyzed 75,777 crisis counseling conversations from a human-staffed WhatsApp helpline in India to characterize how often clients suspected they were speaking to AI, what triggered those doubts, and how counselors responded. Though no conversations actually involved AI assistance, the proportion of conversations where clients suspected AI use increased from 0.8% in June 2024 to 2.6% in March 2025. Within suspicious conversations, 21.5% of clients stated an explicit preference for humans. Client suspicion primarily arose in the first half of messages (68.3%), and when counselors offered reassurance (e.g. 'I assure you; this is not ai!'), clients continued to press or ended the conversation 17.6% of the time. As AI tools get increasingly integrated into counselor workflows, understanding these dynamics is essential for designing AI systems that preserve the therapeutic relationship between counselors and clients.

</details>


### [94] [When Prompts Mislead: Textual Dominance and Diagnostic Bias in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18262)
*Inhyuk Park,Doohyun Park*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper systematically analyzes failure modes of prompting strategies in a medical multimodal large language model (FundusExpert-1B) on a fundus image discrimination task. The study reveals that one-shot textual prompts bias predictions, and when textual claims conflict with visual cues, the model defers to text, causing accuracy to degrade significantly — a problem exacerbated rather than corrected by Chain-of-Thought reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical MLLMs are increasingly used under computational constraints where prompting is the only practical alternative to fine-tuning. Despite widespread assumption that prompting supports diagnostic reasoning, its failure modes in medical contexts remain poorly characterized. This work aims to systematically expose vulnerabilities of prompting in medical MLLMs.

Method: The authors use FundusExpert-1B, an open-source ophthalmology MLLM, evaluated on a hemorrhage vs. drusen discrimination task from the public BRSET dataset. Three experiments are conducted: (1) a controlled probe with artificially injected markers to test spatial grounding; (2) comparison of zero-shot vs. one-shot textual prompts to measure bias; and (3) a conflict condition where overlaid lesion contours are paired with inconsistent textual claims, with and without Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, to assess visual-textual cue dominance.

Result: (i) The model retains coarse, region-level spatial grounding. (ii) One-shot prompts bias predictions toward the prompted finding. (iii) Conflicting textual prompts override correct visual cues, dropping accuracy from 75% to 46%; CoT reasoning worsens rather than corrects this degradation.

Conclusion: Prompting strategies alone may be insufficient for safe clinical deployment of medical MLLMs, as textual prompts can override visual evidence and reasoning chains fail to self-correct — though findings are limited to a single model and dataset.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for medical applications, where computational constraints often make prompting strategies the only practical alternative to fine-tuning. Such strategies are generally assumed to support diagnostic reasoning, yet their potential failure modes in medical MLLMs remain poorly characterized. We analyze FundusExpert-1B, an open-source ophthalmology MLLM, on a hemorrhage versus drusen discrimination task using the public BRSET dataset, adopted here as a controlled testbed for our analysis. (i) A controlled probe with artificially injected markers confirms that the model retains coarse, region-level spatial grounding. (ii) Compared with zero-shot inference, one-shot textual prompts bias predictions toward the prompted finding. (iii) When an overlaid lesion contour is paired with an inconsistent textual claim, the textual prompt overrides the correct visual cue: overall accuracy drops from 75% to 46% relative to the visual-only condition, and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is associated with further degradation rather than self-correction. Although limited to a single model and dataset, our findings suggest that prompting strategies alone may be insufficient for the safe clinical deployment of medical MLLMs.

</details>


### [95] [How Well Do Large Language Models Capture Human Personality?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18263)
*Aanisha Bhattacharyya,Yaman Kumar Singla,Rajiv Ratn Shah,Changyou Chen,Jitendra Ajmera*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Richer persona descriptions in LLMs paradoxically reduce behavioral diversity and simulation fidelity due to "persona manifold collapse," where increased expressivity contracts representational space. Simple Age-Gender personas consistently outperform complex profiles, and certain attribute combinations form "alignment bridges" that preserve human alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are widely used for human population simulation via persona prompting under untested assumptions: (1) richer personas improve fidelity, (2) same-sized attribute sets are equally simulatable, and (3) persona definitions transfer across tasks. The authors aim to systematically test these assumptions.

Method: Systematic evaluation across multiple LLM architectures, scales, and simulation settings. The authors analyze latent-space inter-persona separation, behavioral differentiation in downstream tasks, subgroup disagreement preservation, and prediction accuracy comparisons between simple (Age-Gender) and complex (Ideal Customer Profile) personas across industries.

Result: Increasing persona complexity reduces inter-persona separation and behavioral differentiation — the "persona manifold collapse" phenomenon. Simple Age-Gender personas consistently outperform richly specified ICPs in downstream prediction. Collapse is non-uniform: certain attribute combinations remain stable and preserve human alignment ("alignment bridges").

Conclusion: More expressive persona descriptions do not guarantee better simulation fidelity. Representation-aware persona construction is needed rather than merely increasing persona expressivity. The findings establish empirical foundations for understanding the limits of persona-conditioned LLM simulation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human populations via persona prompting, often under the assumptions that richer persona descriptions improve behavioral fidelity, similarly sized attribute combinations are equally simulatable, and persona definitions generalize across tasks. In this work, we formalize these assumptions and systematically evaluate them across multiple architectures, scales, and simulation settings. We identify a fundamental limitation we term persona manifold collapse, where increasingly expressive persona specifications lead to systematic contraction of representational and behavioral diversity. Across models, increasing persona complexity consistently reduces inter-persona separation in latent space and weakens behavioral differentiation in downstream simulation tasks. These effects persist across multiple analyses as richer personas fail to preserve human subgroup disagreement, performance varies across attribute combinations of similar size, and adding descriptive detail often degrades rather than improves simulation fidelity. Surprisingly, simple Age-Gender personas consistently outperform richly specified Ideal Customer Profiles (ICPs) across industries, achieving substantially higher downstream prediction accuracy. We find that collapse is not uniform across attributes. Certain combinations remain behaviorally stable and preserve stronger alignment with human responses, forming localized regions we term alignment bridges. Together, our results provide empirical and conceptual foundations for understanding the limits of persona-conditioned simulation, highlighting the need for representation-aware persona construction rather than increasing persona expressivity alone.

</details>


### [96] [Synthetic Resonance: A Framework for Growth-Oriented Human-AI Relationships](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18265)
*Richard A. Fabes*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Introduces "synthetic resonance" as a framework for understanding meaningful human-AI relationships without requiring anthropomorphism or mutual subjective experience, emphasizing structured dynamic interaction patterns instead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language and frameworks for human-AI relationships either anthropomorphize AI (e.g., using terms like "friendship" or "mutual understanding") or reductively frame AI as merely a tool or a threat. Neither approach accurately captures the nature of sustained human-AI affiliations.

Method: Conceptual/philosophical analysis introducing a novel theoretical construct ("synthetic resonance") defined as a structured, dynamic pattern of interaction that yields a sense of relationship without requiring a second experiencing subject.

Result: The synthetic resonance framework provides a more precise conceptualization of human-AI relationships, distinguishing the felt sense of relationship from the attribution of shared feelings or mutual awareness, and highlights potential value and ethical implications.

Conclusion: Synthetic resonance offers a theoretically integrative and ethically informative lens for human-AI relationships. The author calls for empirical research to test the processes and outcomes of synthetic resonance.

Abstract: As human relationships with artificial intelligence systems become increasingly frequent and sustained, existing language and theory fail to accurately capture the nature of these affiliations. Common descriptors such as mutual understanding, connection, or friendship risk anthropomorphizing systems that lack subjective experience, while dominant frameworks tend to reduce AI to either a tool or a threat. In this paper, I introduce the concept of synthetic resonance as an integrative framework for understanding human-AI relationships. Synthetic resonance describes how relationships humans define as meaningful can emerge between a human and an AI system without the need to attribute shared feelings or mutual awareness. I argue that synthetic resonance is best understood as a structured, dynamic pattern of interaction that can produce a sense of relationship without the presence of a second experiencing subject. By clarifying this distinction, the concept of synthetic resonance offers a more precise way of conceptualizing human-AI relationships and highlights their potential value and ethical implications. I also call for more research that tests the processes and outcomes of synthetic resonance.

</details>


### [97] [EMORSION: Examining the Impact of Audio Parameters on Emotional Responses and Immersion in Film](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18266)
*Nelly Garcia,Ruby Crocker,Bleiz M Del Sette,Fabrizio Smeraldi,Charalampos Saitis,George Fazekas,Joshua Reiss*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: EMORSION is a proof-of-concept study demonstrating that systematic manipulation of film audio parameters (frequency, dynamics, directionality) measurably shapes audience emotion and immersion, with conventional immersive mixes yielding stronger consensus and unconventional mixes producing greater interpretive variability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish an experimental protocol for investigating how specific, systematically manipulated parameters of film audio design — frequency, dynamics, and directionality — influence audience emotional perception and immersion in a cinema context.

Method: Four film scenes (2 horror, 2 drama; balanced mainstream/independent) were prepared with multiple alternative audio mixes per scene, manipulating frequency (pitch), dynamics (loudness), and directionality (spatial placement). Three audience groups viewed scenes with one manipulated mix plus a control per scene. Responses were captured via a triangulated multimodal framework: self-report questionnaires (emotion/immersion), heart rate monitoring, and video-based motion tracking.

Result: The protocol successfully captured measurable, interpretable differences across audio conditions. Conventional immersive mixes produced stronger cross-audience agreement, while unconventional mixes led to greater interpretive variability.

Conclusion: The EMORSION protocol is feasible and effective; findings motivate larger-scale studies to further characterise how specific audio parameters shape audience experience.

Abstract: EMORSION is an exploratory proof-of-concept study examining how film audio design shapes audience emotion and immersion in acinema setting. Four film scenes were selected across the horror (2) and drama (2) genres, balanced between mainstream and independent productions. For each scene, multiple alternative audio mixes were created by systematically manipulating three core aspects of audio design, frequency (pitch), dynamics (loudness), and directionality (spatial placement). Three audience groups viewed the scenes, with each group exposed to one manipulated mix alongside a control mix for each scene. Audience responses were assessed through a triangulated multimodal framework combining self-reported emotion and immersion via a questionnaire, physiological measures including heart rate monitoring, and video-based motion tracking. The protocol successfully captured measurable, interpretable differences across audio conditions, indicating that even subtle changes in audio design can shape emotional perception and immersion. Unconventional mixes tended to produce greater variability in audience interpretation, while conventional immersive mixes were associated with stronger cross-audience agreement. These findings establish the feasibility of the EMORSION protocol and motivate larger-scale studies to characterise the role of specific audio parameters in shaping audience experience.

</details>


### [98] [Beyond the Algorithm: Professional Experiences and Perceptions of AI Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18289)
*Micarah Malone-Gawu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A qualitative multi-case study of nine AI practitioners reveals that algorithmic bias stems from historical inequities, exclusionary design, and organizational pressures favoring speed over ethics. Technical fixes alone are insufficient; fairness requires structural accountability, diverse participation, embedded ethics, and strengthened governance throughout the development lifecycle.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To examine how social bias emerges, is perceived, and can be mitigated within AI/ML systems from the perspective of practitioners directly involved in design, development, and governance — filling a gap in understanding the lived experiences and professional insights of those building these systems.

Method: Interpretivist qualitative multi-case study using semi-structured interviews with nine AI practitioners, supplemented by document analysis and triangulated case material from healthcare, criminal justice, employment, and education domains. Analysis grounded in Intersectionality Theory and Cognitive Science frameworks.

Result: Algorithmic bias was found to originate from three key sources: historical inequities embedded in data and processes, exclusionary design assumptions, and organizational pressures prioritizing speed/efficiency over ethical reflection. Participants reported limited enforcement of ethical standards and inconsistent organizational support for responsible practice. Technical corrections alone were deemed insufficient for achieving fairness.

Conclusion: Equitable, human-centered AI requires embedding ethics early in design, strengthening governance frameworks, and fostering institutional cultures of reflective decision-making. The study offers practical guidance for organizations pursuing transparent, accountable systems aligned with affected communities.

Abstract: The purpose of this qualitative multi-case study was to examine how social bias emerges, is perceived, and can be mitigated within artificial intelligence and machine learning systems by practitioners directly involved in their design, development, and governance. Although examples from healthcare, criminal justice, employment, and education were used to illustrate domains where automated systems shape everyday life, the study focused on the lived experiences and professional insights of AI practitioners rather than sector-specific populations. Guided by Intersectionality Theory and Cognitive Science, the study employed an interpretivist approach, utilizing semi-structured interviews with nine practitioners, supplemented by document analysis and triangulated case material to enrich contextual understanding. Findings showed that algorithmic bias arises from historical inequities, exclusionary design assumptions, and organizational pressures that prioritize speed and efficiency over ethical reflection. Participants emphasized that technical corrections alone cannot ensure fairness; instead, equitable AI requires structural accountability, diverse participation, and sustained cognitive awareness during the development lifecycle. Many described limited enforcement of ethical standards and organizational cultures that inconsistently support responsible practice. The study concludes that human-centered and socially grounded AI development depends on embedding ethics early in the design process, strengthening governance frameworks, and cultivating institutional environments that encourage reflective decision-making. These insights contribute to ongoing conversations on responsible AI and offer practical guidance for organizations seeking to design systems that are transparent, accountable, and aligned with the communities they affect.

</details>


### [99] [Stitching the Divide: Investigating Mixed Reality as a Bridge Between Paper-Based and Digital Artifacts in UI/UX Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18511)
*Abidullah Khan,Jinghui Cheng*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: UI/UX designers lack tools that bridge paper and digital workflows. Through interviews (N=19) and MR-probe user studies (9 sessions), researchers identified that MR enables hybrid workflows, spatial workspaces, and cross-medium collaboration. Designers envisioned AI-assisted future MR tools, leading to four design dimensions for next-generation MR design systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: UI/UX designers currently rely on both paper-based and digital artifacts in their workflows, yet no existing tools seamlessly integrate these two modalities. Mixed Reality (MR) presents an underexplored opportunity to bridge this gap by combining the tactile affordances of paper with the flexibility of digital environments.

Method: A two-phase qualitative study: (1) semi-structured interviews with 19 professional UI/UX designers to understand current paper-digital workflow practices and pain points; (2) nine conceptual-probe user study sessions where designers interacted with an MR prototype integrating paper and digital prototyping, followed by brainstorming sessions to elicit visions for future MR design tools.

Result: Participants valued MR for four key affordances: (a) enabling continuous hybrid design workflows without disruptive modality switches; (b) reducing manual reconstruction effort when translating between paper and digital; (c) supporting spatially anchored workspaces for persistent design contexts; and (d) facilitating real-time cross-medium collaboration. Designers also envisioned future MR tools featuring AI assistance, richer interactive/dynamic content, and unified management of diverse design artifacts.

Conclusion: The authors derive four design dimensions to guide the development of future MR systems for UI/UX design, aiming to support more fluid, creative, and collaborative design practices. These dimensions synthesize empirical findings into actionable guidance for HCI researchers and tool builders.

Abstract: UI/UX designers work with both paper-based and digital artifacts but lack tools that seamlessly integrate the two. Mixed Reality (MR) offers under-explored opportunities to combine the strengths of both design environments. To examine these opportunities, we first conducted interviews with 19 professional UI/UX designers to understand their current experiences using paper and digital artifacts. Motivated and informed by the interview insights, we organized nine conceptual-probe user study sessions in which designers engaged with a MR-probe that combined paper and digital prototyping processes and brainstormed MR's potential in UI/UX design. We found that participants valued MR for enabling continuous hybrid design workflows, reducing manual reconstruction, supporting spatially anchored workspaces, and facilitating real-time cross-medium collaboration. They also envisioned future MR tools with AI assistance, richer interactive and dynamic content, and the ability to manage diverse design artifacts within a unified environment. From these findings, we derive four design dimensions for future MR systems that could enable more fluid, creative, and collaborative design practices.

</details>


### [100] ["The New Era of Tech-Enabled Traceability": Tensions between the FDA's Data Governance Vision and the Lived Realities of Food Producers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18593)
*Soonho Kwon,Catherine Wieczorek,Heidi Biggs,Shellye Suttles,Tammi S. Etheridge,Annabel Rothschild,Shaowen Bardzell*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The FDA's Food Traceability Rule (effective 2026) mandates detailed record-keeping across the agri-food supply chain, envisioning tech-enabled traceability as public health infrastructure. This paper critiques how the Rule transforms stakeholders into "data laborers," disproportionately burdening smaller, under-resourced actors. Analyzing 1,198 public comments through a Data Feminism lens, the authors identify three tensions: (1) individual labor/financial/educational burdens of becoming data workers; (2) infeasibility of data tracking due to infrastructural, cultural, and production contexts; and (3) how the Rule's intended flexibility creates confusion and burden through ambiguity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The FDA promotes the Food Traceability Rule as a public health advancement through standardized data infrastructure. However, the authors observe a critical gap: the Rule's data mandates reconfigure diverse agri-food stakeholders (farmers, fishers, retail workers) into data laborers without adequate consideration of the unequal capacities to comply, potentially exacerbating inequities for smaller, under-resourced actors.

Method: The study employs Data Feminism as its analytical orientation, specifically focusing on how data-driven policy disproportionately burdens marginalized groups. The authors conduct a qualitative document analysis of 1,198 public comments submitted to Regulations.gov in response to the proposed FDA Food Traceability Rule.

Result: The analysis reveals three key tensions: (1) stakeholders face individual labor, financial, and educational burdens upon being reconfigured into data workers; (2) data tracking requirements become infeasible in contexts with infrastructural limitations, specific cultural practices, and situated production methods; and (3) the Rule's intended flexibility paradoxically introduces confusion and additional burden due to ambiguous language.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the FDA's tech-enabled traceability vision, while promising for public health, imposes disproportionate compliance burdens on smaller, under-resourced stakeholders. The reconfiguration into data laborers creates tensions that undermine the Rule's equity and feasibility, highlighting the need for data-driven policies to account for diverse stakeholder capacities and situated realities.

Abstract: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)'s Food Traceability Rule requires agri-food supply chain stakeholders (stakeholders)--including farmers, fishers, retail workers, and others--to maintain detailed tracking records beginning in January 2026. Through this Rule, the FDA envisions a "New Era of Tech-Enabled Traceability," in which standardized, harmonized tracking data serve as a foundational public health infrastructure, enabling more rapid identification and removal of potentially contaminated food and ultimately reducing the risk of foodborne illness.
  Despite this promising vision, we observe that the Rule reconfigures agri-food stakeholders into data laborers by mandating stringent data collection, formatting, and reporting requirements. In this paper, we examine the tensions and burdens that arise from such reconfiguration. Leveraging Data Feminism as an orientation to attend to how data-driven policy implementation disproportionately burdens smaller, under-resourced stakeholders who lack the infrastructural and financial capacity to comply, we analyze 1,198 public comments submitted to Regulations.gov in response to the proposed Rule. Our qualitative document analysis reveals three key tensions: (1) the individual labor, financial, and educational burdens stakeholders experience as they are reconfigured into data workers; (2) moments where data tracking becomes infeasible due to infrastructural limitations, cultural contexts, and situated production practices; and (3) instances where the Rule's intended flexibility instead introduces confusion and burden due to its ambiguity.

</details>


### [101] [Better Adherence, Richer Context: A Field Evaluation of LLM-Powered Conversational Voice Diaries for Sleep](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18596)
*Amama Mahmood,Bokyung Kim,Honghao Zhao,Molly E. Atwood,Luis F. Buenaver,Michael T. Smith,Chien-Ming Huang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A 4-week field study (N=30) comparing an LLM-powered conversational voice diary (smart-speaker) against a text-based mobile diary for sleep tracking found higher adherence and richer contextual self-report with voice, but lower completeness on structured fields, highlighting a trade-off between expressive richness and structured precision in longitudinal health self-report.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sleep diaries are essential for behavioral sleep medicine and CBT-I, but daily completion is hard to sustain, and static forms lack context for interpreting night-to-night sleep variability. The authors aim to explore whether LLM-powered conversational voice interfaces can improve adherence and contextual richness over traditional text-based mobile diaries.

Method: The authors designed an LLM-powered conversational voice diary deployed via proactive smart-speaker prompts, delivering clinically grounded morning and evening sleep diary questions with adaptive follow-up dialogue. A four-week between-subjects field study was conducted with 30 university students, comparing the voice diary against a text-based mobile diary matched on diary items, reporting windows, and reminder intervals.

Result: The conversational voice diary yielded: (1) higher adherence rates; (2) more detailed contextual self-report about routines, stressors, environmental conditions, and sleep-related factors; (3) greater perceived ease of integration into daily routines despite longer perceived completion time. However, it also produced lower completeness for certain structured diary fields, revealing a trade-off between expressive richness and structured precision.

Conclusion: LLM-powered conversational voice assistants show promise for improving engagement and contextual depth in longitudinal health self-report, but the trade-off between narrative richness and structured data completeness must be addressed for clinical applicability where standardized sleep metrics are required.

Abstract: Sleep diaries are central to behavioral sleep medicine and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, yet daily completion is difficult to sustain, and static forms often provide limited context for interpreting night-to-night sleep variation. We designed an LLM-powered conversational voice diary that delivers clinically grounded morning and evening sleep diary questions through proactive smart-speaker prompts, structured conversational intake, and adaptive follow-up dialogue. We evaluated the system in a four-week between-subjects field study with 30 university students, comparing it with a text-based mobile diary using matched diary items, reporting windows, and reminder intervals. Compared with the text-based diary, the conversational voice diary showed higher adherence and elicited more detailed contextual self-report about routines, stressors, environmental conditions, and other sleep-related factors. Participants also described the voice diary as easier to integrate into daily routines, despite longer perceived completion time. However, voice-based conversational intake produced lower completeness for some structured diary fields, revealing a trade-off between expressive richness and structured precision. These findings show both the promise and the challenge of using LLM-powered conversational voice assistants for longitudinal health self-report.

</details>


### [102] [HANSEL: Extracting Breadcrumbs from Web Agent Trajectories for Interactive Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18671)
*Yujin Zhang,Daye Nam*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: HANSEL is a system that extracts interactive, verifiable evidence from web-agent trajectories, presenting key pages and snippets as navigable views with preserved page state. It flags gaps when agent answers lack evidential support, achieves high precision/recall in evidence identification, and significantly improves user verification efficiency over passive transparency mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verifying the correctness of AI web agent outputs is difficult. Existing transparency mechanisms (full trajectory logs, screenshots, LLM summaries) treat verification as a passive reading task, overwhelming users with data or exposing them to unfaithful explanations. There is a need for an interactive verification approach that lets users efficiently trace how an agent arrived at its answer.

Method: HANSEL takes an agent's trajectory and automatically extracts evidence pages and content snippets, presenting them as interactive, navigable views. Critically, it preserves relevant page state (filters, search queries, scroll positions) so users can inspect the exact context the agent saw. When no visited page supports the agent's answer, HANSEL explicitly flags this evidential gap. The system was evaluated technically on 45 tasks from AssistantBench and Online-Mind2Web, and through a controlled user study with 14 participants comparing HANSEL against a standard agent interface.

Result: Technical evaluation: 83.7% precision and 88.8% recall in identifying evidence pages, with a 61.6% reduction in trajectory volume. User study: HANSEL significantly reduced task completion time and perceived effort, with significantly higher ratings on usability, verification ease, and error identification compared to the baseline interface.

Conclusion: Reframing verification as an interactive activity rather than passive consumption of agent explanations leads to more efficient human oversight of AI agents. HANSEL demonstrates that interactive, evidence-based verification improves both objective performance and subjective user experience in human-AI agent collaboration.

Abstract: AI web agents can perform complex, multi-step tasks such as searching for products, comparing options, and making purchases on behalf of users. However, verifying the correctness of an agent's output remains difficult. Existing transparency mechanisms, including full trajectory logs, source links, screenshots, and LLM-generated summaries, treat verification as a passive reading task, leaving users to sift through overwhelming logs or trust potentially unfaithful explanations. We present HANSEL (Highlighting Agent Navigation Steps as Evidence Links), a system that extracts interactive, verifiable evidence from web-agent trajectories. Given an agent trajectory, HANSEL extracts evidence pages and snippets and presents them as navigable, interactive views with relevant page state preserved (e.g., applied filters, search queries, and scroll positions), enabling users to verify how the agent arrived at its answer. When the agent's answer cannot be traced to any visited page, HANSEL explicitly flags this gap. A technical evaluation on 45 tasks from AssistantBench and Online-Mind2Web shows that HANSEL achieves 83.7% precision and 88.8% recall in identifying evidence pages, while reducing trajectory volume by 61.6%. In a controlled user study with 14 participants, HANSEL significantly reduced task completion time and perceived effort compared to a standard agent interface, while participants rated it significantly higher on usability, verification ease, and error identification. Our results demonstrate that reframing verification as an interactive activity, rather than passive consumption of agent explanations, leads to more efficient human oversight of AI agents.

</details>


### [103] [Human-AI Agent Interaction in a Business Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18716)
*Kathrin Paimann,Elizangela Valarini,Sebastian Juhl*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates principles, criteria, and measurement methods for positive UX in human-AI agent interactions within business contexts, using a mixed-methods exploratory approach to identify user expectations that foster adoption, trust, and user-centered design decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents become embedded in core business processes, there is a pressing need to understand what constitutes effective and positive interaction patterns between humans and AI agents to enable value creation, adoption, and trust.

Method: A mixed-methods approach combining qualitative and quantitative techniques: initial exploratory research identifies user expectations, needs, and interaction patterns, which then informs the design of a larger-scale survey experiment to evaluate specific design elements' effectiveness.

Result: The exploratory phase produced foundational findings on interaction patterns, user expectations, and UX principles/criteria, which serve as the basis for a subsequent survey experiment (results of the experiment not reported in this abstract).

Conclusion: The foundational research contributes to developing more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings, establishing groundwork for evidence-based UX design guidelines.

Abstract: As AI agents are increasingly integrated into core business processes, understanding and designing effective interaction patterns between humans and AI agents becomes crucial for value creation. This study identifies and evaluates principles and criteria for a positive User Experience (UX) with AI agents, along with methods for its measurement. We identify user expectations and needs to facilitate adoption, build trust, and support user-centered decision-making by development teams. Using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative techniques, we explore interaction patterns between humans and AI agents. The findings from this exploratory research serve as the basis to develop a survey experiment which evaluates the effectiveness of specific design elements on a larger scale. This foundational research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings.

</details>


### [104] [SwitchBraidNet: Quantisation-Aware Lightweight Architecture for Hybrid Brain-Computer Interface](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18816)
*Gourav Siddhad,Yogesh Kumar Meena*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: SwitchBraidNet is a compact dual-path EEG architecture with electrode gating and log-variance readout, achieving high hybrid BCI accuracy (MI: 69.49%, SSVEP: 93.48%) at an INT8 footprint of just 3.03 KB for embedded deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid BCIs combining MI and SSVEP offer high-dimensional neural decoding but exceed the computational budgets of embedded hardware. There is a need for ultra-compact, low-power models that maintain accuracy across reduced numerical precisions for real-world wearable deployment.

Method: The authors propose SwitchBraidNet with three key components: (1) a dual-path temporal braid for multiscale oscillatory feature extraction, (2) an adaptive squeeze-and-excitation spatial switch for dynamic electrode gating, and (3) a log-variance readout for direct band-power encoding. Quantisation-aware training is applied across FP32, FP16, and INT8 precisions, with evaluation against four baselines on the OpenBMI dataset.

Result: SwitchBraidNet achieves MI accuracy of 69.49% (FP16), SSVEP accuracy of 93.48% (FP32), and a hybrid information transfer rate of 64.82 bits/min (FP16). Its INT8 model occupies only 3.03 KB while retaining high accuracy, outperforming four established baselines across all tested precisions.

Conclusion: SwitchBraidNet demonstrates that aggressive model compression via quantisation-aware training can yield a hybrid BCI classifier suitable for low-power embedded deployment without sacrificing decoding performance, bridging the gap between high-dimensional neural interfaces and resource-constrained hardware.

Abstract: Hybrid brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) that integrate motor imagery (MI) and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) provide high-dimensional neural decoding but typically exceed the computational limits of embedded hardware. To address this, we propose SwitchBraidNet, a compact EEG classification architecture designed for low-power deployment. The model employs a dual-path temporal braid to extract multiscale oscillatory features, an adaptive squeeze-and-excitation spatial switch for electrode gating, and a log-variance readout layer for direct band-power encoding. Furthermore, through systematic quantisation-aware training on the OpenBMI dataset, we compared SwitchBraidNet against four established baselines across FP32, FP16, and INT8 precisions. Experimental results demonstrate superior efficiency and performance, achieving MI accuracy of 69.49% (FP16), SSVEP accuracy of 93.48% (FP32), and a hybrid information transfer rate of 64.82 bits/min (FP16). With an INT8 footprint of only 3.03 KB, SwitchBraidNet maintains high accuracy across varying numerical precisions, demonstrating its suitability for low-power embedded BCI deployment.

</details>


### [105] [Improving Human-Robot Teamwork in Urban Search and Rescue Through Episodic Memory of Prior Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18836)
*Taewoon Kim,Emma van Zoelen,Mark Neerincx*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A robot in a search-and-rescue task uses knowledge-graph episodic memories of prior team collaboration patterns, selected via graph representation learning, to initialize its behavior. This reuse of a single prior CP significantly boosts rescue success rate and reduces task time, especially early in interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Effective human-robot teamwork requires robots to adapt from the very start of an interaction. Prior collaboration patterns discovered by human teammates are often lost between episodes. The authors investigate whether robots can leverage these historical team experiences to become better teammates in future interactions, addressing the cold-start problem in human-robot collaboration.

Method: Historical collaboration patterns (CPs) from the MATRIX USAR environment are represented as knowledge-graph episodic memories. Graph representation learning with a node-classification objective is applied to identify the most representative and effective memory. The robot is then initialized with this single automatically selected CP before a new collaboration episode. The study involves 20 participants and 160 round-level observations.

Result: Initializing the robot with a single automatically selected prior CP increased rescue success rate from 25.7% to 41.3% (a ~60% relative improvement) and reduced average task time by 283 seconds. The strongest performance gains were observed at the beginning of interactions.

Conclusion: Reusable episodic memory, even a single automatically selected prior collaboration pattern, can equip robots with more effective task knowledge at the outset of teamwork, substantially improving both success rates and efficiency. This supports smoother early-stage human-robot collaboration.

Abstract: Effective human-robot teamwork requires robots to adapt to partners, situations, and task dynamics from the start of an interaction. In the MATRX Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) environment, people can externalize collaboration patterns (CPs) they discover during teamwork through a chat and reflection interface. We study whether a robot can use such prior team experience to become a better teammate in future interactions. To this end, we represent historical CPs as knowledge-graph episodic memories and use graph representation learning with a node-classification objective to identify a representative and effective memory for reuse. We then initialize the robot with this memory before a new collaboration episode begins. Across 20 participants and 160 round-level observations, initializing the robot with a single automatically selected prior CP increases rescue success from 25.7% to 41.3% and reduces average task time by 283 seconds. The strongest gains appear at the beginning of interaction, suggesting that reusable episodic memory can help robots enter collaboration with more effective task knowledge and support smoother early teamwork.

</details>


### [106] [A Clinician-Centered Pipeline for Annotation and Evaluation in Ultrasound AI Studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19174)
*Fangyijie Wang,Jianjun Yu,Wentao Shi,Haixia Huang,Ran Shi,Guénolé Silvestre,Kathleen M. Curran*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A browser-based pipeline enabling remote, blinded, multi-rater clinician evaluation of medical AI systems for ultrasound imaging, validated in a fetal ultrasound segmentation study with six raters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical image platforms focus on dataset labeling and lack integrated support for blinded model comparison and reproducible evaluation workflows. Quantitative metrics alone are insufficient for validating medical AI in ultrasound, necessitating clinician-centered evaluation.

Method: A centralized server with lightweight browser interfaces supports remote annotation, blinded ranking, and review without local dataset downloads. The pipeline enables multi-rater participation, centralized result aggregation, and automated statistical analysis (Spearman correlation, Kendall's τ, top-1 selection statistics).

Result: In a fetal ultrasound segmentation study with six raters (expert, generalist, non-expert), results showed moderate to strong inter-rater agreement. Blinded evaluation revealed a preference for later active learning models.

Conclusion: The pipeline effectively supports clinician-centered annotation and reproducible human-AI evaluation studies in ultrasound imaging. The system is open-sourced on GitHub.

Abstract: Clinician-centered evaluation is critical for validating medical AI systems, especially in ultrasound imaging where quantitative metrics do not always capture clinical usability. Existing medical image platforms primarily focus on dataset labeling. They lack integrated support for blinded model comparison and reproducible evaluation workflows. We present a clinician-centered pipeline for remote annotation and evaluation in ultrasound AI studies. The proposed pipeline uses a centralized server and lightweight browser interfaces to enable clinicians to perform annotation, blinded ranking, and review without local dataset downloads. The pipeline also supports multi-rater participation, centralized result aggregation, and automated statistical analysis. We validate the pipeline in a fetal ultrasound segmentation study with six raters spanning expert, generalist, and non-expert experience levels. The system automatically generated Spearman correlation, Kendall's $τ$, and top-1 selection statistics. Results indicated moderate to strong agreement across experts and other groups. The blinded evaluation results showed a tendency for later active learning models to be preferred. These outcomes suggest that the pipeline can support clinician-centered annotation and reproducible human-\ac{AI} evaluation studies in ultrasound imaging. The proposed pipeline is available on \href{https://github.com/13204942/SonoRate}{GitHub}.

</details>


### [107] [A Taxonomy of Mental Health and Technology Needs for Alzheimer's and Dementia Caregivers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19247)
*Keran Wang,Drishti Goel,Jiayue Melissa Shi,Violeta J. Rodriguez,Daniel S. Brown,Dong Whi Yoo,Ravi Karkar,Koustuv Saha*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Caregiver Mental Health and Technology Taxonomy that systematically maps the psychosocial needs of AD/ADRD informal caregivers to technology-based interventions, identifying gaps such as relational strain and compassion fatigue that are underserved by current digital tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Informal caregivers of individuals with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) — over 11 million in the U.S. alone — are at high risk for mental health problems, yet research reduces their complex psychosocial experiences to a monolithic "caregiver burden" construct. Simultaneously, digital and AI-enabled technologies are proliferating without a shared interdisciplinary framework to align caregiver needs with technological solutions, limiting cumulative progress across medicine, psychology, and technology research.

Method: The taxonomy was developed through an interdisciplinary literature review spanning medicine, psychology, and technology domains, combined with two qualitative studies involving AD/ADRD caregivers. This mixed approach enabled identification of mismatches between caregiver-articulated priorities and existing technological support offerings.

Result: The resulting taxonomy systematically links specific caregiver mental health needs to corresponding classes of technology-based interventions. It reveals critical mismatches between caregiver priorities and available technologies, highlights under-served domains — notably relational strain and compassion fatigue — and proposes design directions for adaptive, responsive systems.

Conclusion: The framework provides a shared vocabulary for clinicians, researchers, and technology designers, enabling more person-centered, clinically grounded innovation in dementia care. It moves the field beyond the reductive "caregiver burden" construct toward nuanced, need-specific technological support.

Abstract: Family members caring for individuals with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) provide the foundation of long-term care worldwide. In 2023, more than 11 million U.S. family and friends contributed 18 billion hours of unpaid care, often at the cost of their own physical and mental health. These informal caregivers -- also referred as the "invisible second patients" -- experience elevated rates of mental health problems. Yet research commonly reduces their complex psychosocial experiences to a single construct of caregiver burden, obscuring which specific needs are unmet or effectively supported. At the same time, digital and AI-enabled technologies are rapidly expanding, from smartphone apps and videoconferencing to sensor platforms and AI chatbots. However, the absence of shared frameworks across medicine, psychology, and technology research limits cumulative progress. This study introduces a Caregiver Mental Health and Technology Taxonomy that systematically links AD/ADRD caregiver needs with corresponding classes of technology-based interventions. Drawing from an interdisciplinary literature review and two qualitative studies with caregivers, the taxonomy identifies mismatches between caregiver priorities and existing technological support, highlights under-served domains such as relational strain and compassion fatigue, and proposes design directions for adaptive, responsive systems. The framework offers a shared vocabulary to guide clinicians, researchers, and technology designers in developing more person-centered and clinically grounded innovation in dementia care.

</details>


### [108] [Correct Yourself, Keep My Trust: How Self-Correction and Social Connection Shape Credibility in Social Chatbots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19286)
*Biswadeep Sen,Yi-Chieh Lee*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: When social chatbots make errors, self-correction preserves both credibility and belief change better than external corrections (webpage retractions or expert chatbot corrections). Social connection amplifies correction effectiveness, but only when the chatbot corrects itself.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social chatbots increasingly pervade daily life but are prone to generating convincing falsehoods. Their social rapport with users makes errors especially damaging, yet little is known about how different error-correction strategies affect trust recovery, credibility, and belief updating.

Method: Between-subjects experiment with N=120 participants, comparing three error correction strategies: (1) webpage retraction, (2) self-correction by the same social chatbot, and (3) correction by an expert chatbot. Social connection was measured via social attraction and self-disclosure.

Result: All three strategies corrected belief in the misinformation equally effectively. However, only self-correction preserved the chatbot's credibility — trustworthiness and perceived expertise ratings were significantly higher than external-correction conditions. Social connection strength predicted belief change magnitude only in the self-correction condition; outsourcing corrections severed this link entirely.

Conclusion: Social chatbots should self-correct their errors rather than defer to external sources. Investing in social connection is a functional mechanism that amplifies correction effectiveness, not merely a design feature. These findings inform design strategies for maintaining long-term credibility in social AI systems.

Abstract: When social chatbots make mistakes, and they do, how they recover determines whether users trust them again. Social chatbots are increasingly integrated into everyday life, yet they remain prone to generating convincing but inaccurate information. The social connection they build with users makes such errors particularly consequential. We conducted a between-subjects experiment (N=120) comparing three error correction strategies: a webpage retraction, self-correction by the same social chatbot, and correction by an expert chatbot. Our results reveal two key findings. First, all three strategies corrected the error equally well, but only self-correction did so without damaging the chatbot's credibility: participants rated self-correcting chatbots significantly higher in both trustworthiness and perceived expertise than chatbots whose errors were corrected by external sources. Second, the strength of the user's social connection with the chatbot, measured through social attraction and self-disclosure, significantly predicted the magnitude of belief change, but only when the chatbot corrected itself. Outsourcing corrections to an external source severed this link entirely. These findings suggest that social chatbots should correct their own mistakes rather than outsource corrections, and that investing in social connection is a functional mechanism that amplifies correction effectiveness, not merely a design feature. We discuss implications for designing chatbots that maintain long-term credibility while effectively addressing their own errors.

</details>


### [109] [Integrating Multi-Label Classification and Generative AI for Scalable Analysis of User Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.23018)
*Sandra Loop,Erik Bertram,Sebastian Juhl,Martin Schrepp*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A major software company integrated supervised machine learning for topic labeling and generative AI for summarization to efficiently analyze large volumes of open-ended UX feedback. Sentiment analysis proved unreliable as a proxy for product satisfaction, which must be measured explicitly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: UX evaluation relies on both quantitative metrics and qualitative open-ended feedback. Manual analysis of large volumes of user comments is time-consuming and challenging, creating a bottleneck for organizations that need to extract actionable insights and communicate findings to stakeholders, including upper management.

Method: The authors developed two techniques within a long-term UX measurement project: (1) supervised machine learning to assign pre-defined topic labels to user comments for high-level overview, and (2) generative AI to produce concise summaries of feedback. They also investigated sentiment analysis as a potential indicator of overall product satisfaction.

Result: The supervised ML approach successfully categorized comments by topic for efficient overview. GenAI produced informative summaries suitable for communicating findings to management. However, sentiment analysis did not reliably reflect user satisfaction; product satisfaction must be assessed explicitly in surveys.

Conclusion: Combining supervised ML for topic classification with GenAI for summarization offers a practical pipeline for processing large-scale UX feedback. Organizations should not rely on sentiment analysis as a proxy for product satisfaction but should instead measure it directly through explicit survey items.

Abstract: In highly competitive software markets, user experience (UX) evaluation is crucial for ensuring software quality and fostering long-term product success. Such UX evaluations typically combine quantitative metrics from standardized questionnaires with qualitative feedback collected through open-ended questions. While open-ended feedback offers valuable insights for improvement and helps explain quantitative results, analyzing large volumes of user comments is challenging and time-consuming. In this paper, we present techniques developed during a long-term UX measurement project at a major software company to efficiently process and interpret extensive volumes of user comments. To provide a high-level overview of the collected comments, we employ a supervised machine learning approach that assigns meaningful, pre-defined topic labels to each comment. Additionally, we demonstrate how generative AI (GenAI) can be leveraged to create concise and informative summaries of user feedback, facilitating effective communication of findings to the organization and especially upper management. Finally, we investigate whether the sentiment expressed in user comments can serve as an indicator for overall product satisfaction. Our results show that sentiment analysis alone does not reliably reflect user satisfaction. Instead, product satisfaction needs to be assessed explicitly in surveys to measure the user's perception of the product.

</details>

### [110] [RankGraph-2: Lifecycle Co-Design for Billion-Node Graph Learning in Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18379)
*Renzhi Wu,Zikun Cui,Junjie Yang,Tai Guo,Hong Li,Xian Chen,Li Yu,Ke Pan,Sri Reddy,Mahesh Srinivasan,Nipun Mathur,Haomin Yu,Hong Yan*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: RankGraph-2 is a Meta-deployed framework that co-designs graph construction, representation learning, and real-time serving for billion-node similarity-based retrieval. By pre-computing multi-hop neighborhoods via personalized PageRank, subsampling edges with popularity bias correction, and co-learning a residual-quantization cluster index, it achieves 83% serving cost reduction with 2.1–3.8× recall gains over prior methods, delivering +0.96% CTR and +2.75% CVR in production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-based retrieval systems treat graph construction, representation learning, and serving as isolated problems. At billion-node scale, these stages are tightly coupled: serving requires cheap ANN lookup which demands a co-learned index; training tolerates pre-computed neighborhoods, eliminating online graph traversals; and construction must support hour-level refresh for item coverage. No prior work jointly addresses all three under these cascading constraints.

Method: RankGraph-2 co-designs three lifecycle stages: (1) Graph Construction: reduces trillions of edges to hundreds of billions via subsampling with popularity bias correction, and pre-computes multi-hop neighborhoods using personalized PageRank to produce self-contained data. (2) Representation Learning: incorporates a co-learned residual-quantization (RQ) cluster index directly into the training objective, optimized for both U2U2I and U2I2I retrieval. (3) Serving: leverages the co-learned RQ index for efficient approximate nearest-neighbor lookup, avoiding expensive online KNN computation.

Result: RankGraph-2 reduces serving computational cost by 83% compared to online KNN. It achieves 3.8× higher recall than GAT + Deep Graph Infomax on bipartite graphs and 2.1× higher recall than PyTorch-BigGraph on item retrieval. In production A/B tests, it delivers up to +0.96% CTR and +2.75% CVR improvements, and has powered over 20 retrieval launches across major surfaces at Meta.

Conclusion: Lifecycle co-design across graph construction, representation learning, and serving is essential for billion-scale graph-based retrieval. By letting each stage's requirements cascade into the others, RankGraph-2 achieves substantial efficiency and quality gains, demonstrating that joint optimization unlocks performance unavailable to isolated approaches.

Abstract: Graph-based retrieval at billion-node scale requires jointly solving three tightly coupled problems -- graph construction, representation learning, and real-time serving -- yet existing work addresses each in isolation. We present RankGraph-2, a framework deployed at Meta that co-designs all three lifecycle stages for similarity-based retrieval (U2U2I and U2I2I), where each stage's requirements shape the others. Serving requires a co-learned cluster index to avoid expensive online KNN -- this pushes index co-training into the training objective. Training benefits from the observation that similarity-based retrieval tolerates pre-computed neighborhoods, eliminating online graph infrastructure -- this requires construction to produce self-contained data. Construction must also support hour-level refresh for item coverage. Acting on these cascading requirements, RankGraph-2 reduces hundreds of trillions of edges to hundreds of billions via subsampling with popularity bias correction, pre-computes multi-hop neighborhoods via personalized PageRank, and co-learns a residual-quantization cluster index that reduces serving computational cost by 83%. This lifecycle co-design enables a simple architecture to achieve 3.8 x higher recall than a GAT + Deep Graph Infomax model on a bipartite graph and 2.1 x higher than PyTorch-BigGraph on item retrieval. RankGraph-2 delivers up to +0.96% CTR and +2.75% CVR, and has powered 20+ retrieval launches across major surfaces.

</details>


### [111] [SHIFT: Semantic Harmonization via Index-side Feature Transformation for Multilingual Information Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18801)
*Youngjoon Jang,Seongtae Hong,Hyeonseok Moon,Heuiseok Lim*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SHIFT is a training-free, indexing-stage method that mitigates language bias in multilingual dense retrieval by subtracting a relative language vector from document embeddings, improving MLIR performance across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual dense retrieval models overly favor documents in the query language, causing language bias where top results are dominated by same-language documents even when semantically superior content exists in other languages.

Method: SHIFT operates at indexing time without additional training. It uses parallel translation pairs to estimate a relative language vector for each target language relative to a source language, then subtracts this vector from document embeddings to correct language-specific offsets.

Result: Comprehensive evaluation on four MLIR benchmarks with diverse dense retrieval models demonstrates that SHIFT effectively reduces language bias and improves multilingual retrieval performance.

Conclusion: SHIFT provides a simple, effective, and training-free solution to language bias in MLIR by applying language vector correction at the indexing stage, validated through extensive empirical results.

Abstract: With the rapid expansion of massive multilingual corpora, Multilingual Information Retrieval (MLIR) has emerged as a critical technology for global information access. MLIR enables users to retrieve semantically relevant documents from multilingual text collections using a single-language query. However, recent multilingual dense retrieval models often exhibit a strong preference for documents in the same language as the query. This leads to severe language bias, where top-ranked results are dominated by documents of specific languages, even when documents in other languages contain more semantically relevant information. To address this issue, we propose SHIFT, a training-free method applicable in the indexing stage. Specifically, SHIFT utilizes parallel translation pairs to estimate a relative language vector for each target language with respect to a source language. Subsequently, SHIFT corrects the language-specific offset by subtracting this relative language vector from document embeddings during indexing. Our comprehensive evaluation across four MLIR benchmarks and diverse dense retrieval models confirms that SHIFT can effectively mitigate language bias and enhance MLIR performance.

</details>


### [112] [Rescaling MLM-Head for Neural Sparse Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18811)
*Youngjoon Jang,Seongtae Hong,Jonah Turner,Heuiseok Lim*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Learned sparse retrieval models like SPLADE fail when using stronger pretrained backbones due to inflated MLM-head L2 norms, which destabilize contrastive training. A simple initialization-time rescaling of the MLM-head projection fixes this, enabling ModernBERT and Ettin to match or surpass BERT-SPLADE baselines at zero cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stronger pretrained encoders (e.g., ModernBERT, Ettin) should intuitively improve SPLADE-style learned sparse retrieval over BERT, but empirically they suffer performance degradation or training collapse. The authors aim to diagnose and fix this failure.

Method: The authors identify the root cause as scale mismatch in the MLM head: SPLADE uses unnormalized dot products over MLM-head outputs to compute query-document relevance, so inflated MLM-head L2 norms amplify sparse activations and distort matching scores. Their fix is a simple initialization-time correction — rescaling the MLM-head projection matrix by a constant factor before SPLADE training — with no architectural or objective changes.

Result: The rescaling correction stabilizes training for large-norm backbones (ModernBERT, Ettin), turning previously unstable runs into competitive sparse retrievers. Corrected models match or surpass the classic BERT-SPLADE baseline on both in-domain and out-of-domain retrieval benchmarks.

Conclusion: The bottleneck in adapting pretrained encoders to LSR is not encoder capacity but proper calibration of the MLM-head scale used for constructing sparse lexical representations. The proposed rescaling provides a zero-cost solution.

Abstract: Learned sparse retrieval (LSR) models such as SPLADE have traditionally used BERT-style masked language models as backbone encoders. A natural expectation is that replacing BERT with stronger pretrained encoders should improve retrieval effectiveness. However, we find that under standard SPLADE training recipes, backbones with large MLM-head L2 norms can suffer performance degradation and even training collapse under standard SPLADE training recipes. We identify this failure as a scale mismatch in the MLM head: SPLADE directly uses MLM-head outputs to construct sparse lexical representations, and query-document relevance is computed by an unnormalized dot product over these representations. As a result, an inflated MLM-head scale can amplify sparse activations, distort matching scores, and destabilize contrastive training under common training settings. To address this issue, we introduce a simple initialization-time correction that rescales the MLM-head projection by a constant factor before SPLADE training. This zero-cost adjustment improves training stability without modifying the model architecture or training objective. Across both in-domain and out-of-domain retrieval benchmarks, this simple correction substantially improves large-norm backbones such as ModernBERT and Ettin, turning unstable training runs into competitive sparse retrievers. In several settings, the corrected models further match or surpass the classic BERT-SPLADE baseline. These findings suggest that the bottleneck in adapting pretrained encoders to LSR is not encoder capacity alone, but the calibration of the MLM-head scale used to construct sparse lexical representations.

</details>


### [113] [LensKit-Auto](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18814)
*Max Breit,Anass Amezian El Idrissi,Rishikesh Giriraj Kulkarni,Luca Quade*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper enhances LensKit-Auto, a black-box framework for automatically finding optimal algorithm-hyperparameter combinations for recommender systems. Key improvements include updating compatibility with the latest LensKit version, adding Tree Parzen Estimator optimization, result reuse, visualization of the optimization process, updated documentation, and preparing a meta-dataset for future meta-learning integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recommender system performance varies significantly across datasets, and no single algorithm works universally. Manually searching for the right algorithm-hyperparameter combination is challenging and repetitive. Automating this process (AutoRecSys) is valuable, especially for non-experts who need an easy-to-use, black-box solution.

Method: The authors upgrade LensKit-Auto to support the new version of the underlying LensKit framework. They integrate the Tree Parzen Estimator as an additional hyperparameter optimization method, implement functionality for reusing discovered algorithms, add visualization capabilities for the optimization process, update documentation, and adapt an existing meta-learning framework to construct a suitable meta-dataset for potential future meta-learning integration.

Result: The enhancements modernize LensKit-Auto and improve its usability, allowing even non-experts to feed in their dataset and receive a recommendation for the best algorithm-hyperparameter combination. The framework now supports multiple optimization strategies, result reuse, and process visualization.

Conclusion: LensKit-Auto is successfully updated and enhanced, broadening its accessibility and functionality. The groundwork for future meta-learning integration is laid via the adapted meta-dataset, further advancing the goal of fully automated recommender system selection.

Abstract: Recommender systems have a wide area of application, e.g. in fields like video streaming, social media, or digital marketplaces. But, for a recommender-system, finding the right algorithm with the right hyperparameters is a reoccurring challenge. There is no one-fits-all solution, since the performance of one algorithm can vary immensely on different data sets. Due to the challenges of finding the right algorithm and the broad use of recommender-systems, it is of interest to create an Automated Recommender System (AutoRecSys) that takes on the task of finding the right algorithm-hyperparameter-combination for a given data set. In this work, we present the enhancement of LensKit-Auto, a framework introduced by Vente et al., that solves exactly this task of finding a fitting algorithm-hyperparameter-combination. LensKit-Auto's biggest strength lies in its ease of use, where it operates as a black-box, into which the user can feed their data set and receive the information of which algorithm and hyperparameters work best on this data set. In this work, we bring LensKit-Auto up to date, so that it works with the new version of its underlying framework, LensKit. We also implement further functionalities, such as the Tree Parzen Estimator as an additional optimization method, the ability to reuse the found algorithm, updated documentation, and the ability to visualize the optimization process. We also adapt an existing meta-learning framework to generate a suitable meta-dataset for LensKit-Auto, which could enable the integration of meta-learning into LensKit-Auto in the future. The presented changes bring LensKit-Auto up to date and enhance its usability, so that even non-experts in the field can find the right algorithm for their use case.

</details>


### [114] [SAERec: Constructing Fine-grained Interpretable Intents Priors via Sparse Autoencoders for Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18897)
*Jiangnan Xia,Xuansheng Wu,Yu Yang,Xin Wang,Ninghao Liu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SAERec uses a sparse autoencoder to extract fine-grained, interpretable intents from LLM text embeddings, then retrieves both personal and public intents to guide sequential recommendation via a multi-branch attention mechanism, outperforming existing intent-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing intent-based recommender systems derive intents via clustering or prototype learning from user sequences, which are sensitive to sequence quality, require presetting the number of intents, and lack explicit semantic grounding — resulting in incomplete, coarse intent sets that limit recommendation effectiveness.

Method: SAERec constructs an intent space from textual corpora in three stages: (1) a sparse autoencoder (SAE) disentangles LLM text embeddings to extract fine-grained, interpretable intents from latent space; (2) for each user, relevant intents are retrieved as priors — personal intents matching current interests and public intents capturing general item patterns (e.g., quality, price); (3) a multi-branch attention mechanism captures temporal dependencies and injects both intent types, followed by adaptive fusion to build the final user representation.

Result: Extensive experiments on public datasets show SAERec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while providing human-understandable explanations.

Conclusion: Leveraging SAE-disentangled LLM embeddings for automatic intent construction offers a more fine-grained, semantically grounded, and interpretable alternative to clustering-based intent modeling in sequential recommendation.

Abstract: Intent-based recommender systems have gained significant attention for improving accuracy and interpretability by modeling the underlying motivations behind user behaviors. Most existing models derive intents directly from user sequences via clustering or prototype learning. However, they are sensitive to sequence quality, require presetting the number of intents, and lack explicit semantic grounding. These issues lead to an incomplete and coarse intent set and limit the effectiveness of recommendation. In this paper, we propose the Sparse Autoencoder for intent-based recommendation (SAERec), a novel recommender that automatically constructs a fine-grained and interpretable intent space from a textual corpus to guide recommendation. Rather than treating texts as side signals, SAERec leverages them as high information density evidence for intent construction. Specifically, we first extract a comprehensive set of fine-grained interpretable intents from the latent space of large language models (LLMs) by using a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to disentangle and interpret text embeddings, which isolates intent-related semantics from textual noise. Then, for each user, we retrieve relevant intents from this set as priors to guide recommendation. It contains personal intents matching a user's current interests and public intents capturing general item patterns shared across users (e.g., quality, price). Finally, to integrate retrieved intents into sequence modeling, we propose a multi-branch attention mechanism that captures temporal dependencies and injects both personal and public intent signals, followed by an adaptive fusion layer to construct the final user representation for recommendation. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of SAERec, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while providing human-understandable explanations.

</details>


### [115] [Querit-Reranker: Training Compact Multilingual Rerankers via Efficient Label-Free Distribution Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19037)
*Yunfei Zhong,Jun Yang,Wei Huang,Yinqiong Cai,Haosheng Qian,Yixing Fan,Ruqing Zhang,Lixin Su,Daiting Shi,Jiafeng Guo*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Querit-Reranker introduces a data-centric pipeline for label-efficient adaptation of multilingual cross-encoder rerankers, using synthetic-query mining with teacher scores and SLERP merging to achieve state-of-the-art performance with models of 0.4B and 4B activated parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployable multilingual rerankers must generalize across languages, domains, and tasks while remaining efficient, but adapting them to new target distributions typically requires costly task-specific relevance annotations. The paper aims to reduce this annotation burden through a data-centric, label-efficient adaptation pipeline.

Method: The pipeline has three stages: (1) learning general relevance modeling from large-scale ranking-oriented data; (2) adapting to target distributions via synthetic-query mining using teacher scores as continuous soft labels; (3) merging complementary task-adapted checkpoints via spherical linear interpolation (SLERP) to consolidate strengths into a single model. Two instantiations are provided: Querit-Reranker-A0.4B (MoE backbone, 0.4B activated parameters) and Querit-Reranker-4B (based on Qwen3-Embedding-4B).

Result: Using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B as the first-stage retriever, Querit-Reranker-A0.4B improves average nDCG@10 from 54.11 to 59.28 on BEIR and from 59.87 to 67.70 on MIRACL. On MTEB Multilingual v2 Reranking, it substantially outperforms larger embedding-based baselines. Querit-Reranker-4B achieves state-of-the-art among publicly available models.

Conclusion: The data-centric pipeline enables label-efficient adaptation of multilingual cross-encoder rerankers, producing compact yet highly performant models. The approach demonstrates that synthetic-query mining with soft teacher labels and SLERP-based checkpoint merging can yield state-of-the-art multilingual reranking without costly manual annotations. Both models are released on Hugging Face.

Abstract: Deployable multilingual rerankers must generalize across languages, domains, and target ranking tasks while remaining efficient enough for second-stage reranking. However, adapting them to new target distributions typically requires extensive task-specific relevance annotations, which are costly to obtain. We present Querit-Reranker, a family of multilingual cross-encoder rerankers trained with a data-centric pipeline for label-efficient adaptation. We instantiate it as Querit-Reranker-A0.4B, initialized from an in-house MoE backbone with 0.4B activated parameters, and Querit-Reranker-4B, initialized from Qwen3-Embedding-4B. Our pipeline first learns general relevance modeling from large-scale ranking-oriented data, then adapts to target distributions through synthetic-query mining with teacher scores as continuous soft labels. To consolidate complementary task-adapted strengths, we further merge checkpoints via spherical linear interpolation, obtaining a single deployable model without runtime ensembling overhead. Using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B as the shared first-stage retriever, Querit-Reranker-A0.4B improves average nDCG@10 from 54.11 to 59.28 on BEIR and from 59.87 to 67.70 on MIRACL. On MTEB Multilingual v2 Reranking, it also substantially outperforms larger embedding-based baselines, while Querit-Reranker-4B further achieves state-of-the-art performance among publicly available models. We release both models on Hugging Face.

</details>
