### [116] [Characterizing Opinion Evolution of Networked LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18276)
*Caleb Probine,Yigit Ege Bayiz,Filippos Fotiadis,Samuel Li,Yunhao Yang,Ufuk Topcu*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Classical opinion dynamics models fail to capture LLM behavior in multi-agent systems, but adding a bias term — an innate opinion toward which agents regress — reduces opinion trajectory error by up to 88%, and this finding generalizes across model families, topics, and network topologies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings (simulations, influence operations, social platforms), creating new regimes of opinion propagation. Existing opinion dynamics models were developed for humans, and it is unknown whether they apply to LLM interactions. This paper investigates that gap.

Method: The authors evaluate classical opinion dynamics models (e.g., averaging-style models) against observed LLM opinion trajectories in multi-agent networks. They then introduce modifications — most notably a "bias" term representing an innate opinion to which agents regress — and measure improvements in modeling fidelity via cumulative estimated mean opinion error.

Result: Naive averaging models fail to track LLM opinion dynamics. Incorporating a bias term substantially improves fidelity, reducing cumulative estimated mean opinion error by up to 88%. Results generalize across different LLM families, discussion topics, and network structures.

Conclusion: LLM opinion dynamics qualitatively differ from classical human models, but simple augmentations — particularly innate bias — can bridge the gap effectively. Bias is a significant driver of LLM opinion propagation in multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with one another in multi-agent systems, from simulations of human discourse to influence operations and fully LLM-driven social platforms. These interactions give rise to new regimes of opinion propagation that are not yet well understood. We investigate whether classical opinion dynamics models, which have long been used to explain how interactions shape collective beliefs in human societies, can capture the behavior of LLM networks. We find that, while naive averaging-style models fail to track LLMs' opinion dynamics, simple modifications yield substantial gains in modeling fidelity. In particular, bias, an innate opinion toward which agents regress, emerges as a significant driver of LLM opinion dynamics, with its inclusion reducing cumulative estimated mean opinion error by up to 88%. We additionally find that these conclusions generalize across model families, discussion topics, and networks.

</details>


### [117] [PersonalPlan: Planning Multi-Agent Systems for Personalized Programming Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18633)
*Zhiyuan Wen,Jiannong Cao,Peng Gao,Haochen Shi,Wengpan Kuan,Bo Yuan,Xiuxiu Qi*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: MAP-PPL is a new dataset for personalized programming learning with multi-agent plans, and PersonalPlan is a two-stage planner using hierarchical SFT with LoRA and Reward-Adaptive GRPO that outperforms frontier LLMs and existing MAS frameworks on plan executability, personalization, and pedagogical quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems for programming education lack profile-grounding (learner-specific adaptation) and pedagogical scaffolding, undermining truly personalized learning experiences.

Method: First, MAP-PPL dataset is constructed with 3,043 query-profile-plan instances from Stack Overflow and 2,738 learner profiles. Then, PersonalPlan is proposed: Stage 1 uses hierarchical supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with separate LoRA adapters for profile-aware task decomposition and step dependency planning; Stage 2 applies Reward-Adaptive GRPO to optimize for executability, personalization, and pedagogical scaffolding.

Result: PersonalPlan (8B and 32B variants) achieves state-of-the-art performance on plan executability, personalization, and pedagogical quality, surpassing frontier LLMs, generic MAS frameworks, and existing agentic planners.

Conclusion: Profile-conditioned planning with dedicated LoRA adapters and reward-adaptive reinforcement learning effectively orchestrates multi-agent systems for personalized programming education.

Abstract: Effective programming education requires personalized instruction adapted to diverse learner backgrounds. However, while LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) excel at complex planning, existing planners often lack profile-grounding and pedagogical scaffolding, thereby undermining personalized programming learning. To fill in the gap, we first introduce \textbf{MAP-PPL} (\textbf{M}ulti-\textbf{A}gent \textbf{P}lans for \textbf{P}ersonalized \textbf{P}rogramming \textbf{L}earning), a profile-conditioned multi-agent planning dataset with 3{,}043 query--profile--plan instances from 1{,}730 Stack Overflow question groups and 2{,}738 learner profiles. Each plan specifies agents, subtasks, executable steps, and prerequisite dependencies. Then, we propose \textbf{PersonalPlan}, a two-stage MAS planner that first performs hierarchical SFT with separate LoRA adapters for profile-aware task decomposition and step dependency planning, then applies a Reward-Adaptive GRPO to encourage the model to generate executable, personalized, and pedagogically scaffolded plans. Extensive experiments on MAP-PPL comparing PersonalPlan against frontier LLMs, generic MAS frameworks, and agentic planners demonstrate its superiority. With only 8B and 32B variants, PersonalPlan achieves state-of-the-art plan executability, personalization, and pedagogical quality, effectively orchestrating MAS for agent-student interactions.

</details>


### [118] [Gender Bias in LLM Hiring Decisions: Evidence from a Japanese Context and Evaluation of Mitigation Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18649)
*Serena A. Hoffstedde,Machiko Hirota,Akshara Nadayanur Sathis Kanna,Rihito Kotani,Ujwal Kumar,Gabriele Trovato,Phan Xuan Tan*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A study examining gender bias in LLM hiring decisions within a Japanese corporate context finds a significant pro-female bias across five LLMs, replicating Western findings. Prompt-level gender-neutrality instructions fail to reduce bias, while name removal effectively eliminates the female advantage. A 42% refusal rate when combining privacy filters with GPT-4o's safety filter reveals a critical deployment challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on gender bias in LLM hiring decisions has predominantly focused on English-language, Western-format resumes, leaving a gap in understanding whether these biases generalize to non-Western contexts. The authors aim to test whether pro-female bias replicates in a Japanese corporate setting and to evaluate practical mitigation strategies applicable to real-world LLM-assisted recruitment pipelines.

Method: The study employs a counterfactual resume design using 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes paired with 12 linguistically grounded gender-signal name pairs. Five state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B) were tested across three conditions — baseline, prompt instruction (gender-neutrality directive), and privacy filter (name anonymization) — totaling 43,200 API calls. A crossed random-effects linear mixed model was used for statistical analysis, complemented by a name-reliance analysis to isolate the primary gender signal channel.

Result: A significant pro-female bias was confirmed across all five models, successfully replicating Western findings in the Japanese context. The prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction produced no meaningful bias reduction. The name-reliance analysis identified candidate name as the primary gender channel: removing the name reduced the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. An unexpected incompatibility between the privacy filter condition and GPT-4o's content safety filter resulted in a 42% refusal rate for that model.

Conclusion: Pro-female gender bias in LLM hiring decisions generalizes beyond Western contexts to Japanese corporate settings. Simple prompt-based debiasing instructions are ineffective, while name anonymization proves potent but introduces practical deployment risks — such as safety filter conflicts — that must be addressed before integrating LLMs into real-world recruitment pipelines.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in hiring workflows, yet most research on gender bias in LLM hiring decisions has focused on English-language, Western-format resumes. This study examines whether pro-female gender bias extends to a Japanese corporate context and evaluates two practical mitigation strategies. Using a counterfactual resume design with 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes, 12 name pairs selected on linguistically grounded gender-signal criteria, and five state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B), we conducted 43,200 API calls across baseline, prompt instruction, and privacy filter conditions. A crossed random-effects linear mixed model confirms a significant pro-female bias across all five models, replicating Western findings in a non-Western context. A prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction produces no meaningful reduction in bias. A name-reliance analysis formally identifies the candidate name as the primary gender channel: removing the name from the prompt reduces the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. An unexpected incompatibility between the privacy filter and GPT-4o's content safety filter, resulting in a 42% refusal rate, highlights a practical deployment challenge for name anonymization in LLM-assisted recruitment pipelines.

</details>


### [119] [EARS: Explanatory Abstention for Reliable Sub-Agent Modeling in Large-scale Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18668)
*Shuang Xie,Yunan Lu,Han Li,Lingyun Wang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: EARS is a framework that improves multi-agent system reliability by having sub-agents detect when they cannot answer a request and return structured failure states with rationales to the coordinator, instead of hallucinating. Fine-tuned with LLM-as-a-Judge-labeled data, it raised production e-commerce assistant pass rates from 68.5% to 78.9%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In centralized multi-agent systems with domain-specialized sub-agents built on smaller fine-tuned models, these sub-agents often fail to recognize their own capability boundaries. They over-answer ambiguous, underspecified, misrouted, or unsupported requests, producing hallucinations rather than actionable feedback. This undermines overall system reliability.

Method: EARS (Explanatory Abstention for Reliable Sub-Agent Modeling) frames sub-agent abstention as an inter-agent communication protocol. It uses an ensemble of calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge models to curate human-agent interaction data, producing structured abstention labels and rationales under a taxonomy of sub-agent failure modes. These data are then used to fine-tune sub-agents to detect failure conditions and return rationales, enabling the coordinator to clarify, reroute, or trigger fallback mechanisms.

Result: In a large-scale production e-commerce assistant for enterprise business intelligence workflows, EARS improved the overall response pass rate from 68.5% to 78.9%.

Conclusion: Sub-agent-side explanatory abstention significantly enhances multi-agent system reliability. By explicitly communicating failure states rather than guessing, fine-tuned sub-agents enable more robust coordinator-level recovery, demonstrating EARS as a practical framework for production MAS deployments.

Abstract: In large-scale enterprise settings, centralized multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly adopted, in which a coordinator delegates user requests to lightweight, domain-specialized sub-agents. While this architecture improves modularity, scalability, and cost efficiency, its reliability depends not only on accurate routing but also on sub-agents' ability to calibrate their responses to capability constraints. In particular, sub-agents built on smaller fine-tuned models often struggle with such calibration, leading them to over-answer ambiguous, underspecified, misrouted, or unsupported requests and produce hallucinated outputs instead of actionable feedback. To address this challenge, we present EARS (Explanatory Abstention for Reliable Sub-Agent Modeling), a production-oriented framework that reframes sub-agent abstention as an inter-agent communication protocol: a sub-agent does not merely abstain, but exposes an actionable failure state to the coordinator. EARS curates human-agent interaction data using an ensemble of calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge models, producing structured abstention labels and rationales under a taxonomy of sub-agent failure modes. These data are used to fine-tune sub-agents to detect failure conditions and return rationales for coordinator-level clarification, rerouting, or fallback. We evaluate EARS in a large-scale production e-commerce assistant supporting enterprise business intelligence workflows. EARS improves the overall response pass rate from 68.5% to 78.9%, demonstrating that sub-agent-side explanatory abstention improves MAS reliability.

</details>


### [120] [Skill-MAS: Evolving Meta-Skill for Automatic Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18837)
*Hehai Lin,Qi Yang,Chengwei Qin*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Skill-MAS proposes a third paradigm for LLM-based multi-agent system generation that decouples experience retention from parametric updates by treating orchestration capability as an evolvable Meta-Skill, optimized through multi-trajectory rollout and selective reflection, achieving strong performance with favorable cost trade-offs and demonstrated robustness/transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MAS generation methods suffer from a dichotomy: inference-time approaches using frozen frontier LLMs fail to retain past experience (repeating searches), while training-time approaches that internalize experience via gradient updates are limited by the capability ceiling of smaller models and cannot scale to large frontier LLMs. A method is needed that combines experience retention with frontier LLM capability.

Method: Skill-MAS introduces an evolvable Meta-Skill that captures high-level orchestration knowledge decoupled from model parameters. It operates via a closed optimization loop with two components: (1) Multi-Trajectory Rollout, which samples behavioral distributions for each task under the current Meta-Skill; and (2) Selective Reflection, which adaptively selects priority tasks and applies hierarchical contrastive analysis to distill systemic experience into generalizable strategy-level principles.

Result: Extensive experiments across four complex benchmarks and four distinct LLMs show that Skill-MAS achieves remarkable performance gains while maintaining a favorable cost-performance trade-off. The evolved Meta-Skills exhibit strong robustness and transferability across unseen tasks and different LLMs.

Conclusion: Skill-MAS successfully bridges the gap between inference-time and training-time MAS paradigms, offering a scalable, experience-retaining approach that works with frontier LLMs and generalizes across tasks and models.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based automatic Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) generation has become a crucial frontier for tackling complex tasks. However, existing methods face a dilemma between model capability and experience retention. Inference-time MAS leverages frozen frontier LLMs but repeats identical searches without learning from past experience. Conversely, Training-time MAS internalizes experience via gradient updates but is constrained by the low capability ceiling of smaller models, and is hard to scale to large frontier LLMs. To bridge this gap, we propose Skill-MAS, a novel third path that decouples experience retention from parametric updates by conceptualizing the high-level orchestration capability as an evolvable Meta-Skill. Skill-MAS refines this architectural knowledge through a closed optimization loop: (1) Multi-Trajectory Rollout samples a behavioral distribution for each task under the current Meta-Skill; and (2) Selective Reflection adaptively selects priority tasks and applies hierarchical contrastive analysis to distill systemic experience into generalizable, strategy-level principles. Extensive experiments across four complex benchmarks and four distinct LLMs demonstrate that Skill-MAS not only achieves remarkable performance gains but also maintains a favorable cost-performance trade-off. Further analysis reveals that the evolved Meta-Skills are highly robust and exhibit strong transferability across unseen tasks and different LLMs.

</details>


### [121] [A Technical Taxonomy of LLM Agent Communication Protocols](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19135)
*Linus Sander,Habtom Kahsay Gidey,Alexander Lenz,Alois Knoll*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper presents a five-dimension taxonomy for classifying LLM agent communication protocols, applies it to nine open-source protocols, identifies architectural patterns and convergence trends, and predicts a federated, layered protocol stack rather than a single dominant standard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-based multi-agent systems proliferate, the fragmented landscape of communication protocols creates interoperability challenges. No systematic classification framework exists to compare, analyze, or guide selection among these emerging protocols.

Method: The authors employed an established iterative taxonomy-building method (Nickerson et al., 2013) with defined purpose, meta-characteristic, and ending conditions. Five iterations were conducted: three empirical-to-conceptual (inductive, based on protocol artifacts) and two conceptual-to-empirical (deductive, driven by theoretical dimensions). Nine actively maintained, open-source protocols with demonstrable adoption were sampled as the empirical basis.

Result: The resulting taxonomy has five dimensions: (1) Counterparty — agent-to-agent vs. agent-to-context; (2) Payload — structured, unstructured, or hybrid; (3) Interaction State — stateless, session-state, or persistent; (4) Discovery Mechanism — centralized, decentralized, or hybrid; (5) Schema Flexibility — fixed, multiple-predefined, or runtime-negotiated. Classification revealed that all sampled agent-to-agent protocols use hybrid payloads with session-state persistence; most support multiple predefined schemas; two negotiate schemas at runtime; and decentralized discovery is rare.

Conclusion: Short-term convergence pressure exists toward protocols unifying agent-to-agent and agent-to-context communication. Long-term, no single protocol can simultaneously maximize versatility, efficiency, and portability — the field will evolve toward a federated, layered protocol stack. The taxonomy serves as a tool for protocol selection and highlights open gaps in privacy and policy enforcement.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance and multi-agent systems aim to overcome the limits of standalone agents, robust communication protocols are becoming essential infrastructure for distributed agent networks. Nonetheless, the fragmented protocol landscape presents a significant interoperability challenge. This study develops a technical taxonomy to classify and analyze LLM agent communication protocols. Following an established iterative method, we defined the taxonomy's purpose, meta-characteristic, and ending conditions, then performed five iterations, three empirical-to-conceptual and two conceptual-to-empirical, on nine actively maintained open-source protocols with demonstrable adoption. The taxonomy comprises five dimensions: counterparty, payload, interaction state, discovery mechanism, and schema flexibility. Classification reveals recurring architectural patterns: all sampled agent-to-agent protocols combine hybrid payloads with session-state persistence; most protocols support multiple predefined schemas, and two negotiate schemas at runtime, indicating a trend toward schema flexibility; decentralized discovery remains rare. Analysis suggests short-term convergence pressure toward protocols unifying agent-to-agent and agent-to-context (tool and data) communication. Long-term, however, no single protocol is likely to maximize versatility, efficiency, and portability simultaneously. The field will more likely evolve toward a federated, layered protocol stack. The framework guides protocol selection and highlights open research gaps such as privacy and policy enforcement.}

</details>


### [122] [Data Intelligence Agents: Interpreting, Modeling, and Querying Enterprise Data via Autonomous Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19319)
*Anoushka Vyas,Aarushi Dhanuka,Sina Khoshfetrat Pakazad,Henrik Ohlsson*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: DIA is a three-agent system (Data Interpreter, Schema Creator, Query Generator) that uses autonomous coding agents to generate, execute, validate, and repair concrete data artifacts. It compresses enterprise data integration workflows, uses shared memory for experience reuse, and achieves state-of-the-art results across seven SQL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise production data integration suffers from repeated, lossy handoffs between data owners, engineers, and analysts during the discover-structure-query pipeline. Existing approaches rely on text-based outputs that lack executability, validation, and repair loops, creating a bottleneck that DIA aims to eliminate by treating executable code generation as a first-class paradigm.

Method: DIA comprises three autonomous coding agents (ACAs): (1) Data Interpreter for data discovery and structuring, (2) Schema Creator for schema design, and (3) Query Generator for SQL generation. Each agent generates, executes, validates, and repairs concrete artifacts (code/schemas/queries) rather than emitting text. A shared memory enables experience reuse across tasks. The system surfaces artifacts for domain expert review. The Query Generator is evaluated in fully autonomous mode across seven SQL benchmarks spanning four task categories and four SQL dialects.

Result: The Query Generator matches or surpasses the best published results on all seven SQL benchmarks, covering four task categories and four dialects. This demonstrates that an execution-grounded architecture built on ACAs with shared memory generalizes across the data intelligence workload while requiring only natural-language instruction adaptation for different contexts.

Conclusion: Treating autonomous coding agents as a first-class abstraction—where agents produce executable, validated, and repairable artifacts—effectively compresses the data integration workflow. The shared memory mechanism and execution-grounded design enable strong generalization across diverse SQL tasks and dialects, validating the architecture for production enterprise deployment.

Abstract: Production data integration is bottlenecked by repeated, lossy handoffs between data owners, engineers, and analysts who must collaboratively discover, structure, and query enterprise data. We present Data Intelligence Agents (DIA), a system of three agents (Data Interpreter, Schema Creator, and Query Generator) that compresses this workflow by treating autonomous coding agents (ACAs) as a first-class abstraction: rather than emitting text, the agents generate, execute, validate, and repair concrete artifacts, draw on a shared memory for experience reuse, and surface each for review by domain experts. DIA is deployed in production for enterprise customers. We study the Query Generator in depth and evaluate it in fully autonomous mode across seven SQL benchmarks spanning four task categories and four dialects. It matches or surpasses the best published results on all seven, demonstrating that an architecture grounded in execution, built on ACAs and a shared memory, generalizes across the data intelligence workload with adaptation confined to natural-language instructions.

</details>

### [123] [Conflict-Aware Retriever Editing for Knowledge Injection Attacks on LLM-Based RAG Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18310)
*Xinru Liu,Xianglong Zhang,Di Cai,Zhumin Chen,Pengfei Hu,Xin Xin*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CAREATTACK is a model-centric attack framework that edits retriever model parameters to inject malicious knowledge into RAG systems, overcoming detectability issues of data-centric methods by directly modifying the retriever through conflict-aware parameter editing and anchor repair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing data-centric RAG injection attacks (e.g., crafting malicious corpus) produce synthetic text that can be detected, causing attack failure. With open-source retrievers becoming prevalent, model-centric attacks present an underexplored and practical threat surface.

Method: CAREATTACK has two stages: (1) Conflict-aware retriever editing — applies closed-form parameter editing to dense retrieval models to boost malicious passages over benign ones, using graph-based conflict detection and parameter projection to resolve parameter conflicts; (2) Attack-preserving anchor repair — lightweight calibration of the edited retriever to preserve attack effectiveness on target prompts while neutralizing side effects on non-target prompts.

Result: Instantiated on Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and BGE-M3 across three benchmark datasets, the method substantially elevates malicious passages into RAG retrieved knowledge and supports batched attacks on multiple target prompts/passages simultaneously.

Conclusion: The work reveals a practical attack surface in RAG systems built on open-source retrieval models, demonstrating that model-centric retriever editing is a viable and effective approach for malicious knowledge injection.

Abstract: Injecting malicious knowledge into retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems can manipulate retrieved evidence and mislead downstream generation, posing a serious security threat for AI applications. Existing RAG injection attacks mainly rely on manipulating external knowledge bases, such as crafting malicious corpus. However, the synthetic text crafted by such data-centric methods could be detectable, leading to the failure of attacks. Beyond corpus manipulation, open-source retrievers are increasingly exposing RAG systems to model-centric attacks. In this paper, we propose conflict-aware retriever editing, i.e., CAREATTACK, a model-centric retriever attack framework for malicious knowledge injection in RAG. Specifically, CAREATTACK consists two stages of conflict-aware retriever editing and attack-preserving anchor repair. Conflict-aware retriever editing adapts efficient closed-form parameter editing to the dense retrieval model, promoting malicious knowledge above benign competing passages and resolving potential parameter conflicts through graph-based conflict detection and parameter editing projection. Then, attack-preserving anchor repair performs lightweight calibration on the edited retriever to further eliminate the impact on non-target prompts while preserving the attack effectiveness for target prompts. We instantiate CAREATTACK on Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and BGE-M3, and conduct evaluation on three benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate our method substantially promote malicious passages into the retrieved knowledge of RAG systems and can perform attacks for batches of target prompts and passages, given the access of retrieval model parameters. Since most RAG systems are built upon open-source retrieval models, this work reveals a practical attack surface in RAG systems. Codes are public accessible at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CareAttack-3F1C.

</details>


### [124] [TIGER: Inverting Transformer Gradients via Embedding-Subspace Distance Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18312)
*William Kalikman,Ivo Petrov,Dimitar I. Dimitrov,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TIGER is a continuous gradient inversion attack that recovers private inputs from federated learning gradient updates by optimizing token embeddings to minimize their distance to a subspace derived from low-rank attention gradients, outperforming prior attacks on both encoder and decoder transformers, especially under differential privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing gradient inversion attacks on transformers are either computationally expensive/unstable (optimization-based) or brittle under numerical noise from quantization/DP and scale poorly for encoder models (subspace-based with discrete token tests). A robust, efficient attack that works under DP for both encoder and decoder architectures is needed.

Method: TIGER exploits the low-rank property of attention gradients to identify a subspace containing true token embeddings. Instead of a discrete membership test over candidate tokens, TIGER introduces a differentiable objective: it directly optimizes continuous token embeddings to minimize their distance to this subspace, enabling gradient-based optimization without searching over discrete token spaces.

Result: On encoder-only models, TIGER substantially improves both reconstruction quality and runtime over existing attacks. On decoder models, TIGER is more robust than prior subspace-based attacks, achieving the first successful reconstructions in DP-defended federated learning settings.

Conclusion: TIGER demonstrates that continuous optimization over the embedding subspace is a more effective and robust approach for gradient inversion on transformers, successfully breaching DP defenses where prior attacks fail.

Abstract: Federated learning allows multiple clients to jointly train a shared model by sending gradient updates to a central server while keeping raw inputs local. However, prior gradient inversion attacks show that these updates can reveal enough information to reconstruct client inputs. Existing attacks on transformers either optimize dummy inputs to match the true client updates, which is costly and unstable for modern models, or exploit the low rank of attention gradients to identify a subspace containing the true layer embeddings, followed by a discrete membership test for candidate tokens. However, this token test is brittle under numerical noise, i.e., from quantization or Differential Privacy (DP), and scales poorly for encoder models with non-causal attention. We introduce TIGER, a continuous gradient inversion attack that turns this subspace signal into a differentiable objective. Instead of searching over tokens or matching full gradients, TIGER directly optimizes token embeddings to minimize their distance to the subspace. Our experiments demonstrate that on encoder-only models, TIGER substantially improves both reconstruction quality and runtime over existing attacks, while on decoder models, TIGER is more robust than prior subspace-based attacks, enabling the first successful reconstructions in DP-defended federated learning settings.

</details>


### [125] [TopVenues: A Reproducible Corpus and Tooling Substrate for Cybersecurity Literature Reviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18320)
*Sidnei Barbieri,Ágney Lopes Roth Ferraz,Lourenço Alves Pereira Júnior*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TopVenues is an open-source system that materializes cybersecurity literature corpus construction as a versioned, reproducible artifact. Using DBLP as a metadata spine and enriching records via scholarly APIs, it produces a monotonic SQLite snapshot with near-perfect abstract/BibTeX coverage, enabling repeatable measurements like preprint analysis and author-based filtering for literature reviews.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cybersecurity literature reviews lack a reproducible denominator—the fixed set of papers included before screening. Current approaches rely on publisher portals, bibliographic indices, and scholarly APIs whose coverage, formats, and query semantics drift over time, undermining auditability and replicability of systematic reviews and bibliometric measurements.

Method: TopVenues declares a venue and year scope, uses DBLP as a metadata spine, and enriches records with abstracts and BibTeX entries via open scholarly APIs (e.g., Crossref, Semantic Scholar) and publisher-specific extractors. Results are stored in a monotonic SQLite snapshot with a CLI, web interface, and export paths. A 250-test suite validates data-integrity invariants.

Result: The May 2026 snapshot contains 9,925 papers from 11 cybersecurity sources (2017–2026), achieving 99.86% abstract coverage and 99.99% BibTeX coverage. Keyword search completes in under 31 ms. Repeatable measurements show 29.2% of 2024–2025 top-venue papers appear as arXiv preprints (median 5 months before publication), and a prior-author-track-record filter yields a 16.5× precision gain at 90% recall for triaging preprints.

Conclusion: TopVenues links corpus construction to auditable cybersecurity measurement by making the corpus executable, inspectable, and citable, thereby establishing a reproducible foundation for systematic literature reviews and bibliometric studies in cybersecurity.

Abstract: Cybersecurity literature reviews require a reproducible denominator: the set of papers that a protocol includes before screening and synthesis begin. Today, that denominator is often reconstructed from publisher portals, bibliographic indices, and scholarly application programming interfaces (APIs) whose coverage, formats, and query semantics change over time. This paper presents TopVenues, an open-source system that materializes corpus construction as a versioned research artifact. TopVenues declares a venue and year scope, uses DBLP Computer Science Bibliography (DBLP) as the metadata spine, enriches records with abstracts and BibTeX entries via open scholarly APIs and publisher-specific extractors, and stores the results in a monotonic SQLite snapshot, accessible via a command-line interface (CLI), a web interface, and export paths for review workflows. The May 2026 snapshot contains 9,925 papers from 11 cybersecurity sources over 2017 to 2026, with 99.86% abstract coverage and 99.99% BibTeX coverage; keyword search over the full corpus completes in under 31 ms, and a 250-test suite validates the data-integrity invariants. The fixed denominator also enables repeatable measurement: 29.2% of 2024 to 2025 papers from the four top-ranked security conferences in our scope appear as arXiv preprints, with a median of five months before publication, and a prior-author-track-record filter yields a 16.5x precision gain at 90% recall for triaging preprints that later appear in the same venue set. TopVenues links corpus construction to auditable cybersecurity measurement by making the corpus itself executable, inspectable, and citable. The artifact is available at https://github.com/sidneibarbieri/topVenues.

</details>


### [126] [Agentra: A Supervisable Multi-Agent Framework for Enterprise Intrusion Response](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18325)
*Raj Patel,Shaswata Mitra,Michele Guida,Stefano Iannucci,Sudip Mittal,Shahram Rahimi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Agentra is a supervisable multi-agent IRS framework that converts IDS/EDR/XDR alerts into structured incident response plans using MITRE ATT&CK, D3FEND, and NIST CSF 2.0. A bounded Planner–Validator loop, Moderator gateway, Action Catalog, risk scoring, and append-only audit log ensure safe, auditable automation. Evaluation on 120 events shows FP-aware IRS F1 improvement from 0.61 to 0.84 while maintaining a 0.0% harmful-action rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise intrusion response remains bottlenecked by static playbooks and manual analyst triage, causing dangerous delays between alert generation and containment. Current automation approaches lack the reasoning flexibility to adapt to novel threats while maintaining safety, auditability, and analyst oversight—prompting the need for a supervisable, ontology-grounded multi-agent framework.

Method: Agentra decomposes response reasoning across role-scoped agents and employs a bounded Planner–Validator review loop to refine proposed response plans. A Moderator security gateway screens retrieved threat intelligence for safety, while an Action Catalog with risk scoring gates all executable actions. An append-only audit log records all decisions for traceability. The system is evaluated on a 120-event corpus from ThreatHunter-Playbook, Splunk BOTSv3, and DARPA OpTC, benchmarked against a static OASIS CACAO v2.0 playbook baseline.

Result: The strongest Agentra configuration improved FP-aware IRS F1 score from 0.61 (static baseline) to 0.84. Planner-only configurations introduced unsafe overreaction, but the full Agentra framework restored the projected harmful-action rate to the static baseline level of 0.0%. This demonstrates that multi-agent response planning can expand ontology-grounded IRS coverage without sacrificing safety or analyst approval.

Conclusion: Multi-agent, ontology-grounded IRS frameworks like Agentra can substantially improve incident response coverage over static playbooks while preserving the safety, auditability, and human oversight essential for enterprise security operations.

Abstract: Enterprise intrusion response still depends on static playbooks and analyst-driven triage, creating delay between alert generation and containment. We present Agentra, a supervisable multi-agent Intrusion Response System (IRS) framework that converts alerts from IDS, EDR, and XDR platforms into structured incident response plans grounded in MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE D3FEND, and NIST CSF 2.0. Agentra decomposes response reasoning across role-scoped agents, validates proposed plans through a bounded Planner--Validator review loop, screens retrieved threat intelligence through a Moderator security gateway, gates actions through an Action Catalog and risk score, and records decisions in an append-only audit log. We evaluate Agentra against a static OASIS CACAO v2.0 cyber-playbook baseline on a 120-event corpus drawn from ThreatHunter-Playbook, Splunk BOTSv3, and DARPA OpTC. The strongest configuration improves FP-aware IRS F1 from 0.61 to 0.84 and restores the projected harmful-action rate to the static baseline level of 0.0% after Planner-only configurations introduce unsafe overreaction. These results indicate that multi-agent response planning can improve ontology-grounded IRS coverage while preserving analyst approval and auditability.

</details>


### [127] [SafeClawBench: Separating Semantic, Audit-Evidence, and Sandbox Harm in Tool-Using LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18356)
*Yuchuan Tian,Mengyu Zheng,Haocheng Mei,Ye Yuan,Chao Xu,Xinghao Chen,Hanting Chen,Yu Wang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SafeClawBench is a staged benchmark with 600 adversarial tasks evaluating tool-using agent security across three distinct endpoints — semantic acceptance, audited harm evidence, and sandbox-observed harm — revealing that these stages capture different failure modes and that models can produce observable harm even when passing semantic checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of tool-using LM agent security collapse multiple attack stages into a single success rate, conflating mere textual agreement with actual observable harm. This makes it impossible to distinguish whether a model simply agreed with an attacker or genuinely produced harmful tool effects and state changes.

Method: The authors introduce SafeClawBench, a benchmark comprising 600 controlled adversarial tasks spanning six attack families (direct/indirect prompt injection, tool-return injection, memory poisoning, memory extraction, ambiguity-driven unsafe inference). It reports outcomes at three staged endpoints: (1) semantic attack acceptance, (2) audit-visible harm evidence, and (3) sandbox-observed tool/state harm. Five agent endpoints are evaluated under four prompt-level policies, with a 12,000-row matched analysis comparing semantic check results against sandbox harm observations.

Result: Semantic failure rates vary widely across models (9.0%–44.2%). Audited harm evidence is narrower than semantic failure. Critically, 291 of 347 observed sandbox harms occurred in rows that passed the semantic check, demonstrating that semantic safety does not guarantee executable safety. Prompt policies shift endpoint outcomes, but effects depend on both model and protocol.

Conclusion: SafeClawBench provides a reproducible, multi-stage framework for comparing agent models and prompt-policy conditions without conflating textual compliance, evidence-supported harm, and executable state changes. The three-endpoint design reveals that safety evaluations must go beyond semantic checks to capture real-world tool-execution risks.

Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents introduce security failures that go beyond unsafe text: they can disclose protected objects, write persistent memory, send messages, modify databases, or trigger harmful code and tool effects. Existing evaluations often collapse these stages into a single attack success rate, making it difficult to tell whether a model merely agreed with an attacker or actually produced observable harm. We introduce SafeClawBench, a staged benchmark for tool-using agent security with 600 controlled adversarial tasks across six attack families: direct and indirect prompt injection, tool-return injection, memory poisoning, memory extraction, and ambiguity-driven unsafe inference. SafeClawBench reports three separate endpoints: semantic attack acceptance, audit-visible harm evidence, and sandbox-observed tool/state harm. Evaluating five agent endpoints under four prompt-level policies, we find that these endpoints capture different failure modes. Without additional prompt protection, semantic failure rates vary widely across models, from 9.0% to 44.2%. Audited harm evidence is narrower than semantic failure, and under a separate executable protocol some matched task identities produce sandbox harm despite passing the Semantic Core call: in a 12,000-row matched analysis, 291 of 347 observed sandbox harms occur in rows that pass the semantic check. Prompt policies change endpoint outcomes, but their effects depend on both model and protocol. SafeClawBench provides a reproducible framework for comparing agent models and prompt-policy conditions without conflating textual compliance, evidence-supported harm, and executable state changes. The open-source dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sairights/safeclawbench.

</details>


### [128] [Evaluating the Effectiveness of LLMs in Aiding Compliance Testing of PKCS#1-v1.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18405)
*Polina Kozyreva,Endadul Hoque*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper investigates using grammar-level mutation with LLM-based code synthesis for binary protocol specification compliance testing, evaluated on PKCS#1 v1.5 signature verification across 48 cryptographic libraries. The approach reproduced 10 of 13 previously known non-trivial specification violation categories and found 1 new discrepancy. LLM hallucination (82.5% of scripts) was the primary limiting factor, with structural mutations achieving only 13.3% fidelity versus 30.3% for constraint mutations. A sharp gap between operational reliability (99.8%) and semantic fidelity (17.5%) was identified.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Testing binary protocol implementations for specification compliance is challenging because purely random generation and primitive mutations fail to explore semantically meaningful behaviors, particularly in TLV-encoded protocols. Domain-specific compliance testing tools demand deep protocol expertise and significant manual effort. The authors investigate whether grammar-level mutation combined with LLM-based code synthesis offers a more generalizable alternative.

Method: Grammar-level mutation strategies combined with LLM-based code synthesis were applied to generate specification-compliance tests. The approach was evaluated on PKCS#1 v1.5 signature verification (a TLV-encoded standard) against 48 cryptographic library implementations. Results were validated using Morpheus, a formally verified testing oracle.

Result: The method reproduced 10 of 13 non-trivial specification violation categories (including all 5 signature forgery categories) and discovered 1 previously unreported discrepancy. LLM hallucination occurred in 82.5% of generated scripts. Five distinct hallucination types were identified with systematic distribution differences: structural mutations had 13.3% implementation fidelity, while constraint mutations achieved 30.3% correctness but suffered 8.1% of mutations being entirely ignored. Operational reliability reached 99.8%, but semantic fidelity was only 17.5%.

Conclusion: LLM-based code synthesis shows promise for specification compliance testing but is severely limited by hallucination. The striking gap between operational reliability and semantic fidelity provides actionable guidance on when LLM-synthesized code can be trusted in specification-driven testing pipelines. Effectiveness depends more on managing hallucination than on mutation strategy design.

Abstract: Testing implementations of binary protocols for specification compliance requires inputs that satisfy both structural and semantic constraints. Purely random generation and primitive mutations are often insufficient for exploring semantically meaningful behaviors in protocols that rely on Type-Length-Value (TLV) encoding, yet domain-specific compliance testing tools require deep protocol expertise and significant manual effort to construct. This work investigates whether grammar-level mutation combined with LLM-based code synthesis can serve as a viable, more generalizable approach to specification compliance testing.
  We evaluate the approach on PKCS#1 v1.5 signature verification -- a widely deployed TLV-encoded standard with a formally verified testing oracle (Morpheus) -- across 48 cryptographic library implementations. We reproduced 10 of 13 non-trivial specification violation categories previously identified by Morpheus, including all 5 signature forgery categories, and discovered 1 previously unreported discrepancy. We found that LLM hallucination -- occurring in 82.5% of generated scripts -- is the primary factor limiting effectiveness, not the mutation strategies. We identify five distinct hallucination types and show that their distribution varies systematically across mutation categories: structural mutations are implemented with 13.3% fidelity while constraint mutations achieve 30.3% correctness but suffer the highest rate of mutations being fully ignored (8.1%). These findings reveal a striking gap between operational reliability (99.8%) and semantic fidelity (17.5%), providing actionable guidance on when LLM-based code synthesis can be trusted in specification-driven testing pipelines.

</details>


### [129] [Understanding the "Airport" Censorship Circumvention Ecosystem in China](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18427)
*Rumaisa Habib,Mingshi Wu,Shiva Shahandeh,Min Ni,Eric Wustrow,Zakir Durumeric*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A systematic study of China's underground "airport" ecosystem — subscription-based censorship circumvention proxies that are the most popular off-the-shelf circumvention tool among Chinese users, offering ease of use and high performance via multi-hop architecture, but introducing new security risks, fragility, and distinct censorship policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the widespread use of censorship circumvention tools in China, no prior research has systematically examined the underground "airport" ecosystem — a commercially operated, subscription-based proxy market. Understanding its scale, popularity, architecture, and risks is essential for informing future circumvention research and policy.

Method: A mixed-methods approach combining: (1) user surveys (n=1,667) to gauge adoption and user perceptions; (2) social media analysis on platforms like Telegram to map the ecosystem; (3) active network measurements, including Internet scanning and Telegram channel scraping to identify 3,431 active airports; and (4) direct subscriptions to 35 airports for performance characterization.

Result: Over 50% of survey respondents use airports, citing ease of use, performance, and access to geo-restricted services (ChatGPT, Netflix). A total of 3,431 active airports were identified, built on a few open-source toolkits. Subscribed airports often outperform direct GFW connections due to a distinctive multi-hop architecture. However, airports rely on commercial payment services (e.g., Alipay), face frequent government takedowns, present configuration difficulties for clients, and many impose their own censorship policies.

Conclusion: Airports represent the dominant practical circumvention tool in China, far exceeding academic tools in adoption. However, their commercial nature introduces new forms of fragility, centralized control, and security risks. These characteristics offer both lessons for designing more usable circumvention tools and opportunities for advancing censorship-resistant network research.

Abstract: In China, a burgeoning underground market sells citizens subscription-based censorship circumvention proxies known as ''airports''. We present the first systematic study of this ecosystem, combining user surveys, social media analysis, and active network measurements. We find that airports are by far the most popular off-the-shelf censorship circumvention tool in China, used by over half of our 1,667~survey respondents, who cite their ease of use, performance, and access to geo-restricted services like ChatGPT and Netflix. By scanning the Internet and scraping Telegram announcement channels, we identify 3,431 active airports built on a handful of open-source toolkits. We subscribe to 35 airports and characterize their performance, which often surpasses direct connections through the Great Firewall due to a distinctive multi-hop architecture. However, airports also pose new challenges and security risks: they accept payment through commercial services like Alipay, suffer frequent government takedowns, and are difficult for clients to configure optimally. Many airports also deploy their own distinct censorship policies. Airports are far more widely used than other circumvention tools from the academic literature, but introduce new forms of fragility and control, offering both lessons and opportunities for future circumvention research.

</details>


### [130] [Ghost Vectors: Soft-Deleted Embeddings Remain Reconstructible in HNSW Vector Databases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18497)
*Chandranil Chakraborttii,Jackeline García Alvarado,Sitora Abdulofizova,Shivanshu Dwivedi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper reveals that soft-deleted vectors in HNSW-based RAG systems remain physically recoverable from raw index files, enabling reconstruction of sensitive data (PII, faces, medical info) via inversion models. The authors propose Epoch Key Rotation, an encryption-based deletion mechanism with cryptographic proof, which reduces PII recovery to 0%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern RAG systems using HNSW vector databases only mark deleted records rather than physically removing embeddings, creating compliance risks under GDPR Article 17 (right to erasure) and HIPAA. The authors aim to empirically demonstrate the severity of this soft-delete vulnerability and propose a practical countermeasure.

Method: The authors analyze three HNSW implementations (Faiss, Hnswlib, pgvector), then apply the Vec2Text inversion model without domain-specific fine-tuning to recover data from soft-deleted embeddings across multiple modalities: text (Wikipedia BLP, NIH Synthea), images (histopathology patches, facial embeddings). They propose Epoch Key Rotation — encrypting vectors at insertion and discarding the encryption key upon deletion, complemented by ECDSA-signed cryptographic proofs for auditable deletion records.

Result: Text recovery: 25.5% exact person names and 46.4% geographic locations (ROUGE-L 0.185) on BLP; 100% recovery of patient age/gender (ROUGE-L 0.290) on NIH Synthea. Image recovery: 100% tissue classification on histopathology (p=1.02e-07); 99% top-1 identity recovery on facial embeddings (p<0.01). Epoch Key Rotation reduces PII recovery to 0% and completes in ~2.5 ms for 500 deleted vectors (~0.005 ms/record).

Conclusion: Soft-delete in vector databases is a significant compliance vulnerability, as deleted embeddings remain physically accessible and recoverable via inversion attacks across modalities. Epoch Key Rotation provides a practical, low-overhead solution that cryptographically ensures unrecoverability and generates auditable deletion proofs, satisfying GDPR and HIPAA obligations.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) allows large language models to access external and private corpora for factual, domain-specific responses. Modern RAG pipelines use hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW) vector databases for efficient similarity search. When a user requests data deletion, the systems typically only mark the record as deleted, leaving the embedding on disk physically unchanged. This soft-delete operation raises compliance concerns under data-erasure and retention requirements such as GDPR Article 17 and HIPAA. Analysis on three HNSW implementations confirms that deleted vectors remain physically recoverable by accessing the raw index files at the storage layer, bypassing API access. Using the Vec2Text inversion model without domain-specific fine-tuning, we show this vulnerability on multiple real-world datasets and data modalities. On Wikipedia biographical living persons dataset (BLP), we successfully recover 25.5% of exact person names and 46.4% of geographic locations (ROUGE-L 0.185). Recovery reaches 100% for both patient age and gender markers (ROUGE-L 0.290) on highly structured, sensitive data (NIH Synthea dataset). On soft-deleted image embeddings, we show 100% tissue classification on histopathology patches (p=1.02e-07) and top-1 identity recovery reaches 99% on facial embeddings (p<0.01). This work introduces Epoch Key Rotation, which encrypts vectors and discards the key upon deletion. Epoch key rotation reduces observed PII recovery to 0% and completes in 2.5 ms for 500 deleted vectors (approximately 0.005 ms/record). Additionally, it generates an ECDSA-signed cryptographic proof as an auditable record of the deletion event.

</details>


### [131] [From Bits to Mixed-Radix Keys: Horner Decomposition, Uniform Sampling, and the Information-Theoretic QKD Interface of the MR-OTP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18526)
*Fabio F. G. Buono*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper extends the classical One-Time Pad to mixed-radix (heterogeneous) alphabets, providing a bias-free method to convert binary entropy from QKD sources into uniform mixed-radix keys using Horner's method and rejection sampling, with proven information-theoretic security and efficiency guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical OTP assumes a single, homogeneous alphabet (typically binary), but real-world applications often involve heterogeneous alphabets (e.g., alphanumeric symbols with different modulus sizes). Naively extending OTP to mixed-radix settings via modular reduction introduces statistical bias, compromising perfect secrecy. There is a need for a principled, provably bias-free method to convert raw binary entropy (e.g., from QKD) into uniform mixed-radix keys.

Method: The authors identify Horner's method (polynomial evaluation) and its inverse as the natural mapping between binary integers and mixed-radix tuples. To eliminate bias from naive modular reduction, they employ rejection sampling and prove it restores uniformity with optimal expected cost. They also present a batched extractor for efficiency, establish end-to-end information-theoretic security proofs for both single- and multi-session pipelines, and analyze the Base Recovery Problem.

Result: The proposed method achieves uniform mixed-radix key generation from binary entropy without bias, preserving perfect secrecy. Rejection sampling is proven to be optimal in expected cost. Efficiency gains are quantified, and both unconditional and conditional hardness results for the Base Recovery Problem are provided.

Conclusion: MR-OTP is a viable and provably secure extension of the classical OTP to heterogeneous alphabets. The combination of Horner's method for mapping and rejection sampling for debiasing yields a practical, information-theoretically secure pipeline suitable for QKD-sourced key material, with formal guarantees of both security and efficiency.

Abstract: The Mixed-Radix One-Time Pad (MR-OTP) extends the classical OTP to heterogeneous alphabets while preserving perfect secrecy. We provide a practical, bias-free method to convert raw binary entropy from a QKD source into uniform mixed-radix keys by identifying Horner's method and its inverse as the natural mapping between binary integers and mixed-radix tuples. We show that naive modular reduction induces bias and prove that rejection sampling restores uniformity with optimal expected cost. We establish end-to-end information-theoretic security for single and multi-session pipelines, quantify efficiency gains, present a batched extractor, and give unconditional and conditional results on the Base Recovery Problem.

</details>


### [132] [Evaluating Prompting-Based Defenses Against Domain-Camouflaged Injection Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18530)
*Aaditya Pai*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Evaluates five prompting-based defenses against domain-camouflaged injection attacks across three LLM families and three domains (3,510 trials). Paraphrasing is the most effective defense (55-84% reduction), but effectiveness is strongly model-dependent; financial domain carries highest residual risk (26-33%). First systematic benchmark of defenses against camouflage-class injections.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Domain-camouflaged injection attacks use domain-appropriate vocabulary to hide malicious instructions in retrieved content, evading standard detectors that rely on syntactic injection markers. When detection fails, practitioners lack guidance on which defense architectures actually reduce attack success. This work fills that gap.

Method: 3,510 trials across three model families (Claude Haiku, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemini 2.0 Flash), three deployment domains (financial, legal, general), and five prompting-based defenses: spotlighting, paraphrasing, prompt sandwiching, and two combinatorial approaches. All tasks use synthetically constructed professional documents. Llama Guard 4 serves as a detection baseline comparator.

Result: Paraphrasing retrieved content before agent processing is the most consistently effective defense, reducing camouflage attack success rate by 55–84% depending on model, and outperforms Llama Guard 4 on every model tested. Spotlighting halves attack success on Claude Haiku but provides no benefit on Llama 3.1 8B. Financial domain faces 26–33% baseline attack success, with no prompting defense fully eliminating the threat on weaker models.

Conclusion: Prompting-based defenses can substantially mitigate domain-camouflaged injection attacks, but effectiveness varies sharply by model and domain. Paraphrasing is the strongest single defense. Benchmark-based recommendations are provided for practitioners, though generalizability to real enterprise documents remains an open question.

Abstract: Domain-camouflaged injection attacks embed malicious instructions in retrieved content using domain-appropriate vocabulary, evading standard detectors that rely on syntactic injection markers. When detection fails, practitioners need to know which defense architectures reduce attack success. We evaluate five prompting-based defenses (spotlighting, paraphrasing, prompt sandwiching, and two combinations) against domain-camouflaged injection across three model families (Claude Haiku, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemini 2.0 Flash) and three deployment domains (financial, legal, general) using 3,510 trials. Paraphrasing retrieved content before agent processing is the most consistently effective defense in this benchmark, reducing camouflage attack success rate by 55-84\% depending on model, and achieves lower attack success rates than our Llama Guard 4 configuration on every model tested. Defense effectiveness is strongly model-dependent: spotlighting halves attack success on Claude Haiku but provides no benefit on Llama 3.1 8B. Financial domain deployments face the highest residual risk at 26-33\% baseline attack success rate, with no prompting-based defense fully eliminating the threat on weaker models. These results provide the first systematic evaluation of prompting-based defenses specifically against camouflage-class injection attacks and establish benchmark-based recommendations for practitioners. All tasks use synthetically constructed professional documents; whether these benchmark rankings generalize to real enterprise documents remains an open question.

</details>


### [133] [AI Sandboxes: A Threat Model, Taxonomy, and Measurement Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18532)
*Inderjeet Singh,Haitham Mahmoud,Andrés Murillo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper formalizes AI sandboxes as controlled environments for testing across digital, embodied, and cyber-physical systems. It introduces a sandbox boundary formalization, a weakest-link composition rule for evidence, a taxonomy of sandbox archetypes, a cyber-physical threat model covering attacks on assurance apparatus, and a measurement framework (fidelity, controllability, observability, containment, reproducibility, governance) validated through three case studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI systems are increasingly evaluated in bounded, instrumented environments, especially for physical AI, AIoT, and cyber-physical systems where sensing, actuation, and failure involve physical processes and human operators. Existing approaches lack a principled, assurance-oriented account of what sandboxes can validly test, which risks they contain, and what evidence they support — creating gaps for safety, security, and regulatory claims.

Method: The authors (1) formalize a sandbox boundary and a weakest-link rule for composing per-dimension evidence into bounded deployment claims; (2) separate major sandbox archetypes; (3) define a cyber-physical threat model that includes attacks on the assurance apparatus itself; and (4) introduce a six-dimensional measurement framework (fidelity, controllability, observability, containment, reproducibility, governance artifacts), instantiated on three real-world worked case studies.

Result: The framework yields a systematic taxonomy for classifying sandbox types, a threat model that surfaces risks to the testing apparatus, and measurement dimensions that characterize the evidentiary strength of sandbox-based evaluations. Three case studies demonstrate practical instantiation of the framework on real sandboxes, showing how per-dimension evidence composes into a defensible bounded deployment claim.

Conclusion: The proposed threat model, taxonomy, and measurement framework clarify the valid scope, risk containment limits, and evidential support capabilities of AI sandboxes for safety, security, and regulatory assurance. The weakest-link composition rule provides a principled basis for reasoning about when sandbox evidence suffices for bounded deployment decisions in cyber-physical contexts.

Abstract: AI systems are increasingly evaluated in bounded environments that combine isolation, simulation, instrumentation, supervision, and evidence capture. For physical AI, AIoT, and cyber-physical systems, this shift is not a matter of terminology: the system under test may sense, decide, actuate, communicate, and fail through physical processes, networked devices, and human operators. This article develops an assurance-oriented account of AI sandboxes as controlled environments for testing, evaluation, verification, and validation across digital AI, embodied autonomy, and cyber-physical deployments. We formalize the sandbox boundary and a weakest-link rule for composing per-dimension evidence into a bounded deployment claim; separate major sandbox archetypes; define a cyber-physical threat model that includes attacks on the assurance apparatus itself; and introduce a measurement framework spanning fidelity, controllability, observability, containment, reproducibility, and governance artifacts, instantiated on three worked case studies of real sandboxes. The resulting threat model, taxonomy, and measurement framework clarify what a sandbox can validly test, which risks it can contain, and what forms of evidence it can support for safety, security, and regulatory assurance.

</details>


### [134] [Confident yet Concerned: Inconsistencies in Computing Students' Attitudes on Cybersecurity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18541)
*Victor Adama,Robert Biddle,Nalin Arachchilage,Danielle Lottridge*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A survey of 236 computing university students reveals that even tech-savvy young adults hold persistent misconceptions about cybersecurity, learn safety practices primarily outside formal education, and fall into two attitudinal clusters differentiated by confidence and self-efficacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Young adults, despite being heavy technology users, feel powerless managing online privacy and are vulnerable to phishing. The study aims to understand how this demographic—specifically computing students as "lead users"—approaches cybersecurity knowledge, attitudes, and experiences, particularly regarding deceptive online communications.

Method: A mixed-methods survey (n = 236) of computing university students, combining thematic analysis of open-ended responses with quantitative data including cluster analysis of attitudes, correlation of established measures (intentions, objective knowledge, self-efficacy) with preparedness and confidence, and regression to predict cluster membership.

Result: Four thematic tensions emerged: (1) knowledgeable yet persistently incorrect beliefs; (2) safety learning occurs outside the classroom; (3) limited assistance and victimization experiences; (4) confidence coexisting with concern about safety and responsibility. Cluster analysis identified two groups—one less prepared and confident but wanting to learn more. Self-efficacy correlated with confidence and predicted cluster membership, while intentions and objective knowledge correlated with preparedness.

Conclusion: Even computing students exhibit inconsistent cybersecurity practices and perceptions, with significant gaps in formal education and support structures. Self-efficacy emerges as a key psychological factor distinguishing confident from non-confident users, suggesting that interventions should target both knowledge and self-efficacy to improve cybersecurity behaviors.

Abstract: Today's young adults are most immersed in technology, leading in feelings of powerlessness in managing online privacy across many platforms, and particularly susceptible to phishing attacks. This raises questions about their general, wide-ranging attitudes towards and management of cybersecurity. How do young, tech-savvy adults approach cybersecurity? We seek a better understanding of their cybersecurity knowledge, attitudes and experiences, in particular in addressing deceptive online communications. We surveyed a group of `lead users': computing university students (n = 236). By combining thematic analysis of open-ended responses with quantitative data, we provide insights into their experiences and perceptions. While students demonstrate reasonable cybersecurity awareness, their cybersecurity experiences vary, and inconsistencies exist around their practices, perceptions of responsibility, and support structures. Findings also reveal four key thematic tensions: 1) Computing students are knowledgeable yet have persistent incorrect beliefs, 2) They learn more about keeping safe from sources outside the classroom, 3) They have limited assistance and have fallen victim to cybercrime, and 4) Many are confident, yet others are concerned about their own safety and responsibility. Through cluster analysis of attitudes, we identify two groups, with one feeling less prepared, less confident, yet expressing a desire to learn more. Established measures of intentions and objective knowledge were correlated to preparedness. Self-efficacy correlated to confidence and predicted cluster membership.

</details>


### [135] [The Gate Is Only as Honest as Its Contracts: ContractGuard for the Contract Layer of Risk-Aware Causal Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18550)
*Laxmipriya Ganesh Iyer,Rahul Suresh Babu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: RACG defends tool-augmented LLM agents against indirect prompt injection by structurally removing dangerous tools from the agent's visible action space. The paper argues that the critical trust assumption shifts to tool contract integrity — specifically effect integrity, not risk labels. ContractGuard, a layered verifier, restores injection success to zero across all tested attacks and six hosted models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Indirect prompt injection attacks can manipulate tool-augmented LLM agents into invoking dangerous tools. Prior defenses rely on the agent's compliance with safety filtering, which is fragile. RACG aims to provide a structural guarantee by removing dangerous tools from the action space entirely, but this relocates the trust assumption to the integrity of tool contracts (preconditions, effects, risk, authorization). The paper investigates which contract element is load-bearing for security and how to protect it.

Method: The proposed system, Risk-Aware Causal Gating (RACG), operates a two-stage gate: a causal gate (which verifies whether a tool lies on a valid causal path) followed by an admissibility gate. The paper formally analyzes the relative danger of forging effect declarations versus risk labels, demonstrating that effect integrity is the load-bearing assumption. To enforce this, the authors introduce ContractGuard — a verifier layered between the registry and gate that combines signed provenance, typed contract attestation, and runtime effect verification. The approach is evaluated on a controlled benchmark against exhaustive white-box adaptive attackers and validated on six hosted LLMs.

Result: ContractGuard restores injection success to zero against every modeled attack, including an exhaustive white-box adaptive attacker, without over-rejecting honest contracts. The structural prediction — that effect integrity is the critical assumption — is confirmed empirically across all six tested models: Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova Premier, Nova 2 Lite, and GPT-OSS-120B.

Conclusion: RACG provides a structural defense by shrinking the agent's action space, but its security hinges on contract integrity — specifically the integrity of declared tool effects, not risk labels. ContractGuard successfully enforces this integrity through provenance, attestation, and runtime verification, achieving zero injection success across diverse models and attack strategies.

Abstract: Risk-Aware Causal Gating (RACG) defends tool-augmented LLM agents against indirect prompt injection by removing dangerous tools from the agent's visible action space, so that even a fully injection-compliant agent cannot call a tool it cannot see. We make three points. First, this structural guarantee does not eliminate the trust assumption behind safe tool use; it relocates it into the integrity of the tool contracts -- declared preconditions, effects, risk, and authorization -- that the gate reads, so an attacker who corrupts a contract can make the gate mis-decide without ever persuading the agent. Second, forging a tool's effects is strictly more dangerous than tampering with its risk label, because RACG applies a causal gate before its admissibility gate: an off-path tool is never exposed, so risk-relabeling alone fails, whereas effect forgery routes the dangerous tool onto the causal path and succeeds. Effect integrity, not the risk label, is the load-bearing assumption. Third, we introduce ContractGuard, a verifier between the registry and the gate that layers signed provenance, typed contract attestation, and runtime effect verification; on a controlled benchmark it restores injection success to zero against every modeled attack -- including an exhaustive white-box adaptive attacker -- without over-rejecting honest contracts, and the structural prediction is confirmed on six current-generation hosted models (Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5; Amazon Nova Premier and Nova 2 Lite; GPT-OSS-120B).

</details>


### [136] [MIDS: Detecting Stealthy Masquerade and Tampering Attacks on CAN Bus via Bidirectional Mamba](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18599)
*Qiqi Liu,Runhan Song,Lei Cui,Heng Zhang,Yuyan Sun,Limin Sun*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MIDS is a dual-stream intrusion detection system for CAN bus that uses bidirectional state-space models to detect masquerade attacks—where an adversary replaces legitimate frames in-situ—achieving 96.94% F1 on a Tesla Model 3 dataset and outperforming baselines by 8+ points, with sub-1.2ms inference latency suitable for real-time deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CAN intrusion detection systems focus on injection-style attacks (DoS, fuzzing, spoofing) that disrupt traffic periodicity, making detection straightforward via inter-arrival statistics. However, masquerade attacks—where an internal adversary replaces a legitimate frame at its original transmission slot—preserve traffic patterns and render statistical defenses ineffective. This harder threat model lacks adequate detection solutions.

Method: MIDS employs a dual-stream architecture that processes CAN identifiers and payloads in parallel, using bidirectional selective state-space modeling (Mamba) to reconstruct joint temporal semantics. The system captures subtle anomalies in the combined ID-data temporal structure that masquerade attacks disturb, even when per-ID traffic statistics remain unchanged.

Result: On a real Tesla Model 3 dataset (100M+ frames, 3 driving regimes, 54 masquerade variants), MIDS achieves 96.94% F1, exceeding the best reproducible baseline by >8 percentage points, with 1.147ms single-window inference latency. On four public benchmarks (ROAD, CrySyS, OTIDS, CT&T), MIDS reaches 93.70–99.61% F1, outperforming eight reproduced baselines by up to 13.94 points under unified 5-fold evaluation.

Conclusion: MIDS demonstrates that bidirectional state-space modeling of joint ID-payload temporal semantics effectively detects masquerade attacks on CAN bus, achieving state-of-the-art performance with real-time inference latency. The dual-stream Mamba architecture generalizes well across diverse datasets and attack scenarios, offering a practical onboard IDS solution for modern vehicles.

Abstract: The Controller Area Network (CAN) protocol is the primary communication standard for Electronic Control Units (ECUs) in modern vehicles, but its lack of encryption and authentication exposes it to a range of security threats. Existing intrusion detection systems are largely tuned to fabrication-style attacks (DoS, fuzzing, ID spoofing realised by frame injection), in which detection signals such as per-ID inter-arrival statistics are readily available. We instead address the harder \emph{masquerade} setting~\cite{b37}, in which an internal adversary substitutes a legitimate frame in-situ at its original transmission slot, preserving traffic periodicity and rendering traffic-statistic defences ineffective. We propose the Mamba Intrusion Detection System (MIDS), an innovative dual-stream framework that processes CAN identifiers and payloads in parallel and reconstructs their joint temporal semantics through bidirectional selective state-space modelling. To evaluate MIDS, we collected over 100 million CAN frames from a physical Tesla Model 3 across three driving regimes and synthesised 54 masquerade attack variants spanning ID-only, data-only, and combined modifications. MIDS attains an F1 of 96.94\% on this dataset, exceeding the strongest reproducible baseline by more than 8 percentage points, while sustaining a 1.147~ms single-window inference latency -- ample headroom for real-time onboard deployment. To verify generalisation, we further evaluate MIDS on four public benchmarks (ROAD, CrySyS, OTIDS, CT\&T) covering both masquerade and injection scenarios; MIDS attains F1 from 93.70\% to 99.61\%, outperforming the strongest of eight reproduced baselines by up to 13.94 percentage points under a unified 5-fold protocol.

</details>


### [137] [Code-Augur: Agentic Vulnerability Detection via Specification Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18619)
*Zhengxiong Luo,Mehtab Zafar,Dylan Wolff,Abhik Roychoudhury*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Code-Augur proposes a security-specification-first paradigm for agentic vulnerability detection that makes LLM agents' tacit assumptions explicit as in-source assertions, then continuously refines them via runtime fuzzing. It found 22 new vulnerabilities in open-source projects and outperforms state-of-the-art agents using widely available LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous LLM agents are discovering long-hidden vulnerabilities in critical software, but their reasoning remains opaque and unvalidated. Incorrect assumptions can lead to missed vulnerabilities and erode trust in agentic analysis.

Method: Code-Augur introduces a two-phase approach: (1) an LLM agent analyzes code, explicitly commits its local invariants as in-source assertions when it deems a component secure, and (2) a guided fuzzer attempts to falsify those assertions. When assertions are triggered, this reveals either a genuine vulnerability or a flawed specification to refine, grounding the agent's understanding against actual code behavior.

Result: Code-Augur detected more vulnerabilities than other state-of-the-art agents on real-world subjects, discovered 22 new vulnerabilities in key open-source projects, and offers effective agentic vulnerability detection using widely available LLMs (Sonnet, DeepSeek) rather than requiring curated specialized models like Claude Mythos.

Conclusion: The security-specification-first paradigm, combining explicit specification generation with runtime falsification, provides a more trustworthy and effective approach to agentic vulnerability detection than purely reasoning-based agent methods.

Abstract: The advent of agentic vulnerability detection is already becoming a watershed moment for software security.
