Audits conducted entirely by autonomous LLM agents are uncovering critical vulnerabilities in fundamental software underpinning digital society. Many of these vulnerabilities remained masked for years, surfacing only now with AI agents. Yet the reasoning behind these discoveries remains alarmingly opaque and unvalidated. What assumptions did the agent make about a function's inputs when it deemed that function to be secure? Failures in reasoning and incorrect assumptions can lead to missed vulnerabilities and reduce trust in agentic analysis.
  We propose a security-specification-first paradigm that (1) exposes the agent's tacit assumptions explicitly as security specifications and (2) continuously refines those specifications via runtime falsification. We realize our approach in Code-Augur, a novel harness for agentic vulnerability detection. Given a codebase, Code-Augur analyzes each component of the system for vulnerable code. When it deems a component to be secure, it commits the local invariants behind that judgment as in-source assertions. In parallel, Code-Augur leverages a guided fuzzer to attempt to falsify those assumptions. When the fuzzer triggers an assertion, this either reveals a genuine vulnerability or a flawed specification to refine. In both cases, this process grounds the agent's understanding, aligning its view of code intent with how the code actually behaves. On real-world subjects, Code-Augur effectively leverages security specifications to detect more vulnerabilities than other state-of-the-art agents. Additionally, Code-Augur found 22 new vulnerabilities in key open-source projects. Compared to curated specialized models like Claude Mythos, Code-Augur offers effective agentic vulnerability detection built on widely available LLMs like Sonnet and DeepSeek.

</details>


### [138] [TGCM: Topic-Guided Generative Disentanglement of Interleaved APT Technique Sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18651)
*Guo-Wei Wong,Ming-Chuan Yang,Shou-De Lin,Wang-Chien Lee,Meng~Chang Chen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TGCM is a generative framework that uses Consistency Models with MITRE ATT&CK topic priors to disentangle interleaved APT campaign sequences, jointly inferring the number of campaigns and technique assignments. It achieves state-of-the-art separation performance and zero-shot generalization on DARPA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise audit logs often contain interleaved traces from multiple concurrent APT campaigns, creating an Unknown-K Interleaved Sequence Demixing (UKISD) problem. Existing methods assume single-campaign settings or rely on rigid heuristics, failing under realistic conditions with overlapping campaigns, shared techniques, and variable execution lengths.

Method: TGCM (Topic-Guided Consistency Modeling) is a generative disentanglement framework that learns a direct inverse mapping from interleaved multi-campaign observations to structured single-campaign sequences in a single inference step using Consistency Models. It incorporates a topic-guided prior derived from MITRE ATT&CK narratives to provide high-level tactical constraints that favor semantically coherent attack chains during decomposition.

Result: TGCM demonstrates improved separation robustness over 15 baselines (spanning pattern mining, deep learning, and LLM-based methods) under heavy interleaving and technique sharing on synthetic, mixed, and DARPA TC-E3 datasets. It also achieves zero-shot generalization to the naturally interleaved DARPA TC-E5 benchmark without retraining.

Conclusion: TGCM effectively addresses the UKISD problem by combining consistency-based generative modeling with domain-aware topic priors, enabling robust multi-campaign disentanglement even under challenging real-world conditions such as zero-shot transfer to unseen interleaved attack traces.

Abstract: In enterprise environments, multiple Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) campaigns often unfold concurrently, producing audit logs in which attack techniques across actors (sources) are interleaved over time. This setting naturally gives rise to an Unknown-K Interleaved Sequence Demixing (UKISD) problem: recovering multiple latent campaigns from an interleaved technique sequence while jointly inferring their number and technique-level assignments. Existing approaches, ranging from statistical pattern mining to provenance-based analysis, typically assume single-campaign settings or rely on rigid heuristics, limiting their effectiveness under realistic conditions involving overlapping campaigns, shared techniques, and variable execution lengths.
  We present Topic-Guided Consistency Modeling (TGCM), a generative disentanglement framework to tackle the UKSID problem. TGCM leverages Consistency Models to learn a direct inverse mapping from interleaved multi-campaign observations to structured single-campaign sequences in a single inference step. To favor semantically coherent attack chains, TGCM incorporates a topic-guided prior derived from MITRE ATT\&CK narratives, providing high-level tactical constraints during decomposition. We evaluate TGCM on synthetic datasets, established mixed datasets, and incident traces from DARPA TC-E3 and TC-E5, comparing against 15 representative baselines spanning pattern mining, deep learning, and LLM-based methods. Results indicate improved separation robustness over baselines under heavy interleaving and technique sharing, and show that TGCM generalizes zero-shot to a naturally interleaved in-the-wild benchmark (DARPA TC-E5) without retraining.

</details>


### [139] [Understanding and Mitigating Prompt Leaking Attacks in Real-World LLM-Based Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18673)
*Yong Yang,Chong Fu,Tong Zhang,Rui Zeng,Qingming Li,Tianyu Du,Zonghui Wang,Shouling Ji,Wenzhi Chen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A systematic study of 1,200 real-world LLM applications reveals over 80% leak their system prompts under adversarial queries. The authors identify "attention drift" as the mechanistic cause—where query-key alignment bias and softmax amplification cause models to ignore defenses. They propose AREA, an attention re-anchoring defense that matches state-of-the-art leakage resistance while improving usability by 33% and reducing optimization overhead by nearly 3x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: System prompts in LLM-based applications encode core logic and constraints, constituting valuable intellectual property. While prompt leaking attacks are known in controlled settings, their real-world prevalence, underlying causes, and effective defenses remain poorly understood. The authors aim to systematically characterize this threat in production deployments and develop a practical defense that does not sacrifice usability.

Method: The study proceeds in four phases: (1) large-scale measurement of 1,200 LLM applications across six commercial platforms using realistic adversarial queries to assess leakage prevalence; (2) evaluation of existing defenses (e.g., prompt hardening, output filtering) against leakage-usability trade-offs; (3) attention-level mechanistic analysis using probing and causal intervention to diagnose why defenses fail, revealing "attention drift" driven by query-key alignment bias and softmax amplification; (4) design and evaluation of AREA, a defense that re-anchors model attention via an optimizable soft prompt, assessed through experiments and real-world case studies.

Result: Over 80% of the 1,200 measured applications leaked system prompts, with some exposing sensitive data like third-party API keys. Existing defenses frequently failed to prevent leakage without degrading usability. Mechanistic analysis identified attention drift as the root failure mode. AREA matched the leakage resistance of state-of-the-art defenses while improving average usability by over 33% and reducing optimization overhead by nearly 3×. Responsible disclosure led two vendors to classify these leaks as medium-severity vulnerabilities.

Conclusion: Prompt leaking is a pervasive real-world vulnerability in LLM-based applications, not merely a laboratory concern. The failure of existing defenses stems from a fundamental attention mechanism flaw—attention drift—rather than superficial prompt engineering weaknesses. AREA demonstrates that attention-level intervention is a viable and practical defense strategy. The authors advocate for platform-level mitigations and increased developer awareness.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based applications rely on system prompts to encode core logic and developer-defined constraints, making these prompts important intellectual property. However, system prompts are vulnerable to prompt leaking attacks. Although prior work has shown such attacks in controlled settings, their prevalence, causes, and defenses in real-world deployments remain unclear.
  This paper presents a systematic study of prompt leaking in real-world LLM-based applications. We measure 1,200 applications across six major commercial platforms and find that over 80% of deployments leak system prompts under realistic adversarial queries, sometimes exposing sensitive information such as third-party API keys. We also show that existing defenses often fail to prevent leakage without degrading usability. To explain these failures, we conduct an attention-level mechanistic analysis and identify attention drift, where query-key alignment bias and softmax amplification cause LLMs to progressively ignore defensive constraints. Guided by this insight, we propose AREA, a practical defense that re-anchors the model's attention using an optimizable soft prompt. Experiments and real-world case studies show that AREA matches the leakage resistance of state-of-the-art defenses while improving average usability by over 33% and reducing optimization overhead by nearly 3x. Our responsible disclosure led two affected vendors to classify these leaks as medium-severity vulnerabilities.

</details>


### [140] [Image Prompt Reconstruction Attacks on Distributed MLLM Inference Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18710)
*Xinjian Luo,Hongyan Chang,Jianxin Wei,Yuncheng Wu,Xiaofeng Gao,Meikang Qiu,Ting Yu,Xue Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper presents the first study of image-prompt leakage in distributed multimodal LLM (MLLM) inference. The authors design an image embedding extraction algorithm and develop two black-box reconstruction attacks (MPAA for pixel-level and IEDA for semantic-level reconstruction), demonstrating consistent effectiveness across four MLLM families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distributed LLM inference frameworks are increasingly adopting multimodal capabilities (MLLMs), where image prompts contain rich visual/semantic information. While text prompt leakage via intermediate embeddings is known, image-prompt leakage in distributed MLLM inference remains unexplored, creating a significant and unaddressed privacy vulnerability.

Method: The authors first analyze information flow from image pixels to intermediate representations. Since image and text embeddings are intertwined across MLLM layers, they design an image embedding extraction algorithm (achieving ~100% extraction accuracy). Building on this, they develop two passive black-box attacks: (1) MPAA — fine-grained pixel-level reconstruction via patch-wise information extraction and assembly; (2) IEDA — coarse-grained semantic reconstruction through embedding-guided diffusion generation. The attacks assume realistic threat models with limited participant knowledge.

Result: Experiments across four MLLM families (Gemma 3, Phi 4 Multimodal, Qwen 2.5 VL, Llama 4 Scout) demonstrate consistently superior reconstruction performance across various settings. The paper also analyzes the effects of MoE architecture, image preprocessing, model size, and text-image dependency on attack performance.

Conclusion: This is the first study to demonstrate image reconstruction attacks on MLLMs in distributed inference settings, revealing a critical privacy vulnerability where intermediate embeddings can leak rich visual information from user prompts, extending the privacy risk landscape beyond text-only LLMs.

Abstract: Distributed large language model (LLM) inference frameworks connect isolated consumer-grade devices for large-scale model inference, substantially reducing hardware constraints. However, recent studies show that intermediate embeddings transmitted among participants can leak private prompts. As LLMs evolve into multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), this risk extends beyond text: image prompts contain rich visual and semantic information, making their intermediate embeddings highly privacy-sensitive. Yet, image-prompt leakage in distributed MLLM inference remains largely unexplored.
  In this paper, we investigate privacy risks to input images caused by intermediate embeddings in distributed MLLM frameworks. We first analyze the information flow from image pixels to intermediate representations. Since image and text embeddings are often intertwined across MLLM layers, we design an image embedding extraction algorithm as a prerequisite for reconstruction attacks, achieving 100% extraction accuracy across almost all MLLM layers in our experiments. Building on this, we develop two passive black-box image reconstruction attacks, MPAA and IEDA, reflecting realistic threats from normal participants with limited knowledge and capability. MPAA performs fine-grained pixel-level reconstruction via patch-wise information extraction and assembly, while IEDA performs coarse-grained semantic reconstruction through embedding-guided diffusion generation.
  We evaluate our attacks on four representative MLLM families: Gemma 3, Phi 4 Multimodal, Qwen 2.5 VL, and Llama 4 Scout. Results show consistently superior reconstruction performance in various settings. We further analyze the effects of MoE architecture, image preprocessing, model size, and text-image dependency on attack performance. To our knowledge, this is the first study of image reconstruction attacks on MLLMs.

</details>


### [141] [A Predictive Neural Network Architecture for Early Detection of Low-Rate Cyberattacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18771)
*Mert Nakıp*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: IDQS is a lightweight LDoS detection framework for IoT networks that uses a recurrent neural network (RTP-QoS) to predict QoS metrics and a pairwise decision model (PDM) to detect attacks by comparing predicted vs. actual QoS, achieving 79-91% accuracy with 0.28s inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-Rate Denial of Service (LDoS) attacks are subtle and prolonged, easily evading traditional intrusion detection systems, and IoT networks are particularly vulnerable due to resource constraints. There is a need for a lightweight, proactive, real-time detection framework tailored to these environments.

Method: The IDQS framework has two components: (1) RTP-QoS, a Recurrent Trend Predictive Neural Network that learns historical traffic patterns to forecast future Quality of Service metrics; (2) PDM, a Pairwise Decision Model that evaluates discrepancies between predicted and actual QoS values to flag potential LDoS attacks. Detection is based on forecasting deviations rather than signature-based or anomaly-based pattern matching.

Result: Evaluated on SDN-SlowRate-DDoS and CIC-IDS2017 datasets, IDQS achieved over 79% and 91% detection accuracy respectively across most attack scenarios, with high recall and low false negatives. End-to-end inference time was just 0.28 seconds, demonstrating suitability for real-time deployment.

Conclusion: IDQS provides an effective and efficient solution for early LDoS attack detection in resource-constrained IoT environments, combining accurate QoS trend prediction with lightweight decision modeling to enable real-time, proactive intrusion detection.

Abstract: Low-Rate Denial of Service (LDoS) attacks pose a significant challenge to IoT networks due to their subtle and prolonged nature, often evading traditional intrusion detection systems. This paper presents IDQS (Intrusion Detection via QoS Prediction), a lightweight and proactive framework for early LDoS attack detection. IDQS integrates two new key components: (i) RTP-QoS, a Recurrent Trend Predictive Neural Network that learns and forecasts future Quality of Service (QoS) based on historical traffic patterns, and (ii) PDM, a Pairwise Decision Model that evaluates discrepancies between predicted and actual QoS to identify potential attacks. Evaluated on the public SDN-SlowRate-DDoS and CIC-IDS2017 datasets, IDQS respectively achieves over 79% and 91% detection accuracy across most attack scenarios with high recall and low false negatives, while maintaining an end-to-end inference time of just 0.28 seconds. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IDQS for real-time deployment in resource-constrained IoT environments.

</details>


### [142] [TRAP: Benchmark for Task-completion and Resistance to Active Privacy-extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18996)
*Moon Ye-Bin,Nam Hyeon-Woo,Baek Seong-Eun,Yejin Yeo,Tae-Hyun Oh*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces TRAP, a benchmark evaluating the trade-off between task accuracy and privacy leakage in document-intensive agent workflows. Evaluating 22 models, all exhibit non-trivial leakage, with instruction-following ability correlating with leakage. The authors prove that soft-constraint defenses (e.g., prompt-based) cannot achieve both high accuracy and zero leakage, and propose structural private field isolation (hash-based replacement) as a solution that largely prevents leakage while maintaining task accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents deployed in document-intensive workflows routinely handle sensitive private information (e.g., passport numbers) and must use it to complete tasks without exposing it in responses, since the agent cannot authenticate the end user. These two obligations — using private data for accuracy and never revealing it — are in fundamental tension: a model capable of the former can be induced to do the latter. No existing benchmark systematically evaluates this trade-off.

Method: The authors introduce TRAP (Task-completion and Resistance to Active Privacy-extraction), a benchmark where each scenario contains: (1) a document with private information, (2) a task query requiring correct tool invocation using private fields, and (3) an attack query attempting to extract the same information in natural language. They evaluate 22 frontier models across multiple scales. They also provide a formal proof that for softmax-based models, no soft-constraint defense can jointly achieve high task success and zero leakage probability. Finally, they propose structural private field isolation, replacing private fields with hash keys before they reach the model.

Result: All model families exhibit non-trivial leakage. Instruction-following ability correlates positively with leakage rate. Existing prompt-based defenses reduce leakage but impose significant costs on task accuracy. Prompt optimization cannot escape this trade-off. The proposed hash-based structural isolation largely prevents leakage while preserving task accuracy.

Conclusion: The accuracy-privacy trade-off in document-intensive agent workflows is fundamental and inescapable via soft-constraint defenses. The impossibility result formalizes this. Structural defenses that prevent private data from ever reaching the model (e.g., hash-key replacement) offer a principled path forward, achieving both strong privacy and high task accuracy.

Abstract: Agents are increasingly deployed in document-intensive workflows where sensitive private information is not an edge case but a routine input, e.g., an agent booking a flight needs passport numbers. In such settings, the agent must use private information to complete tasks accurately while never exposing it in its responses, because it cannot verify who is actually at the keyboard. These two obligations are in fundamental tension. A model capable enough to use private information for task completion can, by the same capability, be induced to reveal it. To evaluate the trade-off of task accuracy and privacy leakage, we introduce Task-completion and Resistance to Active Privacy-extraction (TRAP). Each scenario includes a document containing private information, a task query that requires the agent to invoke the correct tool using private fields, and an attack query that attempts to elicit the same information in natural language. Evaluating 22 models spanning frontier proprietary and open-source models at multiple scales, we find that all model families exhibit non-trivial leakage, and that instruction-following ability correlates with leakage rate. Existing prompt-based defenses reduce leakage but at significant cost to task accuracy. Prompt optimization fails to escape this trade-off. We demonstrate that this failure is not incidental. For any softmax-based model, no soft-constraint defense, e.g., prompt-based defenses, can jointly achieve high task success with zero leakage probability. Motivated by this impossibility result, we propose structural private field isolation, which replaces private fields with hash keys before they reach the model. This approach largely prevents leakage while keeping task accuracy.

</details>


### [143] [Lifecycle-Aware Dynamic Analysis for Secure ML Model Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19023)
*Gabriele Digregorio,Marco Di Gennaro,Francesco Pastore,Stefano Zanero,Stefano Longari,Michele Carminati*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Moat is a dynamic, lifecycle-aware defense that detects malicious ML models by monitoring their runtime interactions with the host system. Evaluated on 77,974 real-world models and 31 CVE PoCs, it detects all attack classes with near-zero false positives, outperforming static signature-based scanners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained ML model sharing introduces attack surfaces where malicious behavior can be embedded in model artifacts. Existing model-scanning solutions rely on static, format-specific rules or known attack signatures, which fail to generalize across frameworks and cannot detect novel exploitation paths. A new approach is needed that catches attacks based on how they manifest at runtime rather than what they look like on disk.

Method: The authors propose Moat, a dynamic lifecycle-aware approach that secures ML model execution by leveraging two key observations: (1) ML models operate within well-defined lifecycle phases (loading, inference, etc.), and (2) within each phase, host-system interactions are highly structured and predictable. By monitoring deviations from expected behavior during each lifecycle phase, Moat detects malicious activity. The reference implementation, Re-Moat, enforces these behavioral invariants at runtime.

Result: Re-Moat was evaluated on 77,974 real-world Hugging Face Hub models, 31 CVE-derived PoCs, and 334 models from a state-of-the-art dataset across multiple ML frameworks. It detected all evaluated attack classes while maintaining a near-zero false-positive rate, outperforming existing model-scanning solutions.

Conclusion: Dynamic, lifecycle-aware analysis is an effective and generalizable strategy for securing ML model execution. By focusing on runtime behavioral invariants rather than static signatures, the approach achieves strong detection coverage and low false positives, motivating broader adoption of dynamic analysis in ML supply-chain security.

Abstract: The growing reliance on pre-trained Machine Learning (ML) models has introduced new attack surfaces. Recent vulnerabilities demonstrate that malicious behavior can be embedded within model artifacts, often bypassing existing defenses. Current model-scanning solutions primarily rely on static, format-specific rules or known attack signatures, which limit their ability to generalize across frameworks and to detect novel exploitation paths. In contrast, we propose a solution that focuses on the effects an attack has on the host system executing the model and builds on foundational intuitions about ML model execution. In particular, we observe that ML models operate within well-defined lifecycle phases and that, within each phase, interactions with the host system are highly structured and predictable. We translate these intuitions into Moat, a dynamic lifecycle-aware approach for securing ML model execution, and instantiate this design in Re-Moat, our reference implementation. We evaluate Re-Moat across multiple ML frameworks using 77,974 real-world model artifacts from the Hugging Face Hub, 31 Proofs-of-Concept (PoCs) from CVEs, and 334 models from a state-of-the-art dataset, and compare it against state-of-the-art model-scanning solutions. Our results show that our approach detects all evaluated attack classes while maintaining a close-to-zero false-positive rate, validating our intuitions and motivating dynamic analysis for securing ML model execution.

</details>


### [144] [PYPILINE: Malicious PyPI Package Detection via Suspicious API Knowledge and Agent Workflow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19063)
*Siyuan Pang,Zhengwei Jiang,Yepeng Yao,Zijing Fan,Haozhe Li,Baoxu Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PYPILINE combines a suspicious API knowledge base with an AI Agent workflow to detect malicious PyPI packages, achieving 96.7% precision and 99.6% recall, significantly outperforming existing tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing malicious PyPI package detection methods rely on rules or traditional ML, which suffer from poor interpretability and cannot easily adapt to novel attack patterns. There is a need for a more interpretable, adaptive, and practical detection solution.

Method: PYPILINE operates in two phases: (1) Construction — static analysis of known malicious packages to extract ASTs and API call graphs, from which a structured suspicious API knowledge base is automatically built. (2) Detection — an Agent workflow performs deep semantic analysis on unknown packages, leveraging the knowledge base for enhanced reasoning, and outputs a structured, interpretable maliciousness assessment report. The system also integrates tool-calling for automated vector database retrieval and mail-based report delivery.

Result: PYPILINE achieved 96.7% precision, 99.6% recall, and 98.1% F1-score, surpassing baseline tools by 5.7–24.2 percentage points in precision. An empirical study also systematically revealed prevalent attack strategies and the most commonly abused APIs in malicious packages.

Conclusion: PYPILINE provides a practical, efficient, and interpretable solution for malicious PyPI package detection, strengthening open-source ecosystem security through automated, Agent-driven analysis and reporting.

Abstract: The detection of malicious PyPI packages is crucial for maintaining the security of the open source software supply chain. Existing methods, which primarily rely on rules or traditional machine learning, suffer from poor interpretability and difficulty in adapting to novel attacks. To address this, we propose PYPILINE, a novel detection method that combines a suspicious API knowledge base with an Agent workflow. PYPILINE first conducts static analysis on known malicious packages, extracting abstract syntax trees and generating API call graphs, from which it automatically extracts and constructs a structured suspicious API knowledge base. During the detection phase, this knowledge base is used to enhance reasoning capabilities. Through an Agent workflow, PYPILINE performs in depth semantic analysis of unknown packages and outputs a structured, interpretable maliciousness assessment report. The experimental results show that PYPILINE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art tools in precision of 96.7\%, recall of 99.6\%, and F1-score of 98.1\%, with its precision surpassing baseline tools by 5.7 to 24.2 percentage points. Additionally, we conducted an empirical study on malicious packages, systematically revealing prevalent attack strategies, as well as the most commonly abused APIs. Equipped with tool-calling AI agent workflows for automated vector database retrieval of suspicious API knowledge and mail server delivery of analysis reports, PYPILINE delivers a practical, efficient, and convenient malicious package detection solution to strengthen open-source ecosystem security.

</details>


### [145] [Compute-Budgeted Exploitability Evidence Graphs for Prospective Vulnerability Triage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19076)
*Faruk Alpay,Taylan Alpay*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a leakage-safe, compute-budgeted triage framework for prospectively predicting CVE exploitability using temporal evidence graphs. It demonstrates that proper prospective evaluation avoids drastic overestimation (8.5x inflation from naive splits), that two evidence documents per CVE suffice, and that semantic relevance alone does not equate to exploitation evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vulnerability exploitability prediction must operate prospectively — at a fixed decision time before exploits are known — because defenders cannot retroactively patch. Existing evaluations often leak future information (e.g., via random splits or unfiltered evidence), inflating apparent performance. A rigorous, leakage-safe evaluation protocol with auditable evidence certificates is needed for contestable, real-world triage.

Method: The authors construct a temporal evidence graph from CVE advisories, exploit archives, fix commits, and hacker-community discourse, each timestamped. A budgeted selector admits only k evidence documents per CVE seen before a fixed cutoff date. CVEs are scored prospectively, and each score is paired with an auditable certificate listing supporting signals, timestamps, source layers, and leakage flags. A cross-encoder reranker is also tested. The framework is evaluated on 12,012 prospective CVEs.

Result: Budgeted evidence selection yields leakage-safe prospective recall@50 of 0.026 vs. 0.010 for a severity-only baseline. Two evidence documents per CVE capture most of the value. A cross-encoder reranker drops recall to 0.016, indicating semantic relevance ≠ exploitation evidence. A naive random split with unfiltered evidence inflates apparent prospective recall by 8.5× and EPSS-high recall by 5.0×.

Conclusion: The primary contribution is a leakage-safe evaluation protocol with reproducible, auditable evidence certificates that enable contestable vulnerability-prioritization claims. The work exposes severe overestimation risks in standard evaluation practices and establishes that lightweight, temporally-constrained evidence selection is both effective and transparent for real-world triage.

Abstract: Defenders cannot patch every newly disclosed vulnerability at once, so exploitability prediction must be evaluated prospectively rather than retrospectively. We study compute-budgeted vulnerability triage in which each CVE is scored only from public evidence visible by a fixed decision time. Advisories, exploit archives, fix commits, and hacker-community discourse are represented as a temporal evidence graph; a budgeted selector admits only a few evidence documents per CVE, and every score is paired with an auditable certificate listing the supporting signals, timestamps, source layers, and leakage flags. On 12012 prospective CVEs from public sources, budgeted evidence selection raises leakage-safe prospective recall@50 from 0.010 for a severity-only baseline to 0.026, while two evidence documents per CVE capture most of the value. A strong cross-encoder reranker lowers prospective recall to 0.016, showing that semantic relevance to a CVE is not the same as evidence of exploitation. Most importantly, a naive random split with unfiltered evidence inflates apparent prospective recall by 8.5x and EPSS-high recall by 5.0x. The main contribution is a leakage-safe evaluation protocol and reproducible evidence certificates for contestable vulnerability-prioritization claims.

</details>


### [146] [Quantifying Compromise Risk in Exceptional Access Architectures Under Sparse and Indirect Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19106)
*Alan Woodward*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper develops a structured uncertainty framework to compare systemic compromise risk in two lawful exceptional access (EA) architectures—transmission-layer EA (T-EA) and over-the-top EA (OTT-EA)—using historical analogues, Monte Carlo simulations, channel-independence decomposition, and a Bayesian Structural Risk Model. It finds that both EA designs carry strictly higher risk than no-EA baselines, with T-EA risk dominated by central tendency and OTT-EA by tail risk under correlated attacks; annual compromise probability for T-EA ranges 1.4%–12.9%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The longstanding debate over EA risks has been hampered by two problems: (1) no public dataset of EA-specific compromise events exists, forcing reliance on sparse indirect evidence, and (2) structurally different EA designs (transmission-layer vs. platform-layer) have been treated as equivalent despite fundamentally different key–ciphertext relationships. A rigorous, uncertainty-aware comparative framework is needed.

Method: Four analytical layers are applied to both T-EA and OTT-EA: (1) historical analogues drawn from comparable compromise events, (2) a Monte Carlo scenario layer for stochastic simulation, (3) a channel-independence decomposition to isolate independent failure pathways, and (4) a Bayesian Structural Risk Model operating on a parallel-subgraph attack graph. The framework separates calibration-dependent findings from calibration-robust structural findings.

Result: Both EA architectures exhibit strictly higher modelled risk than their no-EA counterfactual, robust to calibration. T-EA risk is driven by central tendency; OTT-EA risk concentrates in the tail under correlated campaigns. Annual compromise probability for T-EA spans 1.4%–12.9% across the structured-judgement targeting-premium interval. Over multi-decade horizons, cumulative compromise probability is substantially above zero, with irreversible key-material exfiltration disproportionately impacting OTT-EA's larger user bases.

Conclusion: EA-equipped architectures structurally elevate systemic compromise risk regardless of design class. The framework enables rigorous comparative risk assessment without producing unsupported predictive forecasts, explicitly scoping out consequence modelling and benefit estimation.

Abstract: Lawful exceptional access (EA) systems hold the cryptographic keys that decrypt protected communications for authorised parties. The debate over their risks has been long and qualitative, complicated by two problems: no public dataset of EA-specific compromise events exists, so assessment must use sparse, indirect evidence; and prior work has treated structurally different designs as equivalent, though transmission-layer EA in carrier infrastructure (T-EA) and over-the-top EA at the platform layer (OTT-EA) differ in how cryptographic keys relate to ciphertext data. This paper builds a structured uncertainty framework for evaluating systemic compromise risk in EA architectures. It does not produce predictive forecasts, which the evidence cannot support; it separates findings robust to assumptions from those that depend on calibration. Four analytical layers are applied to T-EA and OTT-EA: three empirical pillars (historical analogues, a Monte Carlo scenario layer, a channel-independence decomposition) plus a Bayesian Structural Risk Model on a parallel-subgraph attack graph. The central findings are structural. First, EA-equipped architectures of either class carry strictly higher modelled risk than their no-EA counterfactual, an ordering independent of calibration. Second, the classes differ in distribution shape: T-EA risk is dominated by central tendency, OTT-EA by the tail under correlated campaigns. Third, calibration-conditional annual probability ranges span 1.4% to 12.9% for T-EA across the structured-judgement targeting-premium interval. Over multi-decade horizons, cumulative compromise is well above zero; key-material exfiltration is irreversible, weighing heavily on OTT-EA's larger user populations. The framework quantifies compromise probability, not expected harm; consequence modelling and benefit estimation are outside its scope.

</details>


### [147] [Giskard : Byzantine Robust and Confidential Aggregation for Large-Scale Decentralized Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19129)
*Ousmane Touat,César Sabater,Mohamed Maouche,Sonia Ben Mokhtar*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Giskard is a protocol for decentralized machine learning that simultaneously achieves confidentiality and Byzantine robustness. It organizes parties into a tree of committees of size O(log n) and computes approximate median aggregation via distributed binary search using BGW-style MPC within committees, reducing per-party communication asymptotically compared to prior work while tolerating up to n/4 Byzantine parties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing decentralized learning solutions address confidentiality (hiding model updates) and Byzantine robustness (detecting poisoned updates) separately. Recent MPC-based approaches that combine both properties scale poorly, requiring either all-to-all communication or overloading a small subset of participants whose load grows linearly with network size.

Method: Giskard organizes n parties into a committee tree with committees of size O(log n). Within each committee, parties use BGW-style secure multi-party computation to perform a distributed binary search over the value domain, computing a coordinate-wise approximate median aggregator. This committee-adapted structure avoids all-to-all communication and balances computational load.

Result: Giskard reduces per-party communication complexity asymptotically compared to closest competitors (e.g., ELSA). It maintains comparable model utility under up to n/4 Byzantine parties, demonstrated through extensive experiments scaling up to one million participants.

Conclusion: Giskard demonstrates that confidential and Byzantine-robust decentralized aggregation can scale efficiently by using a committee-tree structure combined with MPC-based approximate median computation, making it practical for large-scale decentralized learning systems.

Abstract: Dealing simultaneously with confidentiality and Byzantine behaviors in decentralized learning is a challenging problem. Indeed, in decentralized learning, clients train a machine learning model while keeping their data locally and share their model parameters or gradients with a set of neighbors. While enforcing confidentiality calls for hiding the exchanged model parameters/gradients (e.g., by using cryptographic techniques), dealing with Byzantine contributions often requires inspecting the latter. Hence, most research works address these objectives separately. A recent line of work proposes to employ secure multi-party computation (MPC) to implement robust aggregators against model poisoning, thereby enforcing both confidentiality and Byzantine resilience. However, these solutions scale badly: they either require all-to-all communication between participants or delegate the entire computation to a small subset, whose computational and communication load grows proportionally with the size of the network.
  In this paper, we present Giskard, a protocol for confidential and Byzantine-robust decentralized aggregation. Giskard organizes $n$ parties into a tree of committees of size $O(\log n)$ and evaluates a coordinate-wise approximate median via a committee-adapted distributed binary search over the value domain, using BGW-style MPC within each committee. We assess Giskard both theoretically by proving its security and confidentiality properties and experimentally through extensive experiments involving up to one million participants. Compared to its closest competitors, Giskard reduces per-party communication complexity asymptotically while exhibiting comparable model utility under up to $n/4$ Byzantine parties.

</details>


### [148] [OpenAnt: LLM-Powered Vulnerability Discovery Through Code Decomposition, Adversarial Verification, and Dynamic Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19149)
*Nahum Korda,Gadi Evron*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: OpenAnt is an open-source system that combines static program analysis with LLM-based reasoning in a multi-stage pipeline to discover vulnerabilities in large codebases. It reduces analysis surface via reachability filtering, performs adversarial verification through constrained attacker simulation, and validates findings with automated dynamic exploit testing in sandboxed containers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional static analysis suffers from high false-positive rates, and dynamic fuzzing requires heavy infrastructure and targets narrow bug classes. LLMs offer semantic reasoning about program behavior but face challenges in repository-scale analysis around context management, cost, and verification. There is a need for a practical, scalable automated vulnerability discovery system that integrates these approaches effectively.

Method: OpenAnt employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) Codebase decomposition into self-contained analysis units filtered by reachability from external entry points, reducing the analysis surface by up to 97%. (2) Adversarial verification via constrained attacker simulation, where an LLM evaluates exploitability under realistic attacker capabilities. (3) Dynamic verification through automatic generation of exploit environments, executed in sandboxed containers and discarded after use.

Result: Evaluation on OpenSSL, WordPress, and Flowise demonstrated the system can identify previously unknown vulnerabilities while maintaining manageable analysis costs and substantially reducing false positives compared to traditional approaches.

Conclusion: Closed-loop vulnerability discovery pipelines that combine semantic reasoning with exploit validation offer a practical path toward scalable automated security analysis. OpenAnt is released as open source under Apache 2.0.

Abstract: Automated vulnerability discovery in large codebases remains challenging: traditional static analysis produces high false-positive rates, while dynamic approaches such as fuzzing require substantial infrastructure and often target narrow classes of bugs. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable semantic reasoning about program behavior, but applying LLMs to repository-scale security analysis introduces challenges related to context management, cost, and verification.
  We present OpenAnt, an open-source vulnerability discovery system that integrates static program analysis with LLM-based reasoning in a multi-stage pipeline. OpenAnt introduces three key techniques. First, codebases are decomposed into self-contained analysis units filtered by reachability from external entry points, reducing the analysis surface by up to 97% while preserving attack-relevant code. Second, candidate vulnerabilities undergo adversarial verification through constrained attacker simulation, where the model evaluates exploitability under realistic attacker capabilities. Third, findings are validated through dynamic verification, in which exploit environments are generated automatically, executed in sandboxed containers, and discarded after use.
  Evaluation on widely used open-source projects including OpenSSL, WordPress, and Flowise shows that this architecture can identify previously unknown vulnerabilities while maintaining manageable analysis cost and substantially reducing false positives. Our results suggest that closed-loop vulnerability discovery pipelines, combining semantic reasoning with exploit validation, provide a practical path toward scalable automated security analysis.
  OpenAnt is released as open source under the Apache 2.0 license at https://github.com/knostic/OpenAnt.

</details>


### [149] [PhantomSkill: Malicious Code Injection in Agent Skill Ecosystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19191)
*Yu-Ting Lin,Chia-Mu Yu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PhantomSkill is an attack framework that conceals malicious behavior in LLM-based coding agent skills by embedding payloads in auxiliary resources rather than textual descriptions. Its VulMask technique rewrites overtly malicious scripts as vulnerability-masked implementations that activate only under attacker-controlled triggers, evading detection while preserving benign functionality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent skills enable LLM-based coding agents to extend functionality via third-party packages, but this introduces a supply-chain attack surface. Existing defenses focus on inspecting textual descriptions for malicious intent, leaving auxiliary resources (scripts, configurations, dependencies) as an unvetted attack vector.

Method: PhantomSkill uses VulMask, a technique that transforms overt malicious scripts into implementations resembling common software vulnerabilities. The malicious payload is split into a trigger mechanism and a payload, activated only under attacker-specified conditions. This makes the code appear as merely insecure/exploitable rather than explicitly malicious. The framework was evaluated across multiple host skills, attack goals, coding agents, generation models, and automated reviewers.

Result: VulMask successfully preserves benign utility while significantly reducing both warning-level and malware-level detection rates compared to overt malicious scripts. The vulnerability-masked implementations evade current vetting mechanisms across representative coding agents, models, and automated review systems.

Conclusion: Skill ecosystems require three additional security measures: resource-level vetting (beyond textual description inspection), execution-time containment, and security policies that treat exploitable vulnerabilities in agent skills as potential malicious payloads rather than mere bugs.

Abstract: Agent skills allow LLM-based coding agents to acquire domain-specific capabilities from third-party packages, but they also introduce a new supply-chain attack surface. We present PhantomSkill, an attack framework that hides malicious behavior in a skill's auxiliary resources rather than in its textual description. Its core technique, VulMask, rewrites overt malicious scripts into vulnerability-shaped implementations whose malicious behavior is activated only under attacker-controlled trigger conditions. This design shifts the visible signal from explicit malicious intent to ordinary-looking insecure code. Across representative host skills, attack goals, coding agents, generation models, and automated reviewers, VulMask preserves benign utility while reducing warning and malware-level detection compared with overt malicious scripts. Our results show that skill ecosystems require resource-level vetting, execution-time containment, and security policies that treat exploitable vulnerabilities in agent skills as potential malicious payloads.

</details>


### [150] [CodeSentinel: A Three-Layer Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection in Code Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19235)
*Po-Han Cheng,Chia-Mu Yu,Ying-Dar Lin,Yu-Sung Wu,Wei-Bin Lee*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CodeSentinel is a three-layer inference-time sanitizer that protects code LLMs from indirect prompt injection attacks hidden in retrieved code context by detecting and neutralizing adversarial nodes using Tree-sitter AST extraction, syntax-guided pre-filtering, CST-guided Dynamic Min-K% scoring, and node perturbation analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As code LLMs increasingly retrieve external code from repositories, documentation, and agent environments, a new indirect prompt-injection attack surface emerges where adversaries embed malicious instructions in comments, strings, identifiers, or decoy code. Existing defenses are insufficient against both overt adversarial triggers and natural-looking semantic attacks.

Method: CodeSentinel operates at inference time with three layers: (1) Tree-sitter extracts high-risk model-facing CST (Concrete Syntax Tree) nodes; (2) syntax-guided pre-filtering eliminates benign nodes; (3) CST-guided Dynamic Min-K% scoring combined with node perturbation analysis distinguishes adversarial from natural-looking semantic triggers. Detected malicious nodes are then removed or neutralized before the downstream Code LLM processes the input.

Result: Across six recent attack families, CodeSentinel achieves a 0.80 average node-level F1 score, outperforming three baseline defenses: CodeGarrison, DePA, and KillBadCode.

Conclusion: CodeSentinel provides effective, practical defense against indirect prompt injection in code LLM pipelines by leveraging structural code analysis at the syntax-tree level, achieving state-of-the-art detection performance across diverse attack families.

Abstract: Code large language models increasingly retrieve external code context from repositories, documentation, issue threads, and coding-agent environments, creating an indirect prompt-injection surface where attackers hide instructions in comments, strings, identifiers, or decoy code. We propose CodeSentinel, a three-layer inference-time sanitizer. It uses Tree-sitter to extract high-risk model-facing CST nodes, then combines syntax-guided pre-filtering, CST-guided Dynamic Min-K\% scoring, and node perturbation analysis to detect adversarial and natural-looking semantic triggers. Detected nodes are removed or neutralized before reaching the downstream Code LLM. Across six recent attack families, \CodeSentinel achieves 0.80 average node-level F1, outperforming CodeGarrison, DePA, and KillBadCode.

</details>


### [151] [QSignAI: Quantum-Randomness-Seeded Identity Signatures at the Intersection of AI for Science and Science for AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27729)
*Dongping Liu,Aoyu Zhang,Luyao Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: QSignAI is a production-deployed platform that integrates quantum randomness generation with an AI-driven conversational bot for real-time event participation, demonstrating a bidirectional AI-quantum relationship. It uses a Toeplitz two-source extractor over single-qubit Hadamard measurements and Bell states to generate unique quantum-randomness-seeded identity signatures, currently on cloud simulators with physical QPU extension planned.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite simultaneous recognition of AI and quantum science by Nobel and Turing awards (2024-2025), no deployed system has brought these two streams together for the public. The authors aim to bridge this gap by demonstrating a practical, production-deployed platform that unifies AI and quantum computing in a real-time social system.

Method: QSignAI combines a conversational AI bot with a quantum pipeline. Each participant's first message is routed through: (1) a Toeplitz two-source extractor fed by independent single-qubit Hadamard measurements on SV1 and DM1 cloud quantum simulators, (2) a 2-qubit Bell state, and (3) generation of a unique quantum-randomness-seeded identity signature. Three research questions guide evaluation: latency feasibility, perceptual legibility of quantum phenomena via AI, and practical system viability.

Result: The first two research questions are answered affirmatively through system architecture design and qualitative deployment evidence from live events. The third question is satisfied by successful production deployment. The current implementation relies on cloud quantum simulators rather than physical QPUs, with measurable benchmarks deferred to future work.

Conclusion: QSignAI successfully demonstrates a bidirectional AI-quantum integration in a live production system. The combination of quantum-randomness extraction and AI-mediated explanation makes quantum phenomena accessible to general audiences. Physical QPU randomness and rigorous benchmarking are identified as immediate next steps.

Abstract: The 2024-2025 Nobel and Turing awards recognised AI and quantum science simultaneously. Yet no deployed system has brought these streams together for the public. This paper presents QSignAI, a production-deployed platform demonstrating a bidirectional AI-quantum relationship in a real-time event participation system. We address three questions: can quantum-randomness generation via a two-source extractor be embedded in an AI-driven social platform with acceptable latency; can an AI bot make quantum phenomena perceptually legible to general audiences; and does the combined system work in practice? A conversational bot routes each participant's first message through a quantum pipeline comprising a Toeplitz two-source extractor over independent single-qubit Hadamard measurements on SV1 and DM1 simulators, plus a 2-qubit Bell state, producing a unique quantum-randomness-seeded identity signature per participant. The first two questions are answered through system architecture and qualitative deployment evidence from live events; the third through successful production deployment. The current deployment uses cloud quantum simulators; physical QPU randomness is the near-term extension. Measurable benchmarks are identified as priority future work.

</details>
