### [152] [Vibe Coding Ate My Homework: An evaluation of AI approaches to greenfield software engineering and programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18293)
*Callum Barbour*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates the viability of "vibe coding" — using natural language prompts to build software without coding knowledge — for greenfield software engineering tasks. The authors developed an evaluation suite to assess LLM proficiency on simple, isolated Python programming tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid rise of generative AI has enabled non-programmers to build applications using natural language ("vibe coding"), potentially representing the ultimate abstraction in programming. The authors seek to rigorously evaluate whether this paradigm is genuinely viable for greenfield software engineering, beyond anecdotal claims.

Method: The authors developed a custom evaluation suite designed to test LLM performance on simple, isolated greenfield programming tasks in Python. This suite provides a scoped, controlled environment to analyze coding proficiency without confounding factors.

Result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper describes the development of the evaluation suite and its intended use for analyzing LLM proficiency, with results to be derived from its application.

Conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper focuses on establishing the evaluation framework and motivating the inquiry into vibe coding's viability as the next paradigm in programming abstraction.

Abstract: Thanks to rapid developments in generative AI, we are in the midst of a paradigm shift that may change how we interact with computers forever. We have observed a growth in the use of natural language prompts to build applications and coding infrastructures without underlying knowledge of the field, and this practice has been dubbed `vibe coding.' It arguably represents what the field of programming has been building towards since the beginning, with every higher level of abstraction that is conceived. Vibe coding promises to be the endpoint for the meta of high-level programming as far as method of input is concerned: eliminating a human's use of code syntax entirely in favour of programming in their mother tongue. This paper aims to evaluate the viability of vibe coding for greenfield software engineering tasks, as well as analyse the benchmarks that have been used to measure its software engineering prowess. To this end, we have developed an evaluation suite for analysing an LLM's proficiency in carrying out simple, isolated greenfield programming tasks in Python to provide scoped insight on the matter.

</details>


### [153] [Exploring Statistical Change Point Detection Techniques for Performance Anomaly Detection at Mozilla](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18377)
*Mohamed Bilel Besbes,Gregory Mierzwinski,Suhaib Mujahid,Philipp Leitner,Alexander Serebrenik,Dave Hunt,Diego Elias Costa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An empirical study evaluating 25 change-point detection methods and 15 ensemble approaches on Mozilla performance data finds that ensemble voting strategies improve F1-score by 11% over the current T-test approach, reducing false positives while catching missed regressions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mozilla's current Student's T-test-based approach in Perfherder produces 12.5% false positive alert groups and misses 6.8% of actual regressions. This motivates a systematic evaluation of alternative change-point detection methods to improve precision and recall in automated performance regression detection within CI pipelines.

Method: The authors construct a ground-truth dataset of 174 performance time series manually annotated by eleven Mozilla performance engineers. They evaluate 25 CPD methods (offline, online, and hybrid) and 15 ensemble approaches against this benchmark. Results are validated through a practitioner survey and real-world integration into Mozilla's Perfherder system.

Result: Offline and hybrid CPD methods improve recall but at high precision cost. Ensemble voting strategies mitigate this precision-recall trade-off, yielding an 11% F1-score improvement. The study provides one of the first practitioner-annotated CPD benchmarks for performance engineering.

Conclusion: Ensemble change-point detection methods offer more consistent and balanced performance than single-method approaches for automated performance regression detection, and practitioner involvement in both annotation and validation is essential for developing practical, deployable solutions.

Abstract: Software performance regressions can have significant business consequences, making automated detection a critical component of modern continuous integration pipelines. At Mozilla, performance anomaly detection is handled by Perfherder, Mozilla's performance engineering management system that relies on a Student's T-test-based approach to flag regressions across hundreds of daily code changes. However, our preliminary analysis of one year of Mozilla performance data reveals that 12.5% of generated alert groups are false positives, while approximately 6.8% of them contain regressions missed by the automated system.
  This paper presents an empirical study evaluating 25 change-point detection (CPD) methods and 15 ensemble approaches as alternatives to Mozilla's current method. We construct a ground-truth dataset of 174 performance time series manually annotated by eleven Mozilla performance engineers, representing one of the first practitioner-annotated CPD benchmarks for performance engineering. Our results show that while offline and hybrid CPD methods improve recall over Mozilla's method, they do so at a high cost to precision. Ensemble voting strategies alleviate this trade-off and offer more consistent performance, resulting in 11% improvement in the F1-score. We validate the experimental results through a practitioner survey and report on lessons learned from integrating the best methods into Mozilla's performance engineering system.

</details>


### [154] [Finding Compiler-Platform Interaction Bugs in Deep Learning Pipelines via Cross-Layer Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18421)
*Yuxin Qiu,Jiyuan Wang,Ronak Badhe,Ben Limpanukorn,Miryung Kim,Qian Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: XCheck is a DL compiler testing framework that extracts full-stack constraints to find compiler-platform interaction bugs and enable behavior equivalence partitioning, uncovering 2,034 bug-revealing cases across TVM, ONNX-MLIR, and another compiler.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current DL compiler testing focuses narrowly on type constraints and type validation, missing compiler-platform interaction bugs caused by violated assumptions across compilation passes and hardware platforms. These bugs manifest through interleaved effects between compilation and execution environments.

Method: XCheck employs three techniques: (1) automated extraction of full-stack constraints that jointly guide model generation and characterize compilation behaviors; (2) prioritization of constraints that expose interaction-sensitive behaviors to exercise deep compilation logic; and (3) automatic insertion of assertions for behavior equivalence partitioning to monitor distinct compilation symptoms beyond coverage or pass/fail signals.

Result: Evaluation on three widely-used DL compilers (TVM, ONNX-MLIR, and a third) revealed 2,034 bug-revealing cases, including memory overflows, integer overflows, and silent unexpected compilations, all rooted in compiler-platform interactions.

Conclusion: Moving beyond type-level constraints to full-stack constraint extraction and behavior equivalence partitioning significantly improves the detection of subtle compiler-platform interaction bugs that conventional testing approaches miss.

Abstract: The growing deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) necessitates robust deep learning (DL) compilers, such as TVM and ONNX-MLIR. These compilers take as input high-level AI models, lower them through multi-layer transformations, and specialize them to diverse hardware. Testing such compilers is uniquely challenging as correctness depends on implicit constraints embedded throughout the compilation stack. Existing testing approaches largely take type constraints to restrict input model generation and therefore emphasize type validation and monitor compilation crashes or coverage gains. This focus overlooks compiler-platform interaction bugs that arise from interleaved effects across compilation and execution environments.
  In this work, we propose a scalable, automated DL compiler testing framework for, in tandem, (1) finding compiler-platform interaction bugs and (2) enabling behavior equivalence partitioning. Our key insight is that these bugs are caused by violated assumptions arising from interactions across compilation passes and hardware platforms. Therefore, we move beyond constraining input generation and derive full-stack constraints. Our approach is three-fold. First, we design an automated approach to extract full-stack constraints that jointly guide model generation and characterize compilation behaviors. Second, we prioritize constraints that expose interaction-sensitive behaviors, so our generated models are capable of exercising deep compilation logic. Third, we enable behavior equivalence partitioning by automatically inserting assertions to monitor distinct compilation symptoms that coverage or pass/fail signals miss.
  We evaluated our tool, XCheck, on three widely-used DL compilers and found 2,034 bug-revealing cases, including memory overflows, integer overflows, and silent unexpected compilations that were rooted in compiler-platform interactions.

</details>


### [155] [A Critical Discourse Analysis of Gender Representation in Software Engineering Education Videos on YouTube](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18423)
*Isabella Graßl,Alexander Serebrenik,Giuseppe Destefanis*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A critical discourse analysis of 200 YouTube software engineering tutorials (English & German) reveals male-dominated representation, masculine linguistic defaults, and an "agency gap" where technical/decision-making roles are assigned to men while women are absent or relegated to passive roles—potentially reinforcing gendered barriers in the field.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the persistent gender gap in software engineering and the known influence of educational resources on students' perceptions of belonging, little research has investigated the hidden curriculum regarding gender in online learning spaces—specifically, how YouTube tutorials may implicitly signal who belongs in the field.

Method: The authors conducted a critical discourse analysis of 200 manually analyzed software engineering tutorials on YouTube (both English and German), examining gender representation through two lenses: (1) contextual domains (how characters are portrayed in tutorial scenarios) and (2) linguistic identity markers (gendered language patterns in the instructional discourse).

Result: Male characters and masculine linguistic defaults dominate the tutorials. A pronounced "agency gap" was identified: technical and decision-making roles are almost exclusively assigned to male actors, while female actors are either entirely absent or relegated to passive, low-agency roles.

Conclusion: Software engineering education on YouTube may reproduce gendered norms, with linguistic and representational gatekeeping functioning as a symbolic barrier to entry and participation for women in software engineering.

Abstract: Educational resources may frame students' perceptions of who belongs in software engineering, which is relevant given the field's ongoing gender gap. However, we know little about the hidden curriculum regarding gender in online learning spaces. This study presents a critical discourse analysis of 200 manually analysed English and German software engineering tutorials on YouTube, examining gender representation through contextual domains and linguistic identity markers. Our results show that male characters and masculine linguistic defaults dominate the tutorials. We identified an agency gap, in which technical and decision-making roles are almost exclusively assigned to male actors, while female actors are either absent or tend to passive, low-agency roles. The findings indicate that software engineering education on YouTube may reproduce gendered norms, in which linguistic and representational gatekeeping may serve as a symbolic barrier to software engineering.

</details>


### [156] [From Specification to Execution: AI Assisted Scientific Workflow Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18425)
*Komal Thareja,Hamza Safri,Rajiv Mayani,Anirban Mandal,Ewa Deelman*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An AI-assisted scientific workflow system combining specification-driven generation, LLM-based debugging, and distributed execution via Pegasus WMS with MCP integration, validated on a federated learning medical imaging workflow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scientific workflow design, implementation, and debugging are manual, expertise-intensive processes. While LLMs show promise for code synthesis, direct code generation lacks transparency, reproducibility, and seamless integration with existing workflow management systems. There is a need for an end-to-end AI-assisted approach spanning the entire workflow lifecycle.

Method: The authors propose a three-component approach: (1) a structured specification phase separating workflow intent, design, and implementation, enabling validation before code generation; (2) an LLM-based debugging agent that diagnoses and resolves failures across multiple system layers; (3) integration of the Pegasus WMS with a Model Context Protocol (MCP) layer for unified workflow submission, monitoring, and control. Evaluation uses a federated learning workflow for medical imaging due to its parallel, iterative, and dependency-intensive nature.

Result: The system successfully generated and executed large-scale workflows with thousands of jobs. It reduced debugging effort and enabled non-expert users to construct workflows exhibiting expert-level design patterns.

Conclusion: End-to-end AI-assisted workflow generation and execution is feasible, pointing toward AI-driven platforms for managing the complete scientific workflow lifecycle.

Abstract: Scientific workflow management systems (WMS) support scalable and reproducible execution of complex pipelines, but workflow design, implementation, and debugging remain largely manual and require significant expertise. Recent approaches using large language models (LLMs) show promise for workflow generation from natural language, but often rely on direct code synthesis, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and integration with workflow systems. We present an AI-assisted approach to scientific workflow management that combines specification-driven workflow generation, automated debugging, and distributed execution. The method introduces a structured specification phase that separates workflow intent, design, and implementation, allowing validation prior to code generation. We also develop an LLM-based debugging agent that diagnoses and resolves failures across multiple system layers. To support distributed execution and user interaction, we integrate Pegasus, a widely used WMS, with a Model Context Protocol (MCP) layer, providing a unified interface for workflow submission, monitoring, and control. We evaluate the approach using a federated learning workflow for medical imaging, chosen for its parallel, iterative, and dependency-intensive structure. The system generated and executed large-scale workflows with thousands of jobs, reduced debugging effort, and allowed non-expert users to construct workflows with expert-level design patterns. These results indicate that end-to-end AI-assisted workflow generation and execution is feasible, and point toward AI-driven platforms for managing the scientific workflow lifecycle.

</details>


### [157] [Designing L5: A Permacomputing Approach to Creative Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18481)
*Lee Tusman,Kit Kuksenok*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: L5 is a Lua/LOVE-based creative coding library in the Processing/p5 family that applies permacomputing principles to sustainable creative tools. The paper examines design tensions between sustainability and usability through five case studies on simplicity, resource consumption, long-term stability, constrained functionality, and documentation for low-resource access.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creative coding libraries like Processing/p5 have made computational art widely accessible, but sustainability has not historically been a central concern in these communities. The authors aim to introduce permacomputing — a sustainability-oriented computing movement inspired by permaculture — into the creative coding practice through a new library, L5, and explore the inherent design tensions that arise when balancing sustainability with usability.

Method: The authors present L5, a creative coding library implemented in Lua atop the LOVE framework, designed around permacomputing principles. They conduct a reflective design analysis through five case studies, each examining a specific tension: (1) simplicity vs. exposing underlying seams, (2) designing for lower resource consumption, (3) ensuring long-term software stability, (4) intentionally constraining functionality, and (5) creating documentation accessible under resource-constrained conditions.

Result: The case studies reveal that sustainable creative tool design involves navigating competing values rather than optimizing a single metric. Key findings include: exposing seams can conflict with perceived simplicity; lower resource consumption may require sacrificing features or performance expectations; long-term stability demands restraint in dependency management and feature growth; constraining functionality challenges user expectations of continual expansion; and documentation must be designed for offline, low-bandwidth, and low-power contexts.

Conclusion: Sustainable creative coding tools cannot be reduced to a single optimization target. Designers must transparently navigate tensions between competing values — simplicity, resource efficiency, stability, constrained functionality, and accessible documentation. L5 demonstrates that permacomputing principles can be meaningfully applied to creative coding, offering a model for value-driven tool design in this space.

Abstract: Creative coding libraries provide high-level tools that make computational and algorithmic art accessible to artists and learners. Processing/p5 is one such family of libraries, known for its beginner-friendly approach and wide reach across artistic and technical communities. L5 is a new member of this family, implemented in Lua using the LOVE framework. It applies permacomputing principles, a movement addressing sustainability in computing inspired by permaculture, bringing these values to a community of practice not historically centered on them. This paper explores L5's design decisions and tensions between sustainability and usability through five case studies: 1. balancing perceived simplicity versus exposing the seams, 2. designing for lower resource consumption, 3. ensuring long-term stability, 4. constraining functionality, and 5. designing documentation for resource-constrained access. Rather than optimizing for a single metric, sustainable creative tools require navigating competing values transparently.

</details>


### [158] [SWE-Future: Forecast-Conditioned Data Synthesis for Future-Oriented Software Engineering Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18733)
*Qiao Zhao,JianYing Qu,Jun Zhang,Yehua Yang,Hanwen Du,Zhongkai Sun*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SWE-Future proposes a forecast-conditioned method for synthesizing realistic coding benchmarks that avoids replaying historical GitHub issues/PRs. It forecasts future repository tasks (features, bugfixes, refactors) using only pre-cutoff evidence, validates forecasts against actual future PRs (58.1% relevance), then uses validated forecast families to synthesize 200 tasks across 61 repos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing realistic coding-agent benchmarks replay public GitHub issues/PRs, creating data contamination risks through overlap with model pretraining, fine-tuning, or synthetic-data generation. Fully synthetic tasks avoid this but drift from real repository needs. A method is needed that generates realistic, future-oriented tasks without directly depending on historical pull-request replay.

Method: SWE-Future is a two-phase approach: (1) Forecasting: given a snapshot at time T₀, use only pre-T₀ repository evidence to predict future task families (feature implementation/enhancement, bugfix, refactor). Validate retrospectively by comparing predictions against actual post-T₀ pull requests, achieving 58.1% relevance under semantic matching. (2) Synthesis: use validated forecast families as conditioning signals to generate a 200-task coding-agent dataset across 61 repositories from a task-generation snapshot, without replaying the validation PRs.

Result: In an 80-repository retrospective validation study, the forecaster achieved 58.1% future-work relevance under the main semantic matching metric. The final dataset comprises 200 synthesized coding tasks across 61 repositories.

Conclusion: Repository-evolution forecasts can effectively guide realistic, future-oriented coding-task synthesis while reducing direct dependence on historical pull-request replay, offering a contamination-resistant alternative for coding-agent benchmarking.

Abstract: Realistic coding-agent benchmarks often replay public GitHub issues and pull requests, making them vulnerable to overlap with model pretraining, fine-tuning, synthetic-data generation, or benchmark-driven model selection. Fully synthetic tasks avoid direct historical replay, but can drift away from real repository needs. We propose SWE-Future, a forecast-conditioned data synthesis method for future-oriented coding tasks. Given a forecast snapshot at time $T_0$, the method uses only pre-$T_0$ repository evidence to forecast future feature implementation/enhancement, bugfix, and refactor task families. We first validate this forecasting step retrospectively: after forecasts are fixed, later pull requests are used only to measure whether the predicted task families match future repository work. In an 80-repository study, the forecaster achieves 58.1\% future-work relevance under the main semantic matching metric. We then use validated forecast families as conditioning signals to synthesize a 200-task coding-agent dataset across 61 repositories from a task-generation snapshot, rather than replaying the later pull requests used for validation. SWE-Future shows that repository-evolution forecasts can guide realistic, future-oriented coding-task synthesis while reducing direct dependence on historical pull-request replay.

</details>


### [159] [Toward Semantically-Seeded, Graph-Propagated Impact Analysis Across Software Artifacts: A Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18855)
*Momil Seedat*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes a training-free change-impact-analysis method that fuses semantic similarity (embedding-based) and structural dependency (graph propagation) signals over a heterogeneous artifact graph spanning requirements, config, code, and tests. A tunable weight λ balances the two signals, covering blind spots inherent to each approach alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CIA tools rely on either semantic similarity (misses artifacts with no textual overlap) or structural dependencies (misses semantically related but unconnected artifacts, and rarely cover non-code artifacts). Neither approach alone provides complete coverage, and production failures demonstrate that impacts often propagate across heterogeneous artifact types beyond code.

Method: The system models the software as a heterogeneous artifact graph with typed edges from static analysis. It computes a semantic prior via cosine similarity between embeddings of artifacts and the changed artifact, performs multi-hop impact propagation with decay using a row-normalized propagation matrix, and blends both signals with a single tunable weight λ. Evaluation on a payment subsystem with 5 labeled change scenarios.

Result: The fusion approach recovers artifacts with zero textual overlap (via structural propagation) and helper functions unreachable by propagation alone (via semantic similarity). The fused configuration is the only one that covers both blind spots, with λ acting as an explicit precision/recall control.

Conclusion: A training-free, interpretable fusion of semantic and structural signals over a heterogeneous artifact graph provides more complete change-impact coverage than either signal alone, and the formulation naturally extends to operational artifacts that code-only analysis cannot reach.

Abstract: When a single software artifact changes - a requirement, a configuration value, or a function - engineers must determine what else is impacted. Existing change-impact-analysis (CIA) tooling tends to rely on one of two signals in isolation: semantic similarity recovered from text (information-retrieval traceability, code search, embeddings), or structural dependency following (call graphs, IDE "find usages", test-impact selection). Each has a characteristic blind spot. A semantically driven tool misses an impacted artifact whose text shares no vocabulary with the change; a structurally driven tool misses artifacts related in meaning but not joined by an edge, and most operate only over code rather than the Requirement-Config-Service-Test chain. We argue for a training-free and interpretable analyzer that fuses both signals over the same embeddings. We model the system as a heterogeneous artifact graph with typed edges recovered by static analysis, compute a semantic prior by cosine similarity to the changed artifact, propagate impact multi-hop with decay over a row-normalized propagation matrix, and blend the two with a single tunable weight lambda. A small but complete proof-of-concept on a payment subsystem (5 labelled change scenarios) shows the mechanism we care about: artifacts with zero textual overlap with the change are still recovered through propagation, and helper functions that propagation alone cannot reach are recovered through the semantic layer. The fusion is the only configuration that covers both blind spots, and lambda acts as an explicit precision/recall control. Drawing on four publicly documented production failures, we argue that the same formulation extends to operational artifacts (images, metrics, dashboards, data schemas) that code-only analysis cannot reach.

</details>


### [160] [CAPRA: Scaling Feedback on Software Architecture Deliverables with a Multi-Agent LLM System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18976)
*Marco Becattini,Niccolò Caselli,Matteo Minin,Roberto Verdecchia,Enrico Vicario*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CAPRA is a multi-agent LLM system that automates feedback generation for software architecture student deliverables, using PDF parsing, vision-enabled LLMs for UML analysis, and a deterministic Evidence Anchoring mechanism to reduce hallucinations. Evaluated on 10 student reports, it achieved 88.8% criteria satisfaction and moderate inter-rater agreement (κ=0.582) with humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated assessment in software engineering education has advanced for code and essays, but reviewing software architecture deliverables—requiring structural completeness analysis and requirements traceability—remains unautomated. LLMs offer potential but need robust architectures to ensure accurate, reliable technical feedback. The work aims to fill this gap with a system that generates personalized, pedagogically sound feedback.

Method: CAPRA is a multi-agent LLM system with: (1) a Python-based microservice using PyMuPDF and vision-enabled LLMs (gpt-4o) for multi-modal document extraction (text + UML diagrams); (2) multiple specialized agents coordinated for analysis; (3) a deterministic Evidence Anchoring step using fuzzy matching via normalized Levenshtein distance to ground claims in document content and mitigate hallucinations; and (4) a ConsistencyManager agent for cross-verification, deduplication, and merging of findings. Evaluation uses an eight-criterion binary taxonomy covering extraction completeness, feature validation, issue grounding/severity, recommendation specificity/traceability, and template/tone compliance, assessed via a strict two-rater aggregation rule.

Result: On 10 student reports, CAPRA satisfied 88.8% of evaluated criteria under strict two-rater aggregation. Inter-rater agreement with human evaluators was moderate (Cohen's kappa = 0.582). Average processing time was slightly over 4 minutes per report.

Conclusion: LLM-supported architectural feedback is viable, as evidenced by high criteria satisfaction and moderate human agreement. However, human oversight remains essential for subjective assessment dimensions, indicating a human-in-the-loop approach is still necessary.

Abstract: Automated assessment in software engineering education has advanced significantly for code grading and essay scoring. However, reviewing software architecture deliverables, which requires analyzing structural completeness and requirements traceability, has not yet been fully automated. Applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to this task requires robust architectures to ensure technical feedback is accurate and reliable for students. This paper presents CAPRA (Configurable Architecture Proficiency Report Assessment), a multi-agent LLM system that analyzes software architecture deliverables to generate personalized, template-compliant LaTeX feedback. As a core design choice, CAPRA coordinates multiple specialized agents and employs a Python-based microservice for multi-modal document extraction, utilizing PyMuPDF and vision-enabled LLMs (specifically gpt-4o) to parse text and UML diagrams. To ensure educational reliability and mitigate hallucinations, CAPRA introduces a deterministic Evidence Anchoring step using fuzzy matching via normalized Levenshtein distance, along with a ConsistencyManager agent that cross-verifies, deduplicates, and merges findings. System performance is assessed using a structured eight-criterion binary evaluation taxonomy covering: (i) extraction completeness, (ii) feature validation, (iii) issue grounding and severity detection, (iv) recommendation specificity and traceability, and (v) template and tone compliance. A preliminary empirical evaluation on 10 student reports shows that CAPRA satisfied 88.8% of the evaluated criteria under a strict two-rater aggregation rule, achieved moderate inter-rater agreement with human evaluators (kappa = 0.582), and processed each report in slightly over 4 minutes. While these results support the viability of LLM-supported architectural feedback, human oversight remains essential for subjective assessment dimensions.

</details>


### [161] [Where Did the Variability Go? From Vibe Coding to Product Lines by Regeneration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19042)
*Xhevahire Tërnava*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper studies variability in "vibe coding" — where LLMs generate entire programs from prompts. The authors find that LLM-generated code exhibits near-zero compile/runtime variability, with all decisions resolved at generation time. They propose Variability by Regeneration (VbR), where the LLM serves as a derivation engine, producing tailored, dead-code-free binaries from declarative specifications, with a dispatcher routing user requests to the correct variant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vibe coding shifts software creation from manual engineering to LLM-driven generation from natural language. Traditional software engineering carefully builds variability mechanisms (e.g., preprocessor directives, feature flags, polymorphism) into code to support product lines. The authors ask: what happens to variability in this new paradigm? Their exploratory analysis reveals that LLM-generated code resolves all variability at generation time, eliminating traditional in-artifact variability. The motivation is to understand this phenomenon and design a variability approach that embraces — rather than fights — the LLM-centric workflow.

Method: (1) Exploratory analysis of 10 vibe-coded C/C++ projects to assess variability presence. (2) Formalization of Variability by Regeneration (VbR), where a declarative specification defines the product line, the LLM acts as a derivation engine generating a dedicated, dead-code-free binary per variant, and a variant dispatcher transparently routes requests. (3) Demonstration of the full VbR pipeline on a `wc` (word count) product family. (4) Contrast with classical SPL derivation approaches.

Result: The exploratory analysis shows near-zero in-artifact variability (compile-time and runtime) in vibe-coded projects — all variability decisions are resolved at generation time. The VbR approach successfully demonstrates a product-line methodology where variability lives in the specification rather than the code, with the LLM generating purpose-built binaries per variant.

Conclusion: For software product line engineering in the AI era, variability belongs in the specification, not in the generated code. VbR is the first product-line approach using the LLM as a derivation engine, offering a viable path for managing variability in AI-generated software.

Abstract: In vibe coding, an emerging AI-driven paradigm, an LLM generates an entire program from a natural language prompt, but what happens to the variability that traditional software engineering carefully builds into code? To answer this question, we conducted an exploratory analysis on 10 vibe coded C/C++ projects, which suggests that there is near-zero in-artifact variability, i.e., at compile and runtime. All variability decisions are resolved at a single new binding time, generation time, the moment the LLM produces the source code. Rather than treating this as a defect to fix, we propose Variability by Regeneration (VbR), to our knowledge the first product-line approach in which the LLM acts as the derivation engine, generating a purpose-built, free of dead code binary for each variant from a declarative specification, while a variant dispatcher transparently routes user requests to the matching binary. We formalise VbR, contrast it with classical SPL derivation, and demonstrate its full pipeline on a wc product family. For SPL engineering, variability in AI-generated software belongs in the specification, not in the code.

</details>


### [162] [Written by AI, Managed by AI: Semantic Space Control and Index Sickness Elimination Across 391 Consecutive Sessions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19121)
*Hui Zhang,Shuren Song*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Long-horizon LLM collaboration suffers from "Index Sickness," where excessive symbolic constraints cause models to retreat into self-referential reasoning disconnected from reality. The authors propose the "Pang Principle" (natural language outperforms symbolic expression for information quality) and validate a "Baseline-Log Physical Separation" mechanism that reduced AI Instructions volume by ~75% and eliminated recurrence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The dominant engineering approach to conceptual drift in long-horizon LLM collaboration — adding formal constraints, symbolic identifiers, defensive rules, and expanding context — may backfire. The authors observed in practice that beyond a complexity threshold, these strategies degrade rather than improve reliability, motivating a systematic investigation of this failure mode and its remedy.

Method: Action research conducted on a real software project (Bang-v3) spanning ~1 month and 391 collaborative sessions. The authors documented the failure process of symbolic-constraint-heavy strategies, identified a recurring failure pattern ("Index Sickness"), formulated an underlying principle ("Pang Principle / Semantic Vitality Law"), and designed a counter-mechanism ("Baseline-Log Physical Separation") which was then validated over ~150 subsequent sessions.

Result: When symbolic systems exceed a complexity threshold, LLMs abandon genuine business-semantic understanding and shift to self-referential symbolic reasoning, producing internally consistent but reality-disconnected outputs ("Phantom Legislation"). The proposed Baseline-Log Physical Separation mechanism reduced AI Instructions volume by ~75% and eliminated Index Sickness across ~150 sessions with no recurrence.

Conclusion: The "Pang Principle" holds that natural language carrying explicit purpose conveys superior information quality compared to symbolic expression. Engineering practice should favor semantic vitality over formal-symbolic constraint accumulation in long-horizon LLM collaboration systems.

Abstract: The prevailing engineering intuition for addressing conceptual drift in long-horizon LLM collaboration is to trade more formal constraints for more reliable outputs -- designing symbolic identifier systems, accumulating defensive rules in System Prompts, expanding context windows. Our engineering record shows that in long-horizon settings, this direction may produce effects contrary to design intent. Using action research methods in a real software project (Bang-v3) spanning approximately one month and 391 collaborative sessions, we document and analyze the failure process of these strategies. When the symbolic system exceeds a complexity threshold, LLMs do not become more accurate -- instead, they abandon genuine understanding of business semantics, retreat to self-referential reasoning within the symbolic layer, and generate outputs that appear internally consistent but are physically disconnected from reality. We name this failure pattern "Index Sickness," and its canonical manifestation "Phantom Legislation." We name the underlying principle the "Pang Principle (Semantic Vitality Law)": natural language carrying explicit purpose conveys far greater information quality than symbolic expression. From this, we design and validate its physical engineering mechanism: "Baseline-Log Physical Separation." In the same project, this mechanism reduced AI Instructions volume by ~75%, and across the subsequent ~150 sessions, no recurrence of Index Sickness was observed. A bilingual companion version (Chinese) is included as supplementary material.

</details>


### [163] [Teaching Software Engineering with LLM and MCP Integration: From Classroom to Industry Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19167)
*Kehui Chen,Jacky Keung,Weining Li,Xiangbing Shao,Yishu Li,Xiaoxue Ma*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) into software engineering education to bridge the gap between traditional teaching and industrial AI-driven workflows, enhancing students' programming skills and real-world problem-solving abilities through classroom tools, simulations, and industry internships.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid adoption of LLMs and MCP in industrial software engineering has outpaced traditional software engineering curricula, creating a disconnect between academic training and evolving industry demands. There is a pressing need to modernize education to align with these emerging technologies.

Method: The study employs an integrated collaborative teaching model that embeds LLM- and MCP-driven tools into three key areas: (1) daily classroom instruction, (2) code assistance for programming tasks, and (3) engineering simulations that mimic real-world workflows. This is complemented by industry internship partnerships where students apply these technologies in authentic professional settings.

Result: The integrated approach enhanced students' programming competence, practical problem-solving abilities, and proficiency in using intelligent engineering tools. The combination of in-class tool integration and industry internships strengthened the connection between academic preparation and professional practice.

Conclusion: Integrating LLMs and MCP into software engineering education offers a viable and practical pathway for reforming curricula to meet the demands of the AI era, effectively aligning academic training with industrial realities.

Abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) into industrial software engineering has created a pressing need to update software engineering education to align with emerging technologies and evolving industry demands. This study investigates an innovative approach that integrates LLMs and MCP into a collaborative teaching model for software engineering education, aiming to build a practical learning framework closely connected to real-world engineering practices. By embedding LLM and MCP driven tools into daily teaching, code assistance, and engineering simulations, the model effectively bridges the gap between traditional instruction and industrial workflows. This integration enhances students' programming competence, practical problem-solving abilities, and proficiency in using intelligent engineering tools. Furthermore, through partnerships with industry internships, students can apply these technologies in real-world settings, further strengthening the connection between academic preparation and professional practice. Overall, this research offers a practical pathway for reforming and innovating software engineering education in the era of artificial intelligence.

</details>


### [164] [No Two Developers Think Alike: How Problem-Solving Styles and Experience Shape Needs in Conversational Interaction with Copilot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19216)
*Jonan Richards,Bruno Alves de Oliveira,Iury Oliveira,Igor Wiese,Mairieli Wessel*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Through a think-aloud study with 27 participants, the paper identifies 5 interaction modes and 10 developer needs when using GitHub Copilot Chat, linking them to cognitive diversity factors such as problem-solving styles and experience profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research shows that developers have highly varied needs and face distinct challenges when using LLM-based programming assistants, yet the role of cognitive diversity in shaping these interactions remains poorly understood. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically characterizing how individual differences influence the way developers engage with conversational programming assistants.

Method: A mixed-methods think-aloud study with 27 participants (professional developers and students) interacting with GitHub Copilot Chat. Qualitative analysis of think-aloud sessions was used to derive a conceptual model comprising interaction modes and underlying needs, which were then mapped to participants' cognitive profiles (problem-solving styles and experience levels).

Result: The authors identified 5 distinct interaction modes and 10 underlying developer needs, forming a conceptual model. They found demonstrable links between these modes/needs and developers' problem-solving styles and experience profiles, providing evidence that cognitive diversity significantly shapes how developers interact with programming assistants.

Conclusion: Cognitive diversity is a critical factor in shaping developer interactions with LLM-based programming assistants. The authors offer actionable insights and recommendations for designing, researching, and deploying programming assistants that better accommodate the broad spectrum of developer needs.

Abstract: Conversational LLM-based ``programming assistants'' provide a range of benefits to developers. However, recent studies demonstrate the variety in individual developers' needs regarding programming assistants, and challenges encountered by only specific groups of developers. In this study, we explore the role of cognitive diversity in shaping interactions with GitHub Copilot chat. Through a mixed-methods think aloud study with 27 professional developers and students, we characterize 5 distinct ``interaction modes'' and 10 underlying needs in developers' interactions, forming a conceptual model. We characterize links between these modes, needs, and developers' problem-solving styles and experience profiles, showing how cognitive diversity may shape developers' interactions. We provide insights and recommendations for researchers and practitioners on how to design, research, and employ programming assistants to better account for diverse developer needs.

</details>


### [165] [Runtime Compliance Verification for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19242)
*Nafiseh Kahani,Masoud Barati,Diana Addae*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: C-Trace is a runtime GDPR compliance enforcement framework for AI agents that formally encodes consent, purpose limitation, data minimization, and erasure rights as policy predicates over execution traces. A runtime monitor intercepts tool calls and model outputs to reject non-compliant actions. Evaluated under noisy conditions, it achieves ≤12% attack success rate and ≤16% false positives, reaching 0% ASR with perfect extraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents increasingly process personal data through tool use, function calls, and multi-turn dialogue, creating GDPR compliance obligations. Existing testing approaches (offline red teaming, static prompt review) cannot guarantee runtime compliance, necessitating a dynamic enforcement mechanism that verifies agent behavior against regulatory rules during execution.

Method: C-Trace is a verification framework with three components: (1) formalization of GDPR requirements (consent, purpose limitation, data minimization, right to erasure) as policy predicates over agent execution traces; (2) a runtime monitor that intercepts every tool invocation and model output, rejecting non-compliant actions; and (3) adversarial testing with attack dialogues, including DSPy-generated prompts and red-teaming corpus prompts, designed to induce violations. The framework is evaluated across four GDPR-reframed case studies under extractor noise conditions (drop-out and over-typing at 10% per category).

Result: Under 10% per-category extractor noise (including drop-out and over-typing), C-Trace maintains attack success rate ≤12% and false positive rate ≤16%, outperforming baseline comparisons. Under perfect extraction conditions, attack success rate drops to 0%.

Conclusion: Runtime monitoring with formally specified GDPR policy predicates effectively enforces compliance in AI agent systems, substantially reducing attack success rates even under realistic noisy extraction conditions, and eliminating violations entirely under ideal extraction.

Abstract: AI agents now handle personal data through tool use, function calls, and multi turn dialogue, which can create obligations under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Current testing practices mainly rely on offline red teaming or static prompt review, but they do not guarantee at runtime that agent behavior follows regulatory rules. We propose C-Trace (Compliance Trace based Runtime Agent Conformance Enforcement), a verification framework that: (i) expresses a subset of GDPR requirements, including consent, purpose limitation, data minimization, and the right to erasure, as formal policy predicates over agent execution traces; (ii) uses a runtime monitor that intercepts every tool invocation and model output and rejects non-compliant actions; and (iii) tests the agent with attack dialogues, including DSPy generated prompts and verbatim prompts from red teaming corpora, that try to induce violations. We evaluate the framework on four case studies reframed to GDPR. Under 10 percent per-category extractor noise, including drop-out and over-typing, the monitor keeps the attack success rate at less than or equal to 12 percent, below the baselines we compare against, and false positives at less than or equal to 16 percent, and reaches 0 percent ASR under perfect extraction.

</details>

### [166] [Gaussian Mixture Attention: Linear-Time Sequence Mixing via Probabilistic Latent Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18283)
*Yongchao Huang,Hassan Raza*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Gaussian Mixture Attention (GMA) replaces standard dot-product attention's O(N²) pairwise token interactions with routing through K learned Gaussian mixture components. Queries and keys are mapped to responsibility vectors over a shared latent space, and values are stored in a K-slot memory. This achieves O(NK) memory scaling, avoiding materialization of the N×N affinity matrix. GMA supports bidirectional and causal variants, and empirically shows competitive long-context classification performance and interpretable component usage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The dense token-to-token interaction pattern (O(N²) memory and computation) in standard dot-product attention is a central bottleneck for scaling Transformers to long contexts. The authors seek a probabilistic, more memory-efficient alternative that preserves competitive modeling quality while offering interpretability.

Method: GMA replaces explicit query-key dot products with a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) routing mechanism. Queries and keys are projected into a shared latent routing space and softly assigned to K Gaussian mixture components via posterior responsibility vectors. Token interaction is mediated implicitly through responsibility-space affinity rather than direct comparison. Values are aggregated into K learnable memory slots (write) and retrieved (read) using matrix multiplication associativity, avoiding any N×N materialization. Both bidirectional and causal (masked) variants are formulated, with an end-to-end differentiable GMM parameterization.

Result: Empirically, GMA achieves the intended fixed-K linear memory scaling (O(NK)). On long-context classification tasks, it is competitive with standard attention baselines. Causal GMA improves over tested linear/random-feature attention variants on WikiText-103 perplexity, but underperforms optimized causal SDPA and Mamba in the current implementation. Learned responsibility analysis reveals broad component usage and moderate alignment with surface-form token categories (e.g., punctuation, function words), suggesting interpretable structure.

Conclusion: GMA offers a probabilistic, interpretable, fixed-K linear-time attention-style alternative with O(NK) memory. It is not positioned as a universal replacement for optimized softmax attention or state-space models, but rather as a principled and competitive option for specific long-context settings where memory constraints and interpretability are priorities.

Abstract: The dense token-to-token interaction pattern of standard dot-product attention remains a central bottleneck in scaling Transformer architectures to long contexts. We introduce \textbf{Gaussian Mixture Attention (GMA)}, a probabilistic attention-style sequence mixer that replaces explicit pairwise query--key comparison with routing through $K$ learned Gaussian mixture components. Queries and keys are mapped to posterior \textit{responsibility} vectors over a shared latent routing space; their overlap defines an implicit responsibility-space affinity, while values are written into and read from a $K$-slot latent memory. By exploiting the associativity of matrix multiplication, GMA avoids materializing the induced $N\times N$ affinity matrix and instead uses two responsibility matrices whose dominant activation storage scales as $\mathcal{O}(NK)$ rather than $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ for fixed $K$. We formulate bidirectional and causal variants of GMA, provide an end-to-end differentiable parameterization of the Gaussian mixture components, and analyze its responsibility-modulated gradient structure, constrained non-negative low-rank affinity interpretation, and local routing stability. Empirically, GMA exhibits the intended fixed-$K$ linear memory scaling and is competitive with attention-style baselines on long-context classification, while causal GMA improves over tested linear/random-feature attention variants on WikiText-103 but remains behind optimized causal SDPA and Mamba in the current implementation. Analysis of learned responsibilities further shows broad component usage and moderate alignment with surface-form token categories, supporting GMA as a probabilistic, interpretable, fixed-$K$ linear-time attention-style alternative rather than a universal replacement for optimized softmax attention or state-space models.

</details>


### [167] [Breaking the Solver Bottleneck: Training Task Generators at the Learnable Frontier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18284)
*Lorenz Wolf,Connor Watts,Roger Creus Castanyer,Geoffrey Bradway,Maxwill Lin,Augustine N. Mavor-Parker,Matthew Daborn-Sargent*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PROPEL amortizes the cost of solver-in-the-loop task generation by training a lightweight probe to predict solve rate from a frozen reference model, enabling targeted-difficulty task generation with a single forward pass instead of expensive solver rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As RL agents improve, fixed task distributions saturate. Naive synthetic generation produces trivial or ill-posed tasks, while direct RL optimization of a task generator requires repeated solver rollouts — prohibitive for software-engineering tasks where a single rollout takes tens of minutes.

Method: PROPEL trains a lightweight activation probe on a one-time labeled corpus of generated tasks paired with solver outcomes. The probe, operating on a frozen generator reference model, predicts the target-solver pass rate and serves as a proxy reward during generator optimization. This reduces generator evaluation to a single forward pass, amortizing solver costs.

Result: Across math, code, and SWE at multiple model scales, PROPEL shifts generation toward the targeted solve rate. For coding: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct solver sees learnable-frontier tasks rise from 10.1% to 20.0%; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from 5.3% to 12.6%. For SWE with Qwen3.5-27B on unseen repositories, targeted-solve-rate share increases from 9.8% to 19.6%.

Conclusion: PROPEL provides a scalable, solver-amortized approach to training task generators that produce tasks at a desired difficulty level, effectively addressing the frontier task supply bottleneck for RL training of increasingly capable models.

Abstract: The limiting resource for training agents via reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly frontier task supply: valid, solvable tasks just difficult enough to train the current model. As reasoning and agentic models improve, fixed task distributions saturate, while naive synthetic generation yields tasks that are trivial, impossible, or ill-posed. Training a task generator with RL to optimize validity and learnability can address this bottleneck, but direct optimization requires repeated solver rollouts per candidate. For software-engineering (SWE) tasks, a single rollout can take tens of minutes; solver-in-the-loop generator training is intractable. We introduce PROPEL, a solver-amortized framework for training task generators at the targeted solve rate. PROPEL trains a lightweight activation probe on a one-time labeled corpus of generated tasks and solver outcomes. The probe predicts target-solver pass rate from a frozen generator reference model and serves as a proxy for solve rate during generator optimization, reducing generator evaluation to a single forward pass. Across math, code, and software-engineering at multiple model scales, PROPEL shifts generation toward the targeted solve rate: for coding, tasks generated at the learnable frontier increase from $10.1\% \rightarrow 20.0\%$ for a Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct solver and from $5.3\% \rightarrow 12.6\%$ for a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct solver. For SWE, PROPEL increases the share of generations at the targeted solve rate from $9.8\% \rightarrow 19.6\%$ for Qwen3.5-27B on repositories not seen during training of probe and generator.

</details>


### [168] [CODEBLOCK: Learning to Supervise Code at the Right Granularity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18286)
*Zhijie Deng,Ling Li,Jinlong Pang,Kaiqin Hu,Qi Xuan,Zhaowei Zhu,Jiaheng Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CodeBlock proposes a structure-aware sparse supervision framework for code LLM fine-tuning that selects syntactically coherent code blocks (rather than isolated tokens) for loss computation, using only 1.9% of response tokens while outperforming full-token SFT on code generation benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing token-level selection methods for SFT assume all tokens are equally useful, and while NLP has explored sparse supervision, directly transferring token-level masking to code breaks syntactic/semantic coherence (e.g., splitting definition-use chains). Code needs supervision at the granularity of structurally complete program units.

Method: CodeBlock operates in three stages: (1) high-quality instruction-response pair selection, (2) partitioning code responses into syntactically coherent "coding items" and estimating their utility via aggregated generalized cross-entropy over core logic tokens, (3) reranking blocks using data-flow reach and bridge signals to prioritize blocks that propagate or connect important program dependencies. During training, full context is preserved but loss is applied only to selected code blocks and informative NL tokens.

Result: On six code-generation benchmarks, CodeBlock achieves stronger average pass@1 than full-token SFT and competitive selection baselines, while using only 1.9% of supervised response tokens.

Conclusion: Structure-aware sparse supervision at the code-block level is both more efficient (1.9% tokens) and more effective than uniform full-token SFT for code LLMs, validating that respecting code's structural and dependency properties is critical for selective supervision.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of code LLMs typically applies uniform cross-entropy loss to all response tokens, implicitly assuming that every token provides equally useful learning signal. Recent token-level selection methods challenge this assumption in natural-language SFT by supervising only high-value tokens. However, directly transferring token-level masking to code can break syntactically and semantically coherent program units, because code depends on structural completeness and definition-use relations. We therefore propose CodeBlock, a structure-aware sparse supervision framework that selects structure-complete code evidence rather than isolated tokens. CodeBlock first selects high-quality instruction-response pairs, then partitions code responses into syntactically coherent coding items, estimates their utility by aggregating generalized cross-entropy over core logic tokens, and reranks them with data-flow reach and bridge signals to prioritize blocks that propagate or connect important program dependencies. During training, the full response remains available as context, while loss is applied only to selected code items and informative natural-language tokens. Experiments on six code-generation benchmarks show that CodeBlock achieves stronger average pass@1 than full-token SFT and competitive selection baselines, while using only 1.9% of supervised response tokens.

</details>


### [169] [Artemis: Anatomy-Resolved inTervention for Eliminating Multimodal NeuroImage confounderS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18287)
*Siyuan Dai,Yang Du,Kun Zhao,Zhusuyi Chen,Heng Huang,Paul Thompson,Chao Shi,Haoteng Tang,Liang Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Artemis is a region-level causal intervention framework for multimodal brain network analysis that learns region-specific confounder representations to mitigate demographic biases (age, sex) in GNN-based neuroimaging, serving as a plug-in module compatible with any GNN backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Demographic confounders like age and sex cause GNNs to learn spurious shortcuts rather than causally invariant representations in brain network analysis. Existing causal GNN methods are domain-agnostic and fail to account for real-world clinical confounders, and they ignore that different brain regions have distinct sensitivities to demographic factors, requiring region-aware adjustment.

Method: Artemis performs causal intervention at each brain region independently by learning region-specific confounder representations with lightweight parameters. It comprehensively utilizes both multimodal functional (fMRI) and structural (DTI) connectivity features for graph reasoning and is designed as a plug-in module compatible with arbitrary GNN backbones.

Result: Experiments on three benchmarks — ADNI (disease diagnosis), OASIS (dementia staging), and HCP (sex classification) — demonstrate consistent improvements over representative GNN-based baselines. Additional experiments confirm statistical significance and neuroscientific interpretability.

Conclusion: Region-level causal intervention with learned region-specific confounder representations effectively mitigates demographic confounding in multimodal brain network analysis, yielding robust and interpretable GNN-based predictions across diverse clinical neuroimaging tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal neuroimaging, integrating functional connectivity from fMRI and structural connectivity from DTI, enables non-invasive analysis of brain networks using graph neural networks. However, demographic factors such as age and sex systematically confound the relationship between brain connectivity and clinical outcomes, causing GNNs to exploit spurious shortcuts rather than learning causally invariant representations. While recent causal GNN methods introduce causality at the graph-modeling level, their causal mechanisms remain domain-agnostic without accounting for the real-world confounders inherent in clinical neuroimaging data. Moreover, brain networks are constructed from atlas-based parcellations where each region exhibits distinct sensitivity to demographic factors, necessitating region-aware adjustment. We propose Artemis, a region-level causal framework that bridges this gap with causal intervention at each brain region independently by learning region-specific confounder representations with lightweight parameters. Our adjustment comprehensively utilized the multimodal functional and structural features for graph reasoning as a plug-in module compatible with arbitrary GNN backbones. Experiments on three benchmarks, ADNI for disease diagnosis, OASIS for dementia staging, and HCP for sex classification, demonstrate consistent improvements over representative GNN-based baselines. Multiple supporting experiments further demonstrate statistical significance and neuroscientific interpretability.

</details>


### [170] [A Link between Shock-wave Theory and Symmetry-reduced Stochastic Gradient Descent for Artificial Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18303)
*Taiki Miyagawa*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper establishes a rigorous mathematical connection between stochastic gradient descent dynamics and shock-wave theory by quotienting parameter symmetries. Under coarse-graining, the effective dynamics obey a viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation, and the gradient of the loss evolves according to a Burgers-type equation, enabling shock formation analysis across various neural architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Raw parameter dynamics in deep learning are confounded by symmetry redundancies (e.g., permutation symmetries in MLPs, weight rescalings in Transformers), making it difficult to obtain a principled, geometry-aware description of training dynamics. The authors seek a mathematically rigorous framework that quotients out these symmetries to reveal universal effective dynamics.

Method: The authors apply differential geometry and Lie group theory to quotient out parameter symmetries, then use local-entropy coarse-graining to derive an effective viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation on the quotient manifold. Assuming the raw dynamics reduce to a gradient field, they show the gradient of the coarse-grained loss satisfies a Burgers-type PDE, enabling rigorous shock-formation analysis.

Result: The framework is shown to apply to multilayer perceptrons, CNNs, Transformers, and mean-field networks, all obeying either Hamilton-Jacobi or Burgers-type equations. The authors conjecture that symmetry-corrected quotient observables offer principled diagnostics for monitoring, forecasting, and controlling phase transitions during training, in contrast to raw parameter norms distorted by symmetry redundancy.

Conclusion: Symmetry-quotiented learning dynamics provide a unifying mathematical framework linking SGD to shock-wave theory. Quotient observables, unlike raw parameter norms, offer a geometrically faithful basis for analyzing training-phase transitions, with potential practical utility as diagnostics for deep learning.

Abstract: We develop a mathematically explicit link between shock-wave theory and the symmetry-quotiented learning dynamics of stochastic gradient descent, drawing on differential geometry, Lie group theory, and fluid mechanics. Specifically, after quotienting parameter symmetries and applying local-entropy coarse-graining, the effective dynamics satisfy a viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equation on the quotient manifold. Moreover, under the assumption that the raw parameter dynamics can be summarized by a gradient field on the quotiented space, the gradient of the coarse-grained loss function obeys a Burgers-type equation, and shock formation can be established rigorously. We apply our theory to multilayer perceptrons, convolutional neural networks, Transformers, and mean-field networks, and show that they obey the Hamilton--Jacobi or Burgers-type equations. We conjecture that this framework also yields practical diagnostics for deep learning. In architectures such as Transformers, raw parameter norms are often distorted by symmetry redundancy and may therefore be misleading, whereas symmetry-corrected quotient observables provide a principled basis for monitoring, forecasting, and controlling training-phase transitions.

</details>


### [171] [Attribution-Guided and Coverage-Maximized Pruning for Structural MoE Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18304)
*Yifu Ding,Jiacheng Wang,Ge Yang,Yongcheng Jing,Jinyang Guo,Xianglong Liu,Dacheng Tao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MoE models are efficient to scale but costly to deploy due to memory and inference overhead. Prior expert-level pruning is too coarse. The authors observe that critical information concentrates in few channels within experts, motivating a fine-grained channel-level structural pruning framework. They formulate prune-ratio allocation as a channel-score coverage maximization problem solved via attribution-based approximation, achieving strong accuracy retention at 50%/25% pruning with 4-bit quantization, and a 5.27× memory reduction on Qwen3-30B-A3B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE models are compute-efficient at scale but suffer from large memory footprints and inference overhead during deployment. Existing compression methods prune at the coarse expert level, which cannot capture fine-grained redundancy within individual experts and leads to suboptimal pruning budget allocation.

Method: A structural pruning framework specific to MoE models that: (1) identifies that expert knowledge concentrates in a small subset of channels, (2) reformulates the prune-ratio allocation problem as a channel-score coverage maximization problem, and (3) solves it efficiently using an attribution-based approximation rather than per-channel combinatorial search.

Result: On DeepSeek and Qwen MoE models, the method preserves accuracy under 50% or 25% structured pruning when combined with 4-bit quantization. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it achieves a 5.27× memory footprint reduction and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks.

Conclusion: Fine-grained, channel-level structural pruning within MoE experts—guided by attribution-based coverage maximization—substantially outperforms coarse expert-level pruning. The approach enables aggressive compression (5.27× memory reduction) while maintaining accuracy, making MoE deployment significantly more practical.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale compute efficiently, yet remain expensive to deploy due to their substantial memory footprint and inference overhead. Prior compression methods mainly operate at the expert level, either removing entire experts or ranking experts by coarse-grained importance scores. However, such expert-wise decisions are often too coarse to capture fine-grained redundancy, leading to misallocated pruning budgets and limited compression. To address this problem, we observe that information within MoE experts is highly concentrated in a small subset of channels, leaving substantial redundancy even in experts deemed important. Based on this observation, we propose a structural pruning framework tailored for MoE models. Our method reformulates prune-ratio allocation as a channel-score coverage maximization problem and solves it efficiently using an attribution-based approximation. Experiments on DeepSeek and Qwen MoE models show that our method preserves model accuracy under 50% or 25% structured pruning when combined with 4-bit quantization. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, our approach reduces memory footprint by 5.27$\times$ and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks.

</details>


### [172] [Fisher Width: A Geometric Measure of Complexity on Statistical Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18306)
*Vu Khac Ky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Fisher width, a Fisher-geometric analog of Gaussian width adapted to statistical manifolds. By replacing the Euclidean metric with the Fisher information metric tensor, Fisher width captures local statistical curvature, remains invariant under reparameterization, and retains key properties like concentration and stability. The authors prove a generalization bound for Fisher-Lipschitz classes and provide empirical validation on MNIST.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gaussian width is a foundational complexity measure in high-dimensional probability and learning theory, but it is inherently Euclidean. Statistical models possess a natural Riemannian geometry via the Fisher information metric, where distances reflect statistical distinguishability. The authors aim to port the utility of Gaussian width to this curved geometric setting, enabling complexity analysis that respects the intrinsic geometry of statistical manifolds.

Method: The authors define Fisher width at a parameter θ by rescaling the set with the local metric tensor G(θ)^{1/2} (the square root of the Fisher information matrix), then taking the Gaussian width of the transformed set. They develop its theoretical properties—concentration inequalities, perturbation stability under metric changes, and spectral comparison bounds relating Fisher width to Euclidean Gaussian width. For application, they derive a generalization bound for hypothesis classes satisfying a Fisher-Lipschitz condition and design computable estimators, tested on MNIST across three model classes.

Result: Fisher width retains Gaussian width's structural properties (concentration, stability, spectral comparisons) while additionally capturing anisotropic geometric effects invisible to Euclidean measures. The derived generalization bound for Fisher-Lipschitz classes provides a formal learning-theoretic guarantee. Empirical evaluation on MNIST demonstrates the practical computability of Fisher width estimators across multiple model architectures.

Conclusion: Fisher width serves as the natural complexity measure for statistical manifolds, analogously to Gaussian width for Euclidean convex bodies. The framework opens the door to studying complexity and generalization on curved statistical manifolds with intrinsic geometric fidelity.

Abstract: Gaussian width is a central geometric complexity measure in high-dimensional probability, compressed sensing, convex optimization, and learning theory. It quantifies the average extent of a set along random directions, thereby capturing the effective dimension of constraint sets, hypothesis classes, and descent cones. However, this notion is intrinsically Euclidean. Statistical models instead carry a natural Riemannian geometry induced by the Fisher information metric, where directions are scaled according to statistical distinguishability rather than ambient Euclidean length.
  We introduce Fisher width, a Fisher-geometric analogue of Gaussian width for statistical manifolds. At a parameter point $θ$, Fisher width replaces the Euclidean identity by the local metric tensor $G(θ)^{1/2}$, measuring the Gaussian width of the Fisher-rescaled set. This makes the resulting quantity sensitive to local statistical curvature and invariant under smooth reparameterizations.
  We develop the basic theory of Fisher width, showing that it retains key structural features of Gaussian width, including concentration, metric perturbation stability, and spectral comparison bounds with the Euclidean baseline, while also capturing anisotropic geometric effects invisible to Euclidean measures. As an application, we prove a generalization bound for Fisher-Lipschitz hypothesis classes and propose computable estimators, which we evaluate empirically on MNIST across three model classes.
  Fisher width is to statistical manifolds what Gaussian width is to Euclidean convex bodies. This work lays the foundation for studying complexity and learning on curved statistical manifolds.

</details>


### [173] [Zero-Shot Active Feature Acquisition via LLM-Elicitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18933)
*Binyamin Perets,Natalie Mendelson,Shiran Vainberg,Yehuda Chowers,Shai Shen-Orr,Shie Mannor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A zero-shot active feature acquisition framework that elicits only discriminative statistics from LLMs to construct Markov random fields, resolving gauge ambiguity via maximum-entropy closure. Outperforms LLMs and existing methods on IBD patient classification, especially for hardest cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional active feature acquisition (AFA) requires large labeled datasets to fit probabilistic models, which is impractical in many real-world settings. LLMs offer unsupervised domain knowledge but are poor sequential planners. The insight is to decouple knowledge elicitation from decision-making: ask LLMs only for reliable pairwise and unary statistics (MRF sufficient statistics) rather than full acquisition policies.

Method: The framework elicits unary deviations and pairwise co-variations from an LLM as sufficient statistics of a Markov random field. Since LLMs reliably return only discriminative statistics (class differences, not absolute class descriptions), classical AFA fails. A maximum-entropy closure resolves this gauge ambiguity, yielding a properly normalized joint distribution. This MRF then drives zero-shot active feature acquisition for binary classification and top-k identification tasks.

Result: Evaluated on a cohort of Inflammatory Bowel Disease patients — a setting with diagnostic ambiguity and patient heterogeneity. The framework outperforms the LLM both on ground-truth labels and on the LLM's own extracted beliefs. On the hardest patients, the top-k acquisition policy markedly outperforms all existing methods.

Conclusion: Disciplined LLM elicitation — asking only for what LLMs can reliably return (discriminative statistics) and using proper probabilistic machinery (MRF with maximum-entropy closure) for planning — enables effective zero-shot active feature acquisition, particularly valuable in high-stakes clinical settings with limited labeled data.

Abstract: Active feature acquisition (AFA) sequentially selects which features to observe to reach a classification or ranking decision. Its central limitation is reliance on large amount of labeled data to fit probabilistic models guiding acquisition. Large language models (LLMs) supply unsupervised domain knowledge, but are poor sequential planners. Asking one to both know and decide conflates capabilities best kept separate. Here, we develop a framework for zero-shot AFA through disciplined elicitation: asking the LLM only for what it can be trusted to return, the unary deviations and pairwise co-variations that are the sufficient statistics of a Markov random field (MRF). We apply our framework to two settings: binary classification and top-$k$ identification. In practice, the LLM reliably returns only discriminative statistics, what distinguishes the classes rather than each class in isolation, which precludes classical AFA. We apply a maximum-entropy closure that resolves this gauge ambiguity. We evaluate on a cohort of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) patients, an active clinical setting where diagnostic ambiguity and patient heterogeneity obstruct stable treatment strategies. Our framework outperforms the LLM both on real labels and on its own extracted beliefs. Where it matters most, on the hardest patients, our top-$k$ acquisition policy markedly outperforms all existing methods.

</details>


### [174] [DRIFT: Refining Instruction Data via On-Policy Data Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18307)
*Zefan Wang,Lincheng Li,Tianyu Yu,Yuan Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DRIFT improves SFT data refinement by using on-policy rollouts as IF validation targets, addressing proximity gap and gradient norm bias. It applies signed weighting and debiasing to elevate LLM performance ceilings beyond existing data curation methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing data curation methods optimize for training efficiency under budget constraints (finding smaller subsets that preserve performance) but fail to elevate the capability upper bound. The goal shifts to refining the data distribution toward instances that maximally improve the final model, which standard Influence Functions cannot handle due to structural limitations.

Method: DRIFT introduces three key innovations: (1) using the model's own on-policy rollouts as validation targets instead of external reference data, minimizing the parameter proximity gap and aligning with IF's local neighborhood assumption; (2) signed weighting based on trajectory correctness (correct vs. incorrect rollouts); and (3) debiasing influence scores against gradient hacking (gradient norm bias). A small set of validation queries serves as reliable anchors for attributing the full training dataset.
