Result: Experiments on 7B-parameter instruction and reasoning models demonstrate that DRIFT consistently raises the performance ceiling, outperforming existing data curation baselines on both instruction-following and reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: DRIFT effectively refines SFT data distributions by addressing fundamental limitations of standard Influence Functions, enabling the curation of training data that elevates rather than merely preserves LLM performance, and establishing on-policy validation as a superior attribution strategy.

Abstract: Optimizing the training data distribution for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) dictates the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs). While existing data curation methods excel at accelerating training under constrained budgets, they are less suited to elevating the capability upper bound. The challenge here is no longer to identify a smaller subset that preserves performance, but to refine the data distribution toward instances most capable of improving the final model. To address this problem, we explore instance-level data attribution using Influence Functions (IF). We identify that standard IF formulations struggle in this setting due to two structural limitations: a proximity gap caused by off-policy validation targets, and a severe bias towards gradient norm. We propose DRIFT (Data Refinement via On-Policy Influence Functions for Supervised Fine-Tuning). Instead of relying on external reference data, DRIFT utilizes the model's on-policy rollouts as validation targets, which empirically minimizes the parameter proximity gap and better aligns with the local neighborhood assumption of IF. It further applies signed weighting based on trajectory correctness and debiases influence scores against the gradient hacking issue, allowing a small set of validation queries to act as reliable anchors for attributing the full dataset. Experiments on 7B-parameter instruction and reasoning models show that DRIFT consistently raises the performance ceiling on both, outperforming existing data curation baselines.

</details>


### [175] [LLMZero: Discovering Adaptive Training Strategies for RL Post-Training via LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18388)
*Haoyang Fang,Wei Zhu,Boran Han,Alex Zhang,Zhenyu Pan,Shuo Yang,Shuai Zhang,Jiading Gai,Peng Tang,Cuixiong Hu,Xuan Zhu,Huzefa Rangwala,George Karypis,Bernie Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMZero uses LLM agents with tree search to discover multi-stage RL post-training strategies, revealing that capacity parameters accumulate monotonically while regularization parameters oscillate. Discovered strategies outperform baselines by 9–140% over base models and 6–15% over grid search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL post-training strategies are dataset-dependent, and existing fixed schedules cannot adapt to the non-stationary exploration-exploitation tradeoffs required across training stages. There is a need for automated discovery of dynamic, multi-stage training strategies.

Method: LLMZero: an LLM-agent system that performs tree search over training trajectories. At each checkpoint, agents diagnose training pathologies and propose coordinated multi-parameter transitions, dynamically adjusting both capacity and regularization parameters across stages.

Result: Across 4 GRPO tasks, LLMZero-discovered strategies improve 9–140% over base models and 6–15% over grid search, consistently beating random search and skill-based agents. A structural principle emerges: capacity parameters accumulate monotonically across stages, while regularization parameters oscillate to track shifting training dynamics.

Conclusion: Fixed schedules are fundamentally limited because they cannot express non-stationary exploration-exploitation tradeoffs. The discovered monotonic-vs-oscillatory parameter principle transfers across tasks and provides actionable design rules for multi-stage RL post-training.

Abstract: RL post-training strategies are dataset-dependent and reveal a recurring empirical pattern: capacity parameters accumulate monotonically across stages, while regularization parameters predominantly oscillate in response to shifting training dynamics. This distinction matters because fixed schedules commit all parameters to fixed trajectories and therefore cannot express the non-stationary exploration-exploitation tradeoffs that regularization must track; the principle provides actionable design rules for multi-stage training. We discover this through LLMZero, a system where LLM agents search over training trajectories via tree search, diagnosing pathologies at each checkpoint and proposing coordinated multi-parameter transitions. Across 4 diverse GRPO tasks, LLMZero discovers strategies that improve over the base model by 9% to 140% relative and over grid search by 6% to 15% relative, consistently outperforming random search and the skill-based agent. The structural principle transfers across tasks, providing an explanation for why discovered strategies take qualitatively different forms yet share similar parameter dynamics.

</details>


### [176] [TRIDENT: Breaking the Hybrid-Safety-Physics Coupling for Provably Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18308)
*Zijie Meng,Ziwei Li,Yufei Liu,Zhiyu Li,Jiyuan Liu,Wenhua Nie,Bingcai Wei,Miao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRIDENT is a co-designed MARL framework that addresses the three-way coupling of hybrid discrete-continuous actions, hard safety constraints, and physics-governed dynamics. It uses Richardson-Romberg gradient correction, Lyapunov-constrained trust-region updates, and a physics-informed residual critic to achieve O~(1/√K) convergence to a constrained Nash equilibrium, reducing training-time violations by 76–95% over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safe coordination in networked cyber-physical systems presents three entangled challenges: hybrid (discrete-continuous) action spaces, hard safety constraints that must hold during training, and physics-governed dynamics. The authors identify that naively combining off-the-shelf modules for each challenge creates a directed cycle of biases, formalized as a three-way coupling lemma, which fundamentally degrades learning. No existing MARL framework simultaneously addresses all three features.

Method: TRIDENT co-designs three components to mutually cancel biases: (1) a Richardson-Romberg gradient correction that reduces Gumbel-Softmax discretization bias from O(τ) to O(τ²); (2) a Lyapunov-constrained sequential trust-region update enforcing per-iterate feasibility of safety constraints; and (3) a physics-informed residual critic that decomposes the value function rather than the reward, integrating physics priors directly into the critic architecture.

Result: Theoretical results: O~(1/√K) convergence rate to a constrained Nash equilibrium and O(√K) cumulative-violation bound. Empirical results on multi-UAV mobile-edge computing, autonomous intersection management, and a hybrid SMAC variant: TRIDENT reduces training-time violations by 95.5% over MADDPG and 76.3% over MACPO, while achieving 13.5% higher reward than the strongest unconstrained baseline.

Conclusion: TRIDENT demonstrates that co-designing policy gradient correction, safe policy optimization, and physics-informed value decomposition is essential for safe MARL in cyber-physical systems. The framework validates its theoretical guarantees empirically and sets a new state-of-the-art for constrained multi-agent coordination under hybrid dynamics.

Abstract: Safe coordination in networked cyber-physical systems forces learning algorithms to simultaneously handle hybrid discrete-continuous actions, hard training-time safety constraints, and physics-governed dynamics. We show that these three features form a directed cycle of biases that defeats any naive composition of off-the-shelf modules, and formalize this as a three-way coupling lemma. We then introduce TRIDENT, the first MARL framework whose three components are co-designed to cancel each leak: a Richardson-Romberg gradient correction reducing Gumbel-Softmax bias from O(tau) to O(tau^2), a Lyapunov-constrained sequential trust-region update enforcing per-iterate feasibility, and a physics-informed residual critic that decomposes value rather than reward. We prove an O~(1/sqrt(K)) convergence rate to a constrained Nash equilibrium and an O(sqrt(K)) cumulative-violation bound. On multi-UAV mobile-edge computing, autonomous intersection management, and a hybrid SMAC variant, TRIDENT cuts training-time violations by 95.5% over MADDPG and 76.3% over MACPO, while improving reward by 13.5% over the strongest unconstrained baseline.

</details>


### [177] [SAGE: Retain-Aware Post-Hoc Sanitization of Final Unlearning Vector](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18309)
*Jingyuan Zhang,Yucheng Bai,Peixi Wen,Zhehao Huang,Zhengbao He,Hanling Tian,Xinwen Cheng,Haiyin Ran,Xiaolin Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGE proposes a post-hoc sanitization method for LLM unlearning that corrects final update vectors by suppressing components aligned with retained knowledge directions, restoring retention without rerunning the original unlearning pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM unlearning methods all suffer from a trade-off between forgetting undesirable knowledge and retaining useful capabilities. The authors observe that retention damage can be quantified via activation bias regardless of the unlearning method, motivating a universal post-hoc correction.

Method: SAGE operates in a complementary post-hoc setting: (1) collects real module inputs from a small retain proxy dataset, (2) extracts dominant activation geometry, (3) solves a source-anchored optimization in closed form that suppresses update components aligned with high-energy retained directions while preserving the original unlearning method's forgetting signal.

Result: Across multiple unlearning methods, model scales, and benchmarks, SAGE consistently relieves the retain-forget trade-off, demonstrating that post-hoc sanitization of final vectors is a practical and effective axis for machine unlearning.

Conclusion: Post-hoc sanitization of final unlearning update vectors is an underexplored but highly practical direction. SAGE provides a source-agnostic, plug-and-play correction that restores retention performance for any unlearning method without requiring re-execution of the original pipeline.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning aims to remove undesirable knowledge or behaviors while preserving retained capabilities. Current unlearning methods all involve a trade-off between unlearning and retention. We have found that the retention activation bias can also be used to quantify the damage an unlearning method inflicts on retention, without considering the specific implementation of the unlearning process. This allows us to restore retention performance for any unlearning method using a post-hoc approach. Therefore, we propose a complementary post-hoc setting to sanitize the final update vector without rerunning the original unlearning pipeline. In this setting, we design SAGE, Spectral Activation-GEometry Sanitization, a source-agnostic correction for final unlearning updates. SAGE collects real module inputs from a small retain proxy, extracts their dominant activation geometry, and solves a source-anchored optimization objective in closed form, which suppresses update components aligned with high-energy retained directions while preserving the source method's forgetting carrier. Across multiple unlearning methods, model scales, and benchmarks, SAGE consistently relieves the retain-forget trade-off, identifying post-hoc sanitization of final vectors as a practical and underexplored axis for machine unlearning.

</details>


### [178] [Ghost Attractor Networks: Basin-Structured Dynamical Decoders for Closed-Loop Sequential Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18315)
*Tianyu Wang,Ying Wang,Zhihao Liu,Xi Vincent Wang,Lihui Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Ghost Attractor Networks replace large Transformer/diffusion decoders with a compact dynamical system whose latent state evolves under a learned potential, creating stable basins that enable efficient closed-loop robotic action generation. A 2.3M-parameter model matches a 1.07B-parameter Diffusion Transformer at 462× fewer parameters and 32× lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Transformer and diffusion decoders incur memory costs scaling with sequence length and expensive iterative computation. Small feed-forward decoders are efficient but produce unstructured latent representations that cannot support closed-loop control primitives: phase-conditioned action generation and cross-step latent carry-over require structured latent geometry with stable basins. The paper seeks an architecturally grounded decoder that is simultaneously efficient (constant memory, single-pass) and structurally organized (multi-modal basins, attractor dynamics).

Method: Ghost Attractor Networks formulate the decoder as a continuous-time dynamical system where the latent state evolves under a learned potential with explicit drift and diffusion terms. The potential is designed to produce multiple stable fixed points (basins of attraction) by construction. Mode transitions are modeled as saddle-node bifurcations with ghost-attractor escape dynamics. A hierarchical phase-space decomposition separates first-order basin convergence from second-order proprioceptive refinement. The architecture is trained end-to-end using a behavioral cloning objective combined with a contrastive loss, and the potential's gradient-flow contraction is verified empirically (67% gradient norm decay over five integration steps).

Result: A 2.3M-parameter Ghost decoder matches offline accuracy of a 1.07B Diffusion Transformer (462× parameter reduction, 32× latency reduction). Ghost outperforms five alternative 2M-parameter decoders (MLP, Neural ODE, CVAE, Transformer, 1-step Diffusion) by 5.9–29% on offline MSE. On LIBERO-10 closed-loop benchmark, phase conditioning on Ghost's basin-structured latent yields +13.5 percentage points success rate over an MLP baseline; persistent-latent ensembling achieves 95.7% final success rate. Gradient norm decays by 67% across five integration steps on 1430 held-out samples, confirming predicted contraction.

Conclusion: Ghost Attractor Networks demonstrate that a theoretically grounded dynamical decoder with explicitly structured basin-attractor geometry can match or exceed the performance of orders-of-magnitude larger models while enabling closed-loop control capabilities that unstructured feed-forward decoders cannot provide. The work establishes a new Pareto frontier for efficient, controllable sequential generation.

Abstract: Sequential output generation with large-scale Transformer and diffusion decoders pays a memory cost that grows with sequence length, plus iterative per-step computation. Replacing them with small feed-forward decoders restores efficiency but produces unstructured latent representations that limit closed-loop control: phase-conditioned action generation and cross-step latent carry-over both require a latent geometry with stable basins. This article proposes Ghost Attractor Networks, a theoretically derived dynamical decoder whose latent evolves under a learned potential with drift and produces a basin-attractor structure by construction. Three desiderata (multi-modality, decoder-level single-pass switching, and constant memory) motivate the potential-drift form, and mode transitions arise as saddle-node bifurcations with ghost-attractor escape. A hierarchical phase-space decomposition separates first-order basin convergence from second-order proprioceptive refinement. Empirically, a Ghost trained end-to-end with a behavioral-cloning and contrastive objective exhibits the predicted gradient-flow contraction in its potential, with the gradient norm decaying by 67 percent across five integration steps on 1430 held-out samples. Ghost is evaluated as a robotic action decoder. A 2.3-million-parameter Ghost matches the offline accuracy of a 1.07-billion-parameter Diffusion Transformer at 462 times fewer parameters and 32 times lower latency, and beats five alternative 2M-parameter decoders (MLP, Neural ODE, CVAE, Transformer, 1-step Diffusion) on offline mean squared error by 5.9 to 29 percent. On the LIBERO-10 closed-loop benchmark, phase conditioning on Ghost's basin-structured latent yields a 13.5 percentage-point success-rate gain over a feed-forward MLP baseline, and persistent-latent ensembling reaches a 95.7 percent final success rate.

</details>


### [179] [A Survey on Data-Driven Models for Soil Moisture Regression and Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18316)
*Ilektra Tsimpidi,George Georgoulas,Vidya Sumathy,George Nikolakopoulos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A structured survey categorizing AI-based soil moisture estimation and classification models into five groups: statistical time-series, geostatistical, classical ML, deep learning, and probabilistic/Bayesian methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Soil moisture modelling is a complex spatiotemporal problem hindered by nonlinear environmental interactions, heterogeneous data, and scarce ground observations. Physics-based models are computationally expensive and poorly scalable, motivating the need for flexible data-driven AI alternatives that require fewer modelling assumptions.

Method: The paper presents a structured literature survey that organizes existing AI-based soil moisture models into five categories: (a) statistical time-series models, (b) geostatistical methods, (c) classical machine learning, (d) deep learning, and (e) probabilistic/Bayesian methods. These models utilize inputs such as historical soil moisture, meteorological variables, vegetation indices, topography, soil characteristics, and geolocation data for regression or classification.

Result: The survey provides a taxonomy of AI-driven soil moisture modelling approaches, highlighting how each category leverages different environmental variables and modelling paradigms to address the spatiotemporal complexity of soil moisture dynamics.

Conclusion: AI-based methods offer flexible and scalable alternatives to physics-based water balance models for soil moisture estimation and classification, with each of the five identified categories presenting distinct strengths in handling the nonlinear and heterogeneous nature of the problem.

Abstract: Soil Moisture (SM) modelling constitutes a complex spatiotemporal learning problem characterised by nonlinear environmental interactions, heterogeneous data sources, and limited ground observations. Physics-based approaches, such as water balance models, rely on explicit hydrological equations and high-quality inputs, but their computational cost and scalability limitations restrict large-scale deployment. Data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) methods have emerged as flexible alternatives, enabling the extraction of empirical relationships between soil moisture and environmental variables with reduced modelling assumptions. This work presents a structured survey of AI-based models for soil moisture estimation and classification. Existing approaches are organized into five categories: (a) statistical time-series models, (b) geostatistical methods (c) classical machine learning (ML) models, (d) Deep Learning (DL) models and (e) Probabilistic/Bayesian methods. These models leverage historical soil moisture records, meteorological variables, vegetation indices, topography, soil characteristics, and geolocation data to perform regression or classification tasks.

</details>


### [180] [Enhanced Graph Neural Networks using K-Hop Gaussian Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18317)
*Xuling Zhang,Peng Wang,Daiyan Li,Aoran Huang,Zeiwei Chen,Yongkui Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes K-Hop Gaussian (KHG), a diffusion kernel that preprocesses graph data with multi-hop Gaussian-weighted propagation, outperforming standard GNNs and existing diffusion methods (PPR, Heat Kernel) on noisy/complex graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard GNN message passing is limited to single-hop neighbors, making it vulnerable to noisy or poorly defined edges. Existing global diffusion kernels (PPR, Heat Kernel) improve propagation but still struggle with complex local structures and noise from distant nodes.

Method: KHG diffusion kernel operates as a preprocessing module that performs multi-hop diffusion with Gaussian weighting for remote nodes, balancing local and global information before feeding into standard GNN architectures.

Result: KHG significantly outperforms traditional message-passing GNNs, PPR, and Heat Kernel diffusion across multiple benchmark datasets, with particularly strong gains on noisy and structurally complex graphs.

Conclusion: KHG effectively addresses the limitations of both local message passing and existing global diffusion methods by introducing Gaussian-weighted multi-hop propagation, offering a robust preprocessing strategy for graph neural networks.

Abstract: Most graph neural network (GNN) cores rely on graph convolutions, typically implemented as message passing between direct (single-hop) neighbors. In many real-world graphs, edges can be noisy or poorly defined, limiting information propagation to local neighborhoods. Existing diffusion kernels, such as Personalized PageRank (PPR) and Heat Kernel, alleviate this issue through global propagation, but still struggle with complex local structures and distant node noise. To address these limitations, we propose a K-Hop Gaussian (KHG) diffusion kernel as a preprocessing module for graph data. KHG introduces multi-hop diffusion with Gaussian weighting for remote nodes, balancing local and global information propagation before applying standard GNNs. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that KHG significantly outperforms traditional message-passing GNNs, as well as PPR and Heat Kernel diffusion, particularly in noisy or structurally complex graphs.

</details>


### [181] [ASTRA: A Scalable Next-Generation ATCO Training Simulator with Autonomous Simpilots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18319)
*Ethan Chew,Enjia Wu,Iruss Eng Wei Yeow,Ian Weiqin Lim,Ranen Sim,Brandon Koh Ziheng,Kaleb Nim,Caden Toh Jun Yi,Wei Dong Soin,Darius Kai Keat Koh,Galen King Yu Tay,Prannaya Gupta,Jonathan Ee Fang Koong,Yong Zhi Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ASTRA is an end-to-end air traffic control training simulator that automates simpilot roles using fine-tuned Singaporean-accented ASR (reducing WER from 107.80% to 23.45%) and provides AI-driven trainee evaluation across accuracy, brevity, and completeness metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ATCO training capacity is bottlenecked by reliance on human simpilots, and existing Western-centric speech models fail dramatically on Singaporean-accented aviation speech (WER up to 107.80%), motivating a locally-adapted automated solution.

Method: ASTRA uses a pipeline that transcribes ATCO speech via fine-tuned ASR, interprets instructions, and generates pilot/ATCO responses with locally adapted voice models. An AI-assisted evaluation framework (built on DSPy and Unsloth) scores trainee communications on accuracy, brevity, and completeness.

Result: Fine-tuned ASR achieves 23.45% WER, dramatically outperforming off-the-shelf systems. Post-optimization evaluation scores reach 91.7% (accuracy), 88.2% (brevity), and 86.9% (completeness).

Conclusion: ASTRA enables scalable, standardized ATCO assessment while reducing instructor workload, leveraging open-source foundations to address domain-specific speech challenges in non-Western operational contexts.

Abstract: Air Traffic Control Operators (ATCOs) are vital in ensuring the safe, orderly, and efficient flow of air traffic, yet training capacity is constrained by reliance on specialized human trainers known as simpilots, who must role-play both pilots and ATCOs in a simulated airspace. Existing automated solutions rely on Western-centric speech models that perform poorly in Singaporean operational contexts, with off-the-shelf systems exhibiting Word Error Rates (WER) of up to 107.80% on Singaporean-accented aviation speech. We introduce ASTRA, an end-to-end training simulator that automates these simpilot roles through a pipeline that transcribes ATCO speech, interprets instructions, and generates appropriate pilot and ATCO responses using locally adapted voice models. Our fine-tuned Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) pipeline reduces WER to 23.45%, substantially outperforming existing approaches in this domain. Beyond traffic simulation, ASTRA incorporates an AI-assisted performance evaluation framework that assesses trainee radiotelephony communications across accuracy, brevity, and completeness, achieving post-optimization scores of 91.7%, 88.2%, and 86.9%, respectively. Built on open-source foundations such as DSPy and Unsloth, this approach enables scalable, standardized ATCO assessment while reducing instructor workload.

</details>


### [182] [SAE Interventions are Unreliable: Post-Intervention Recovery of Suppressed Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18322)
*Mingyue Cui,Linghui Shen,Xingyi Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features can be causally intervened upon, but clamping "unsafe" features does not reliably prevent the underlying misbehavior. The paper formalizes "post-intervention recovery," where optimized residual perturbations restore the original behavior while maintaining the clamped feature values, exposing a critical gap between feature-level control and behavioral guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent latent-space defenses assume that identifying and clamping unsafe SAE features provides reliable behavioral control. This paper challenges that assumption, investigating whether feature-level intervention genuinely eliminates harmful behaviors or merely blocks one visible pathway while leaving the behavior recoverable.

Method: The authors formulate post-intervention recovery as a constrained residual-space optimization problem: starting from a post-intervention residual state, they optimize perturbations to restore pre-intervention behavior while preserving targeted SAE feature values. To ensure the intervention remains active, they employ encoder-orthogonal updates (single-layer) and feature-map Jacobian constraints (cross-layer). Experiments span TPP, unlearning, IOI, and refusal steering, with recovery-path attribution localizing the source of recovery.

Result: Recovery remains possible even under a strong threat model where the intervention is active throughout optimization and generation. In refusal steering, they achieve a 95.8% recovery rate on valid samples with defended-feature relative drift of only 0.131, substantially outperforming suffix-based baselines. Attribution analysis localizes recovery to the SAE reconstruction residual — the component unexplained by the SAE.

Conclusion: SAE features support causal intervention, but controlling them does not guarantee behavioral control. The SAE reconstruction residual represents a fundamental blind spot, exposing an incompleteness in current latent-space safety paradigms that rely solely on feature-level monitoring and intervention.

Abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose residual-stream activations into interpretable features. Recent latent-space defenses increasingly rely on these decompositions, assuming that identified "unsafe" SAE features serve as actionable handles for monitoring and intervention. In this paradigm, clamping a specific harmful feature is expected to reliably prevent model misbehavior. However, we show that this success may hide a recoverable failure mode: the clamp may block one visible route to a behavior without eliminating the behavior itself. We formulate this vulnerability as post-intervention recovery, a constrained residual-space optimization problem. Starting from the post-intervention residual state, we optimize residual perturbations to recover the pre-intervention behavior while preserving the post-intervention values of the targeted SAE features. Even under a strong threat model where the intervention remains active throughout optimization and generation, recovery remains possible. To rule out that recovery simply undoes the intervention, we use encoder-orthogonal updates for single-layer interventions and the corresponding feature-map Jacobian in the cross-layer setting. Across TPP, unlearning, IOI, and refusal steering experiments, this stress test reveals recoverable behavior despite successful feature-level intervention. Especially in the safety-critical refusal-steering setting, we achieve a 95.8% recovery rate on valid samples while keeping defended-feature relative drift to 0.131, substantially below suffix-based baselines. A recovery-path attribution analysis further localizes this recovery to the SAE reconstruction residual, the component left unexplained by the SAE. These results expose a gap between feature-level control and behavioral completeness: SAE features can support causal intervention, but controlling them does not guarantee control over the underlying behavior.

</details>


### [183] [Why SWAVE May Not Be All You Need:A Concept-Evolution Retrospective on Complex-Valued Recurrent Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18324)
*Ramprasath Ganesaraja,Swathika N,Sahil Dilip Panse*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SWave is a complex-valued recurrent language model exploring whether representing language as rotating complex waves in a unitary hidden state improves long-sequence modeling. The project iterated through three architectural phases, identified and resolved a failure mode ("cos-domination collapse"), and ultimately distilled transferable engineering principles for complex-valued RNN training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors hypothesize that representing language as complex waves—rather than real-valued numbers—enables richer information encoding. Three core premises drive the design: (1) complex-valued representations encode more information; (2) a Cayley-parameterized unitary transition matrix mathematically guarantees no state explosion or decay; (3) a hidden state that rotates rather than shrinks preserves signal integrity over arbitrarily long contexts.

Method: SWave (169.26M parameters, D=384, L=16, T=2048) was trained on FineWeb-Edu using 2 H100 NVL GPUs across three development phases. Key architectural components include: (1) Cayley-parameterized unitary recurrent transitions; (2) ComplexNorm and Wave Propagation Scan (proven load-bearing throughout); (3) Phase-Associative Memory (PAM) with independent real/imaginary embedding tables replacing the earlier Resonance Head; (4) ProtectGatedScan reframed as a structural prior; (5) a squared-ReLU channel mixer replacing the ComplexGatedUnit. Four multi-scale retention mechanisms and auxiliary training objectives were tested and eliminated as non-load-bearing. The parallel scan uses a log-space backward pass for numerical stability.

Result: The Resonance Head exhibited "cos-domination collapse," a failure mode where imaginary-channel collapse becomes a global loss minimum. Replacing it with PAM's untied head resolved this, enabling stable 200,000-step training (best PPL 22.0 at step 89,861). ComplexNorm and Wave Propagation Scan were load-bearing across all phases. Multi-scale retention showed no measurable improvement. The ComplexGatedUnit was successfully replaced by a simpler squared-ReLU mixer with fewer parameters. Auxiliary training objectives provided no benefit once structural constraints were resolved.

Conclusion: The investigation yields: (1) a formal characterization of cos-domination collapse; (2) a parallel scan with log-space backward pass for numerical stability; (3) six transferable engineering principles for complex-valued recurrent training; and (4) a plan-to-code traceability methodology for detecting structural divergences missed by conventional test suites.

Abstract: SWave is a complex-valued recurrent language model (169.26M parameters, D=384, L=16, T=2048) trained on FineWeb-Edu using 2xH100 NVL. It was designed around three founding premises: that representing language as complex waves rather than real-valued numbers enables richer information encoding; that a Cayley-parameterised unitary transition provides a mathematical guarantee against state decay or explosion; and that a hidden state which rotates rather than shrinks preserves signal integrity over arbitrarily long contexts. The core of SWave evolved substantially across three development phases. The Resonance Head was found to structurally admit imaginary-channel collapse as a global loss minimum (a failure mode we term cos-domination collapse) and was superseded by an untied head with independent real and imaginary embedding tables from the Phase-Associative Memory (PAM) architecture. This resolved the degenerate minimum and enabled stable 200,000-step training (best-step PPL 22.0 at step 89,861). ComplexNorm and the Wave Propagation Scan proved load-bearing throughout all three phases and were retained to the final architecture. ProtectGatedScan was reframed as a structural prior rather than a learned behaviour. The four multi-scale retention concepts showed no measurable improvement under controlled evaluation and were found non-load-bearing. The ComplexGatedUnit was superseded by a real-valued squared-ReLU channel mixer with fewer parameters. The auxiliary training objectives showed no benefit once structural constraints were resolved. The investigation yields a formal characterisation of cos-domination collapse, a parallel scan with a log-space backward pass for numerical stability, six transferable engineering principles for complex-valued recurrent training, and a plan-to-code traceability methodology for catching structural divergences that conventional test suites miss.

</details>


### [184] [Neural Network Implementation of the Renormalization Group for Fault Diagnosis with Class Imbalance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18326)
*Evgeny Nikulchev,Dmitry Ilin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RGNet proposes a neural network inspired by the renormalization group concept from physics, which hierarchically coarse-grains feature space and concatenates multi-scale representations for classification. It introduces RG-flows — interpretable low-dimensional representations that exhibit discrete curvilinear structure in t-SNE — and demonstrates competitive fault prediction performance on the imbalanced AI4I dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practical machine learning applications suffer from class imbalance and multidimensional noise, which degrade model performance and interpretability. There is a need for architectures that can robustly handle these challenges while providing interpretable representations.

Method: RGNet uses a hierarchical coarse-graining architecture inspired by the renormalization group (RG). The model sequentially compresses input dimensionality and concatenates features from all scales prior to classification, enabling joint capture of local details and global patterns. The concept of RG-flows is introduced as interpretable low-dimensional representations, visualized via t-SNE to reveal discrete curvilinear structure.

Result: On the imbalanced AI4I dataset, RGNet achieves competitive fault prediction performance. The t-SNE visualization of RG-flows reveals a discrete curvilinear structure, confirming the effectiveness of the coarse-graining process and supporting model interpretability.

Conclusion: RGNet is a universal, interpretable, and competitive solution for fault prediction tasks characterized by class imbalance. The architecture's multi-scale representation and RG-flow visualizations provide both predictive power and mechanistic insight.

Abstract: The application of machine learning models in practical tasks faces challenges such as class imbalance and multidimensional noise. This paper proposes RGNet, a neural network architecture based on the concept of the renormalization group (RG), for hierarchical coarse-graining of the feature space. The model sequentially compresses the input dimensionality and concatenates all scales before classification, allowing it to capture both local details and global patterns. The notion of RG-flows is introduced - interpretable low-dimensional representations whose visualization via t-SNE reveals a discrete curvilinear structure confirming the effectiveness of coarse-graining. Experimental results are presented on the imbalanced AI4I dataset. The obtained results demonstrate that RGNet is a universal, interpretable, and competitive solution for fault prediction in applications with imbalanced classes.

</details>


### [185] [Self-CTRL: Self-Consistency Training with Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18327)
*Itamar Pres,Laura Ruis,Melat Ghebreselassie,Belinda Z. Li,Jacob Andreas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-CTRL uses reinforcement learning to align language model self-explanations with actual behavior, improving transparency and controllability. The method works bidirectionally: updating explanations to match behavior, or updating behavior to match explanations. Tested on probabilistic reasoning and constitutional AI tasks, it significantly improves explanation fidelity and behavioral alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models that can faithfully describe their own behavior are easier to audit, understand, and trust. Current LMs often produce explanations inconsistent with their actual behavior, limiting transparency and safety.

Method: Self-Consistency Training with Reinforcement Learning (Self-CTRL), which operates in two directions: (1) updating self-explanations to better predict observed behavior, and (2) updating behavior to better match stated explanations. This creates a self-consistent loop between what an LM says it does and what it actually does.

Result: On probabilistic reasoning: correlation between self-reported and actual latent biases improved from R²=0.24 to R²=0.64, matching ground-truth supervision. On constitutional AI: explanation fidelity for a third-party auditor rose from 36% to 92%; behavior updates reduced HarmBench failure rate from 15.0% to 0.5% without significantly increasing harmless-prompt refusals.

Conclusion: Self-CTRL provides a general recipe for training safer, more transparent, and more controllable AI models by aligning self-explanations with behavior bidirectionally.

Abstract: Language models (LMs) that faithfully describe their own behavior can more easily be audited, understood, and trusted by users. This paper describes Self-Consistency Training with Reinforcement Learning (Self-CTRL), a method that optimizes for consistency between a LM's self-explanations and behavior on related inputs by updating explanations to better predict behavior or updating behavior to better match explanations. We apply our method in two domains. First, we study a formal probabilistic reasoning task in which LMs must learn to imitate a family of biased samplers and evaluated on their ability to report the associated biases. We find that consistency training improves the correlation between self-reported and behaviorally-measured latent biases from $R^2=0.24$ to $R^2=0.64$ on a set of held-out distributions, matching the generalization of direct ground-truth supervision. Second, we study a constitutional AI domain in which LMs must describe when they will refuse or comply with user requests. Here, Self-CTRL produces rules that faithfully describe the model's behavior on held-out requests, improving the refusal predictions of a third-party auditor model from $36\%$ to $92\%$. In the other direction, behavior updates improve alignment, reducing HarmBench failure rate from $15.0\%$ to $0.5\%$ without substantially increasing refusal on harmless prompts. By aligning explanations and behavior, our work provides a general recipe for training AI models to be safer, more transparent, and more controllable.

</details>


### [186] [ThousandWorlds: A benchmark for climate emulation of potentially habitable exoplanets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18338)
*Edward T. Stevenson,Mei Ting Mak,Eric Wolf,Denis E. Sergeev,Tobi Hammond,N. J. Mayne,Miles Cranmer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ThousandWorlds is an ML-ready benchmark dataset of ~1800 exoplanet climate simulations from 5 GCMs, enabling research on low-data, multi-simulator emulation of 3D atmospheric fields.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interpreting exoplanet atmospheric biosignatures requires understanding host planet climate via GCMs, but GCM runs are computationally expensive (millions of core-hours) and require domain expertise. ML emulators could bypass this bottleneck, but progress is hindered by the lack of a curated, multi-model exoclimate dataset.

Method: The authors introduce ThousandWorlds, a benchmark comprising ~1800 simulations from five distinct GCMs (ExoCAM, LMD-G, ROCKE-3D, THOR, Unified Model). Eight planetary parameters (e.g., stellar flux, rotation rate, surface pressure, radius, gravity, atmospheric composition) map to 3D atmospheric fields (temperature, humidity, winds, clouds, radiation). Three nested subsets create escalating challenges: (1) single-simulator regression, (2) multi-simulator regression with complete observations, and (3) multi-simulator regression with structured missingness. Two evaluation protocols are proposed: ranking-based and performance relative to inter-GCM disagreement. Seven baselines (simple methods, deep learning, Gaussian processes) are evaluated.

Result: GP-based methods outperform deep learning baselines, indicating ThousandWorlds defines a low-data regime where off-the-shelf deep learning fails. The benchmark exposes structured challenges like sim-to-sim generalization and missing-data robustness.

Conclusion: ThousandWorlds fills a critical gap as the first curated, multi-GCM exoclimate benchmark, enabling ML research on parameter-to-field regression under data-scarcity and multi-simulator conditions relevant to exoplanet science and beyond.

Abstract: The search for life beyond Earth will depend on detecting faint signatures in the atmospheres of potentially habitable exoplanets. Interpreting those signatures requires understanding the host planet's climate: the same molecule may signal life on one planet and abiotic chemistry on another. Global climate models (GCMs) provide this understanding, but individual runs can require up to millions of core-hours and substantial domain expert time. Machine-learning emulators could remove this bottleneck, but progress has been limited by the absence of a curated, multi-model exoclimate dataset. We introduce ThousandWorlds, an ML-ready benchmark for exoclimate emulation and for the broader regime of low-data, multi-simulator, parameter-to-field regression. The dataset contains approximately 1800 simulations from five GCMs, mapping eight planet parameters to 3D atmospheric fields including temperature, humidity, winds, clouds, and radiation. Three nested subsets define progressively harder challenges: single-simulator regression, multi-simulator regression with complete observations, and multi-simulator regression with structured missingness. We propose two evaluation protocols: one for ranking methods, and one that measures performance relative to the disagreement between GCMs themselves. We evaluate seven baselines spanning simple methods, deep learning, and Gaussian processes. GP-based methods perform best, suggesting that ThousandWorlds exposes a regime where off-the-shelf deep learning does not yet succeed. Data: https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/8695. Code: https://github.com/edstevenson/ThousandWorlds.

</details>


### [187] [Do Time Series Foundation Model Benchmarks Hide Regime-Dependent Failures? Evidence from Traffic Speed Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18367)
*Yingshuo Wang,Xian Sun,Lingdong Kong,Wei Gao,Yanhang Li,Zhichao Fan,Zexin Zhuang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Aggregate metrics in time series foundation model benchmarks conceal catastrophic failures during abrupt regime transitions (e.g., free-flow to congested traffic). Authors introduce regime-stratified evaluation, revealing severe accuracy and prediction-interval coverage degradation during transitions, and propose Bimodal Mixture Augmentation (BMA) to mitigate these failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard aggregate evaluation metrics for time series foundation models (TSFMs) mask severe performance failures in critical operating regimes. In traffic forecasting, abrupt regime switches between free-flow and congested states produce bimodal speed distributions during transitions, and poor performance during these transitions is statistically invisible because free-flow observations dominate the sample.

Method: The authors apply regime-stratified evaluation to three TSFMs on two standard traffic speed benchmarks, stratifying predictions by traffic regime (free-flow, congested, transition). They then propose Bimodal Mixture Augmentation (BMA), a post-hoc method that combines TSFM forecasts with per-sensor historical conditional distributions to recover transition-regime prediction-interval coverage while preserving the TSFM's point-forecast accuracy.

Result: Regime-stratified evaluation reveals that transition-regime MAE reaches 11 mph (vs. 3 mph overall), and empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals drops as low as 55%. A simple historical conditional baseline achieves superior transition coverage but far worse overall accuracy. BMA approaches the historical baseline's transition coverage while preserving the TSFM's accuracy.

Conclusion: TSFM benchmarks should adopt regime-aware evaluation to expose failures that aggregate metrics hide. BMA offers a practical post-hoc remedy, but the broader implication is that evaluation methodology must account for distributional heterogeneity in critical operating regimes.

Abstract: Standard benchmarks evaluate time series foundation models (TSFMs) using aggregate metrics, but these can mask severe failures in critical operating regimes. We introduce regime-stratified evaluation and apply it to three TSFMs on two standard traffic speed benchmarks. Traffic exhibits abrupt regime switching between free-flow and congested states, producing bimodal speed distributions during transitions. When we stratify by traffic regime, both accuracy and prediction-interval coverage degrade sharply during transitions: transition-regime MAE reaches 11 mph (versus 3 mph overall), and empirical coverage of 90% prediction intervals drops as low as 55%. These failures are invisible in aggregate metrics because free-flow observations dominate the sample. A simple historical conditional baseline (sampling from per-sensor training distributions) achieves better transition coverage than any TSFM, but has far worse overall accuracy. We propose bimodal mixture augmentation (BMA), a post-hoc method that combines TSFM forecasts with historical distributional knowledge, approaching the historical baseline's transition coverage while preserving the TSFM's accuracy. Our results suggest that TSFM benchmarks should incorporate regime-aware evaluation to surface failures that aggregate metrics hide.

</details>


### [188] [From Sparse Features to Trustworthy Proxies: Certifying SAE-Based Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18383)
*Dibyanayan Bandyopadhyay,Asif Ekbal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a statistical learning framework that certifies when sparse autoencoder (SAE) explanations faithfully represent a frozen language model, deriving an upper bound on expected risk via four measurable quantities and empirically validating it across GPT-2 Small, Gemma-2B, and Llama-3-8B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SAEs are widely used to extract interpretable features from LMs, but there is no rigorous criterion for determining when an SAE-based explanation can be considered a faithful, trustworthy representation of the underlying frozen model's behavior.

Method: The authors propose a post-hoc generalization framework that replaces a native hidden activation with its pretrained SAE reconstruction to form a sparse proxy. They derive a PAC-style upper bound on the base model's expected risk expressed as: proxy risk + SAE reconstruction gap + concept-pool mismatch + sparse complexity. This bound serves as an operational certificate of explanatory faithfulness, where non-vacuousness indicates retained predictive information and small reconstruction/mismatch errors indicate behavioral closeness.

Result: The bound becomes non-vacuous on GPT-2 Small, Gemma-2B, and Llama-3-8B at practical sample sizes. Layerwise analysis of Llama-3-8B reveals strong depth dependence: later layers are easier to certify due to stronger local fidelity and weaker downstream error amplification. Feature-shuffling ablations confirm the decomposition distinguishes genuine semantic alignment from mere statistical sparsity.

Conclusion: The proposed certificate provides a principled, operational criterion for SAE faithfulness. Non-vacuous bounds indicate trustworthy explanations, while the decomposition helps diagnose when SAE-based explanations become unreliable, particularly revealing that deeper layers yield more faithful sparse representations.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly used to extract interpretable features from language models (LMs), yet a central question remains: when can an SAE-based explanation be treated as a faithful view of an underlying frozen LM We study this through a post-hoc generalization framework that certifies the LM via a sparse proxy, obtained by replacing a native hidden activation with its pretrained SAE reconstruction. Our framework derives an upper bound on the base model's expected risk using four measurable quantities: proxy risk, SAE reconstruction gap, concept-pool mismatch, and sparse complexity. We interpret this certificate as an operational criterion for explanatory faithfulness. In particular, a non-vacuous bound indicates that the extracted sparse features retain meaningful predictive information, while small reconstruction and mismatch errors indicate that the proxy remains behaviorally close to the original model. Empirically, we show that the bound becomes non-vacuous on GPT-2 Small, Gemma-2B, and Llama-3-8B at practical sample sizes. A detailed layerwise analysis of Llama-3-8B reveals a strong depth dependence, with later layers becoming much easier to certify, associated with both stronger local fidelity and weaker downstream error amplification. Finally, through feature-shuffling ablations, we show that the decomposition distinguishes genuine semantic alignment from mere statistical sparsity, providing a useful diagnostic for when SAE-based explanations become less reliable.

</details>


### [189] [SCOPE-FL: A Strategy-proof Chain-based Optimal pareto efficient Federated Learning System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18384)
*Seyed Salar Ghazi,Kaiwen Zhang,Mehdi feizi,Hans-Arno Jacobsen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCOPE-FL proposes a hierarchical federated learning framework that uses the Top Trading Cycle algorithm for client selection (achieving both Pareto efficiency and strategy-proofness) and Shapley value approximation for fair reward distribution, all secured by blockchain smart contracts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing HFL client selection methods sacrifice Pareto efficiency by over-prioritizing stability and lack strategy-proofness, incentivizing participants to misrepresent preferences. Both failures degrade overall system welfare.

Method: SCOPE-FL formulates client selection as a two-sided school choice problem solved via the Top Trading Cycle (TTC) algorithm, guaranteeing both Pareto efficiency and strategy-proofness. Reward distribution uses a scalable One-Round Reconstruction (OR)-based Shapley value approximation. The entire mechanism executes on blockchain smart contracts for tamper-proof SP guarantees.

Result: On MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, SCOPE-FL outperforms DA, IAS, and other baselines in model accuracy, convergence rate, and reward efficiency, with communication latency comparable to DA and significantly lower blockchain overhead than DA at scale.

Conclusion: SCOPE-FL successfully addresses strategic inefficiency in HFL by combining TTC-based client selection with fair Shapley-based rewards under blockchain enforcement, yielding superior performance across multiple metrics.

Abstract: Hierarchical Federated Learning (HFL) enables scalable collaborative model training across distributed devices while preserving data privacy. However, existing HFL client selection mechanisms suffer from a fundamental strategic inefficiency. By prioritizing stability over Pareto efficiency (PE), they produce suboptimal resource allocations, and without strategy proofness (SP), participants are incentivized to misrepresent their true preferences, both failures degrading system overall welfare in the Pareto sense in practice. To address it, we propose SCOPE-FL (Strategy-proof Chain-based Optimal pareto efficient Federated Learning), a synchronous HFL framework that formulates client selection as a two-sided school choice problem solved through the Top Trading Cycle (TTC) algorithm that simultaneously guarantees PE and SP. For reward distribution, SCOPE-FL employs a scalable Shapley value approximation based on One-Round Reconstruction (OR), ensuring compensation proportional to each client's contribution. The entire mechanism executes via blockchain smart contracts, providing the tamper-proof environment required for the SP guarantees to hold in practice. A comprehensive evaluation on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 demonstrates that SCOPE-FL outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, including DA, IAS, and other methods across model accuracy, convergence rate, and reward efficiency, while achieving communication latency comparable to DA and blockchain overhead significantly lower than DA at scale.

</details>


### [190] [MOLAR: Learning Multimodal Molecular Representations from Noisy Labels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18390)
*Yingxu Wang,Kunyu Zhang,Nan Yin,Yu Li,Eran Segal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MOLAR is a noise-aware multimodal molecular representation learning framework that separates clean-property inference from noisy label observation using graph and text modalities, achieving superior performance on noisy benchmarks while providing interpretable reliability diagnostics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular property prediction suffers from noisy labels due to assay-based annotations, curated databases, and weak annotation pipelines. Treating these as clean supervision causes models to memorize corrupted observations. In multimodal settings (graph-text), label noise can propagate across modalities through fusion or alignment, amplifying the problem.

Method: MOLAR decouples latent clean-property inference from recorded-label observation via: (1) graph and text views contributing residual evidence to a clean-property distribution, and (2) a categorical label-observation channel mapping this clean distribution to recorded (noisy) labels for training. This formulation enables deriving posterior label reliability and modality-specific molecular evidence from the model itself.

Result: MOLAR consistently outperforms representative baselines on both naturally noisy molecular benchmarks and controlled label-flipping benchmarks. Visualization analyses demonstrate that the framework provides interpretable reliability estimates and modality-evidence diagnostics.

Conclusion: MOLAR offers a principled noise-aware approach to multimodal molecular representation learning by explicitly modeling the label corruption process, leading to both improved robustness and interpretability in noisy-label molecular property prediction.

Abstract: Motivation: Noisy labels are a common challenge in molecular property prediction because molecular annotations are often obtained from assays, curated databases, or weak annotation pipelines rather than directly observed clean biological states. Treating recorded labels as reliable supervision can cause models to memorize corrupted observations and learn misleading molecular evidence. In multimodal molecular representation learning, this issue can be amplified by graph-text fusion or alignment, which may propagate label-induced errors across modalities. Results: We propose MOLAR, a noise-aware framework for learning multimodal molecular representations from noisy labels. MOLAR separates latent clean-property inference from recorded-label observation: graph and text views contribute residual evidence to a clean-property distribution, and a categorical label-observation channel maps this distribution to recorded labels for training. This formulation derives posterior label reliability and modality-specific molecular evidence from the model. Experiments on naturally noisy molecular benchmarks and controlled label-flipping benchmarks show that MOLAR consistently outperforms representative baselines. Visualization analyses further show that MOLAR provides interpretable reliability and modality-evidence diagnostics.

</details>


### [191] [P$^2$CE: Model-Agnostic Plausible Pareto-Optimal Counterfactual Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18418)
*Arthur Hendricks Mendes de Oliveira,Giovani Valdrighi,Marcos Medeiros Raimundo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: P²CE introduces a Pareto-optimal counterfactual explanation algorithm that uses isolation forest for plausibility and SHAP values for efficiency, outperforming existing methods on three datasets in both quality and speed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods struggle to simultaneously balance feasibility, plausibility (alignment with data distribution), and computational efficiency. Users need a diverse set of optimal trade-offs between different feasibility notions.

Method: P²CE combines two key components: (1) an auxiliary isolation forest outlier detector to ensure generated explanations conform to the underlying data distribution (plausibility), and (2) SHAP values to guide the search for Pareto-optimal counterfactuals efficiently, yielding a diverse set of optimal feasibility trade-offs in short computing time, independent of the underlying model type.

Result: Empirical evaluation on three datasets showed P²CE achieves superior solution quality and computational efficiency compared to related counterfactual explanation techniques.

Conclusion: P²CE successfully addresses the trilemma of feasibility, plausibility, and computational efficiency in counterfactual explanations by leveraging isolation forest and SHAP values, producing diverse Pareto-optimal explanations suitable for real-world social applications.

Abstract: The increasing use of machine learning algorithms in social applications has raised concerns about fairness and transparency, leading to the development of counterfactual explanations. These explanations supports individuals to understand and potentially alter unfavorable decisions in areas such as loan applications, job selections, and more, by providing actionable changes to input features that would lead to a desired outcome. Existing methods often struggle to balance feasibility, plausibility, and computational efficiency. To address this, we introduce P$^2$CE, an algorithm for generating plausible Pareto-optimal counterfactual explanations, offering users a diverse set of optimal trade-offs between different notions of feasibility. P$^2$CE employs an auxiliary isolation forest outlier detector to ensure that explanations are in accordance with the data distribution and leverages SHAP values to obtain optimal results with short computing times, regardless of the underlying model. Our algorithm was empirically evaluated on three datasets, demonstrating superior performance in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency compared to related techniques.

</details>


### [192] [Measurement noise limits the advantage of nonlinear models over linear models in biomedical prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18420)
*Marc-Andre Schulz,Kerstin Ritter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In biomedical tabular data, nonlinear models often fail to outperform linear models not because the models are inadequate, but because measurement noise attenuates nonlinear structure faster than linear structure. The authors derive an exact excess-risk identity showing that feature reliability, sample size, and feature representation must all align for flexible models to help — a narrow window most biomedical tasks miss. Empirical validation across 140 UK Biobank tasks confirms the predicted noise signature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the persistent puzzle in biomedical machine learning: despite the presumed nonlinearity of biological systems, flexible models (deep networks, gradient-boosted trees, kernel methods) routinely fail to beat linear/logistic regression on tabular biomedical data. The standard response is to blame model inadequacy — insufficient data, poor architecture, or suboptimal tuning. The authors challenge this assumption, arguing the binding constraint is often measurement reliability, not model capacity.

Method: The authors synthesize classical results from measurement-error statistics, psychometrics (attenuation theory), and Gaussian analysis into an exact excess-risk identity. The key theoretical insight: additive measurement noise attenuates a degree-k interaction by the k-th power of feature reliability (e.g., reliability coefficient ρ), while the linear component is attenuated only by ρ. Thus, nonlinear structure is exponentially more vulnerable to measurement noise. The framework identifies three necessary conditions for flexible models to outperform linear ones: sufficient measurement reliability, adequate sample size, and appropriate feature representation. The theory is tested across 140 UK Biobank prediction tasks.

Result: Across 140 UK Biobank tasks, the performance gap between flexible and linear models, when present, exhibits the predicted noise signature — i.e., the gap shrinks systematically as measurement reliability decreases. The three conditions (reliability, sample size, representation) can be disentangled through intervention but not through benchmarking alone, meaning standard benchmark comparisons cannot distinguish between "nonlinearity is absent" and "nonlinearity is hidden by noise."

Conclusion: When linear and flexible models tie on biomedical data, this does not constitute evidence against nonlinear biology. The nonlinearity may be present but hidden by measurement noise, and no amount of additional data or model flexibility can recover what noise has erased — only better measurement can. The window where flexible models can help is narrow, defined by the joint satisfaction of reliability, sample size, and representation conditions, and most biomedical tasks fall outside it.

Abstract: On biomedical tabular data, flexible models such as deep networks, gradient-boosted trees, and kernel methods are repeatedly matched or beaten by linear and logistic regression given the same features. The usual reaction is to treat this as a model-side shortfall, to be fixed with more data, a better architecture, or tuning, on the assumption that the nonlinear structure is there and the model has failed to capture it. We argue that these fixes cannot help when the binding limit is the measurement rather than the model, as it frequently is in biomedicine. Additive noise blurs the population-optimal predictor, and because blurring removes a function's fine, rapidly varying detail before its broad shape, it erases nonlinear structure faster than linear structure. A degree-$k$ interaction is attenuated by the $k$-th power of feature reliability, while the linear part is attenuated only once. At the reliabilities typical of biomedical measurement, the nonlinear advantage can vanish even when the underlying biology is strongly nonlinear, and what the noise removes cannot be recovered by a larger cohort or a more flexible model, only by better measurement. The nonlinearity is hidden, not absent, and a tie between linear and flexible models is not by itself a verdict on the biology. These pieces are classical, drawn from measurement-error statistics, psychometrics, and Gaussian analysis, and we assemble them into an exact excess-risk identity. Measurement reliability is one of three conditions, alongside sample size and feature representation, that must align for a flexible model to help, and together they leave only a narrow window that most biomedical tasks fall outside. Across 140 UK Biobank tasks, the gap between flexible and linear models, where it exists, carries the predicted noise signature, and the three conditions can be separated by intervention but not by a benchmark alone.

</details>


### [193] [Signature filtering: a lightweight enhancement for statistical watermark detection in large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18430)
*Chih-Duo Hong,Yen-Pang Chen,Fang Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Signature filtering is a detection-time module that learns a small set of "signature" tokens whose presence makes watermark tests unreliable, removes them before detection, and significantly boosts watermark detection rates in weak-signal and low-entropy settings without modifying watermark embedding or text generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM watermark detectors struggle when watermark signals are weak, texts are repetitive (low-entropy), or watermarks are edited. The authors aim to improve detection robustness without altering the watermark embedding process or the text generation pipeline.

Method: A detection-time module that identifies "signature" tokens — tokens whose presence degrades watermark test reliability — by solving a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) on a small training set. The optimization maximizes true positive rate under constraints. These signature tokens are then removed (filtered out) prior to running the watermark detector. The approach is model-agnostic and works as an add-on to existing detectors. Finite-sample and asymptotic detection bounds are derived under color-blind, color-adaptive, and distributionally correlated attacker models.

Result: Evaluated across four watermark families (Kgw, Sweet, Unigram, Exp), four corpora (C4, MBPP, HumanEval, Code-Search-Net), and six LLMs (Opt-1.3b, Opt-6.7b, Llama2-13b, Llama3.1-8b, Qwen2.5-14b, Phi-3-medium-14b). 2- and 3-gram signature filters raised detection rates from 8–31% (without filtering) to 78–99% (with filtering) in weak-signal and low-entropy settings, with controlled false positives. Under stress tests with scrambling and 25–50% token perturbations (dilution, deletions, substitutions), 2-gram filters preserved most detection gains and often matched or outperformed the WinMax detector.

Conclusion: Signature filtering offers a simple, scalable, model-agnostic add-on that significantly strengthens watermark-based provenance checks for LLM-generated text, particularly in challenging weak-signal, low-entropy, and adversarially perturbed scenarios.

Abstract: Statistical watermarks help organizations attribute large language model (LLM) outputs, yet existing detectors often struggle when watermark signals are weak, texts are repetitive, or watermarks are edited. We propose signature filtering, a detection-time module that enhances watermark detection without modifying watermark embedding and text generation. It learns a small set of ``signature'' tokens whose presence makes watermark tests unreliable, and removes these tokens before detection. The signatures are obtained by solving a mixed-integer linear program on a small training set, with constraints that maximize the true positive rate. We additionally derive finite-sample and asymptotic bounds under several attacker models (color-blind, color-adaptive, and distributionally correlated). On four well-known watermark families (Kgw, Sweet, Unigram, Exp), four benchmark corpora (C4, MBPP, HumanEval, Code-Search-Net), and six LLMs (Opt-1.3b, Opt-6.7b, Llama2-13b, Llama3.1-8b, Qwen2.5-14b, Phi-3-medium-14b), 2- and 3-gram signatures raise detection rates in weak-signal and low-entropy settings from 8~31% without filtering to 78~99% with filtering, while keeping false positives controllable and often negligible. In stress tests where we scramble sentences and perturb 25~50% of tokens by dilution, deletions, and substitutions, 2-gram filters for Kgw-style watermarks preserve most of the clean-text detection gains, often matching or outperforming the advanced WinMax watermark detector. Signature filtering thus provides a simple, scalable, and model-agnostic add-on to strengthen watermark-based provenance checks for LLM text in information processing workflows.

</details>


### [194] [Beyond Prediction: Tail-Aware Scheduling for LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18431)
*Yueying Li,Yuanfan Chen,Jiayang Chen,Esha Choukse,Haoran Qiu,G. Edward Suh,Rodrigo Fonseca,Ziv Scully,Udit Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a distribution-aware, prediction-free scheduling framework for LLM serving that uses soft priority boosting based on lightweight statistical signals instead of explicit decode-length prediction. It co-optimizes scheduling with cache-aware preemption, achieving 35-50% P99 TTLT reduction over SRPT with perfect length knowledge and 34-47% TTFT reduction across diverse workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM schedulers rely on predicted decode lengths or ranks to approximate SJF/SRPT, but these prediction-driven policies are fragile under distribution shifts, bursty arrivals, and GPU memory pressure. They also offer limited control over tail latency (P90-P99) that dominates user experience. Even with perfect decode-length knowledge, current approaches fall short on tail metrics.

Method: The authors introduce a distribution-aware, prediction-free scheduling framework that replaces explicit length prediction with soft priority boosting using lightweight statistical signals. The design co-optimizes scheduling and cache-aware preemption to handle memory-coupled decode dynamics across workload mixes. Priority boosting is driven by observed statistical properties of requests rather than point predictions of remaining decode length.

Result: Evaluated on production and open-source traces, the method reduces P99 TTLT by 35-50% relative to SRPT with perfect length knowledge, and reduces TTFT by 34-47% across workloads including reasoning-heavy and chat-heavy tasks.

Conclusion: The framework provides a robust alternative for optimizing tail latency in online LLM serving, demonstrating that prediction-free, distribution-aware scheduling can outperform even oracle-assisted SRPT on tail metrics while being resilient to real-world variability.

Abstract: LLM serving exhibits extreme length variability, making size-based scheduling difficult in practice. Recent LLM schedulers approximate SJF/SRPT using predicted decode lengths or ranks and primarily report mean-centric metrics such as TTFT and TBT. We show that these prediction-driven policies can be fragile under distribution shifts, bursty arrivals, and GPU memory pressure, while offering limited control over the tail latency (P90-P99) that dominates user experience, even with perfect decode-length knowledge. We introduce a distribution-aware, prediction-free scheduling framework that replaces explicit length prediction with soft priority boosting driven by lightweight statistical signals. Our design co-optimizes scheduling and cache-aware preemption to account for memory-coupled decode dynamics across workload mixes. Evaluated on production and open-source traces, our method reduces P99 TTLT by up to 35-50% relative to SRPT with perfect length knowledge and reduces TTFT by 34-47% across workloads, including reasoning-heavy and chat-heavy tasks. These results demonstrate a robust alternative for optimizing tail latency in online LLM serving.

</details>


### [195] [A Human-in-the-Loop Bayesian Optimization Framework for Constraint-Aware Bioprocess Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19230)
*Samuel Stricker,Claus Wirnsperger,Alessandro Butté,Laura Helleckes,Gonzalo Guillén Gosálbez,Antonio del Rio Chanona,Mehmet Mercangöz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Extension of Pareto Front Guided Sampling (PFGS) — a Human-in-the-Loop BO framework — to handle constrained and robust optimization by incorporating probabilistic constraint satisfaction and Monte Carlo–estimated input robustness as explicit Pareto objectives, demonstrated on an 8D CHO cell culture simulator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard BO returns a single automated recommendation, which is insufficient when domain experts need to balance multiple competing objectives (predicted performance, uncertainty, feasibility under constraints, and robustness to input perturbations) and iteratively refine selection criteria as development goals evolve.

Method: The PFGS framework reformulates GP surrogate-derived quantities into multi-objective optimization objectives visualized as a Pareto front. Two extensions: (1) constrained optimization via analytical computation of posterior probability of satisfying specification limits as a Pareto objective; (2) robust optimization via Monte Carlo sampling estimating expected lower-confidence performance over user-defined input variability. The multi-dimensional Pareto set is rendered as pairwise 2D projections on an interactive dashboard for expert-driven candidate selection.

Result: Demonstrated on an 8D fed-batch CHO cell culture simulator, the framework systematically identifies operating conditions that are simultaneously high-performing, constraint-compliant, and resilient to perturbations. Expert-defined requirements provide a principled stopping criterion and guide efficient allocation of experimental resources.

Conclusion: Integrating probabilistic constraints and input robustness as explicit Pareto objectives within a HitL BO framework enables transparent, multi-criteria decision-making. The approach allows selection criteria to evolve alongside model improvement and provides a principled basis for terminating the optimization cycle.

Abstract: This work presents an extension to Pareto Front Guided Sampling (PFGS), a Human-in-the-Loop (HitL) Bayesian Optimization (BO) framework in which Gaussian process (GP) surrogate-derived quantities are reformulated as objectives of a multi-objective optimization problem, and the resulting Pareto front is exposed to a domain expert for interactive candidate selection rather than returning a single automated recommendation. The framework is extended in two directions: constrained optimization is addressed by incorporating the posterior probability of satisfying output specification limits as an explicit Pareto objective, computed analytically from the GP posterior distribution; robust optimization is addressed by a Monte Carlo sampling strategy that estimates expected lower-confidence performance over a user-defined variability of input perturbations, capturing performance degradation under likely implementation deviations. The resulting multi-dimensional Pareto representation renders trade-offs between predicted performance, model uncertainty, probabilistic constraint satisfaction, and input robustness simultaneously visible through pairwise two-dimensional projections on an interactive dashboard, enabling selection criteria to be iteratively refined as the surrogate model improves and development objectives evolve. The framework is showcased on an eight-dimensional fed-batch Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cell culture simulator demonstrating systematic identification of high-performing, feasibility-compliant, and perturbation-resilient operating conditions, and illustrating how expert-defined requirements provide a principled stopping criterion and support informed allocation of experimental resources.

</details>


### [196] [TMR-GGNN: Credit Card Fraud Detection based on Time-Aware Multi-Relational Guided Graph Neural Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18444)
*Rohit Tewari,Shubhankar Shilpi,Navin Chhibber,Devendra Singh Parmar,Sunil Khemka,Piyush Ranjan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes TMR-GGNN, a time-aware multi-relational graph neural network for credit card fraud detection that uses dynamic heterogeneous graphs, temporal attention, contrastive learning, and a composite InfoNCE + Focal Loss to handle class imbalance and evolving fraud patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address three core challenges in credit card fraud detection: (1) highly imbalanced transaction data where fraud cases are rare; (2) continuously evolving fraud patterns that static models fail to capture; and (3) complex relational structures among transaction entities (customers, merchants, devices, IPs) that simple models cannot exploit.

Method: The TMR-GGNN framework extends an encoder-decoder GNN architecture with three key innovations: (1) constructs a dynamic multi-relational graph modeling heterogeneous interactions among customers, merchants, devices, and IPs over temporal windows; (2) introduces a time-aware relational attention mechanism in the encoder that adaptively weights transaction relevance based on temporal proximity and semantic context; (3) employs a contrastive learning module in the decoder to distinguish real from synthesized transactions, improving generalization on rare fraud cases. A composite loss function combining InfoNCE-based contrastive loss with Focal Loss addresses severe class imbalance and emphasizes discriminative learning.

Result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper claims the framework improves fraud identification and mitigates false negatives through the composite loss design, but specific quantitative results are not provided.

Conclusion: The TMR-GGNN framework effectively integrates temporal modeling, multi-relational graph learning, and contrastive representation learning to tackle class imbalance, evolving fraud patterns, and complex entity relationships. The InfoNCE + Focal Loss combination enhances fraud detection while reducing false negatives.

Abstract: In recent years, credit card fraud detection has faced significant challenges due to highly imbalanced data, evolving fraud patterns, and complex relational structures among transaction entities. To address these issues, this research proposes a novel framework called Timeaware Multi Relational Guided Graph Neural Network (TMR GGNN). Particularly, the proposed TMR GGNN extends the encoder decoder Graph Neural Network GNN architecture by modeling heterogeneous interactions across customers, merchants, devices, and IPs over temporal windows.
