Subsequently, the proposed TMR GGNN approach constructs a dynamic, multi relational graph and incorporates a time aware relational attention mechanism within the encoder to adaptively weigh the transaction relevance based on temporal proximity and semantic context. Consequently, the decoder employs a contrastive learning module to distinguish between real and synthesized transaction patterns, while improving the models generalization of rare fraud cases. Additionally, to effectively manage severe class imbalances and emphasize discriminative learning, a composite loss function combining Information Noise Contrastive Estimation (InfoNCE) based contrastive loss with Focal Loss is introduced. This integration assists in improving fraud identification while mitigating false negatives.

</details>


### [197] [A Cross-Model VLM-Judge Protocol for Single-Image 3D Mesh Quality (and Why Cheap Proxies Fall Short)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18451)
*Ali Asaria,Tony Salomone,Deep Gandhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a VLM-judge evaluation protocol for single-image-to-3D generation that is reproducible and human-free, shows that two judge families agree substantially, and demonstrates that commonly used cheap proxies (render-space CLIP similarity, geometry validity) fail to substitute for it, being either near chance or only weakly correlated when defects are visually salient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No agreed-upon, human-free evaluation protocol exists for single-image-to-3D generation. Practitioners default to cheap automatic proxies (render-space CLIP similarity, mesh geometry-validity statistics), but their alignment with perceived quality is unestablished. The work aims to fill this gap.

Method: The authors propose a VLM-judge protocol: a fixed 24-view headless render rig, two independent vision-language model judge families, and a mandatory position-bias correction that queries both presentation orders and retains only order-consistent verdicts. This protocol serves as reference to evaluate cheap proxies. They also train a learned Bradley-Terry model over extracted features to see if proxy weighting improves performance.

Result: The two VLM judge families agree substantially (Cohen's kappa = 0.66). Geometry validity is only a weak bimodal signal, below the pre-registered target; render-CLIP performs at chance. The learned Bradley-Terry head collapses onto a single manifoldness statistic with negative CLIP weight, matching geometry-only performance. The proxy is bimodal: above chance on contrasts with visible geometric defects, at chance on ambiguous ones.

Conclusion: The VLM-judge protocol is recommended as a reliable, reproducible evaluator (under the tested conditions: two feed-forward generators on Google Scanned Objects, face-drop degradation). Geometry/CLIP proxies are not recommended as optimization targets.

Abstract: Single-image-to-3D generators are improving quickly, but there is no agreed, human-free way to tell whether one generated mesh is better than another. Practitioners commonly rely on cheap automatic proxies (render-space CLIP similarity and mesh geometry-validity statistics), yet how well these track perceived quality is unestablished. We make two contributions. First, we propose and validate a reproducible VLM-judge evaluation protocol: a fixed 24-view headless render rig, two independent vision-language judge families, and a mandatory position-bias correction that queries both presentation orders and keeps only order-consistent verdicts. The two judge families agree substantially with each other (Cohen's kappa = 0.66), well above the chance-agreement floor. Second, using this protocol as the reference, we show the cheap proxies do not substitute for it. Geometry validity is only a weak signal on average (because, as we show, it is bimodal) and stays below our pre-registered target, while render-CLIP is at chance. A learned Bradley-Terry head collapses onto a single manifoldness statistic (giving render-CLIP a negative weight) and matches geometry-only exactly, so learning the feature weights buys nothing. The proxy is also bimodal: it is significantly above chance on contrasts with visible geometric defects but at chance on ambiguous contrasts, consistent with geometry validity tracking the judge only when the defect is visually salient. We therefore recommend the VLM-judge protocol as a reliable, reproducible evaluator under the conditions tested (two feed-forward generators on Google Scanned Objects, with a face-drop degradation regime) and advise against geometry/CLIP proxies as optimization targets.

</details>


### [198] [Stealthy World Model Manipulation via Data Poisoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18697)
*Yibin Hu,Xiaolin Sun,Zizhan Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SWAAP is a two-stage data poisoning attack against learned world models that manipulates fine-tuning trajectories to corrupt downstream planning, achieving substantial performance degradation while evading standard defenses across continuous-control tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models are increasingly used in model-based RL for planning, but the fine-tuning phase—where models are updated from collected experience—creates an underexplored attack surface. No prior work has investigated how adversarially poisoned fine-tuning data can manipulate learned dynamics to corrupt planning.

Method: SWAAP operates in two stages: (1) Target identification via first-order bilevel optimization using a novel transition-gradient theorem to find a harmful world model close to clean dynamics; (2) Stealth-constrained gradient matching that modifies a limited fraction of transition targets, with a prediction-error regularizer keeping poisoned samples near the model's natural approximation error, so training gradients steer the victim toward the adversarial target.

Result: SWAAP causes substantial performance degradation across diverse continuous-control tasks. Poisoned transitions remain close to clean data and evade non-adaptive residual, CUSUM, and TRIM-style defenses evaluated at three stages: pre-training detection, robust fine-tuning, and test-time monitoring.

Conclusion: World-model adaptation pipelines exhibit a practical vulnerability to data poisoning, and current defenses are insufficient. Robustness methods must protect both training data and learned dynamics in world-model systems.

Abstract: Model-based learning agents use learned world models to predict future states, plan actions, and adapt to new environments. However, the process of updating world models from collected experience creates a training-time attack surface: adversarially poisoned fine-tuning trajectories can manipulate the learned dynamics and thereby corrupt downstream planning. In this paper, we propose SWAAP, the first two-stage data poisoning framework for learned world models. In the first stage, SWAAP identifies a harmful target world model that induces low-return behavior under planning while remaining close to clean dynamics, using first-order bilevel optimization enabled by a transition-gradient theorem. In the second stage, SWAAP realizes this target through stealth-constrained gradient matching, modifying only a limited fraction of fine-tuning transition targets so that the induced training gradients steer the victim model toward the adversarial target, while a prediction-error regularizer encourages the poisoned targets to remain close to the world model's natural approximation error. To assess attack stealthiness, we evaluate defenses and detectability across three stages of the poisoning pipeline: pre-training detection of poisoned transitions, robust training during fine-tuning, and test-time monitoring of the resulting world model. Across diverse continuous-control tasks, SWAAP causes substantial performance degradation while keeping poisoned transitions close to clean data and evading the evaluated non-adaptive residual/CUSUM/TRIM-style defenses. These results reveal a practical vulnerability in world-model adaptation pipelines and highlight the need for robustness methods that protect both world-model training data and learned dynamics.

</details>


### [199] [Veriphi: Attack-Guided Neural Network Verification with Dataset-Dependent Training Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18454)
*Pratik Deshmukh,Kartik Arya,Vasili Savin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Veriphi combines GPU-accelerated adversarial attacks with α,β-CROWN formal bound certification, demonstrating that training method effectiveness for neural network verification is fundamentally dataset-dependent. IBP excels on simple MNIST but fails on CIFAR-10 where PGD adversarial training dominates. The system achieves 5x verification speedup and scales to 105.8M-parameter production models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper is motivated by the need to challenge the prevailing assumption that certified training (e.g., IBP) universally outperforms adversarial training for neural network verification. The authors aim to demonstrate that context—specifically dataset complexity—critically determines which training and verification strategy is optimal, and to bridge the gap between fast adversarial attacks and formal bound certification in a scalable, production-ready system.

Method: Veriphi integrates adversarial attack-based falsification (for fast counterexample discovery) with formal bound certification using α,β-CROWN methods on GPU-accelerated infrastructure. The system is evaluated through systematic experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 across three training paradigms: standard training, adversarial training (PGD), and certified training (IBP). An attack-guided falsification pipeline is employed to accelerate verification. The approach is scaled to production-size models with 105.8M parameters for aerospace logistics optimization use cases.

Result: Key results: (1) IBP achieves 78% certified accuracy on MNIST (784 dimensions) but negligible certification on CIFAR-10. (2) PGD adversarial training dominates on CIFAR-10 with 94% certification at small perturbation radii. (3) Attack-guided falsification yields a 5x verification speedup. (4) The system successfully scales to 105.8M-parameter production models for real-world aerospace logistics optimization.

Conclusion: The assumption that certified training universally outperforms adversarial training is refuted. Dataset complexity fundamentally mediates training method effectiveness for verification: IBP suffices for low-dimensional problems like MNIST, while PGD adversarial training is superior for more complex datasets like CIFAR-10. Context-aware verification strategy selection is critical, and hybrid systems combining falsification with formal certification can achieve both speed and scalability for industrial applications.

Abstract: We present Veriphi, a GPU-accelerated neural network verification system that combines fast adversarial attacks with formal bound certification using alpha,beta-CROWN methods. Through systematic experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 using three training methodologies (standard, adversarial, certified), we demonstrate that training method effectiveness is fundamentally dataset-dependent. Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) achieves 78% certified accuracy on simple MNIST (784 dimensions) but provides negligible certification performance on the more complex CIFAR-10 dataset, where PGD adversarial training dominates with 94% certification at small perturbations. We achieve 5x verification speedup through attack-guided falsification and scale our approach to production-size models (105.8M parameters) for real-world aerospace logistics optimization. Our results challenge the assumption that certified training universally outperforms adversarial training, showing context matters critically for verification strategy selection.

</details>


### [200] [Task-Restricted Symmetries in Recurrent Weight Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18457)
*Simon Dräger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: One-layer tanh RNNs exhibit substantial functional redundancy in weight space. Using Schur decomposition, the authors perform structured ablations showing that certain nonnormal couplings can be removed with minimal loss, while others are essential. The ablation profile varies by task and solution, revealing approximate functional invariances rather than universal symmetries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recurrent networks often have many weight configurations that produce nearly identical input-output behavior, yet similarly-sized weight changes can catastrophically disrupt function. The authors aim to systematically characterize this functional redundancy — distinguishing which structural components of a recurrent weight matrix are dispensable versus essential — using a mathematically principled coordinate system rather than arbitrary weight perturbations.

Method: The authors use the ordered real Schur decomposition to represent one-layer tanh RNN weight matrices in a coordinate system that separates spectral (eigenvalue) blocks from directed nonnormal (strictly upper-triangular) couplings. They then perform structured ablations by zeroing out specific Schur-coordinate components (while keeping input and readout maps fixed) and measure the resulting loss on trained tasks: fixed-length copy, flip-flop, sine generation, and context-dependent integration.

Result: Selected nonnormal Schur couplings can be removed with negligible performance degradation in some trained solutions, while other couplings are critical for accurate autonomous replay. The ablation-vulnerable versus ablation-robust components differ across tasks (copy vs. flip-flop vs. sine generation vs. context-dependent integration) and across different trained solutions for the same task, indicating approximate invariances rather than universal symmetries of RNN weight space.

Conclusion: Schur-coordinate ablations provide a practical diagnostic tool for identifying which structured perturbations preserve a trained RNN's computation and which disrupt it. The observed invariances are approximate and solution-specific, not universal symmetries, highlighting that functional redundancy in recurrent networks is nuanced and task-dependent.

Abstract: Recurrent networks can contain substantial functional redundancy in
  weight space: changing a recurrent matrix may leave the input-output
  rollout nearly unchanged on a task distribution, while similar-scale
  changes can destroy the same behavior. We study this redundancy in
  one-layer tanh RNNs using ordered real Schur coordinates. The Schur
  form separates spectral blocks from directed nonnormal couplings,
  giving a diagnostic basis for structured ablations that keep the input
  and readout maps fixed. In a fixed-length copy task, selected
  nonnormal Schur couplings can be removed with little loss in some
  trained solutions, whereas other couplings are necessary for accurate
  autonomous replay. Across flip-flop, sine generation, and
  context-dependent integration, the loss-preserving ablation profile
  varies across tasks and trained solutions. These results identify
  candidate approximate functional invariances, not universal symmetries
  of recurrent weight space. Schur-coordinate ablations provide a
  practical diagnostic for which structured perturbations preserve a
  trained recurrent solution and which ones disrupt its computation.

</details>


### [201] [What Does the Weight Norm Control in Grokking? Logit-Scale Mediation under Cross-Entropy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18465)
*Truong Xuan Khanh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Grokking delay is primarily controlled by the logit scale (softmax temperature), not weight norm directly. Weight norm acts merely as an upstream handle; the proximal mechanism is logit scale and softmax saturation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokking — the delayed transition from memorization to generalization — is empirically associated with weight norm, but the causal mechanism remains unclear. The authors aim to identify what the weight norm actually controls in the grokking phenomenon.

Method: The authors decouple weight norm from logit scale by clamping the norm and independently varying output temperature. They sweep across a grid of norms and temperatures under cross-entropy loss, measure grokking delay, and perform regression (R²=0.97). Control experiments include: MSE loss (where logit scale is pinned), float64 softmax-collapse audits, no-LayerNorm transformers, and forking from identical states to rule out rescaling artifacts.

Result: Under cross-entropy, grokking delay collapses almost entirely onto logit scale alone (R²=0.97), with weight norm contributing only 1-2% beyond it. Under MSE, the logit scale is pinned and norm acts through a different route. Forking experiments confirm delay follows the held norm value, not the clamp operation. The proximal variable is the logit scale and resulting softmax saturation.

Conclusion: The weight norm is not the direct causal agent of grokking; it is an upstream handle on the logit scale. The true proximal driver of grokking delay is the logit scale and softmax saturation it induces.

Abstract: Grokking, the delayed jump from memorization to generalization, is usually tied to the weight norm: a smaller norm generalizes sooner. We ask what the norm actually controls. Holding the weight norm fixed by clamping and varying only an output temperature, we slide the grokking delay across its entire norm-induced range under cross-entropy; matching the effective logit scale back to baseline recovers about 85% of the delay at two moduli. Across a grid of norms and temperatures the delay collapses onto the logit scale alone (R2 = 0.97), with the norm adding 1-2% beyond it. The effect is loss-dependent: under mean-squared error the logit scale is pinned and the norm acts through a different route. A memorization control, a float64 softmax-collapse audit, and a no-LayerNorm transformer point to the same channel. Forking arms from one identical state, the delay follows the held norm value and not the clamp operation, which closes a rescaling-artifact concern. The proximal variable is the logit scale and the softmax saturation it drives; the weight norm is only an upstream handle. All numbers, tables, and figures reproduce from released code and data.

</details>


### [202] [Structured Representation Learning with Locally Linear Embeddings and Adaptive Feature Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18469)
*Somjit Nath,Jackson J Cone,Derek Nowrouzezahrai,Samira Ebrahimi Kahou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Inspired by how the brain uses low-dimensional manifolds and adaptive gating to encode behavior, the authors propose an RL framework that disentangles dynamics-specific features (via locally linear embeddings) from reward-specific features, then fuses them with an attention mechanism. The method outperforms conventional RL on benchmark tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neuroscientific evidence shows the brain encodes complex behaviors using structured, low-dimensional manifolds and adaptively fuses multiple information sources via gating mechanisms. Existing RL methods do not explicitly model these principles—specifically, the disentanglement of dynamics-relevant and reward-relevant features combined with adaptive per-state fusion. The paper aims to bridge this gap by designing an RL framework that directly mirrors these biological strategies for more efficient decision-making.

Method: The proposed framework has three core components: (1) Locally Linear Embeddings (LLEs) that capture the intrinsic, locally linear structure of state spaces, analogous to local smoothness in neural population activity—these yield dynamics-specific features; (2) a standard RL objective that learns reward-specific features; and (3) an attention mechanism (analogous to cortical gating) that adaptively fuses these two complementary feature sets on a per-state basis, dynamically weighting their contributions depending on context.

Result: Experimental evaluation on benchmark RL tasks shows that the proposed method improves both learning efficiency (sample efficiency/speed of convergence) and overall performance (final return) compared to conventional RL baselines.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling local state structure and incorporating adaptive, attention-based feature fusion—principles grounded in neuroscience—yields tangible benefits in RL. The results underscore the value of drawing on biological computation principles (manifold structure, disentanglement, and dynamic gating) to enhance artificial learning systems.

Abstract: Neuroscientific research has revealed that the brain encodes complex behaviors by leveraging structured, low-dimensional manifolds and dynamically fusing multiple sources of information through adaptive gating mechanisms. Inspired by these principles, we propose a novel reinforcement learning (RL) framework that encourages the disentanglement of dynamics-specific and reward-specific features, drawing direct parallels to how neural circuits separate and integrate information for efficient decision-making. Our approach leverages locally linear embeddings (LLEs) to capture the intrinsic, locally linear structure inherent in many environments, mirroring the local smoothness observed in neural population activity, while concurrently deriving reward-specific features through the standard RL objective. An attention mechanism, analogous to cortical gating, adaptively fuses these complementary representations on a per-state basis. Experimental results on benchmark tasks demonstrate that our method, grounded in neuroscientific principles, improves learning efficiency and overall performance compared to conventional RL approaches, highlighting the benefits of explicitly modeling local state structures and adaptive feature selection as observed in biological systems.

</details>


### [203] [The Illusion of Improvement: Reject Inference Strategies in Credit Scoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18479)
*Bruno Scarone,Ricardo Baeza-Yates*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Credit scoring models retrained under survival bias can exhibit improved accuracy while rejection quality collapses — a structural failure mode. The authors propose controlled exploration (approving a small fraction of rejected applicants) to break the feedback loop, showing that 2–5% exploration suffices to diagnose the problem, and that standard accuracy metrics are misleading under selection bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reject inference methods are commonly used to address survival bias in credit scoring, but their effectiveness is poorly understood. The paper aims to systematically evaluate these methods and uncover structural failure modes in the retraining cycle that standard evaluation metrics fail to detect.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate several reject inference methods across retraining cycles, tracking both accuracy and rejection quality. They then propose a controlled exploration strategy: deliberately approving a random fraction of otherwise-rejected applicants to observe true outcomes, breaking the feedback loop without parametric assumptions. Experiments are conducted across two ML methods (logistic regression and XGBoost) and three real-world datasets.

Result: A structural failure mode is identified where accuracy improves over retraining cycles while recall/rejection quality collapses, creating an illusion of improvement. Accuracy and rejection quality give opposite recommendations on exploration: accuracy favors no exploration, while rejection quality improves with it. Exploration rates as low as 2–5% suffice to diagnose feedback loop severity at near-zero cost.

Conclusion: Standard evaluation protocols relying on accuracy are inadequate for assessing models trained under survival bias. Rejection quality must be monitored separately, and minimal controlled exploration provides a practical, assumption-free mechanism to detect and mitigate feedback-loop degradation in credit scoring systems.

Abstract: Reject inference methods are widely used to mitigate survival bias in credit scoring, yet their effectiveness remains poorly understood. We systematically evaluate several such methods and uncover a structural failure mode: in a natural retraining cycle, models whose accuracy improves while recall collapses create an illusion of improvement that leads practitioners to believe the system is getting better when, in fact, its rejection quality -- the ability to correctly screen out defaulters -- is deteriorating. We then propose a controlled exploration strategy that breaks the feedback loop without statistical assumptions: the lender deliberately approves a fraction of rejected applicants and observes their true outcomes. We show that accuracy and rejection quality give opposite recommendations on whether to explore: accuracy favors no exploration, while rejection quality improves with it, confirming that standard evaluation metrics are misleading under selection bias. Even minimal exploration rates (2--5\%) prove sufficient in our experiments to diagnose the severity of the feedback loop at near-zero cost. Our findings are consistent across two machine learning methods and three real-world datasets, and suggest that standard evaluation protocols are inadequate for assessing models trained under survival bias.

</details>


### [204] [SFT Overtraining Predicts Rank Inversion via Entropy Collapse Under RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18487)
*Siddharth Aphale,Kelly Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Standard SFT checkpoint selection via pass@1 can backfire for GRPO when SFT overfits, compressing the rollout distribution. Low diversity leads to within-group reward homogeneity, collapsing the advantage signal. The authors propose a two-stage diagnostic (pre-RL entropy + early GRPO entropy monitoring) to flag failing runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper identifies a failure mode in GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization): selecting the SFT checkpoint with highest pass@1 can paradoxically yield the worst downstream GRPO performance. This occurs because excessive SFT compresses response diversity, causing most rollout groups to have uniform rewards and thus no group-relative advantage signal — a phenomenon the authors formalize mathematically.

Method: The authors analyze the expected within-group advantage variance under binary rewards, showing it equals $p(1-p)(g-1)/g$, where $p$ is the solve rate and $g$ is group size. When early GRPO pushes $p$ below a threshold $p^*(g)$, groups collapse. They conduct empirical studies on Qwen2.5-Coder-3B (5 SFT depths, 3 seeds) and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B (4 depths, 3 seeds), measuring pre-RL pass@1, pass@10, and entropy. They propose a two-stage diagnostic: pre-RL entropy triage plus early GRPO entropy monitoring, and test KL regularization and label smoothing as potential remedies.

Result: On Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, higher SFT depth raises pre-RL pass@1 but drops peak GRPO pass@10 from 0.806 to 0.481; pre-RL entropy correlates positively with GRPO outcome (ρ=+0.69). On DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, pass@1 stays well above p*(8)=0.083, and GRPO outcomes compress rather than invert. The two-stage diagnostic successfully flags high-risk checkpoints. KL regularization and label smoothing fail to rescue collapsed Qwen runs, indicating the failure is not a trivial hyperparameter artifact.

Conclusion: The highest-pass@1 SFT checkpoint is not always optimal for GRPO initialization; low entropy signals risk of advantage collapse. The proposed entropy-based diagnostic enables early detection of failing runs, and simple regularization remedies prove insufficient, suggesting deeper architectural or algorithmic interventions are needed.

Abstract: The standard heuristic of selecting the SFT checkpoint with the highest pass@1 for GRPO can fail when SFT compresses the rollout distribution. For binary rewards, the expected within group advantage variance is $p(1{-}p)(g{-}1)/g$; when early GRPO drives $p$ below $p^*(g)$, most groups have identical rewards and provide no group relative signal. We study SFT depth ladders for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B. We test Qwen2.5-Coder-3B across five depths and three seeds, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B across four matched depths and three seeds. On Qwen, pre RL pass@1 rises with SFT depth, but peak GRPO pass@10 falls from $0.806$ to $0.481$ (3 seed mean, $n{=}20$); pre RL entropy is positively associated with the GRPO outcome ($ρ{=}{+}0.69$). On DeepSeek, pass@1 remains far above $p^*(8){=}0.083$, and GRPO outcomes compress rather than invert. A two stage diagnostic, combining pre RL entropy triage with an early GRPO entropy monitor, flags high risk checkpoints and can stop failing runs early. Simple KL to reference regularisation and label smoothing variants do not rescue the collapsed Qwen checkpoint in our setting, suggesting the failure is not a trivial GRPO hyperparameter artefact.

</details>


### [205] [Quantum Annealing Enhanced Reinforcement Learning for Accurate Remaining Useful Lifetime Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18503)
*Manoranjan Gandhudi,Arunkumar V.,G. R. Anil,Gangadharan G. R*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A quantum annealing-enhanced Q-learning framework (QAQL) is proposed for RUL estimation, where each Q-value update is encoded as a QUBO solved on a D-Wave Advantage system. The annealer's stochastic action selection from near-optimal solutions provides exploration that prevents premature convergence, outperforming classical and quantum baselines on NASA C-MAPSS and device-fleet datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Statistical degradation models fail to capture the strong nonlinearity of real systems, while data-driven models tend to converge to suboptimal solutions in high-dimensional, non-convex search spaces. There is a need for an optimizer that balances exploration and exploitation within the reinforcement-learning loop to handle nonlinear degradation trajectories effectively.

Method: The QAQL framework encodes each Q-value update as a small quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem. The ground state of the QUBO corresponds to the greedy action. Rather than deterministic optimization, the D-Wave Advantage quantum annealer returns a distribution over near-optimal actions across many reads via minor embedding. This stochastic action selection is woven directly into the RL loop to supply exploration and curb premature convergence.

Result: Evaluated on the NASA C-MAPSS turbofan engine datasets and a device-fleet predictive maintenance dataset, QAQL outperformed all classical and quantum baselines across six error metrics, averaged over multiple independent runs, with statistically significant improvements.

Conclusion: Quantum annealing is demonstrated to be a practically usable optimizer within a reinforcement-learning loop for industrial predictive maintenance, not merely a theoretical construct. The stochastic sampling behavior of the annealer effectively addresses the exploration-exploitation trade-off in nonlinear RUL estimation.

Abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) estimation is central to predictive maintenance, where an unplanned failure can cost far more than the asset itself. Statistical degradation models miss the strong nonlinearity of real systems, and data-driven models often converge to suboptimal solutions in high-dimensional, non-convex search spaces. We propose a Quantum Annealing enhanced Q-Learning (QAQL) framework that couples the sampling behaviour of quantum annealing with the sequential decision making of Q-learning. Each Q-value update is encoded as a small quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) whose ground state is the greedy action; rather than acting as a deterministic optimizer, the annealer returns a distribution over near-optimal actions across many reads, and this stochastic action selection supplies the exploration that curbs premature convergence on nonlinear degradation trajectories. The QUBO is solved on the D-Wave Advantage system using minor embedding, with the annealer woven into the reinforcement-learning loop rather than bolted on after training. We validate QAQL on two public benchmarks: the NASA C-MAPSS turbofan engine datasets and a device-fleet predictive maintenance dataset. Averaged over many independent runs and across six error metrics, QAQL outperforms the classical and quantum baselines considered in this study, with statistically significant improvements. The results indicate that quantum annealing is a usable, not merely theoretical, optimizer inside a reinforcement-learning loop for industrial predictive-maintenance applications.

</details>


### [206] [Beyond AHI: An Interpretable Causal-Discovery-Guided Framework for Sleep Recovery in Connected Health](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18506)
*Saba A. Farahani,Elahe Khatibi,Manoj Vishwanath,Amir M. Rahmani,Hung Cao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a causal-discovery-guided hierarchical Sleep Recovery Score (SRS) derived from multimodal polysomnography data, spanning five physiological domains (respiratory burden, hypoxic burden, sleep fragmentation, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation). The SRS demonstrates up to 2.5× stronger alignment with patient-reported recovery outcomes than the standard Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI), validated across two large cohorts (MESA: n=1540; MrOS: n=825).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PSG summary indices like AHI poorly capture the multidimensional physiological processes underlying functional recovery as perceived by patients (e.g., sleepiness, fatigue). There is a need for an interpretable, multidomain metric that better aligns objective sleep physiology with patient-reported outcomes, and that can bridge clinical PSG with emerging wearable/connected-health sensor streams.

Method: The authors apply directed acyclic graph (DAG) learning on multimodal PSG data from two cohorts to identify candidate physiological drivers across five domains: respiratory burden, hypoxic burden, sleep fragmentation, sleep architecture, and autonomic regulation. A two-stage screening process combines physiology-based constraints with constrained LLM-assisted auditing to remove structural confounders and construct-overlapping variables. The resulting hierarchical Sleep Recovery Score (SRS) is then derived and validated against patient-reported outcomes.

Result: The five physiological domains consistently emerge as recurrent domains associated with recovery across both cohorts. The SRS shows up to 2.5× stronger alignment with perceived recovery (sleepiness, fatigue) compared to AHI, demonstrating superior patient-centered validity.

Conclusion: The SRS framework provides an interpretable, bias-aware, domain-structured approach linking multimodal sleep physiology to patient-centered outcomes. It offers a practical foundation for recovery modeling in both clinical sleep studies and emerging smart/connected health settings, with natural mapping to wearable ECG, oximetry, and sleep-stage estimation devices.

Abstract: Objective sleep assessment relies on polysomnography (PSG), yet clinical impact is often better reflected in patient-reported outcomes (PROs) such as sleepiness and fatigue. Existing summary indices, including the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI), provide limited insight into the multidomain physiology underlying functional recovery. We propose an interpretable, causal-discovery--guided framework for deriving a hierarchical Sleep Recovery Score (SRS) from multimodal PSG. Using two large population cohorts (MESA: n=1540; MrOS: n=825), we apply directed acyclic graph (DAG) learning to identify candidate physiological drivers spanning respiratory burden, hypoxic burden, sleep fragmentation, sleep architecture, and autonomic regulation. Although derived from clinical PSG, these domains map naturally to sensing streams increasingly available in connected health technologies, including wearable ECG, oximetry, and sleep-stage estimation devices. To preserve mechanistic plausibility, we introduce a two-stage screening process that combines physiology-based constraints with constrained LLM-assisted auditing to identify and remove structural confounders and construct-overlapping variables. Across cohorts, these five domains emerge as recurrent physiological domains associated with recovery, and the resulting SRS shows up to 2.5$\times$ stronger alignment with perceived recovery than AHI. By linking multimodal sleep physiology to patient-centered outcomes through an interpretable, bias-aware, and domain structured framework, this work provides a practical foundation for recovery modeling across both clinical sleep studies and emerging smart and connected health settings.

</details>


### [207] [Concept Modulation Models: A Unified Framework for Identifiability and Extrapolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18509)
*Soheun Yi,Yizhou Lu,Chandler Squires,Pradeep Ravikumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Concept Modulation Models (CMMs), a unifying framework for conditional latent variable models that separates generic lifting arguments from model-specific rigidity proofs, using attribute potentials to characterize both identifiability and extrapolation guarantees across diverse model classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing identifiability and extrapolation guarantees for conditional latent variable models (nonlinear ICA, causal representation learning, perturbation modeling) are developed in a model-specific, fragmented manner. There is no unified framework that reveals the common mathematical structure underlying these diverse results, particularly how observed variation across attributes constrains latent structure and enables generalization to unseen attributes.

Method: The authors propose CMMs with structure A→Λ→C→X (attributes→modulators→latent concepts→observed features). They introduce a generic "lifting" step showing that feature agreement on observed attributes induces latent concept transitions, then characterize these transitions via attribute potentials (log-density ratios between attribute-conditioned concept laws). Extrapolation is analyzed through whether transported attribute-potential identities extend to unseen attributes.

Result: The framework yields algebraic extrapolation criteria and identifies common potential-based proof objects shared across several existing identifiability and extrapolation results. When combined with model-specific rigidity arguments from prior works, the framework recovers their stated conclusions, demonstrating its unifying power.

Conclusion: CMMs provide a unified lens for conditional latent variable model identifiability and extrapolation, separating the generic structure (attribute potentials and lifting) from model-specific rigidity constraints. This clarifies the shared mathematical foundations across disparate model classes and offers systematic extrapolation criteria.

Abstract: Reliable generalization in conditional latent variable models requires understanding both identifiability and extrapolation: how observed variation across attributes determines latent structure, and how that structure determines distributions at unseen attributes. However, existing identifiability and extrapolation guarantees are largely model-specific, with separate analyses in nonlinear ICA, causal representation learning, perturbation modeling, and related conditional latent variable models. We introduce concept modulation models (CMMs), an attribute-indexed class of conditional generative models with structure $A\to Λ\to C\to X$, where attributes select modulators, modulators induce latent concept laws, and concepts generate observed features. CMMs lift transition-based identifiability to conditional settings by showing that feature agreement on observed attributes induces a latent concept transition constrained by the CMM class. We express these constraints through attribute potentials, log-density ratios between attribute-conditioned concept laws, separating the generic lifting step from model-specific rigidity arguments. The same potentials control extrapolation: agreement at unseen attributes holds exactly when the transported attribute-potential identities extend to those attributes. This yields algebraic extrapolation criteria, identifies the common potential-based proof objects behind several existing identifiability and extrapolation results, and, when combined with the model-specific rigidity arguments in those works, recovers their stated conclusions.

</details>


### [208] [PSyGenTAB: A Privacy-Preserving Framework for Synthetic Clinical Tabular Data Generation via Constrained Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18518)
*Arshia Ilaty,Hossein Shirazi,Manasi Chitale,Kedar Hegde,Dhanalakshmi Ramesh,Rashmi S. Manjunath,Amir Rahmani,Hajar Homayouni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PSyGenTAB is a privacy-preserving synthetic healthcare data generator that frames the privacy-utility trade-off as a constrained optimization problem solved via the Augmented Lagrangian Method, enabling configurable privacy guarantees while preserving clinically meaningful patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical AI development is bottlenecked by restricted access to clinical data due to institutional silos and regulations like HIPAA/GDPR. Existing synthetic data methods lack principled mechanisms to explicitly control the privacy-utility trade-off, often either degrading clinical patterns or risking re-identification.

Method: PSyGenTAB formulates synthetic healthcare tabular data generation as a constrained optimization problem using the Augmented Lagrangian Method. Privacy constraints (e.g., minimum thresholds against membership inference and exact record reproduction) are embedded directly into the generative model training, allowing the framework to maximize utility while strictly enforcing configurable privacy bounds.

Result: PSyGenTAB preserved inter-feature clinical relationships and minority-class diagnostic patterns across multiple clinical benchmarks. In downstream evaluations (Train-on-Synthetic/Test-on-Real and Train-on-Real/Test-on-Synthetic), models trained on synthetic data matched performance of those trained on real records. Privacy audits confirmed reduced exact record reproduction and strong resistance to membership inference attacks.

Conclusion: PSyGenTAB provides a principled, tunable framework for generating synthetic healthcare data that demonstrably balances privacy protection with clinical utility, enabling secure cross-institutional AI development without compromising patient confidentiality or data fidelity.

Abstract: The development of medical AI is constrained by limited access to high-quality clinical data due to institutional silos and strict privacy regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR. Synthetic data generation offers a potential solution, but existing methods lack principled mechanisms to explicitly manage the privacy-utility trade-off, often degrading clinically meaningful patterns or risking patient re-identification. We present PSyGenTAB, a privacy-preserving generative framework that formulates synthetic healthcare data generation as a constrained optimization problem solved using the Augmented Lagrangian Method. By embedding configurable privacy constraints directly into model training, PSyGenTAB enforces minimum privacy thresholds while maximizing clinical data utility. Across multiple clinically motivated benchmarks, PSyGenTAB preserves inter-feature clinical relationships and minority-class diagnostic patterns essential for reliable health AI. Downstream evaluation using Train-on-Synthetic, Test-on-Real and Train-on-Real, Test-on-Synthetic protocols shows that models trained on synthetic data achieve performance comparable to those trained on real patient records. Privacy auditing further demonstrates reduced exact record reproduction and strong resilience to membership inference attacks. These results establish PSyGenTAB as a principled framework for balancing privacy protection and clinical utility in synthetic healthcare data, supporting secure cross-institutional AI development.

</details>


### [209] [Sparsity Curse: Understanding RLVR Model Parameter Space from Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18521)
*Chenrui Wu,Zexi Li,Jiajun Bu,Jiangchuan Liu,Haishuai Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RLVR produces sparse, off-principal parameter updates that — counterintuitively — make model merging fragile due to near-orthogonal "shortcuts" spread far apart in parameter space. The authors characterize this sparsity curse and propose SAR-Merging, which uses Fisher Information sensitivity arbitration, magnitude-aware sparsification, and rescaling to resolve conflicts, significantly outperforming existing merging methods for RLVR models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLVR is known to produce sparse parameter updates and resist catastrophic forgetting, suggesting it might be naturally amenable to model merging for scalable aggregation of diverse reasoning capabilities. However, the authors discover a "sparsity curse" — sparse RLVR updates are widely dispersed and near-orthogonal, causing standard merging to catastrophically degrade performance. This motivates designing a merging method specifically tailored to RLVR's unique parameter geometry.

Method: The authors first conduct systematic empirical analysis of RLVR update geometry to characterize why standard merging fails. They then propose SAR-Merging (Sensitivity-aware Resolving Merging), which operates in three stages: (1) Fisher Information-based sensitivity arbitration to resolve conflicts in overlapping update regions, (2) magnitude-aware sparsification, and (3) rescaling to preserve fragile reasoning pathways.

Result: SAR-Merging substantially outperforms existing merging methods when applied to RLVR-trained models on mathematical and coding benchmarks, successfully enabling both single-task enhancement and multi-capability fusion that standard methods fail to achieve.

Conclusion: Contrary to intuition, the sparsity of RLVR updates is a curse rather than a blessing for model merging, due to near-orthogonal, dispersed parameter shortcuts. SAR-Merging effectively addresses this by resolving conflicts through sensitivity-aware arbitration, offering a scalable, training-free path to aggregate reasoning capabilities from independently trained RLVR models.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful post-training paradigm that surpasses Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) in eliciting reasoning intelligence and resisting catastrophic forgetting. Recent studies further reveal that RLVR induces highly sparse and off-principal parameter updates compared to SFT. This naturally raises the question: does such sparsity make RLVR models more amenable to model merging? If so, model merging would offer a scalable, training-free path to aggregate diverse reasoning capabilities from independently trained RLVR models. Surprisingly, we find the opposite, uncovering a sparsity curse: the sparse RLVR updates are spread farther apart in parameter space, forming near-orthogonal shortcuts that make aggregation inherently fragile. This is likely rooted in the stochasticity of RL optimization and the diversity of emergent reasoning patterns. Unlike SFT models that converge to shared, flat basins and merge naturally, RLVR models suffer severe degradation under standard merging methods. Through systematic empirical analysis of the update geometry, we characterize the mechanisms behind this failure and propose Sensitivity-aware Resolving Merging (SAR-Merging), a merging recipe tailored for the unique structure of RLVR parameter spaces. SAR-Merging resolves conflicts in overlapping update regions via Fisher Information-based sensitivity arbitration, followed by magnitude-aware sparsification and rescaling to preserve fragile reasoning pathways. Experiments on mathematical and coding benchmarks demonstrate that SAR-Merging substantially outperforms existing merging methods on RLVR models, enabling both single-task enhancement and multi-capability fusion.

</details>


### [210] [On the Residual Scaling of Looped Transformers: Stability and Transferability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18524)
*Shaowen Wang,Bingrui Li,Ge Zhang,Wenhao Huang,Shen Yan,Jian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Looped (weight-tied) Transformers require stronger depth scaling (ε = 1/N) than standard residual networks (ε = 1/√L) because weight sharing correlates residual updates across iterations. For multi-layer looped blocks, the authors derive a factored parameterization ε = λ/(N√L) that decouples loop-correlation control (1/N) from cross-layer variance control (1/√L), enabling hyperparameter transfer from small to large loop counts without retuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard depth-scaling prescriptions (ε = 1/√L) for residual networks fail for looped/weight-tied Transformers because weight sharing introduces correlations between residual updates across iterations. The authors aim to derive the correct scaling laws for looped architectures to enable stable training and hyperparameter transfer.

Method: The authors derive theoretical scaling prescriptions for looped residual architectures. For single-layer blocks looped N times, they show ε = 1/N is required. For multi-layer blocks with L unique layers looped N times, they propose a factored parameterization ε = λ/(N√L) that separates two variance sources: 1/N for within-layer loop correlation and 1/√L for cross-layer variance. They validate these findings experimentally on looped Transformers.

Result: Experiments confirm that 1/N scaling improves trainability and yields lower loss compared to 1/√N scaling across various loop counts. A key practical finding is that the optimal learning rate depends only on L (unique layers), not N (loop count), enabling direct hyperparameter transfer from small to large N without retuning.

Conclusion: Weight-tied looped architectures demand fundamentally different depth-scaling rules than standard residual networks due to update correlation. The proposed 1/N and factored λ/(N√L) scalings are both theoretically motivated and empirically validated, with the practical benefit of loop-count-invariant optimal learning rates.

Abstract: Looped (weight-tied) Transformers apply a shared residual block $N$ times ($h \leftarrow h + \varepsilon\,f(h)$, same $f$ at each step), increasing effective depth without adding parameters. Prior depth-scaling analyses prescribe $\varepsilon = 1/\!\sqrt{L}$ for depth-$L$ residual networks. We show that this is insufficient for looped architectures: weight sharing makes residual updates correlated across iterations, requiring the stronger scaling $\varepsilon = 1/N$. For multi-layer blocks ($L$ unique layers looped $N$ times), we derive a factored parameterization $\varepsilon = λ/(N\!\sqrt{L})$ that separates the two sources of growth: $1/N$ controls the within-layer loop correlation, and $1/\!\sqrt{L}$ controls the across-layer variance. A key consequence is that the optimal learning rate depends only on the number of unique layers $L$, not on the loop count $N$, enabling direct hyperparameter transfer from small to large $N$ without retuning. Experiments on looped Transformers confirm that $1/N$ scaling improves trainability and yields better loss than $1/\!\sqrt{N}$ scaling across loop counts.

</details>


### [211] [Hierarchical Attention via Domain Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18525)
*Stephan Köhler,Oliver Rheinbach*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hierarchical attention mechanism inspired by two-level overlapping Schwarz domain decomposition is proposed, combining local subdomain attention blocks with a coarse global attention block. Tested on a 1D diffusion problem, it trains faster, achieves higher accuracy, and uses fewer parameters than a global low-rank attention baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two-level Schwarz domain decomposition methods effectively combine local subdomain corrections with a coarse-level correction that captures global, long-range information. This observation motivates adapting the same structural principle to design more efficient attention mechanisms for operator learning, where approximating the inverse of a discretized PDE operator is the core task.

Method: The authors replace a dense global softmax-free low-rank attention operator (of the form QK^T) with a two-level additive structure: (1) local low-rank attention blocks on overlapping subdomains, each weighted by a partition-of-unity matrix D_i and restricted via R_i; (2) a coarse attention block using a prolongation matrix Φ. The resulting operator is M_θ^{-1} = Φ Q_0 K_0^T Φ^T + Σ R_i^T D_i^{1/2} Q_i K_i^T D_i^{1/2} R_i. Evaluation uses a 1D diffusion problem with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and synthetic Fourier right-hand sides.

Result: Numerical experiments show that the domain-decomposition attention operator trains faster and yields more accurate approximations than the global low-rank attention baseline, while using significantly fewer parameters.

Conclusion: Incorporating domain decomposition structure into attention mechanisms is a promising direction for finite-dimensional operator learning, offering gains in efficiency, accuracy, and parameter economy even on simple benchmark problems.

Abstract: We propose a hierarchical attention mechanism based on two-level overlapping Schwarz domain decomposition. The method is motivated by the observation that two-level Schwarz domain decomposition methods combine local subdomain corrections with a coarse level that communicates global, long-range information. We test its usefulness in the context of finite-dimensional operator learning using a simple, one-dimensional diffusion problem with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Although elementary, this problem provides a controlled sequence-to-sequence setting in which the exact nonlocal solution operator is known. After discretization, learning the solution operator amounts to approximating the inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix. As a baseline, we use a global softmax-free low-rank attention operator of the form $QK^T$. The proposed construction replaces this dense global factorization by a two-level additive structure: local low-rank attention blocks on overlapping subdomains are combined with a coarse attention block. The resulting operator has the form $$M_θ^{-1}
  =
  ΦQ_0 K_0^T Φ^T
  +
  \sum_{i=1}^{N}
  R_i^T D_i^{1/2} Q_i K_i^T D_i^{1/2} R_i.$$ Here $R_i$ restricts to an overlapping subdomain, $D_i$ is a partition-of-unity weight, and $Φ$ is a coarse interpolation (or prolongation) matrix. Numerical experiments for synthetic Fourier right-hand sides indicate that the domain-decomposition attention operator is able to train faster and can give more accurate approximations than a global low-rank attention baseline while using significantly fewer parameters.

</details>


### [212] [Do as the Romans Do: Learning Universal Behaviors from Heterogeneous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18537)
*Caleb Chang,Davin Win Kyi,Natasha Jaques,Karen Leung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GRID is a social learning method that disentangles reward functions from heterogeneous demonstrators into a shared "general reward" (universal behaviors) and agent-specific rewards (individual preferences). Training on the general reward produces a generalist agent that avoids mode-averaging bias and serves as an effective prior for fine-tuning to downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Observational learning from a heterogeneous population is challenging because different demonstrators pursue different goals, creating conflicting behavioral signals. Standard imitation learning methods suffer from mode-averaging bias when aggregating over diverse behaviors. The authors aim to extract universally useful competencies from diverse demonstrations while preserving the ability to later specialize to individual preferences.

Method: GRID decomposes each agent's reward function into two components: (1) a general reward shared across all agents, capturing universally useful behaviors (e.g., safety, basic task proficiency), and (2) agent-specific rewards capturing individual goals/preferences. The method infers this disentangled reward structure from heterogeneous demonstrations. Training exclusively on the general reward yields a generalist agent, which can then be fine-tuned on specific rewards for downstream specialization.

Result: Experiments across three domains—synthetic basis function decomposition, multi-agent Craftax, and Highway-Env (autonomous driving)—demonstrate that GRID successfully disentangles rewards in a semantically meaningful way, outperforms standard learning-from-demonstration baselines, and enables more efficient and stable fine-tuning to downstream tasks, including previously unseen preferences.

Conclusion: GRID provides a principled approach to social learning from heterogeneous populations by separating shared environmental competencies from individual preferences. The resulting generalist agent avoids mode-averaging bias and serves as a superior pretrained prior, enabling robust and efficient specialization to diverse downstream tasks.

Abstract: Humans often acquire new skills by observing others, since observed behaviors implicitly reveal how to act in an environment. However, observations drawn from a heterogeneous population introduce conflicting behavioral signals, making it difficult to determine which behaviors are worth imitating. We address this challenge with General Reward Inference and Disentanglement (GRID), a social learning method that extracts universally useful behaviors from a heterogeneous population of demonstrators pursuing different goals. GRID decomposes per-agent reward functions into a general reward, capturing behaviors shared across all agents, and specific rewards, capturing individual preferences and objectives. Training exclusively on the general reward provides a new paradigm of generalist pretraining. It yields a generalist agent that internalizes universal environmental competencies, such as safety and basic task proficiency, without the mode-averaging bias that afflicts standard learning from demonstration techniques. This generalist serves as a superior prior for fine-tuning to downstream tasks, including preferences unseen during training. Experiments across a synthetic basis function decomposition, multi-agent Craftax, and a continuous autonomous driving simulator (Highway-Env) confirm that GRID successfully disentangles reward structure in a semantically meaningful way, outperforms standard learning from demonstration baselines, and enables more efficient and stable specialization.

</details>


### [213] [Effects of sparsity and superposition on loss in simple autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18538)
*Mriganka Basu Roy Chowdhury,Eric McLaughlin Weiner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a rigorous mathematical analysis of superposition in neural networks, deriving tight L2 reconstruction loss bounds for power activation functions in the very sparse regime, while corroborating the empirical findings of Elhage et al. (2022).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Polysemanticity—where individual neurons encode multiple features—hinders mechanistic interpretability. Elhage et al. (2022) attributed this to superposition, where networks compress sparse features into non-orthogonal directions in lower-dimensional space. However, a formal mathematical foundation for why and when superposition occurs optimally was lacking.

Method: The authors mathematically analyze the sparse autoencoder setting of Elhage et al. (2022), deriving rigorous upper and lower bounds on the L2 reconstruction loss for power activation functions. The analysis focuses on the very sparse input regime to establish tightness of the bounds.

Result: The paper provides tight upper and lower bounds for L2 reconstruction loss in the very sparse regime under power activation functions, formally corroborating key claims from Elhage et al. (2022) regarding the occurrence and optimality of superposition as a compression strategy.

Conclusion: Superposition is mathematically justified as an optimal compression strategy for sparse features. The rigorous bounds confirm the empirical hypotheses of prior work, and several open problems are identified for future investigation.

Abstract: One of the major difficulties in the mechanistic interpretability of neural networks is the occurrence of polysemanticity, which suggests that each neuron is typically responsible for multiple different tasks, impeding a clean interpretation of their function. The seminal paper of Elhage et al. (2022) argues that this occurs due to superposition, a phenomenon where the neural network represents distinct features as non-orthogonal directions in a lower-dimensional space, a strategy that allows much greater compression of the data without sacrificing fidelity due to the feature sparsity of input vectors. Elhage et al. (2022) empirically validates these hypotheses in a rather natural and simple autoencoder with sparse inputs. The contribution of the present work is to analyze the mathematical basis for the occurrence and optimality of superposition, while rigorously corroborating some of their findings. In particular, we provide upper and lower bounds for the L2 reconstruction loss, tight in the very sparse regime, for power activation functions. A short list of interesting open problems are also included at the end.

</details>


### [214] [TS-Fault: Benchmarking Time Series Forecasters Against Structural Faults](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18539)
*Yuyang Zhao,Lian Xu,Hao Miao,Chenxi Liu,Hao Xue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TS-Fault is a benchmark that evaluates time series forecasting models under structured, parameterized fault scenarios (observation/mechanism-level, univariate/multivariate), revealing that clean-data accuracy anti-correlates with robustness and foundation models are most fragile under mechanism-level faults.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current TSF model evaluation relies on single-number metrics over clean data, implicitly assuming this predicts real-world reliability. However, real faults are structured (temporal shapes, broken cross-variable dependencies, regime changes with missingness, causal propagation) rather than i.i.d. noise. There is a need to systematically test robustness against the structures models actually rely on.

Method: TS-Fault organizes failures into four modes along two orthogonal axes: observation-level vs mechanism-level, and univariate vs multivariate. Faults are injected into the most prediction-critical window using a unified importance score. A paired clean/corrupt protocol evaluates 21 models across 6 datasets, 4 modes, and 5 difficulty levels.

Result: Three key findings: (1) clean-data accuracy anti-correlates with robustness; (2) clean rankings are preserved under observation-level faults but reshuffled under mechanism-level faults; (3) all catastrophic failures occur under mechanism-level faults, with foundation models showing highest clean accuracy but greatest fragility.

Conclusion: TS-Fault demonstrates that clean-data leaderboard rankings are misleading for real-world reliability. Robustness must be evaluated under structured, mechanism-level fault scenarios, particularly for high-performing foundation models that prove unexpectedly brittle.

Abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) underpins consequential decisions in energy, transportation, finance, and healthcare, yet TSF models are almost universally ranked by a single number (e.g., average error) on clean held-out data, under the implicit assumption that it predicts deployed reliability. However, real faults are not i.i.d noise but structured events with temporal shape, broken cross-variable dependencies, regime change coupled with missingness, and causal propagation across a sensing pipeline. Treating TSF robustness as a data-quality problem, we present TS-Fault, a benchmark that evaluates forecasting models under explicit, parameterized fault scenarios with controllable semantic difficulty. TS-Fault organizes recurring failures into four modes along two orthogonal axes (observation- vs mechanism-level; univariate vs multivariate) and injects each fault into the most prediction-critical window via a unified importance score. This design enables robustness to be tested against the structures models actually rely on, rather than reduced to generic noise sensitivity. We evaluate 21 models across 6 datasets, 4 modes, and 5 difficulty levels under a paired clean/corrupt protocol. The results reveal three findings that contradict common leaderboard intuition: (i) clean-data accuracy anti-correlates with robustness; (ii) clean rankings are preserved under observation-level faults but reshuffled under mechanism-level faults; and (iii) all catastrophic failures occur under mechanism-level faults, with foundation models achieving the highest clean-data accuracy yet exhibiting the greatest fragility. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Ray-zyy/TS-Fault.

</details>


### [215] [Correcting Sensor-Induced Distribution Drift with Wasserstein Adversarial Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18561)
*Saraa Ali,Vladimir Bocharnikov,Fedor Ratnikov,Mikhail Hushchyn,Artem Ryzhikov,Denis Derkach*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Wasserstein-GAN-based unsupervised method infers physically interpretable calibration parameters to correct sensor degradation by matching changed detector response distributions to a nominal reference distribution, validated on tracking-detector toy models and Geant4 calorimeter simulations with cell-wise aging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sensor motion and aging degrade data quality and downstream data-driven method performance. Direct labels for degradation parameters are often unavailable, motivating an unsupervised approach to recover calibration transformations.

Method: A Wasserstein-GAN-inspired framework where the generator serves as a learnable calibration transformation with trainable weights representing physically interpretable parameters, while the critic provides a distributional distance signal via the Wasserstein objective to map degraded distributions back to a nominal reference.

Result: Validated on a tracking-detector toy model with controlled layer shifts and on Geant4-simulated high-granularity calorimeter data with cell-wise aging. The method recovers aging coefficients correlated with ground truth, improves agreement between calibrated and reference energy-sum distributions, and shows expected degradation under increasing channel-to-channel noise.

Conclusion: Adversarial distribution matching is viable as a data-driven calibration component when direct degradation labels are unavailable, with promising performance on both toy and realistic detector simulations.

Abstract: The quality of recorded data depends on the stability of the sensor system that acquires it. Sensor motion and aging can degrade the performance and stability of downstream data-driven methods. We present a Wasserstein-GAN-inspired approach for unsupervised inference of physically interpretable transformation parameters that map a changed detector response distribution back to a nominal reference distribution. In contrast to standard generative modeling, the generator is used as a learnable calibration transformation whose trainable weights represent the sought parameters, while the critic provides a distributional distance signal via the Wasserstein objective. We validate the approach on a tracking-detector toy model with controlled layer shifts and demonstrate its application on high-granularity Geant4-simulated calorimeter data with cell-wise aging effects. The method recovers aging coefficients for individual cells with correlation to ground truth and improves agreement between calibrated and reference energy-sum distributions, while exhibiting the expected degradation at increasing channel-to-channel noise levels. These results indicate that adversarial distribution matching can serve as a data-driven component of calibration strategies in settings where direct labels for degradation parameters are unavailable.

</details>


### [216] [Fair Cognitive Impairment Detection Through Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18571)
*William Nguyen,Jiali Cheng,Hadi Amiri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multimodal framework for MCI detection that uses cross-modal fusion (speech, text, image) and gradient reversal-based demographic unlearning to improve classification accuracy while reducing performance disparities across sex and language subgroups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MCI detection models from spontaneous speech exploit demographic cues (sex, language) correlated with labels, leading to biased, subgroup-dependent performance. The authors aim to build a fairer classifier that maintains accuracy while closing the performance gap across demographics.

Method: A multimodal framework combining: (1) cross-modal fusion across speech, text, and image modalities; (2) adversarial demographic unlearning via gradient reversal layers that discourage shared embeddings from encoding sex and language information. Evaluated on TAUKADIAL and PREPARE multilingual benchmarks.

Result: The proposed method surpasses the state-of-the-art multilingual and multimodal baseline in MCI classification accuracy while substantially narrowing the performance gap across sex and language subgroups. Cross-dataset transfer analysis shows that demographic unlearning yields more robust representations.

Conclusion: Demographic unlearning via gradient reversal, combined with multimodal fusion, produces both more accurate and fairer MCI detection models. The approach generalizes across datasets and languages, suggesting that removing demographic confounds leads to more clinically meaningful representations.

Abstract: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a medical condition characterized by a noticeable decline in memory, language, or thinking abilities. MCI detection from spontaneous speech is promising for scalable screening. However, learned models often exploit demographic cues correlated with labels, resulting in a large performance gap across subgroups. We present a multimodal framework that combines (i) cross-model fusion between modalities (speech, text, and image), and (ii) unlearning using gradient reversal that discourages the shared embedding from encoding task-irrelevant demographic attributes. Evaluated on the multilingual benchmarks TAUKADIAL and PREPARE, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art multilingual and multimodal baseline in MCI classification while substantially reducing the performance gap across patient subgroups (sex and language). We further analyze transfer across datasets, showing that demographic unlearning helps learn more robust representations for MCI detection.

</details>


### [217] [Towards Anomaly Detection on Relational Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18621)
*Shiyuan Li,Yunfeng Zhao,Yue Tan,Qingfeng Chen,Yixin Liu,Shirui Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RelAD is a reconstruction-based anomaly detection framework for relational databases that uses conditional sparse-gated attribute reconstruction and dual-view multi-relational edge reconstruction to capture anomalies in both multi-table attributes and foreign-key connection patterns, outperforming baselines on 6 newly constructed benchmark datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing anomaly detection methods are inadequate for relational data because: (1) multi-table attributes are high-dimensional and heterogeneous, allowing sparse abnormal signals to be overwhelmed by normal/irrelevant information; (2) anomalies can manifest as abnormal connection patterns across foreign-key relations, which tabular and graph-based methods fail to capture effectively.

Method: RelAD employs a reconstruction-based framework with two core modules: (1) Conditional sparse-gated attribute reconstruction, which suppresses redundant multi-table attributes and emphasizes abnormal semantic blocks; (2) Dual-view multi-relational edge reconstruction, which detects relation-specific abnormal connections using both intrinsic and behavioral entity profiles. These signals are integrated via a lightweight fusion module to produce final anomaly scores. The authors also construct 6 benchmark datasets with systematic anomalies for evaluation.

Result: Extensive experiments on the 6 constructed benchmark datasets demonstrate that RelAD consistently outperforms other baseline methods while maintaining competitive computational efficiency.

Conclusion: RelAD effectively addresses the under-explored problem of relational database anomaly detection by jointly modeling attribute-level and relational-level reconstruction, with the sparse-gated mechanism and dual-view edge reconstruction proving critical for isolating anomalous patterns in complex multi-table settings.

Abstract: Relational databases are widely used for managing structured data in real-world systems. Detecting anomalies from such relational data is crucial for identifying fraud, risks, and abnormal behaviors, yet remains under-explored. The key challenges lie in the intrinsic complexity of relational data: multi-table attributes are high-dimensional and heterogeneous, making sparse abnormal clues easy to overwhelm by normal or irrelevant information; and anomalies may further manifest as abnormal connection patterns across different foreign-key relations, which existing tabular and graph anomaly detection methods are ill-suited to capture. To address them, we propose RelAD, a reconstruction-based framework that captures anomalies from both attribute and relational edge reconstruction. RelAD contains two core modules: conditional sparse-gated attribute reconstruction, which suppresses redundant multi-table attributes and emphasizes abnormal semantic blocks, and dual-view multi-relational edge reconstruction, which detects relation-specific abnormal connections from both intrinsic and behavioral entity profiles. The resulting attribute and relational signals are integrated through a lightweight fusion module to produce the final anomaly score. We further construct 6 benchmark datasets with systematic anomalies, on which extensive experiments show that RelAD consistently outperforms other baselines while achieving competitive efficiency.

</details>


### [218] [PACT: Preserving Anchored Cores in Task-vectors for Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18627)
*Ningyuan Shi,Zhipeng Zhou,Hao Wang,Chunyan Miao,Peilin Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies "Load-Bearing Wall (LBW) dimensions" — task-critical knowledge that remains in pre-trained weights rather than being transferred to task vectors — challenging the core assumption of Task Arithmetic merging. The authors propose PACT, which aligns and removes LBW-orthogonal subspaces from task vectors before merging, achieving consistent SOTA improvements when integrated with existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing model merging methods following the Task Arithmetic paradigm assume task-specific knowledge is fully encoded in task vectors (fine-tuned minus pre-trained weights). The authors argue this assumption fails because pre-trained models exhibit intrinsic task preferences, leaving critical knowledge "anchored" in pre-trained weights. Ignoring these LBW dimensions leads to unresolved task conflicts and degradation of task-specific knowledge during merging.

Method: The authors first characterize LBW dimensions from both scalar-weight and subspace perspectives. They then propose PACT (Preserving Anchored Cores within Task vectors), which: (1) identifies LBW dimensions in task vectors, (2) aligns the orthogonal complement of these LBW dimensions with the pre-trained weight subspace, (3) removes these aligned components from task vectors prior to merging, and (4) applies any existing merging algorithm on the cleaned task vectors. An efficient randomized SVD variant is developed for scalability. PACT is designed as a plug-and-play module compatible with mainstream merging methods.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PACT consistently enhances mainstream model merging approaches and establishes new state-of-the-art performance.

Conclusion: The Task Arithmetic assumption that task knowledge resides solely in task vectors is flawed due to LBW dimensions embedded in pre-trained weights. PACT effectively addresses this by preserving anchored task-specific cores and removing conflicting subspace components, serving as a general-purpose enhancer for existing merging techniques.

Abstract: Model merging has emerged as a training-free alternative to multi-task learning, aiming to combine multiple task-specific fine-tuned models into a single multi-task model. Most existing model merging approaches follow the Task Arithmetic paradigm, which decomposes fine-tuned weights into pre-trained parameters and task vectors, and performs merging exclusively in the task-vector space. The effectiveness of this paradigm implicitly relies on the assumption that task-specific knowledge is encoded solely within task vectors. We argue that this assumption generally does not hold due to the intrinsic task preferences of pre-trained models. Specifically, we identify \textbf{Load-Bearing Wall (LBW) dimensions}, namely some task-critical knowledge that remains embedded in the pre-trained weights rather than being fully transferred into task vectors. We characterize LBW dimensions from both scalar-weight and subspace perspectives, thereby covering the major paradigms of existing model merging methods. Our analysis reveals that, by ignoring LBW dimensions, task-vector-based approaches fail to fully resolve task conflicts and may inadvertently damage task-specific knowledge encoded in the pre-trained model, leading to degradation. To address this issue, we propose PACT, which preserves the anchored task-specific cores (i.e., LBW dimensions) within task vectors by aligning their orthogonal complements with the subspace of the pre-trained weights. These aligned subspace components are then removed from the task vectors before applying existing model merging algorithms. Furthermore, we develop an efficient variant based on randomized SVD to improve scalability. PACT can be seamlessly integrated with existing methods. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PACT consistently enhances mainstream model merging approaches and establishes new state-of-the-art performance.

</details>


### [219] [MetaboNet-Bench: A Multi-modal Benchmark for Glucose Forecasting in Type 1 Diabetes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18640)
*Nathaniel Jeffries,Miriam Wolff,Sam Royston,Elizabeth Healey,Caleb Mayer,David Klonoff,Michael Snyder,Tao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG
