TL;DR: MetaboNet-Bench is an open-source benchmark for evaluating multimodal glucose forecasting algorithms in type 1 diabetes, using glucose, insulin, and carbohydrate data. Benchmarking various models reveals that the benefit of additional data modalities depends on model complexity, and incorporating richer clinical metrics helps pinpoint research gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The lack of standardized benchmarks for glucose forecasting algorithms in type 1 diabetes hinders fair comparison and innovation. Additionally, most published methods rely solely on CGM data, ignoring multimodal signals (insulin, carbohydrates) that could improve prediction.

Method: The authors introduce MetaboNet-Bench, an extensible open-source evaluation framework that standardizes comparison of multimodal glucose forecasting algorithms using glucose, insulin, and carbohydrate data. They benchmark several recently published models alongside a custom multimodal time-series model representing diverse architectures.

Result: Results demonstrate that the benefit of incorporating additional data modalities (insulin, carbohydrates) is conditional on model complexity. Including more clinically relevant evaluation metrics helps reveal meaningful performance gaps and directions for future work.

Conclusion: Standardized multimodal benchmarking is essential for advancing glucose forecasting research. Model architecture complexity mediates the utility of extra data modalities, and richer clinical evaluation metrics are necessary to guide future innovation effectively.

Abstract: Glucose forecasting algorithms are an important aspect of glycemic control management in type 1 diabetes. So far, the research community has developed numerous algorithms and models for forecasting. However, it is well-recognized that the lack of standardized model performance evaluation benchmarks makes fair comparison difficult and hinders further innovation, and thus benchmark standardization is in urgent need. Furthermore, many published glucose forecasting algorithms are limited to CGM data alone, ignoring other multimodal signals such as insulin dosing and carbohydrate intake. Here, we introduce MetaboNet-Bench, a benchmark for multimodal glucose forecasting for patients with type 1 diabetes that provides an extensible open-source evaluation framework for comparison of glucose forecasting algorithms that leverage glucose, insulin, and carbohydrate data. We then demonstrate its utility by benchmarking several recently published glucose forecasting models and a custom multimodal time-series model, representing different model architectures. The results show that the benefit of adding data modalities is conditioned on the complexity of the model and that incorporating more clinical metrics helps identify meaningful gaps to fill for future research.

</details>


### [220] [BLADE: Scalable Bi-level Adaptive Data Selection for LLM Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18650)
*Jiaxing Wang,Deping Xiang,Jin Xu,Zirui Liu,Zicheng Zhang,Guoqiang Gong,Jun Fang,Chao Liu,Pengzhang Liu,Tongxuan Liu,Ke Zhang,Qixia Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BLADE reformulates influence-based data selection as a penalized single-level optimization, avoiding expensive inverse-Hessian computations while dynamically synchronizing the reference model with training. It outperforms existing methods in LLM training experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current data selection for LLM training faces a trade-off: influence-based methods are principled but computationally intractable due to inverse-Hessian requirements; excess-loss methods are efficient but rely on a static reference model that becomes misaligned during training. A method combining the strengths of both paradigms is needed.

Method: BLADE reformulates the bi-level influence-based optimization as a penalized single-level objective using Lagrange multipliers, eliminating the need for inverse-Hessian computations. The resulting objective takes an excess-loss form but uses a dynamically synchronized reference model instead of a static one. For efficient online batch selection, BLADE is instantiated as a memoryless randomized block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm. First-order convergence is theoretically proven.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that BLADE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data selection baselines, providing a practical and effective recipe for large-scale LLM training data selection.

Conclusion: BLADE bridges the gap between influence-based and excess-loss data selection paradigms, offering both theoretical guarantees (first-order convergence) and practical efficiency. It establishes a new state-of-the-art for online data selection in LLM training.

Abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) datasets scale to trillions of tokens, data selection has emerged as a critical frontier to filter out uninformative noise and construct adaptive learning trajectories. Beyond static heuristic filtering, advanced data selection methods for LLM training largely follow two paradigms, each with fundamental limitations. Influence-based methods provide principled bi-level objectives but require intractable inverse-Hessian computations, while excess-loss methods are computationally efficient but rely on a static reference model that becomes misaligned with the evolving proxy model during training. We propose BLADE (Bi-Level Adaptive Data sElection), a Hessian-free framework for data selection. BLADE reformulates the bi-level optimization problem underlying influence-based methods as a penalized single-level objective via Lagrange multipliers, avoiding inverse-Hessian computation while revealing a principled connection to excess-loss based data selection. The resulting objective recovers an excess-loss form but replaces the static reference model with a dynamic one that stays synchronized with training. Theoretically, we prove that this penalized formulation guarantees first-order convergence. For efficient online batch selection, we instantiate BLADE as a memoryless randomized block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm. Extensive experiments show that BLADE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data selection baselines, providing a practical recipe for LLM training.

</details>


### [221] [scGTN: Deep Siamese Graph Transformer Network for Single-cell RNA Sequencing Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18672)
*Jinke Wu,Yifan Wang,Siyu Yi,Caiyang Yu,Ziyue Qiao,Nan Yin,Jiancheng Lv,Wei Ju*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes scGTN, a deep Siamese Graph Transformer Network for single-cell RNA-seq clustering that integrates gene expression with intercellular structural dependencies, using dual graph augmentation, shortest-path encoding, and optimal transport-based self-supervised clustering to address sparsity, noise, and complex cell-cell relationships.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scRNA-seq clustering methods ignore data sparsity, noise, and the complex intercellular structural information inherent in the data, limiting clustering performance and the accurate characterization of cellular heterogeneity.

Method: scGTN formulates scRNA-seq data as a graph and constructs two augmented graph views for complementary intercellular information. A Siamese graph transformer network explicitly incorporates shortest-path information and node-wise distances to capture richer structural relationships. Clustering is guided by an optimal transport strategy in a self-supervised manner.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark scRNA-seq datasets demonstrate that scGTN consistently outperforms existing methods.

Conclusion: scGTN provides a robust and effective framework for scRNA-seq clustering by jointly modeling gene expression and intercellular structure, with superior performance validated across benchmarks. Code is publicly available.

Abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) serves a pivotal role in characterizing gene expression at the cellular level, enabling the identification of cell types and advancing the understanding of cellular heterogeneity. Despite the significant progress in scRNA-seq data clustering, we argue that current methods always ignore the sparsity and noise, as well as the complex intercellular structural information inherent in scRNA-seq data. Toward this end, in this paper, we propose a novel single-cell RNA-seq clustering framework via deep Siamese Graph Transformer Network (termed scGTN), which explicitly integrates gene expression profile and intercellular structural dependencies for cell clustering. In particular, we formulate scRNA-seq data as a graph and construct two augmented graph views that serve as dual views to capture complementary intercellular information. Then, a Siamese graph transformer network is employed to explicitly incorporate shortest-path information and node-wise distances for capturing richer structural relationships between cells. Finally, we employ an optimal transport strategy to guide the cell clustering in a self-supervised manner. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark scRNA-seq datasets demonstrate that our scGTN consistently outperforms existing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/W-RMSL/scGTN.

</details>


### [222] [InTrain: Intrinsic Trainability for Zero-Cost Neural Architecture Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18676)
*Qinqin Zhou,Fuhai Chen,Jipeng Wu,Zhiwei Chen,Zhikai Hu,Weiwei Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Intrinsic Trainability (InTrain), a unified theoretical proxy for training-free neural architecture search that combines geometric capacity (via activation covariance eigenspectrum) and optimization resilience (via cumulative gradient health) through multiplicative coupling to predict architecture performance without training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing zero-cost NAS proxies rely on fragmented heuristics and fail to address the fundamental question of what makes a neural architecture inherently trainable. There is a need for a principled, unified theoretical framework that captures the essential properties determining an architecture's capacity to be effectively trained.

Method: InTrain operationalizes trainability through two synergistic components: (1) Geometric capacity, quantified via the participation ratio of the activation covariance eigenspectrum, which measures the effective dimensionality of representation manifolds; (2) Optimization resilience, measured through cumulative gradient health that assesses backpropagation robustness across network depth. These are combined via a scale-invariant multiplicative coupling, hypothesized to capture their synergistic, non-additive relationship. The proxy is computed without any training.

Result: Extensive experiments on standard NAS benchmarks and search spaces show InTrain achieves ranking correlations on par with state-of-the-art ensemble-based proxies and outperforms other single-metric methods.

Conclusion: Intrinsic trainability, formalized as the multiplicative synergy between geometric capacity and optimization resilience, provides a principled and effective zero-cost proxy for NAS, matching ensemble methods with a single unified metric.

Abstract: Training-free neural architecture search promises efficient discovery of high-performance networks without costly training. However, existing zero-cost proxies rely on fragmented heuristics that fail to capture the fundamental question: what makes an architecture trainable? This paper introduces Intrinsic Trainability (InTrain), a unified theoretical proxy that formalizes trainability as an architectural invariant emerging from two synergistic components: geometric capacity and optimization resilience. We operationalize intrinsic trainability through analysis of neural information processing. Geometric capacity is quantified via the participation ratio of activation covariance eigenspectrum, capturing the effective dimensionality of representation manifolds. Optimization resilience is measured through cumulative gradient health, assessing the robustness of backpropagation across network depth. InTrain synthesizes these dimensions through a scale-invariant multiplicative coupling, which we hypothesize is essential for capturing their synergistic, non-additive relationship. Extensive experiments on standard NAS benchmarks and search spaces demonstrate that InTrain achieves ranking correlations on par with state-of-the-art ensemble-based proxies and outperforms other single-metric methods.

</details>


### [223] [Bounded Context Management for Tabular Foundation Models on Stream Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18677)
*Jinmo Lee,Doyun Choi,Moongi Choi,Jaemin Yoo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CURE is a context management policy for tabular foundation models in stream learning that uses entropy-gated admission and redundancy-aware eviction to select which examples to keep in context, achieving up to 27% improvement over classical stream learners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular stream learning faces distribution shift as examples arrive sequentially. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer an in-context learning alternative to standard state-updating methods, but this shifts the challenge from model updating to context management. The paper identifies a gap: there are no principled policies for managing which examples to retain in the limited context window of TFMs during streaming.

Method: The authors derive three requirements for context management from a "future information view": preserve recent examples (temporal relevance), retain uncertain examples (high-entropy instances for learning), and remove redundant examples (to maximize context diversity). These are instantiated as CURE, which employs (1) entropy-gated admission — only admitting examples where the model's predictive entropy exceeds a threshold, and (2) redundancy-aware eviction — removing the most redundant example when the context is full, measured via similarity or representational overlap.

Result: CURE achieves up to 27.0% relative improvement over classical stream learning methods across seven benchmark streams. The policy remains robust across multiple TFM backbones and ranks first among all compared policy variants.

Conclusion: Effective context management is critical for deploying TFMs in streaming settings. CURE provides a simple yet principled policy that outperforms both classical stream learners and alternative context management strategies by balancing recency, uncertainty, and diversity in the retained context.

Abstract: Tabular stream learning requires predictions on sequentially arriving examples under distribution shift. While standard methods adapt by updating model states, tabular foundation models (TFMs) make predictions conditioned on a labeled context in an in-context manner, making them a natural alternative for stream learning. This shifts the challenge from how to update the model to how to manage the context. We propose a future information view that yields three practical requirements for context management: preserve recent examples, retain uncertain examples, and remove redundant examples. We instantiate these requirements as CURE (Context management via Uncertainty-aware admission and Redundancy aware Eviction), a context-managing policy with entropy-gated admission and redundancy-aware eviction. Across seven streams, CURE shows up to 27.0% relative improvement over classical stream learners, remains robust across multiple TFM backbones, and ranks first among other policy variants. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/morcellinus/CURE-ICML-FMSD.

</details>


### [224] [Dual-Channel Grounded World Modeling (DCGWM): Structural Prevention of Objective Interference Collapse via Heterogeneous External Grounding with Inward-Only Gradient Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18688)
*Akshay Hazare*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JEPA-based world models suffer from Objective Interference Collapse (OIC) when jointly learning from distinct physical and social-behavioral signals. The authors propose Dual-Channel Grounded World Modeling (DCGWM), which partitions the latent space to structurally prevent one channel from dominating the other, backed by three theoretical results. Experimental validation is pending.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identify and resolve a failure mode (OIC) in JEPA-based world models where joint grounding against qualitatively distinct external signals — sparse, high-magnitude physical dynamics versus diffuse, distribution-matching social-behavioral dynamics — causes the dominant channel to collapse the subordinate channel's representational subspace, a problem that loss weighting alone cannot fix.

Method: DCGWM partitions the latent space into a physical subspace (Z_p) and a behavioral subspace (Z_b) with inward-only gradient flow. A Physical Grounding Channel updates Z_p via VICReg-style alignment; a Social-Behavioral Grounding Channel updates Z_b via alignment to multi-agent simulation trajectories. An Inter-Channel Interface Module couples subspaces at the task level without cross-subspace gradients. An Asymmetric Grounding Adherence Loss uses a hard hinge for physical violations and a soft KL for behavioral divergence. A Generative Rendering Layer is architecturally isolated from the latent world model. Three theoretical results are provided: (1) partition removes the gradient-interference pathway, (2) each subspace inherits anti-collapse guarantees from its alignment objective, and (3) generative isolation is necessary under an assumption on the generative objective's geometry.

Result: The manuscript establishes the problem formulation and architecture with three theoretical results. Experimental validation is ongoing and not yet reported.

Conclusion: DCGWM theoretically addresses OIC through structural latent space partitioning, and the authors frame this as a necessary architectural intervention beyond mere loss reweighting. Empirical validation remains future work.

Abstract: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are a leading approach to world model representation learning. We identify a failure mode in JEPA-based world models grounded against two qualitatively distinct external signals: physical dynamics (sparse, high-magnitude, constraint-satisfying gradient corrections) and social-behavioral dynamics (diffuse, distribution-matching corrections). We term this Objective Interference Collapse (OIC): we argue that joint learning in a shared latent space causes the dominant channel to systematically collapse the subordinate channel's representational subspace, in a manner not resolvable by loss weighting alone. We propose Dual-Channel Grounded World Modeling (DCGWM), designed to structurally prevent OIC through a partitioned latent space (physical subspace Z_p, behavioral subspace Z_b) with inward-only gradient flow. A Physical Grounding Channel updates only Z_p via VICReg-style alignment to physical measurements; a Social-Behavioral Grounding Channel updates only Z_b via alignment to trajectories from an emergent multi-agent simulation. An Inter-Channel Interface Module couples the subspaces at the task level without cross-subspace gradients. An Asymmetric Grounding Adherence Loss penalizes rollout drift with a hard hinge for physical violations and a soft KL for behavioral divergence. A Generative Rendering Layer is architecturally isolated from the latent world model. We present three theoretical results: the partition removes the gradient-interference pathway implicated in OIC; each grounded subspace inherits anti-collapse guarantees from its alignment objective; and generative isolation is necessary under a stated assumption on the generative objective's geometry. This manuscript establishes the problem formulation and architecture; experimental validation is ongoing and will be reported in a future revision.

</details>


### [225] [Robust and Interpretable Adaptation of Equivariant Materials Foundation Models via Sparsity-promoting Fine-tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18691)
*Youngwoo Cho,Seunghoon Yi,Wooil Yang,Sungmo Kang,Young-woo Son,Jaegul Choo,Joonseok Lee,Soo Kyung Kim,Hongkee Yoon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method for E(3)-equivariant materials foundation models that matches full fine-tuning performance while updating as few as 0.5–3% of parameters, with interpretable sparsity patterns revealing physical signatures like enhanced d-orbital contributions in transition metals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained materials foundation models (ML interatomic potentials) need domain-specific calibration due to physicochemical diversity and mismatches between practical computational settings and pre-training data. Existing fine-tuning approaches either update all parameters (full fine-tuning) or use low-rank adaptations, but both lack parameter efficiency and physical interpretability.

Method: The authors propose a sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method that selectively updates model parameters by exploiting structural properties of E(3)-equivariant architectures. The approach identifies and updates only the most important parameters for a given downstream task, achieving extreme parameter sparsity (as low as ~0.5%) while maintaining or improving accuracy on energy and force predictions, and extending to magnetic property modeling.

Result: The method matches or surpasses full fine-tuning and equivariant low-rank adaptation on energy and force prediction tasks across molecular and crystalline benchmarks while updating only ~3% of parameters (as low as ~0.5%). It generalizes to magnetic moment prediction and magnetism-aware total energy modeling. Sparsity patterns show physically interpretable signatures, including enhanced d-orbital contributions in transition metal systems.

Conclusion: Sparsity-promoting fine-tuning is established as a flexible, parameter-efficient, and physically interpretable method for domain specialization of equivariant materials foundation models, with broad applicability beyond energy and force calibration.

Abstract: Pre-trained materials foundation models, or machine learning interatomic potentials, leverage general physicochemical knowledge to effectively approximate potential energy surfaces. However, they often require domain-specific calibration due to physicochemical diversity as well as mismatches between practical computational settings and those used in constructing the pre-training data. To address this, we propose a sparsity-promoting fine-tuning method that selectively updates model parameters by exploiting the structural properties of E(3)-equivariant materials foundation models. On energy and force prediction tasks across molecular and crystalline benchmarks, our method matches or surpasses full fine-tuning and equivariant low-rank adaptation while updating only $\sim$3~\% of parameters, and in some cases as little as $\sim$0.5~\%. Beyond energy and force calibration, we further demonstrate task generalizability by applying our method to magnetic moment prediction and magnetism-aware total energy modeling. Finally, analysis of sparsity patterns reveals physically interpretable signatures, such as enhanced $d$-orbital contributions in transition metal systems. Overall, our results establish sparsity-promoting fine-tuning as a flexible and interpretable method for domain specialization of equivariant materials foundation models.

</details>


### [226] [Attention as Frustrated Synchronization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18694)
*Joshua Nunley*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces the Frustrated Synchronization Network (FSN), a novel attention architecture where token states are phases on a torus and computation emerges from structured departures from synchronization, achieving superior validation loss compared to tuned RoPE-SwiGLU transformers at matched parameter and training budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A perfectly synchronized oscillator network computes nothing; meaningful computation must arise from structured departures from agreement. The authors leverage this insight from synchronization theory to design an attention mechanism where next-token prediction is naturally implemented as synchronization frustrated by the data itself.

Method: The FSN represents token states as phases on a torus with a learned complex coupling kernel composed of three frustration components: (1) static Kuramoto-Sakaguchi frustration angles as complex phases, (2) repulsive Daido components as signed harmonics, and (3) a delay term coupling each token to successors of attended tokens, algebraically identical to Kuramoto-Sakaguchi coupling with the data's own transition as the frustration angle. A variant replaces feed-forward blocks with mean-field coupling to learned collective modes.

Result: At one-million-parameter scale on character-level text and code: FSN validation loss is below a tuned RoPE-SwiGLU transformer at every measured epoch. Every thirty-epoch enwik8 seed finishes below the transformer's converged fifty-epoch loss of 1.611; FSN's fifty-epoch runs converge to 1.5953 ± 0.0014. The mean-field variant without MLPs tracks the transformer. On natural text, the unfrustrated base layer underperforms on long-range copy events, but the kernel reverses the deficit at depth ≥4. The advantage persists at four-million-parameter scale.

Conclusion: Structured frustration in oscillator synchronization provides a viable and competitive alternative to standard transformer attention, with the FSN demonstrating consistent loss advantages across scales. The architecture suggests a principled connection between synchronization dynamics and sequence modeling, where next-token prediction emerges naturally from frustrated coupling.

Abstract: A network of oscillators that synchronizes perfectly computes nothing further, so an attention architecture built from synchronization must locate its computation in structured departures from agreement. We introduce the Frustrated Synchronization Network (FSN), whose token states are phases on a torus and whose entire value pathway is one learned complex coupling kernel over harmonics and a one-step delay. Each component of the kernel is a frustration in the sense of the synchronization literature. The complex phases are static Kuramoto-Sakaguchi frustration angles, the signed harmonics are repulsive Daido components, and the delay term, which couples each token to the successors of the tokens it attends to, is algebraically identical to Kuramoto-Sakaguchi coupling whose frustration angle is the data's own transition, so next-token prediction is implemented as synchronization frustrated by the data. At matched one-million-parameter and training budgets on character-level text and code, the FSN's validation loss is below a tuned RoPE-SwiGLU transformer's at every epoch measured, and the comparison survives training the baseline to convergence: every thirty-epoch enwik8 seed finishes below the transformer's converged fifty-epoch loss of 1.611, and the FSN's completed fifty-epoch runs converge to 1.5953 +/- 0.0014. A variant with every feed-forward block replaced by mean-field coupling to learned collective modes, leaving no multilayer perceptron in the stack, tracks the transformer. On natural text the unfrustrated base layer falls behind the converged transformer at every copy depth, worst on long-range copy events; the kernel reverses the deficit at every depth of four and beyond. Headline comparisons are at the one-million-parameter scale; a scale ladder is complete through four million parameters with the advantage persisting, and remaining arms are marked as in progress.

</details>


### [227] [Contextualizing Biological Language Models across Modalities via Logit-Space Contrastive Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18703)
*Yanjun Shao,Yundi Chen,Yashvi Patel,Aurelien Pelissier,María Rodríguez Martínez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LOGICA introduces a contrastive learning framework that operates directly in the output logit space of pretrained biological language models, preserving their native token-likelihood interface while conditioning predictions on biological context (ligands, TCR–peptide, drugs). It outperforms latent-space and conditional masked language modeling baselines on variant scoring and drug-resistance prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained biological language models provide useful per-token probability distributions, but these are not conditioned on task-specific contexts (e.g., binding partners, cellular environments). Existing methods that add context typically distort the likelihood interface through pooled embeddings or task-specific heads, losing the interpretability and generative capability of the original model. There is a need for context conditioning that preserves the native token-level interface.

Method: LOGICA performs contrastive learning directly in logit space (output logits before softmax). It uses gated cross-modal adapters that are compatible with each model's native token head, converting contextualized token log-likelihoods into matching scores. Alignment is defined via context-sensitive token probabilities rather than embedding proximity, enabling learning from sparse paired data across models with distinct vocabularies and without requiring a shared tokenizer or decoder. For variant ranking, comparisons reduce to context-conditioned likelihoods of mutant tokens at perturbed sites.

Result: LOGICA outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods (matched latent-contrastive and conditional MLM baselines) across protein–ligand binding, TCR–peptide activity, and drug-conditioned resistance prediction. On held-out-gene single-mutation drug-resistance prediction, LOGICA improves AUC from near-random (~0.55) to ~0.65 compared to latent-space baselines.

Conclusion: Aligning biological language models through logit-space contrastive learning effectively conditions token-level predictions on biological context while preserving the pretrained likelihood interface. This enables both improved predictive performance and retained interpretability/generative capability.

Abstract: Pretrained biological language models expose per-token probability distributions through masked-token prediction, providing the likelihood interface central to sequence design, variant scoring, and mechanistic interpretation. Yet these distributions are learned from broad unlabeled corpora and are not naturally conditioned on task-specific biological contexts such as interaction partners, cellular environments, or therapeutic interventions. Existing contextual matching methods often distort this interface through pooled embeddings, contrastive latent spaces, or task-specific prediction heads. We introduce LOGICA (Logit-space Contrastive Alignment), a framework for context-conditioned prediction that performs contrastive learning directly in output-logit space. Using gated cross-modal adapters compatible with each model's native token head, LOGICA preserves the pretrained likelihood interface and converts contextualized token log-likelihoods into matching scores. Alignment is defined through context-sensitive token probabilities rather than proximity in a shared embedding space, enabling learning from sparse paired data across models with distinct vocabularies, without a shared tokenizer or decoder. LOGICA is particularly effective for mutation-local variant ranking, where comparisons reduce to context-conditioned likelihoods of mutant tokens at perturbed sites. Across protein--ligand binding, TCR--peptide activity, and drug-conditioned resistance prediction, LOGICA improves over prior state-of-the-art methods, including matched latent-contrastive and conditional MLM baselines, while retaining a token-level interface for interpretation and generation. On held-out-gene single-mutation drug-resistance prediction, LOGICA improves AUC from near-random latent-space baselines of $\sim$0.55 to $\sim$0.65.

</details>


### [228] [Trainable Photonic Measurement for Physics-Informed PDE Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18713)
*Jiale Linghu,Hao Dong,Yangshuai Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Photonic Quantum Neural Field (PQNF), where trainable optical phases, multi-photon Fock-space interference, and photon-number measurements serve directly as a learnable representation for solving PDEs, achieving superior accuracy and parameter efficiency in challenging regimes compared to classical neural fields.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore and establish the role of photonic quantum machine learning in scientific ML, specifically for physics-informed neural fields solving PDEs. The key insight is that differential equations require trial spaces preserving phase, frequency, and derivative structure — properties naturally offered by photonic systems — but this potential has remained unexplored.

Method: The PQNF encodes spatial/temporal coordinates as trainable optical phases, processes them through multi-photon Fock-space interference in a photonic circuit, and decodes representations via photon-number measurements. Crucially, the circuit is optimized as the neural-field representation itself (not a fixed feature map), and the physics-informed residual is minimized directly on the photonic measurement statistics. Ablation studies use frozen/shuffled controls and noise stress tests to attribute gains to learned interference and stable Fock-probability readout.

Result: Across seven benchmarks (elliptic, wave, nonlinear dispersive, and inverse PDEs), a "phase-complexity transition" is observed: classical coordinate and Fourier-feature networks perform adequately in smooth regimes, but PQNF achieves highest accuracy when residual derivatives amplify phase mismatch. In the hardest regimes, PQNF yields errors up to an order of magnitude lower than classical baselines while using approximately one-quarter of the trainable parameters.

Conclusion: Photonic quantum measurement constitutes a representation-learning principle for scientific machine learning. The learned interference and stable Fock-probability readout under compound perturbations enable accurate and parameter-efficient PDE solving, particularly in regimes with strong phase complexity.

Abstract: Photonic quantum machine learning offers a route to trainable physical representations built from phase, interference and measurement. However, its role in scientific machine learning remains largely unexplored. Physics-informed neural fields provide a natural setting, because differential equations require trial spaces that preserve phase, frequency and derivative structure. Here we introduce a photonic quantum neural field in which coordinates become trainable optical phases, are mixed by multi-photon Fock-space interference and are decoded from photon-number measurements. The photonic circuit is optimized as the neural-field representation itself, not as a fixed feature map or hardware accelerator. Photonic measurement is therefore a trainable representation on which the physics-informed residual is minimized. Across seven elliptic, wave, nonlinear dispersive and inverse PDE benchmarks, we observe a phase-complexity transition: classical coordinate and Fourier-feature networks suffice in smooth regimes, whereas the photonic field is most accurate when residual derivatives amplify phase mismatch. In the hardest regimes it gives the lowest errors, with margins reaching an order of magnitude and about one quarter of the trainable parameters of classical baselines. Frozen and shuffled controls, together with noise stress tests, attribute this gain to learned interference and stable Fock-probability readout under compound perturbations. These results identify photonic quantum measurement as a representation-learning principle for scientific machine learning.

</details>


### [229] [Graph Grounded Cross Attention Transformer Neural Network for Structurally Constrained Full Event Sequence Generation in Predictive Process Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18726)
*Fang Wang,Ernesto Damiani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GGATN proposes a single-pass, graph-constrained Transformer for full event sequence generation in predictive process monitoring, achieving zero hallucination and strong similarity metrics across six benchmarks, outperforming LLM baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PPM research tackles only component tasks (next activity, remaining time, etc.) rather than full event sequence generation. Full generation is structurally constrained — paths must respect transition feasibility, temporal order, termination, and attribute consistency — which remains unsolved.

Method: GGATN combines three components: (1) a global process graph encoder serving as structured activity memory; (2) Transformer self-attention for contextualizing sequence positions; and (3) graph-grounded cross-attention that injects process topology into the decoder. Generation occurs in a single non-autoregressive pass — producing activities, timestamps, length, and both event-level and sequence-level attributes — followed by Viterbi-style graph-constrained decoding to enforce feasible paths and explicit termination.

Result: On six benchmark event logs, GGATN surpasses local instruction-prompted LLM baselines in generation reliability. It achieves strong performance on sequence similarity, Damerau-Levenshtein similarity, bigram-based control-flow similarity, and duration distribution, while maintaining zero hallucinated activities and zero sequence-level attribute inconsistency.

Conclusion: The global graph encoder provides a stable structural prior (confirmed by ablation), and interpretability analyses reveal how graph structure, sequence context, feedback refinement, and constrained decoding jointly shape generation quality.

Abstract: Structurally constrained event sequence generation remains challenging because generated paths must preserve transition feasibility, temporal order, termination, and attribute consistency. In predictive process monitoring (PPM), this challenge appears as full event sequence generation, whereas existing work mainly addresses component tasks such as next activity, remaining time, outcome, and attribute prediction. This paper proposes the Graph Grounded Cross Attention Transformer Neural Network (GGATN) for this unified PPM task. GGATN uses a global process graph as structured activity memory, contextualizes sequence positions through Transformer self attention, and injects process topology through graph grounded cross attention. Unlike autoregressive decoding, GGATN generates activities, timestamps, length, and event level and sequence level attributes in a single pass, followed by Viterbi style graph constrained decoding for feasible paths and explicit termination. Experiments on six benchmark event logs show more reliable generation quality than local instruction prompted LLM baselines. GGATN achieves strong performance on sequence similarity, Damerau Levenshtein similarity, bigram based control flow similarity, and duration distribution, while maintaining zero hallucinated activities and zero sequence level attribute inconsistency. Ablation analyses confirm the global graph encoder as a stable structural prior. Interpretability analyses show how graph structure, sequence context, feedback refinement, and constrained decoding shape generation.

</details>


### [230] [Low-Cost Neuromorphic Fall Detection Using Synthetic Event Data and Hybrid SNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18732)
*Guillermo Rojas,Gonzalo Soto,Daniel Yunge*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid SNN-CNN models process simulated DVS event data from smartphone videos for human fall detection, achieving significant efficiency gains without accuracy loss compared to traditional ML models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To leverage the energy efficiency and spatio-temporal processing capabilities of SNNs combined with event-based DVS data for practical fall detection, addressing the need for efficient real-world monitoring systems.

Method: Conventional smartphone video frames are converted into simulated DVS event-based data. Hybrid models integrating SNN and CNN components are then trained and evaluated on this event data across multiple datasets, with performance benchmarked against traditional machine learning models.

Result: The hybrid SNN-CNN models achieved significant efficiency gains while maintaining accuracy comparable to traditional machine learning approaches across multiple datasets.

Conclusion: Combining SNNs with DVS event-based technology shows strong potential for enabling energy-efficient, accurate fall detection and other complex tasks in real-world environments.

Abstract: This work presents the development of hybrid models that integrate spiking neural networks (SNNs) with components of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to learn from simulated event-based camera data (Dynamic Vision Sensor, DVS) generated from conventional smartphone videos. Aimed primarily at human fall detection, the approach leverages the energy efficiency and spatio-temporal processing capabilities of SNNs by converting video frames into event-based data. The proposed models are evaluated through simulations on multiple datasets, comparing their performance to that of traditional machine learning models. Results demonstrate significant gains in efficiency without sacrificing accuracy, underscoring the potential of combining SNNs and DVS technology for complex tasks in real-world environments.

</details>


### [231] [Private Learning with Public Feature Conditioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18773)
*Shuli Jiang,Walid Krichene,Nicolas Mayoraz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cond-DP is a conditioned variant of DPSGD that uses public, non-sensitive features to construct a data-driven conditioning matrix, reshaping the optimization landscape for faster convergence under label differential privacy in regression tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While label-DP and semi-sensitive-feature settings have been studied for classification, effective DP regression methods remain underexplored. Public feature matrices in applications like recommendation systems often exhibit rapidly decaying spectra, presenting an opportunity to accelerate private optimization.

Method: Cond-DP extends DPSGD by incorporating a conditioning matrix derived from public features to reshape gradients. This matrix preconditions the optimization problem, improving the condition number and accelerating convergence. The authors provide convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex settings, with standard DPSGD recovered as a special case (identity conditioning matrix). The conditioning matrix is constructed solely from public data, incurring no additional privacy cost.

Result: Cond-DP achieves provably faster convergence than DPSGD in private linear regression. Empirically, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse datasets and model architectures under label DP, demonstrating robust practical performance.

Conclusion: Leveraging public feature structure via data-driven preconditioning is an effective and practical strategy for improving differentially private regression, with strong theoretical guarantees and empirical results.

Abstract: We study differentially private (DP) regression in settings where each data sample includes public, non-sensitive features -- common in applications such as recommendation and advertising systems. While such label-DP or semi-sensitive-feature settings have been primarily explored in the context of classification, effective approaches for regression remain underexplored. We introduce Cond-DP, a conditioned variant of DPSGD that leverages the structure of public feature matrices to improve optimization under privacy constraints. Motivated by the observation that these public features often exhibit rapidly decaying spectra, Cond-DP incorporates a data-driven conditioning matrix to reshape the optimization landscape and accelerate convergence. We provide convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex settings, and recover standard DPSGD as a special case when the conditioning matrix is the identity. We show how to construct an effective conditioning matrix for Cond-DP directly from public features, enabling provably faster convergence than DPSGD in private linear regression without incurring additional privacy cost. Empirically, Cond-DP with this conditioning matrix consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across a wide range of datasets and model architectures under label DP, demonstrating strong and robust performance in practice.

</details>


### [232] [RouteJudge: An Open Platform for Reproducible and Preference-Aware LLM Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18774)
*Guannan Lai,Haoran Hu,Han-Jia Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RouteJudge is an online platform for evaluating LLM routing systems via anonymous pairwise user preference comparisons at the router level, complemented by ORBIT, a modular toolbox that standardizes routing algorithm development, benchmarking, and submission.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation methods for LLMs focus on model-level response quality, but there is a lack of frameworks for evaluating router-level decision quality—i.e., how well different routing strategies select models under shared constraints. The authors aim to fill this gap with a preference-based, cost-aware, and task-conditioned evaluation framework.

Method: RouteJudge collects user queries, has multiple routing strategies independently recommend models under the same model pool and budget, and presents responses via anonymous pairwise comparisons. User preferences are attributed back to the routing strategies. Each record captures query, routing decisions, responses, preference labels, cost, latency, and metadata. ORBIT provides unified interfaces for benchmark loading, query representation, router implementation, budget-aware evaluation, and method comparison, serving as both a development toolkit and the submission layer for RouteJudge.

Result: The paper describes the system design and release of the RouteJudge platform (routejudge.cn) and the ORBIT toolbox (open-sourced on GitHub), enabling online preference-based evaluation and standardized routing algorithm development respectively.

Conclusion: RouteJudge and ORBIT together provide a comprehensive ecosystem for evaluating and developing LLM routing methods, shifting evaluation from model-level response quality to router-level decision quality through real user preferences, while ORBIT ensures reproducibility and extensibility in routing research.

Abstract: We present RouteJudge, an online pairwise preference evaluation framework for LLM routing systems, with a public platform available at https://routejudge.cn. Different from model-level response evaluation, RouteJudge focuses on router-level decision quality. For each user query, multiple routing strategies independently recommend candidate models under the same model pool and budget constraints. The selected model responses are then presented to users through anonymous pairwise comparisons, and the resulting user preferences are attributed back to the routing strategies behind the compared responses. Each evaluation record stores the query, routing decisions, model responses, preference labels, cost, latency, and task metadata, enabling preference-aware, cost-aware, and task-conditioned analysis of LLM routers. To support the continuous expansion of routing methods in RouteJudge, we further release ORBIT (Optimal Routing and Budgeted Inference Toolbox), a modular and extensible toolbox that standardizes the end-to-end workflow of LLM routing. ORBIT provides unified interfaces for benchmark loading, query representation, router implementation, budget-aware evaluation, and method comparison, allowing researchers to develop and evaluate routing algorithms under consistent protocols. It also serves as the submission and integration layer for RouteJudge: researchers can implement routing methods within ORBIT, validate them on existing routing benchmarks, and submit compatible routers for online preference-based evaluation. The code of ORBIT is available at https://github.com/AIGNLAI/LAMDA-ORBIT.

</details>


### [233] [Online Distributional Prediction via Latent Cluster Geometry Under Drift and Corruption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18778)
*Navyansh Mahla,Prateek Chanda,Ganesh Ramakrishnan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Bayesian nonparametric framework for online distributional prediction under drift and corruption, using latent cluster geometries with reversible-jump MCMC. A restarted quasi-Bayesian update achieves sublinear cumulative Wasserstein-1 regret, with bounds decomposing into PAC-Bayesian complexity, corruption perturbation, and optimal-transport drift terms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing online learning in non-stationary streams focuses on point estimates, but many real-world applications (e.g., risk assessment, decision-making under uncertainty) require predicting the full data-generating distribution. Furthermore, streams may exhibit both gradual drift and adversarial corruption, and imposing parametric assumptions is often unrealistic. The gap is a method that tracks the full predictive distribution online without parametric constraints, while providing theoretical guarantees under both drift and corruption.

Method: Each candidate law is represented by a latent cluster configuration — a variable-size set of centers organizing probability mass — which induces a predictive distribution. A Gibbs quasi-posterior is placed over these variable-dimensional configurations, and posterior averaging yields the online predictor. Sampling uses reversible-jump MCMC to handle the varying dimensionality. To combat staleness from long-horizon memory under drift, a restarted variant temporally localizes the quasi-Bayesian update within windows.

Result: The cumulative Wasserstein-1 regret bound decomposes into: (1) a PAC-Bayesian complexity term, (2) a corruption-sensitive posterior perturbation term, and (3) a dynamic optimal-transport term A_T^OT = Σ W₂²(p*_{t-1}, p*_t). Under conditions of bounded support, stable latent geometry, predictive-map regularity, oracle realizability, localized restart windows, sublinear transport action, and sublinear corruption budget, the restarted predictor achieves sublinear cumulative Wasserstein regret.

Conclusion: The proposed method provides a principled, nonparametric approach to online distributional prediction that gracefully handles both distribution drift and adversarial corruption, with formal sublinear regret guarantees requiring no parametric assumptions on the stream, drift mechanism, or corruption process.

Abstract: Online learning in non-stationary streams is often formulated as tracking a point estimate, but many applications require predicting the full data-generating distribution. We study online distributional prediction under drift and adversarial corruption. Our approach represents each candidate law through a latent cluster geometry: a variable-size configuration of centers that organizes probability mass and induces a predictive distribution. A Gibbs quasi-posterior over these configurations yields an online predictor by posterior averaging, and the resulting variable-dimensional posterior can be sampled with reversible-jump MCMC. The method therefore avoids specifying a parametric streaming law while retaining a structured latent space for uncertainty, regularization, and comparison.
  We evaluate performance by cumulative Wasserstein-1 regret against the time-varying true law. The analysis separates two effects: corruption perturbs the loss-based posterior update, whereas drift makes long-horizon posterior memory stale. We address the latter with a restarted variant that temporally localizes the same quasi-Bayesian update. The resulting high-probability bounds decompose into a PAC-Bayesian complexity term, a corruption-sensitive posterior perturbation term, and a dynamic optimal-transport term driven by \(A_T^{\mathrm{OT}}=\sum_{t=2}^T W_2^2(p_{t-1}^*,p_t^*)\). Under bounded support, stable latent geometry, predictive-map regularity, oracle realizability, localized restart windows, sublinear transport action, and sublinear corruption budget, the restarted predictor achieves sublinear cumulative Wasserstein regret. These guarantees require no parametric model for the stream, drift mechanism, or corruption process.

</details>


### [234] [Bayesian Anytime Pareto Set Identification for Multi-Objective Multi-Armed Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18785)
*Lennert Saerens,Bram Silue,Eleni Litsa,Peter Vrancx,Pieter Libin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces TTPFTS, the first anytime Bayesian Multi-Objective Multi-Armed Bandit algorithm for Pareto Set Identification, validated on synthetic benchmarks and a molecular discovery application, with a novel uncertainty quantification metric and asymptotic correctness proof.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Pareto Set Identification algorithms are fixed-budget and lack anytime capability. There is a need for an anytime Bayesian approach that can efficiently identify Pareto optimal arms in multi-objective bandit settings and provide confidence estimates for the identified set, especially for real-world applications like molecular discovery where evaluation budgets are uncertain.

Method: Proposes Top-Two Pareto Front Thompson Sampling (TTPFTS), a Bayesian MO-MAB algorithm that combines Thompson Sampling with a top-two sampling mechanism adapted for multi-objective Pareto front identification. Introduces a novel uncertainty quantification metric to estimate confidence in the predicted Pareto set. Provides a theoretical proof of asymptotic correctness.

Result: TTPFTS is benchmarked against state-of-the-art fixed-budget algorithms on synthetic environments. It demonstrates practical utility by efficiently exploring an ultra-large synthesis-on-demand molecular library for multi-objective molecular discovery. The uncertainty quantification metric is shown to effectively proxy true performance, enabling robust learning progress monitoring.

Conclusion: TTPFTS provides an effective anytime solution for Pareto Set Identification, bridging theory and practice through both asymptotic correctness guarantees and demonstrated real-world utility in molecular discovery, with the uncertainty metric serving as a practical tool for deployment in complex settings.

Abstract: Identifying Pareto optimal solutions is critical to support multi-objective decision-making. We introduce the first anytime Multi-Objective Multi-Armed Bandit algorithm for the Pareto Set Identification problem, taking a Bayesian approach: Top-Two Pareto Front Thompson Sampling (TTPFTS). We benchmark TTPFTS against state-of-the-art fixed-budget Pareto Set Identification algorithms on synthetic environments. Next, we demonstrate its practical utility in a challenging multi-objective molecular discovery setting by efficiently exploring an ultra-large synthesis-on-demand molecular library. Furthermore, we introduce a novel uncertainty quantification metric that estimates our algorithm's confidence in the predicted Pareto set. We demonstrate that this metric effectively proxies true performance, yielding a robust methodology for monitoring learning progress in complex settings. Finally, we complement these empirical findings with a theoretical proof of the algorithm's asymptotic correctness.

</details>


### [235] [GateMem: Benchmarking Memory Governance in Multi-Principal Shared-Memory Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18829)
*Zhe Ren,Yibo Yang,Yimeng Chen,Zijun Zhao,Benshuo Fu,Zhihao Shu,Bingjie Zhang,Yangyang Xu,Dandan Guo,Shuicheng Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GateMem is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in multi-principal shared-memory settings (hospitals, workplaces, etc.), jointly testing utility, access control, and forgetting. No current method excels at all three, revealing that existing memory agents are unreliable for shared institutional deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM memory benchmarks assume single-user settings, neglecting shared-assistant scenarios where multiple principals interact with a common memory pool under distinct roles, scopes, and relationships. In such deployments, memory quality depends on both recall and governance (access control, deletion compliance), which are unaddressed by current evaluations.

Method: GateMem jointly evaluates three dimensions: (1) utility for long-horizon requests with state updates; (2) access control across contextual authorization boundaries; and (3) active forgetting after explicit deletion requests. It spans four domains (medical, office, education, household), featuring long-form multi-party episodes, incremental memory injection, hidden checkpoints, structured judging, and leak-target annotations.

Result: No baseline method or backbone model simultaneously achieves strong utility, robust access control, and reliable forgetting. Long-context prompting yields the best governance scores but at high token cost, while retrieval-based and external-memory methods reduce cost but leak unauthorized or deleted information.

Conclusion: Current memory agents fall far short of the reliability required for shared institutional deployment, as governance (access control and forgetting) remains fundamentally unsolved alongside utility.

Abstract: Memory benchmarks for LLM agents largely assume single-user settings, leaving shared assistants for hospitals, workplaces, campuses, and households understudied. In these deployments, multiple principals write to a common memory pool and query it under different roles, scopes, and relationships, so memory quality requires governance as well as recall. We introduce GateMem, a benchmark for multi-principal shared-memory agents. GateMem jointly evaluates utility for legitimate long-horizon requests with state updates, access control across contextual authorization boundaries, and agent-facing active forgetting after explicit deletion requests. It spans medical, office, education, and household domains, with long-form multi-party episodes, incremental memory injection, hidden checkpoints, structured judging, and leak-target annotations. Across diverse baselines and backbone models, no method simultaneously achieves strong utility, robust access control, and reliable forgetting. Long-context prompting often yields the best governance score at high token cost, while retrieval-based and external-memory methods reduce cost yet still leak unauthorized or deleted information. These results show current memory agents remain far from reliable shared institutional deployment.

</details>


### [236] [Learning from Own Solutions: Self-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18810)
*Yingyu Shan,Yuhang Guo,Zihao Cheng,Zeming Liu,Xiangrong Zhu,Xinyi Wang,Jiashu Yao,Wei Lin,Hongru Wang,Heyan Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SC-GRPO introduces self-conditioned KL divergence as per-token gradient weights to replace GRPO's uniform credit assignment, achieving superior reasoning performance without external teachers or process reward models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GRPO assigns uniform credit across all tokens, wasting gradient on routine tokens while under-crediting pivotal reasoning steps. Existing solutions (process reward models, knowledge distillation) require external resources beyond the model's own rollouts, limiting pure RLVR applicability.

Method: SC-GRPO conditions the model on its own verified trajectories, measures per-token KL divergence between original and conditioned distributions, and uses this divergence as a multiplicative weight on GRPO gradients. The paper also proves that naive self-distillation from verified trajectories leads to infeasible weighted-average solutions when multiple verified trajectories exist.

Result: Across five benchmarks (math, code, agentic tasks), SC-GRPO outperforms GRPO by 8.1%, DAPO by 5.9%, and OPD, with stronger out-of-distribution generalization.

Conclusion: Self-conditioned token-level credit assignment is both theoretically sound and empirically effective, enabling pure RLVR without external dependencies while significantly boosting reasoning performance and OOD robustness.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has driven substantial progress in training LLMs for reasoning tasks, but representative methods such as GRPO assign uniform credit across all tokens, wasting gradient on routine tokens while under-crediting pivotal reasoning steps. Existing token-level credit assignment methods require resources beyond the model's own rollouts. GRPO variants rely on process reward models or ground-truth answers. Knowledge distillation assigns credit through per-token divergence but requires external teachers (On-Policy Distillation) or privileged information (On-Policy Self Distillation). However, these dependencies limit applicability in the pure RLVR setting. We observe that conditioning the model on its own verified trajectories induces a measurable per-token KL divergence between the original and conditioned distributions, and prove that distilling from a self-teacher constructed by verified trajectories leads to infeasible weighted-average solutions when multiple verified trajectories exist. We propose SC-GRPO (Self-Conditioned GRPO), which uses KL divergence mentioned before as a multiplicative weight on GRPO gradients. Across five benchmarks spanning math, code, and agentic tasks, SC-GRPO consistently outperforms 8.1% over GRPO and 5.9% over DAPO with stronger OOD performance. Moreover, SC-GRPO achieves higher performance than OPD.

</details>


### [237] [REVES: REvision and VErification--Augmented Training for Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18910)
*Yuanxin Liu,Ruida Zhou,Xinyan Zhao,Amr Sharaf,Hongzhou Lin,Arijit Biswas,Mohammad Ghavamzadeh,Zhaoran Wang,Mingyi Hong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage iterative framework that alternates between online data augmentation and policy optimization, converting "near-miss" intermediate steps into decoupled revision and verification prompts to improve LLM multi-step reasoning via test-time scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard post-training methods optimize single-shot objectives, misaligning with multi-step inference dynamics. Existing multi-turn RL approaches optimize over full trajectories but fail to exploit high-quality mistakes in intermediate steps that models could learn from correcting.

Method: A two-stage iterative framework: (1) online data/prompt augmentation that extracts "near-miss" answers from successful recovery trajectories and converts them into decoupled revision and verification prompts; (2) policy optimization on this augmented data. This enables efficient off-policy data generation and reduces long-horizon sampling overhead versus standard multi-turn RL.

Result: On LiveCodeBench: +6.5 points over RL baseline, +4.0 over standard multi-turn training. Matches SOTA on circle packing using only a 4B model with far fewer rollouts. Math results with ground-truth verification confirm improved correction ability. Generalizes to OOD constraint-satisfaction puzzles (n_queens, mini_sudoku).

Conclusion: Decoupling revision from verification and training on intermediate "near-miss" corrections significantly boosts multi-step reasoning performance across coding, math, and constraint-satisfaction domains, outperforming both standard multi-turn RL and single-shot post-training baselines.

Abstract: Test-time scaling via sequential revision has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. However, standard post-training methods primarily optimize single-shot objectives, creating a fundamental misalignment with multi-step inference dynamics. While recent work treats this as multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL), conventional approaches optimize over the multi-step trajectories directly, failing to further exploit the high-quality mistakes in intermediate steps that model can learn from correcting them. We propose a two-stage iterative framework that alternates between online data/prompt augmentation and policy optimization. By converting the intermediate steps (``near-miss'' answers) in the successful recovery trajectories into decoupled revision and verification prompts, our approach concentrates training on both effective answer transformation and error identification. This approach enables efficient off-policy data generation and reduces the computational overhead of long-horizon sampling compared to standard multi-turn RL. On LiveCodeBench, using publicly available test cases as feedback, we observe gains of +6.5 points over the RL baseline and +4.0 points over standard multi-turn training. Beyond coding, our approach matches the previously reported SOTA result on circle packing while using the smallest base model (4B) and far fewer rollouts than the much larger evolutionary search systems. Math results under ground-truth verification further confirm improved correction ability. It also generalizes to out-of-distribution constraint-satisfaction puzzles such as n\_queens and mini\_sudoku, where correctness is defined entirely by problem constraints. Code is available at https://github.com/yxliu02/REVES.git.

</details>


### [238] [Reinforcement Learning Foundation Models Should Already Be A Thing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18812)
*Abdelrahman Zighem,Jill-Jênn Vie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that reinforcement learning is a conspicuous gap in the trend toward foundation models for structured domains, proposes that MDPs admit a fixed-size sufficient statistic making them amenable to attention-based architectures, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept model trained entirely on synthetic MDPs that solves held-out tabular RL benchmarks in context without task-specific tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models have revolutionized language and vision through internet-scale data, but structured domains like tabular prediction, time-series, and graph learning have instead turned to synthetic data with carefully designed priors (e.g., TabPFN). Reinforcement learning remains a conspicuous gap: no in-context RL work treats prior design over MDPs as a primary objective, despite synthetic MDP sampling being just as feasible as synthetic tabular data generation.

Method: The authors leverage the observation that MDPs admit a fixed-size sufficient statistic that is independent of the number of observed episodes and tabular in shape. This statistic directly fits attention-based architectures (transformers) previously used for tabular foundation models. The model is trained entirely on synthetic MDPs sampled from a designed prior. A policy head replaces the supervised target, enabling in-context reinforcement learning. The approach handles both online and offline RL settings.

Result: Without any task-specific fine-tuning, the single pretrained model solves held-out tabular RL benchmarks in context. In the online setting, it requires far fewer episodes than UCB-VI and tabular Q-learning. In the offline setting, it performs competitively with VI-LCB.

Conclusion: The paper establishes the agenda for an RL foundation model by showing that (1) MDP prior design should be a primary research objective, and (2) the tabular structure of MDP sufficient statistics makes them naturally compatible with transformer architectures. The proof-of-concept results demonstrate that this approach is viable and competitive with classical algorithms.

Abstract: Foundation models for language and vision are powered by internet-scale data, while structured domains (tabular prediction, time-series forecasting, graph learning, reinforcement learning) are not. The substitute is synthetic data, which shifts the burden from collection to prior design. Such priors already exist for many structured tasks: TabPFN and its successors solve tabular classification with a transformer pretrained on a synthetic Bayesian prior.
  We make two points. \textbf{First}, reinforcement learning is the conspicuous gap: sampling a synthetic MDP is as feasible as sampling a synthetic tabular dataset, yet no in-context RL work treats prior design as a primary objective. \textbf{Second}, MDPs admit a fixed-size sufficient statistic, independent of the episodes observed and tabular in shape, which makes them directly amenable to the attention-based architectures used for tabular foundation models, with a policy head replacing the supervised target. Together these define the agenda for an RL foundation model.
  As a proof of concept, we train one model entirely on synthetic MDPs and show that, with no task-specific tuning, it solves held-out tabular benchmarks in context, both online and offline: online, in far fewer episodes than UCB-VI and tabular Q-learning, and offline, competitively with VI-LCB.

</details>


### [239] [Maturing Markov Decision Processes: Decision Making under Increasing Information and Shrinking Action Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18820)
*Jiaxi Liu,Aiping Yang,Yuhang Yang,Shuqi Zhang,Zewei Dong,Jiangming Yang,Xuebin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Maturing Markov Decision Processes (MMDPs), a formulation that explicitly models the asymmetric evolution of information and action expiration in sequential decision problems. It derives an expiring-action priority principle, and develops a structure-aware RL framework with stage-aware policies and search-augmented distillation. Experiments on supply-chain and cash-management tasks show improved learning efficiency, especially as problems scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MDP formulations flatten the temporal structure of sequential decisions, obscuring the asymmetry between incoming information (richer over time) and expiring feasible actions (due to cutoffs, commitments, or constraints). This makes it hard to distinguish urgent actions from deferrable ones, harming learning efficiency in large-scale problems.

Method: The authors propose Maturing Markov Decision Processes (MMDPs), formalizing the information-action asymmetry. They characterize an expiring-action priority principle that identifies which actions must be resolved before the next decision stage. Building on this, they develop a structure-aware reinforcement learning framework featuring: (1) stage-aware policy design, (2) expiring-action abstraction, and (3) search-augmented learning with policy distillation.

Result: Experiments across three domains—a controlled multi-supplier replenishment problem, simplified cash-management environments of increasing complexity, and a production-scale simulator—demonstrate that explicitly modeling the information-action asymmetry improves learning efficiency. The benefits grow as the decision problem scales in complexity and size.

Conclusion: Explicitly capturing the asymmetric evolution of information and action expiration via MMDPs and leveraging it through structure-aware RL yields substantial gains in learning efficiency, particularly for large-scale sequential decision problems where distinguishing urgent from deferrable actions is critical.

Abstract: Sequential decision problems often exhibit an asymmetric evolution of information and decision flexibility: as a decision cycle unfolds, the agent receives richer information while feasible actions expire due to operational cutoffs, commitments, or resource constraints. Standard MDP formulations typically flatten this structure into stage-dependent state descriptions and action masks, thereby obscuring the nested information--action asymmetry that determines which decisions are urgent and which can be deferred. We introduce Maturing Markov Decision Processes (MMDPs), a formulation built around this information--action asymmetry. We characterize one of its key consequences through an expiring-action priority principle, which identifies the actions that must be resolved before the next stage. Motivated by this structure, we develop a structure-aware reinforcement learning framework with stage-aware policy design, expiring-action abstraction, and search-augmented learning with distillation. Experiments on a controlled multi-supplier replenishment problem, simplified cash-management environments of increasing complexity, and a production-scale simulator show that explicitly modeling this asymmetry improves learning efficiency and becomes increasingly valuable as decision problems scale.

</details>


### [240] [Target-confidence Recourse Using tSeTlin machines: TRUST](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18832)
*K. Darshana Abeyrathna,Sara El Mekkaoui,Nils Enric Canut Taugbøl,Anuja Vats*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRUST leverages Probabilistic Tsetlin Machines with Bayesian optimization to generate counterfactuals that explicitly satisfy user-specified confidence targets, yielding more robust and interpretable recourse than conventional boundary-based approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing counterfactual methods minimize input change to flip a decision, but counterfactuals that barely cross the decision boundary are fragile under noise and model variation. Decision-makers in high-stakes settings care about prediction confidence, not just the label, yet no method directly incorporates confidence targets into the recourse search.

Method: The TRUST framework allows users to specify a desired prediction confidence. It uses a Probabilistic Tsetlin Machine (PTM), whose clause-based structure links confidence to rule stability, and employs Bayesian optimization to directly search for minimal changes that meet the confidence target. This also enables comparison of recourse options along cost, confidence, and robustness axes.

Result: Target-confidence counterfactuals achieve perfect robustness while maintaining low recourse cost across benchmarks. On the Haberman dataset, TRUST attains an L2 distance of 0.10 at 0.92 confidence. The framework also reveals that counterfactuals satisfying identical rules can differ substantially in reliability based on how securely those rules are activated.

Conclusion: By explicitly controlling confidence and exposing rule-level stability, TRUST provides actionable, robust recourse suitable for high-stakes decision support, outperforming conventional boundary-based counterfactual methods.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are widely used to provide algorithmic recourse in high-stakes decision-making systems. Most existing methods seek the smallest change to an input that flips a model's decision. However, decision-makers often rely not only on predicted labels but also on confidence thresholds and risk margins. Counterfactuals that barely cross a decision boundary can be fragile and unstable under noise or model variation.
  In this paper, we propose Target-confidence Recourse Using tSeTlin machines (TRUST), a framework in which users explicitly specify the desired prediction confidence for recourse. Rather than generating counterfactuals and evaluating confidence afterward, TRUST directly searches for minimal changes that satisfy a user-defined confidence target, enabling comparison of recourse options in terms of cost, confidence, and robustness.
  We instantiate TRUST using a Probabilistic Tsetlin Machine (PTM) combined with Bayesian optimization. The probabilistic clause-based structure of PTM links prediction confidence to the stability of decision rules. We show that counterfactuals satisfying the same rules can still differ substantially in reliability depending on how securely they satisfy those rules, revealing whether decisions are supported by robust or fragile clause activations.
  Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that target-confidence counterfactuals produce more robust and interpretable recourse than conventional boundary-based approaches. Across multiple benchmarks, TRUST achieves perfect robustness while maintaining low recourse cost, including an L2 distance of 0.10 on the Haberman dataset at 0.92 confidence. By explicitly controlling confidence and exposing rule-level stability, TRUST provides actionable recourse for high-stakes decision support.

</details>


### [241] [STARE: Surprisal-Guided Token-Level Advantage Reweighting for Policy Entropy Stability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19236)
*Haipeng Luo,Qingfeng Sun,Songli Wu,Can Xu,Wenfeng Deng,Han Hu,Yansong Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GRPO-style RL suffers policy entropy collapse due to a token-level credit assignment mismatch. The authors analyze this theoretically, revealing an advantage-surprisal four-quadrant structure, then propose STARE — a method that reweights advantages on entropy-critical tokens using surprisal quantiles with a target-entropy gate — achieving stable training and 4–8% accuracy gains on AIME benchmarks across 1.5B–32B models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (e.g., GRPO) has become dominant for post-training LLM reasoning, but suffers from policy entropy collapse during training, which degrades exploration and limits RL potential. The root cause — a token-level credit assignment mismatch — lacks rigorous gradient-level analysis and a principled remedy.

Method: The authors (1) derive first-order token-level entropy dynamics under GRPO, decomposing per-token entropy variation into the product of trajectory-level advantage and an entropy sensitivity function over the next-token distribution, yielding an advantage-surprisal four-quadrant structure with near-criticality; (2) propose STARE: identify entropy-critical token subsets via batch-internal surprisal quantiles, selectively reweight their effective advantages, and incorporate a target-entropy closed-loop gate for stable regulation.

Result: STARE sustains stable RL training over thousands of steps while keeping policy entropy within the target band across 1.5B–32B models on Short CoT, Long CoT, and Multi-Turn Tool Use tasks. On AIME24/AIME25, it outperforms DAPO and other baselines by 4%–8% average accuracy, with reflection tokens and response length growing in tandem, indicating sustained exploration-exploitation balance.

Conclusion: The identified token-level credit assignment mismatch and advantage-surprisal structure provide a principled lens on GRPO entropy collapse. STARE offers an effective, lightweight fix that stabilizes entropy, boosts benchmark performance, and unlocks further RL training potential for LLM reasoning.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards algorithms like GRPO have emerged as the dominant post-training paradigm for complex reasoning in LLMs, yet commonly suffer from policy entropy collapse during training.
