We conduct a first-order gradient analysis of token-level entropy dynamics under GRPO and identify a token-level credit assignment mismatch: the per-token entropy variation decomposes into the product of the trajectory-level advantage and an entropy sensitivity function over the next-token distribution, yielding an advantage-surprisal four-quadrant structure and a near-criticality property. Motivated by it, we propose STARE (Surprisal-guided Token-level Advantage Reweighting for policy Entropy stability), which identifies entropy-critical token subsets via batch-internal surprisal quantiles, selectively reweights their effective advantages, and incorporates a target-entropy closed-loop gate for stable entropy regulation. Across model scales from 1.5B to 32B and three task families (Short CoT, Long CoT, and Multi-Turn Tool Use), STARE sustains stable RL training over thousands of steps while maintaining policy entropy within the target band. On AIME24 and AIME25, STARE outperforms DAPO and other competitive baselines by 4%-8% in average accuracy, with reflection tokens and response length growing in tandem, indicating sustained exploration-exploitation balance that further unlocks RL training potential.Code is available at https://github.com/hp-luo/STARE.

</details>


### [242] [Seed-Guided Semi-Supervised Clustering by A-Contrario Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18833)
*Nassir Mohammad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A semi-supervised clustering framework that defines clusters via anomaly detection duality, using a-contrario reasoning and minimal seeds to iteratively exclude outliers without manual parameter tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Partitioning algorithms (e.g., k-means) over-assign outliers into clusters, while density-based methods (e.g., DBSCAN) rely on sensitive global parameters. Both lack principled mechanisms for handling noise and defining robust cluster boundaries in noisy environments.

Method: The Perception algorithm uses a-contrario reasoning with a null hypothesis of uniform randomness. A cluster is defined as a maximal subset containing no anomalies, where anomaly detection uses an expectation-based threshold (E < 1). The "clustering-by-exclusion" mechanism works iteratively: (1) user-provided seeds (10–30 per cluster) initialize robust cluster medians, (2) initial groups form around seeds, (3) non-anomalous points are admitted to expand clusters, (4) fringe points and isolated noise are naturally isolated. Emerging unknown clusters remain unassigned.

Result: With only 10–30 seeds per cluster, the method achieves competitive to very strong performance on synthetic and real-world benchmarks (image and text datasets, using raw, PCA-reduced, and neighborhood-preserving embeddings) under a practical low-tuning protocol. Linear scalability in observations and dimensionality is maintained for a fixed number of seeded clusters and iterations.

Conclusion: The statistical duality between clustering and anomaly detection, operationalized through a-contrario reasoning and clustering-by-exclusion, yields a robust, low-tuning, seed-guided clustering framework that handles noise effectively and scales linearly.

Abstract: This paper introduces a semi-supervised clustering framework grounded in the statistical duality between grouping principles and anomaly detection. We address the challenge of robust cluster definition in noisy environments -- a task where partitioning algorithms often over-assign outliers and density-based methods remain sensitive to heuristic global parameters. Drawing on \textit{a-contrario} statistical reasoning and Gestalt proximity principles, we define a cluster as a maximal subset of data points containing no anomalies relative to a null hypothesis of uniform randomness. Central to this approach is the Perception algorithm, which utilises a principled expectation-based threshold ($\mathbb{E} < 1$) to identify outliers without manual parameter tuning. By treating clustering as the dual of anomaly detection, we employ an iterative ``clustering-by-exclusion'' mechanism. The algorithm is seed-guided, leveraging minimal user-provided labels to initialise robust cluster medians and form initial groups, which are subsequently expanded by admitting non-anomalous points. This approach naturally isolates fringe points, isolated noise, and emerging unknown clusters. We evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including image and text datasets represented through raw, linear-reduced, and neighbourhood-preserving embeddings. Results demonstrate that with as few as 10--30 seeds per cluster, the proposed method achieves competitive and often very strong performance under a practical low-tuning benchmarking protocol, while maintaining linear scalability with respect to both observations and dimensionality for a fixed number of seeded clusters and iterations.

</details>


### [243] [Structured Inference with Large Language Gibbs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19264)
*Sanghyeok Choi,Henry Gouk,Esmeralda S. Whitammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Large Language Gibbs (LLG), a method that treats LLM conditional distributions as Gibbs sampling transition operators for structured probabilistic inference. Instead of single-pass autoregressive generation, LLG iteratively resamples individual variables conditioned on all others, avoiding order-dependent biases and converging to a stationary distribution that balances all local conditionals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs encode substantial world knowledge, extracting this knowledge for coherent probabilistic reasoning over structured variables is challenging. Single-pass autoregressive generation introduces order-dependent biases and fails to produce globally consistent samples. The authors aim to leverage LLM conditional distributions within a principled MCMC framework to achieve coherent structured inference.

Method: Large Language Gibbs (LLG) uses an LLM's next-token conditional distributions as transition operators in a Gibbs sampling scheme. For structured objects (e.g., tuples, graphs), variables are iteratively resampled one at a time, conditioning on the current values of all other variables via appropriately formatted prompts. This yields a Markov chain whose stationary distribution represents a compromise among all local conditionals, free from the biases of sequential generation order.

Result: LLG was evaluated on three tasks: (1) sampling from synthetic distributions, where it recovered the target distribution more faithfully than autoregressive generation; (2) consistent reasoning tasks, where it produced more logically coherent outputs; and (3) Bayesian structure learning, where it discovered plausible graphical structures. Across all settings, LLG outperformed single-pass generation baselines in terms of distributional fidelity and consistency.

Conclusion: LLM conditionals can serve as effective transition operators within MCMC, specifically Gibbs sampling, offering a practical and principled alternative to one-pass autoregressive generation for structured probabilistic inference under noisy world priors encoded in LLMs.

Abstract: The knowledge encoded in large language models (LLMs) can serve as a substrate for structured reasoning over variables describing a complex world, but accessing this knowledge in a probabilistically coherent manner poses a difficult inference problem. We propose Large Language Gibbs, a scheme for structured probabilistic inference that uses conditional distributions of an LLM as transition operators. Rather than sampling structured objects through single-pass autoregressive generation, we iteratively resample individual variables conditioned on others using an LLM's next-token conditionals. This approach avoids order-dependent biases and produces a stationary distribution that reflects a compromise between all local conditionals. We apply this approach to sampling from synthetic distributions, consistent reasoning tasks, and Bayesian structure learning. The results suggest that the use of LLM conditionals in MCMC is a practical alternative to one-pass generation for structured probabilistic inference under a world prior accessible through noisy LLM conditionals.

</details>


### [244] [Identifying Structural Biases from Causal Mechanism Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18834)
*Praharsh Nanavati,Jilles Vreeken,David Kaltenpoth*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces StruBI, an algorithm that identifies hidden confounding and selection biases in causal discovery by detecting dependent mechanism shifts across multiple environments, using a mutual information-based criterion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard causal discovery assumes i.i.d. data and no unmeasured confounders, but real-world data often violates these assumptions. Existing methods struggle to distinguish between different types of structural biases (hidden confounding vs. selection bias), motivating a principled approach to identify which variables are affected by which bias.

Method: The authors theoretically demonstrate that structural biases (hidden confounding and selection bias) induce dependent mechanism shifts across environments. They develop an empirically testable criterion based on conditional mutual information to detect these dependencies. The StruBI algorithm operationalizes this criterion to classify each variable as unbiased, hidden-confounded, or selection-biased by analyzing mechanism shift patterns across multiple environments.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that StruBI accurately recovers both the set of affected variables and the type of bias, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: Structural biases leave detectable signatures in the form of dependent mechanism shifts across environments. StruBI exploits this insight to reliably identify hidden confounding and selection bias without requiring strong parametric assumptions, offering a practical tool for more robust causal discovery.

Abstract: Causal discovery methods commonly assume that all data is independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) and that there are no unmeasured variables affecting the system. In practice, these assumptions are often violated, leading to inaccurate inference. In this paper, we study how to identify hidden confounding and selection biases from causal mechanism shifts. In particular, we show that structural biases lead to dependent mechanism shifts. That is, by considering for which variables the mechanisms change given data from different environments, we can tell which variables are unbiased, which are subject to hidden confounding, and which are undergoing selection bias. We formalize this into an empirically testable criterion based on mutual information, and show under which conditions it identifies structural biases. To tell which nodes are subject to what kind of bias, we introduce the StruBI algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that StruBI works well in practice, accurately recovering affected variable sets and types of biases, outperforming the state-of-the-art by a wide margin.

</details>


### [245] [Semantic Robustness Certification for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18839)
*Peiyu Yang,Paul Montague,Feng Liu,Andrew C. Cullen,Amardeep Kaur,Christopher Leckie,Sarah M. Erfani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first framework for certifying VLM robustness under semantic-level distribution shifts (e.g., shape, size, style) by using text prompts as semantic proxies to construct parameterized transformations. It quantitatively certifies the extent interval over which predictions remain stable without requiring additional data per variation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing robustness certification methods for vision-language models focus only on geometric or pixel-level input transformations, overlooking semantic-level variations (shape, size, style) that commonly occur in real-world deployments. There is a need for a principled certification framework that handles these semantically meaningful distribution shifts.

Method: The framework leverages VLMs' open-vocabulary capability to use text prompts as semantic proxies, constructing transformations parameterized by an "extent" that controls the degree of semantic variation. It characterizes the VLM decision boundary in closed form, then quantitatively certifies extent intervals within which the predicted class remains invariant under the semantic transformation. No additional data per variation is required.

Result: Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that the framework successfully certifies VLM robustness under diverse semantic variations across various scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed framework is the first to enable practical, data-free certification of VLM robustness under semantic-level transformations, filling a critical gap between geometric/pixel-level certification and real-world semantic distribution shifts.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are now widely used in downstream tasks. However, real-world applications often expose VLMs to distribution shifts induced by semantic variation (e.g., shape, size, and style). Robustness certification determines if a model's prediction changes when transformations are applied to its input. While most certification frameworks study geometric or pixel-level transformations over inputs, this work proposes a novel framework that enables certifying VLM robustness under semantic-level transformations. Leveraging the open-vocabulary capability of VLMs, we use text prompts as semantic proxies to construct transformations parameterized by an extent that controls the degree of semantic variation. By characterizing the VLM decision boundary in closed form, our framework quantitatively certifies extent intervals for which the predicted class remains unchanged under the semantic transformation. Our framework is the first to certify VLM robustness under semantic-level variations without requiring additional data for each variation, making it practical to apply. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data show that our framework enables certifying robustness under diverse semantic variations across scenarios.

</details>


### [246] [Learning from Your Own Mistakes: Constructing Learnable Micro-Reflective Trajectories for Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18844)
*Zhilin Huang,Hang Gao,Ziqiang Dong,Yuan Chen,Yifeng Luo,Chujun Qin,Jingyi Wang,Yang Yang,Guanjun Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TAPO improves LLM reasoning by replacing implicit KL-based self-distillation with explicit contrastive trajectory construction, where the model's own correct and incorrect rollouts are used to build micro-reflective corrections that diagnose failures and insert corrected reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-distillation methods (e.g., KL divergence minimization) align the model toward a privileged distribution via uncontrolled sampling, but fail to provide diagnostic insight into specific errors or fine-grained corrective guidance. The model merely imitates rather than understanding where and why its reasoning fails.

Method: TAPO (Trajectory-Augmented Policy Optimization) constructs contrastive rollouts (correct + incorrect) per query. It builds micro-reflective correction trajectories that preserve erroneous reasoning up to the failure point, then inserts a natural-language diagnosis and corrected reasoning from a correct reference. Key components include difficulty-aware candidate selection at the capability boundary and decoupled advantage estimation to avoid gradient contamination.

Result: TAPO achieves consistent improvements over GRPO on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 under equal training steps. It strengthens both first-pass reasoning and error-correction effectiveness.

Conclusion: Explicit trajectory-level correction with contrastive supervision — rather than implicit distributional alignment — provides more effective reasoning improvement, preserving on-policy distribution and targeting individual failure patterns.

Abstract: Self-distillation improves reasoning in large language models by using the model's own rollouts as training signal, typically through implicit logit-level alignment that minimizes KL divergence toward a privileged target distribution. However, because this supervision is generated via uncontrolled sampling, it provides no diagnostic insight into the model's specific errors or corrective guidance for its individual failure patterns. Consequently, the model learns to imitate a privileged distribution rather than receiving fine-grained corrections that pinpoint where and why its reasoning fails. In this paper, we propose Trajectory-Augmented Policy Optimization (TAPO), which advances self-distillation from implicit distributional alignment to explicit trajectory construction. During RL training, the model produces both correct and incorrect rollouts to the same query, and TAPO leverages this contrastive structure to construct micro-reflective corrections, new training trajectories that retain the model's erroneous reasoning up to the point of failure, then insert a natural-language diagnosis and corrected reasoning guided by a correct reference from the same sampling group. Since each trajectory is anchored in the learner's own prefix and solutions, the corrective signal preserves the model's on-policy distribution to a greater extent than the position-wise alignment imposed by KL-based methods. To integrate these trajectories, TAPO introduces difficulty-aware candidate selection at the model's capability boundary and decoupled advantage estimation to prevent gradient contamination. Experiments on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that TAPO achieves consistent improvements over GRPO under the same number of training steps. Further analysis demonstrates that TAPO strengthens both first-pass reasoning and error-correction effectiveness.

</details>


### [247] [Investigating Inductive Biases for Machine Learning Emulation of Sudden Stratospheric Warmings in Idealised Isca Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18857)
*Oskar Bohn Lassen,Simon Driscoll,Stephen I. Thomson,Sebastian Schemm,Francisco C. Pereira*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study evaluates how architectural inductive biases in machine-learning weather emulators affect their ability to capture sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) dynamics and stratosphere-troposphere coupling, finding that explicit 3D vertical coupling is crucial but that low error metrics can mask physically unfaithful wave-mean-flow interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine-learning weather emulators show promise for subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction, but it is unclear whether they can exploit stratospheric predictability anchors like SSWs. The authors aim to test whether architectural choices (inductive biases) affect emulation of stratospheric dynamics and physically faithful wave-mean-flow interaction.

Method: Paired idealized Isca model simulations differing only in an imposed wave-2 heating perturbation are used. Convolutional, transformer, and graph-based neural network architectures are trained for one-step prediction. Performance is compared under dynamically quiet vs. SSW-active stratospheric conditions, with evaluation using both standard forecast error metrics and Eliassen-Palm flux diagnostics to assess physical fidelity of wave-mean-flow interaction.

Result: Architectural differences are modest during quiescent stratospheric conditions but become substantial when SSW-like variability is active. Explicit three-dimensional vertical coupling emerges as a key inductive bias for emulating stratospheric dynamics. Critically, low forecast error does not guarantee physically accurate wave-mean-flow interaction: coherent errors persist in stratospheric wave-driving structure even when bulk error metrics appear favorable.

Conclusion: Explicit 3D vertical coupling is essential for machine-learning emulators to capture stratospheric dynamics. Standard error metrics are insufficient for validating physical fidelity; Eliassen-Palm flux diagnostics reveal hidden structural errors in wave driving. Architectural inductive bias matters most under active dynamical regimes like SSWs.

Abstract: Machine-learning emulators are increasingly used for weather prediction and have the potential to extend skill on subseasonal-to-seasonal timescales by learning dynamically important sources of predictability. A key challenge is whether the models can exploit predictability anchors, such as stratospheric variability, that influence tropospheric circulation beyond short lead times. We test how architectural inductive bias affects emulation of sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) dynamics using paired idealised Isca simulations that differ only in an imposed wave-2 heating perturbation. Across convolutional, transformer, and graph-based architectures trained for one-step prediction, model differences are modest when the stratosphere is dynamically quiet but widen substantially when SSW-like variability is active. Our results identify explicit three-dimensional vertical coupling as a key inductive bias for machine-learning emulation of stratospheric dynamics. However, Eliassen-Palm flux diagnostics show that low forecast error does not guarantee physically faithful wave-mean-flow interaction, with coherent errors remaining in stratospheric wave-driving structure.

</details>


### [248] [Scaling Learning-based AEB with Massive Unlabeled Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18864)
*Xiangyu Wang,Yang Zhan,Mengxiang Hao,Chuanchuan Zhong,Yansong Jia,Junjie Zhang,Yu Han,Xin Jiang,Zhen Cao,Ying Wang,Yulun Song,Zhitao Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A stabilized meta-feedback semi-supervised learning framework scales automatic emergency braking (AEB) using up to 1B unlabeled driving windows. It introduces Noise-Aware Decoupling and kinematics-gated pseudo-labeling with teacher conflict penalty to mitigate pseudo-label errors from anchor ambiguity and data mismatch, achieving a 100:1 positive-to-false activation ratio and 35% improvement in accident-free driving mileage in deployed fleet validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling learning-based AEB with massive unlabeled fleet data is attractive but challenging under production constraints. The core problem is that systematic pseudo-label errors — arising from (1) anchor ambiguity in the small labeled set used for teacher updates and (2) labeled-unlabeled data distribution mismatch — can cause spurious braking triggers, compromising safety and comfort. A practical solution is needed to safely leverage billion-scale unlabeled data.

Method: The proposed stabilized MF-SSL framework extends meta-feedback semi-supervised learning with two key mechanisms: (1) **Noise-Aware Decoupling** — ambiguity-prone anchors (samples where expert label confidence is low) are removed from the teacher model's supervised update path, preventing noisy gradient signals from corrupting pseudo-label quality. (2) **Kinematics-gated pseudo-labeling with teacher conflict penalty** — a kinematics-based gating function filters unlabeled samples unlikely to require braking, and a teacher conflict penalty term suppresses risk hallucinations (false-positive braking predictions) on unlabeled data when the teacher disagrees with the student, all while preserving broad coverage of genuine braking scenarios.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance gains as unlabeled data scales from 1M to 1B windows. The 1B-trained student model, deployed to hundreds of thousands of vehicles and validated over 10^9 km of real-world driving, achieves: (1) a positive-to-false activation ratio exceeding 100:1, and (2) a 35% improvement in accident-free driving mileage compared to a production rule-only AEB baseline, all while maintaining stable comfort metrics.

Conclusion: Stabilized MF-SSL with Noise-Aware Decoupling and kinematics-gated pseudo-labeling effectively mitigates the compounding pseudo-label error problem in large-scale semi-supervised AEB learning. The approach demonstrates that billion-scale unlabeled fleet data can be safely harnessed to significantly improve real-world AEB performance, surpassing rule-based systems while meeting stringent production safety and comfort requirements.

Abstract: This paper studies how to scale learning-based automatic emergency braking (AEB) with massive unlabeled fleet data under production constraints. Our approach is based on meta-feedback semi-supervised learning (MF-SSL), where a teacher generates pseudo labels for unlabeled driving data and is updated using a small labeled anchor set as safety-critical feedback. In production, anchor ambiguity and labeled-unlabeled mismatch can amplify systematic pseudo-label errors, leading to spurious triggers. We propose a stabilized MF-SSL framework with (i) Noise-Aware Decoupling, which removes ambiguity-prone anchors from the teacher's supervised update path, and (ii) kinematics-gated pseudo-labeling with a teacher conflict penalty to suppress mismatch-induced risk hallucinations on unlabeled data while maintaining broad coverage. Extensive experiments show consistent gains as unlabeled data scale from 1M to 1B windows, improving safety while keeping comfort stable. The 1B-trained student model is deployed to hundreds of thousands of vehicles and validated over \$10^9$ km of driving, achieving a positive-to-false activation ratio exceeding 100:1 and a 35% improvement in accident-free driving mileage over a production rule-only baseline.

</details>


### [249] [Strategic Feature Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18867)
*Jivat Neet Kaur,Pratik Patil,Divya Shanmugam,Emma Pierson,Michael I. Jordan,Nika Haghtalab,Meena Jagadeesan,Ahmed Alaa,Serena Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formally studies strategic classification through joint feature selection and ridge regularization, showing that excluding features based solely on manipulability is suboptimal. The authors provide theoretical characterization of feature subset performance under optimal regularization and develop a practical algorithm for joint selection, validated on a healthcare payments benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In high-stakes domains like healthcare, decision-makers often rely on coarse, practical levers—such as excluding manipulable features or applying ridge regularization—within existing prediction pipelines to mitigate strategic manipulation, rather than redesigning predictors from scratch. There is no formal understanding of how feature selection and regularization interact in strategic settings.

Method: The authors initiate a formal study of strategic classification through the lens of feature selection combined with ridge regularization. They derive a fine-grained theoretical characterization of how a given feature subset performs under optimally tuned ridge regularization, then develop a practical algorithm that jointly optimizes the feature set and the regularization parameter.

Result: The central finding is that naively excluding features based solely on their manipulability is generally suboptimal. The interaction between feature selection and regularization yields non-trivial trade-offs. The proposed joint selection algorithm is demonstrated on a real-world healthcare payments benchmark, showing practical utility in guiding coarse policy design.

Conclusion: The paper provides a principled, practical framework for mitigating strategic manipulation in algorithmic decision-making by jointly optimizing feature selection and ridge regularization, offering actionable insights for policy design without requiring full predictor redesign.

Abstract: When algorithmic predictors inform resource allocation in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, these predictors must account for strategic manipulation of input features. The typical solution is to redesign the predictor itself to explicitly account for strategic interactions. In practice, however, decision makers are often constrained to adjusting coarser levers within existing prediction pipelines. For example, healthcare organizations often select which features to exclude based on perceived manipulability, while using standard regularization procedures to shrink the coefficients of retained features. In this work, we initiate a formal study of strategic classification through feature selection and its interaction with ridge regularization. Our main finding is that excluding individual features based on their manipulability alone is generally suboptimal. We provide a fine-grained characterization of the performance of a feature subset under optimal regularization, yielding new insights for policy design. Motivated by this characterization, we develop a practical algorithm for jointly choosing the feature set and the level of ridge regularization. Through a real-world case study on a healthcare payments benchmark, we illustrate how our algorithm can guide the design of coarse policy levers in practice. Our results provide a principled, practical framework for mitigating the effects of strategic behavior in algorithmic decision-making systems.

</details>


### [250] [Domain-Shift Aware Neural Networks for Unbalance Characterization in Rotating Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18882)
*Bernardo Feijó Junqueira,Claudio Kiyoshi Umezu,Bruno Bilhar Karaziack,Tomaz Junior,Daniel Alves Castello*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A domain-shift aware neural network using maximum mean discrepancy is applied to estimate unbalance masses in rotating shafts under varying operating conditions, demonstrating improved prediction accuracy when domain discrepancies are present and not fully characterized.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional regression models for unbalance mass estimation in rotating machinery degrade when operating conditions shift (e.g., activation of a secondary shaft, varying rotational speeds). The authors aim to address this domain discrepancy problem where the system's physical behavior and sources of domain shift are not fully known, limiting generalization beyond training conditions.

Method: A domain adaptation framework is employed, training a neural network with a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) strategy to align feature representations across source and target distributions. Experimental data were collected from a test rig featuring a primary shaft with a flange carrying unbalanced masses at fixed radial distances, driven at different rotational speeds. A secondary shaft could be optionally activated to introduce domain discrepancy. Triaxial accelerometers captured the dynamic response, and the inverse problem of mass estimation was solved under this domain-shift aware paradigm.

Result: Explicitly addressing domain shift via MMD-based feature alignment significantly improves prediction accuracy for unbalance mass estimation, particularly when the system's physical behavior and sources of domain discrepancy fall outside the training conditions.

Conclusion: Domain-shift aware models hold strong potential for regression tasks in Structural Health Monitoring, enabling robust mass estimation even under unforeseen or poorly characterized operating condition changes.

Abstract: This work investigates the application of a domain-shift aware neural network for regression tasks aimed at estimating unbalance masses in rotating shafts under varying operating conditions. Experimental data were collected from a test rig in which a primary shaft, equipped with a flange carrying unbalanced masses, was driven at different rotational speeds, while a secondary shaft could be optionally activated to introduce domain discrepancy. The unbalance masses were positioned at a fixed radial distance, and the dynamic response of the system was recorded using triaxial accelerometers. The inverse problem of mass estimation is formulated within a domain adaptation framework, where the network is trained with a maximum mean discrepancy strategy to align feature representations across source and target distributions. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly addressing domain shift in improving prediction accuracy, especially when the system's physical behavior and sources of domain discrepancy are not fully known and fall outside the training conditions. These findings highlight the potential of domain-shift aware models for regression tasks in Structural Health Monitoring.

</details>


### [251] [Anomaly Detection for Sparse and Irregular Multivariate Time Series with Latent SDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18898)
*Martin Uray,Dominik Geng,Florian Graf,Stefan Huber,Roland Kwitt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a generative MTSAD method using Latent Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) that handles irregular sampling and missing data by modeling time series as continuous-time stochastic dynamical systems. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on six benchmarks and remains robust under severe data sparsity where baselines degrade.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MTSAD methods assume uniformly sampled, complete time series, but real-world data is often sparse, irregularly sampled, or partially observed. Additionally, many real-world processes exhibit cyclic behavior that existing methods fail to capture naturally.

Method: A generative approach based on Latent SDEs that projects observed time series onto a continuous-time stochastic dynamical system. This formulation inherently handles missing observations and irregular sampling, and naturally captures cyclic behavior through its continuous-time stochastic dynamics.

Result: The proposed method ranks first among state-of-the-art baselines across six anomaly detection benchmark datasets. It remains robust under severe data sparsity, while baseline methods exhibit significant performance degradation.

Conclusion: Latent SDEs provide a natural inductive bias for MTSAD, particularly advantageous when real-world irregularities such as missing data and non-uniform sampling are present.

Abstract: Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) is critical for a wide range of application areas, such as industrial monitoring, cybersecurity, or healthcare. Real-world data is often sparse, irregularly sampled or partially observed, yet existing methods assume uniformly sampled time series. We propose a generative approach based on Latent SDEs that projects the observed time series on a continuous-time stochastic dynamical system, directly being able to handle missing observations and irregular sampling, while also naturally capturing possible cyclic behavior that many real-world use cases inherently possess. Experiments on six anomaly benchmark datasets show that our proposed method ranks first among state-of-the-art baselines. We further demonstrate that our method remains robust under severe data sparsity, while performance significantly degrades for the tested baseline methods. These results highlight latent SDEs as a natural inductive bias for anomaly detection in multivariate time series, especially in presence of real-world irregularities.

</details>


### [252] [Some Complexity Results for Robustness Verification for Binarized Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18918)
*Harshit Goyal,Sudakshina Dutta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BNN satisfiability is NP-complete (reduction from SAT), while robustness under uniform occlusion can be checked in polynomial time due to piecewise-constant output structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To characterize the computational complexity of verification problems for Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs), specifically satisfiability and robustness under uniform image occlusion.

Method: For satisfiability, a reduction from the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) to BNN satisfiability is used to prove NP-completeness. For robustness, the paper exploits the piecewise-constant structure induced in the network output by uniform image occlusion to devise a polynomial-time algorithm.

Result: BNN satisfiability is NP-complete. Uniform occlusion causes the network output to exhibit a piecewise-constant structure, which enables a polynomial-time algorithm for robustness verification.

Conclusion: Verifying BNNs is computationally hard in general (NP-complete for satisfiability), but structural properties induced by uniform occlusion make robustness checking tractable (polynomial time).

Abstract: This paper studies the computational complexity of verification problems for Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs), where activations (and sometimes weights) are binary. We analyze two problems: satisfiability and robustness under uniform image occlusion. We show that BNN satisfiability is NP-complete via a reduction from Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT), and that uniform occlusion induces a piecewise-constant structure in the network output, enabling a polynomial-time robustness-checking algorithm.

</details>


### [253] [GrapNet: A Programmable Dynamic-Architecture Neural Graph Substrate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18923)
*Zirong Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GrapNet proposes neural networks where the computation graph is a first-class programmable entity. Nodes own child references and trainable allocation vectors; structural edits (deletion, freezing, routing) are native operations. Evaluated as a programmability stress suite, GrapNet outperforms parameter-larger MLPs on Split Fashion-MNIST (+12.08 pts) and Split CIFAR-10 (+3.81 pts), demonstrating structural programmability as a viable neural substrate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current fixed-tensor neural networks lack programmability as a first-class interface. Operations like editing relations, freezing subgraphs, auditing local functions, or changing execution backends require ad-hoc parameter surgery rather than being native operations on the neural program itself. The authors argue the computation graph should be the architecture and executable program, not merely an input data structure.

Method: GrapNet treats the neural network as an editable graph where each compute node owns its child references and a trainable allocation vector. Structural rules and execution policies are external to node cores, enabling: deletion (removes child reference + allocation coordinate), freezing subgraphs, structural editing, grouping into trainable family blocks, attention-based routing over active relations, and lowering to dense snapshots post topology stabilization. GrapNet composes with conventional modules (dense layers, CNNs, ResNets, attention, transformers) via a vector-valued parent interface, where each sensory GrapNode receives one coordinate.

Result: On Split Fashion-MNIST (10 seeds), GrapNet+ER achieves 63.16% seen-class accuracy vs. 51.08% for a parameter-larger dense MLP+ER (Δ=12.08 points, p=1.3e-5). On Split CIFAR-10 with frozen ImageNet ResNet-18 encoder, GrapNet improves over MLP-256 by 3.81 points (p=0.0026).

Conclusion: GrapNet demonstrates that structural programmability — treating the neural graph as an editable, first-class program — provides a viable substrate for neural computation, offering faithful execution views alongside competitive performance on continual learning-style evaluations.

Abstract: Programmability is a missing first-class interface in fixed-tensor neural networks: editing a relation, freezing a subgraph, auditing a local function, or changing the execution backend should be an operation on the neural program rather than ad-hoc parameter surgery. GrapNet studies this graph-as-network setting. The graph is the architecture and executable program, not an input data graph. Each compute node owns its next-layer child references and a trainable allocation vector aligned with those references; deleting a relation physically removes both the child reference and the corresponding allocation coordinate. Structural rules and execution policies live outside the node core, so the same child-owned graph can be grown, frozen, structurally edited, grouped into trainable family blocks, routed by attention over active relations, or lowered to dense snapshots after topology stabilizes. GrapNet composes with conventional modules through a vector-valued parent interface: dense layers, CNN encoders, ResNet feature extractors, attention blocks, and transformer representations can all feed one sensory GrapNode per coordinate. The evaluation is organized as a programmability stress suite rather than as a new replay benchmark. In a matched ten-seed Split Fashion-MNIST study, a plastic GrapNet+ER head reaches 63.16 percent seen-class accuracy versus 51.08 percent for a parameter-larger dense MLP+ER under the same seen-class loss and replay memory, with paired delta 12.08 points and p=1.3e-5. On Split CIFAR-10 with a frozen ImageNet ResNet-18 encoder, the same substrate improves the online head over MLP-256 by 3.81 points, with p=0.0026. These results support GrapNet as an editable neural graph substrate whose core value is structural programmability with faithful execution views.

</details>


### [254] [Be Your Own Teacher: Steering Protein Language Models via Unsupervised Reward Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18961)
*Lanqing Li,Shentong Mo,Yang Yu,Pheng-Ann Heng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces unsupervised reward optimization for protein language models (PLMs), enabling steerable protein generation without ground-truth labels. The authors propose two offline algorithms—Soft Reward Optimization (SRO) and Binarized Reward Optimization (BRO)—that leverage task-agnostic rewards combining model uncertainty and semantic consistency. These methods outperform DPO and KTO baselines and approach oracle performance across diverse protein design tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training adaptation of PLMs for controllable biomolecular design typically depends on costly wet-lab validation or curated preference datasets. The authors aim to overcome this supervision bottleneck by enabling PLM self-improvement without labeled preferences or experimental feedback.

Method: The authors propose a framework based on task-agnostic proxy rewards that combine (1) intrinsic model uncertainty and (2) extrinsic semantic consistency from protein representation models. These rewards correlate strongly with controllability measures. They then introduce two offline RLHF algorithms: Soft Reward Optimization (SRO), which uses continuous reward signals, and Binarized Reward Optimization (BRO), which binarizes rewards. Both maximize the classical RLHF objective using these unsupervised proxy rewards without ground-truth labels.

Result: Extensive experiments on compositional out-of-distribution prompts show that SRO and BRO significantly outperform competitive baselines (DPO, KTO), approaching oracle performance across multiple sampling temperatures, model scales, and protein families. Fine-tuned PLMs also achieve consistently higher coverage than base models in pass@k evaluations.

Conclusion: The framework provides a scalable pathway toward controllable biomolecular design without requiring labeled preferences or experimental feedback, enabling PLM self-improvement through their own generated experience.

Abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for controllable biomolecular design, yet their post-training adaptation typically relies on costly wet-lab validation or curated preference datasets. To overcome this supervision bottleneck, we introduce unsupervised reward optimization of PLMs, a comprehensive framework for steerable protein generation without ground-truth labels. Our key insight is that task-agnostic rewards, which combine intrinsic model uncertainty with extrinsic semantic consistency informed by protein representation models, exhibit strong correlation with controllability measures across base models and temperature regimes. Building upon this discovery, we propose two offline algorithms: Soft Reward Optimization (SRO) and Binarized Reward Optimization (BRO), which effectively maximize the classical RLHF objective induced by these proxy rewards. Extensive experiments on compositional out-of-distribution prompts demonstrate that both methods significantly outperform competitive baselines (DPO, KTO), while approaching oracle performance across multiple sampling temperatures, model scales and protein families. Moreover, PLMs fine-tuned with unsupervised rewards can achieve consistently higher coverage compared to their base model in pass@k evaluations. By enabling self-improvement of PLMs through their own generated experience, our framework provides a scalable pathway toward controllable biomolecular design in settings where labeled preferences or experimental feedback are scarce or unavailable.

</details>


### [255] [Online Reward-Punishment Learning from Fixed-Channel Perceptual Event Streams without Environment Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18963)
*Zirong Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces OHIRL (Online Hidden-schema Intrinsic Reward Learning), a framework where an agent learns from raw perceptual streams without explicit rewards. Four specialized modules handle next-packet prediction, residual dynamics modeling, fixed trajectory evaluation, and value-evidence-based policy optimization. The system uses a recovery-positive, persistence-negative orientation, achieving high accuracy in sign attribution and optimal-action selection across various benchmark tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address online reward-punishment learning when the environment provides no scalar reward or evaluative labels — only fixed-channel perceptual packets. The agent must infer valence (positive/negative) of perceptual dimensions from transition consequences, mirroring how biological systems might assign value without explicit external reinforcement signals.

Method: OHIRL separates learning into four roles: (1) M_ψ for next-packet prediction, (2) D_ω for residual dynamics modeling, (3) C_η as a fixed internal post-transition trajectory evaluator using a recovery-positive and persistence/growth-negative residual-regulation orientation, and (4) B_ξ for converting value evidence into policy updates and action scoring. A conditional error decomposition separates evidence-estimation error from policy-optimization error. The protocol withholds environment rewards, delayed external evaluators, success labels, and action-goodness labels.

Result: In a 2×2-XOR packet task, medicine and chili acquire opposite value under visual XOR contexts, with B_ξ reaching 0.952 balanced reward-sign accuracy. In full online-interleaved audit: M_ψ holdout R²=0.907, B_ξ sign accuracy=0.940, policy optimal-action accuracy=0.979. Controls using immediate packet scores, prediction-error rewards, shuffled targets, zero reward, and error-reduction all collapse. Coefficient-origin audit shows equal-unit, raw-equal, and random monotone C_η variants preserve >92% of top-action rankings; sign inversion preserves 0%. Hidden-reward CartPole and Taxi controls further validate the framework.

Conclusion: The OHIRL framework demonstrates that effective reward-punishment learning is possible without explicit environment rewards by inferring valence from transition consequences. The four-module architecture successfully separates concerns, and the recovery-positive orientation proves robust across C_η variants, suggesting a general principle for intrinsic motivation in reinforcement learning.

Abstract: We study online reward-punishment learning when the environment provides no scalar reward or evaluative label. At each step the agent receives only a fixed-channel perceptual packet, and quantities such as pain, energy, contact, damage, or cognitive error are treated as perceptual dimensions whose valence must be inferred from transition consequences. OHIRL separates four roles: M_psi learns next-packet prediction, D_omega models residual dynamics, C_eta is a fixed internal post-transition trajectory evaluator, and B_xi learns to use the resulting value evidence for later policy updates and action scoring. C_eta uses a recovery-positive and persistence/growth-negative residual-regulation orientation; a coefficient-origin audit shows that equal-unit, raw-equal, and random monotone variants preserve more than 92% of the released top-action rankings, while sign inversion preserves 0%.
  The reward-free protocol exposes observation transitions while withholding environment rewards, delayed external evaluators, success labels, and action-goodness labels. A conditional error decomposition separates B_xi evidence-estimation error from residual policy-optimization error. In a 2x2-XOR packet task, medicine and chili acquire opposite value under visual XOR contexts, and the same pain or spice increase can be positive or negative depending on consequence structure; B_xi reaches 0.952 balanced reward-sign accuracy. In a full online-interleaved audit, M_psi reaches holdout R2=0.907, B_xi reaches 0.940 sign accuracy, and the policy reaches 0.979 optimal-action accuracy, while immediate packet scores, prediction-error rewards, shuffled targets, zero reward, and error-reduction controls collapse. Hidden-reward CartPole and Taxi controls, public-context no-leakage audits, and module-role ablations further test information boundaries and component necessity.

</details>


### [256] [EfficientRollout: System-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for RL Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18967)
*Minseo Kim,Minjae Lee,Seunghyuk Oh,Kevin Galim,Donghoon Kim,Coleman Hooper,Harman Singh,Amir Gholami,Hyung Il Koo,Wonjun Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EfficientRollout is a system-aware self-speculative decoding framework that accelerates RL training rollouts for LLMs by using a quantized drafter derived from the evolving target model and a toggle policy that activates speculation only in beneficial compute regimes, achieving up to 19.6% rollout and 12.7% end-to-end latency reduction without degrading model quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL post-training of LLMs suffers from a rollout latency bottleneck because autoregressive decoding is sequential and dominated by long-tailed generations. While speculative decoding (SD) can reduce serving latency, its benefits do not directly transfer to RL rollouts due to two issues: (1) a fixed drafter becomes mismatched with the evolving target policy during training, and (2) shrinking batch sizes during rollout decoding shift from compute-bound to memory-bound regimes, where naive SD can actually hurt throughput.

Method: EfficientRollout introduces (1) self-speculative decoding with a quantized drafter derived from the target model itself, keeping the drafter aligned with the evolving policy without separate pretraining or online adaptation; (2) a system-aware SD toggle policy that activates speculation only in memory-bound regimes and deactivates it in compute-bound regimes; and (3) acceptance-aware draft-length adaptation that adjusts the drafting budget based on the evolving drafter quality to avoid wasted compute.

Result: EfficientRollout reduces rollout latency by up to 19.6% and end-to-end training latency by up to 12.7% over an accelerated autoregressive rollout baseline, while preserving final model quality.

Conclusion: Self-speculative decoding combined with system-aware scheduling effectively bridges the gap between SD and RL rollouts, enabling meaningful latency reductions without sacrificing the quality of the trained policy.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a representative post-training paradigm for LLMs, enabling strong reasoning and agentic capabilities. However, rollout generation remains a dominant latency bottleneck because autoregressive sampling decodes responses sequentially and a small number of long-tailed generations often determine completion time. Speculative decoding (SD) offers a natural way to address this bottleneck, as it is a well-established technique for serving fixed LLMs that reduces latency by rapidly drafting tokens and accepting them through parallel verification while preserving the target-model distribution. However, its practical speedups do not directly carry over to RL rollouts: (i) the evolving target policy makes any fixed drafter increasingly mismatched with the policy's output distribution; and (ii) active batch sizes shrink throughout rollout decoding, shifting decoding from compute-bound to memory-bound regimes where parallel verification can exploit underutilized compute. Therefore, accelerating RL rollouts requires both a drafter that remains effective under long, high-temperature generations from an evolving policy and system-aware use of SD that avoids compute-bound regimes. We present EfficientRollout, a system-aware self-SD framework designed to address this gap for RL rollouts. EfficientRollout induces a quantized drafter from the target model (i.e. self-speculative decoding), keeping it coupled to the evolving policy without separate drafter pretraining or online adaptation. It further coordinates a system-aware SD toggle policy with acceptance-aware draft-length adaptation, enabling speculation only in beneficial regimes while matching the drafting budget to evolving drafter quality. EfficientRollout reduces rollout and end-to-end latency by up to 19.6% and 12.7%, respectively, over an accelerated AR rollout baseline, while preserving final model quality.

</details>


### [257] [A Controlled Benchmark of Quantum-Latent GAN Augmentation for Brain MRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18970)
*Syed Mujtaba Haider,Silvia Figini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A controlled benchmark comparing quantum vs. classical generative augmentation for brain MRI classification finds no significant benefit from either over real-data-only training, with quantum and classical generators statistically indistinguishable and suffering from mode collapse in low-data regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work claiming accuracy gains from quantum generative augmentation in medical imaging suffers from critical methodological flaws: single training runs, unmatched parameter budgets between quantum and classical models, and no characterization of the data regime where benefits supposedly emerge. A rigorous, controlled study is needed.

Method: Images are encoded into a KL-regularized latent space. A conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (cWGAN-GP) is trained with either a variational quantum generator (1,648 parameters) or a classical generator (1,632 parameters) — nearly identical budgets. Synthetic samples are decoded and used to augment a pretrained classifier across labeled data fractions (5%–100%), evaluated over eight random seeds with paired significance testing (with multiple-comparison correction), intraset diversity analysis, and latent-distribution analysis.

Result: Across all data fractions, no augmentation variant significantly outperforms real-data-only training. The quantum and classical generators are statistically indistinguishable. In low-data settings, synthetic samples are off-distribution and severely mode-collapsed; the quantum generator shows no greater diversity. Any apparent low-data benefit reflects regularization, not faithful data expansion.

Conclusion: Claims of quantum advantage for generative medical image augmentation are unsupported under controlled, matched-budget conditions. The authors release their protocol as a testbed for rigorous future evaluation.

Abstract: Medical image classification is often constrained by limited labeled data, motivating generative augmentation; recently, quantum generative models have been proposed for this purpose, frequently reporting accuracy gains. However, such claims are typically based on single training runs, do not match the parameter budgets of the quantum and classical generators, and do not characterize the data regime in which any benefit appears. We present a controlled benchmark that isolates the contribution of a quantum generator to brain-MRI augmentation. Images are encoded into a KL-regularized latent space in which a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty is trained using either a variational quantum generator or a classical generator of near-identical parameter count (1648 vs. 1632). Synthetic samples are decoded and used to augment a pretrained classifier across labeled data fractions from 5% to 100%, evaluated over eight random seeds with paired significance testing (with multiple-comparison correction) and with intraset diversity and latent-distribution analyses. Across all fractions, no augmentation variant significantly outperforms real-data-only training, and the quantum and classical generators are statistically indistinguishable. Any low-data benefit behaves as regularization rather than faithful data expansion:synthetic samples are off distribution and severely mode collapsed precisely where data is scarce, and the quantum generator is no more diverse thanits classical counterpart. We release the protocol as a testbed for rigorous evaluation of quantum generative augmentation in medical imaging.

</details>


### [258] [DIPHINE: Diffusion-based $Φ$-ID Neural Estimator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18997)
*Simon Pedro Galeano Munoz,Mustapha Bounoua,Giulio Franzese,Pietro Michiardi,Maurizio Filippone*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DIPHINE introduces a diffusion-model-based neural estimator for Integrated Information Decomposition (ΦID), extending the framework beyond Gaussian/discrete systems to continuous non-Gaussian dynamics. It jointly estimates all required mutual information terms via a single amortized network, recovers sixteen information atoms via Möbius inversion, and provides theoretical error propagation analysis showing the synergy-to-synergy atom is the hardest to estimate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ΦID is a powerful framework for characterizing multivariate information dynamics (redundant, unique, synergistic storage, transfer, and integration), but existing computational methods are limited to Gaussian or discrete systems, barring application to real-world continuous non-Gaussian dynamical systems. A general-purpose estimator is needed.

Method: DIPHINE uses score-based diffusion models as a neural mutual information estimator to jointly estimate all mutual information terms needed for ΦID from a single amortized network. The sixteen ΦID atoms are then recovered via Möbius inversion. A theoretical analysis of error propagation through the inversion is provided, including the result that the Jacobian is integer-valued and the synergy-to-synergy atom has the highest error amplification.

Result: DIPHINE achieves accurate recovery of ground-truth atoms on synthetic benchmarks, outperforms established mutual information estimators, and successfully extracts physiologically interpretable information-dynamic structure from real-world data without distributional assumptions.

Conclusion: DIPHINE enables ΦID analysis on arbitrary continuous dynamical systems for the first time, removing restrictive distributional assumptions. The theoretical error analysis provides practical guidance on which atoms are reliably estimable, with synergy-to-synergy being the most challenging.

Abstract: Uncovering the true informational architecture of real-world complex systems requires disentangling how their components uniquely store, redundantly share, and synergistically integrate information over time. Integrated Information Decomposition ($Φ$ID) is a framework for decomposing the information dynamics of multivariate systems into sixteen non-overlapping atoms that characterize redundant, unique, and synergistic modes of information storage, transfer, and integration. Existing methods to compute $Φ$ID are restricted to Gaussian or discrete systems, preventing its application to continuous non-Gaussian dynamical systems. We address this limitation by proposing DIPHINE (Diffusion-based $Φ$-ID Neural Estimator), the first neural estimator that leverages score-based diffusion models to jointly estimate all the mutual information terms required by $Φ$ID from a single amortized network, recovering the sixteen atoms through Möbius inversion. We provide a theoretical analysis of error propagation through the inversion, showing that the Jacobian of the mapping from mutual informations to atoms is integer-valued and that the synergy-to-synergy atom is provably the hardest to estimate. We demonstrate accurate recovery of ground-truth atoms on synthetic benchmarks, superior performance compared to established mutual information estimators, and the ability to extract physiologically interpretable information-dynamic structure on an application involving real data without any distributional assumptions.

</details>


### [259] [FoMoE: Breaking the Full-Replica Barrier with a Federation of MoEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19025)
*Lorenzo Sani,Zeyu Cao,Meghdad Kurmanji,Alex Iacob,Andrej Jovanovic,Yan Gao,Wanru Zhao,Nicholas D. Lane*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FoMoE introduces a geographically distributed training system for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs that partitions expert layers across workers instead of requiring full model replicas at each site, achieving significant reductions in communication costs and throughput improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing distributed MoE training methods (DiLoCo, Photon) require full model replicas at every data center, creating prohibitive memory constraints and communication overhead. The authors aim to overcome this fundamental inefficiency while preserving the benefits of low-communication, cross-datacenter training.

Method: FoMoE partitions expert layers across geographically distributed workers rather than replicating them. It employs partial expert replication to reduce communication, introduces a skip-token mechanism for throughput gains, and uses system modeling to project benefits to 100B-parameter scale configurations.

Result: FoMoE reduces communication costs by up to 1.42x over efficient baselines and 45.44x over DDP. The skip-token mechanism yields empirical throughput speedups up to 1.4x. The system demonstrates stable routing in trained proxy regimes and projects communication/memory benefits to 100B-scale models via system modeling.

Conclusion: Breaking the full-replica paradigm by partitioning expert layers is a viable and efficient strategy for distributed MoE training across weakly-connected data centers, offering substantial communication and memory savings that scale to very large models.

Abstract: Pre-training Large Language Models (LLMs) typically demands large-scale infrastructure with tightly coupled hardware accelerators. While increasing model and dataset scale remains the dominant driver of performance, Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) architectures have recently achieved state-of-the-art results by decoupling parameter count from computational cost. This efficiency enables training massive models on constrained compute budgets, yet it typically requires the high-speed interconnects of a single datacenter. To overcome these physical limits, recent approaches such as DiLoCo and Photon use low-communication data-parallel methods to enable scaling across geographically distributed, weakly connected data centers. However, these methods suffer from a fundamental inefficiency: they require full model replicas at every site, which imposes prohibitive memory constraints and communication overheads. In this work, we introduce FoMoE, a system that breaks the full-replica paradigm by partitioning expert layers across workers. We demonstrate that FoMoE: (I) reduces communication costs by up to 1.42x over efficient baselines and 45.44x over DDP via partial expert replication in the studied regimes; (II) achieves empirical throughput speedups of up to 1.4x through a novel skip-token mechanism; and (III) shows stable routing in the trained proxy regimes and projects the communication/memory benefits to 100B-scale configurations through system modelling.

</details>


### [260] [A Hybrid LSTM--Vision Transformer Architecture for Predicting HRRR Forecast Errors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19026)
*David Aaron Evans,Jay C. Rothenberger,Kara J. Sulia,Nick P. Bassill,Chris D. Thorncroft*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid LSTM-Vision Transformer (LSTM-ViT) model that combines surface observations with atmospheric profile data outperforms baseline LSTM networks in predicting HRRR forecast errors, particularly for precipitation and during active PBL periods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecast errors in high-resolution NWP are linked to unresolved boundary layer processes and vertical atmospheric structures. Previous LSTM-based error prediction degrades during complex vertical atmospheric evolution, motivating integration of vertical profile information.

Method: The authors develop an LSTM-ViT hybrid framework that combines LSTM temporal sequence learning from surface observations with Vision Transformer attention mechanisms operating on atmospheric profiles from the NYS Mesonet profiler network. The model predicts HRRR forecast errors for hourly precipitation, 10 m wind speed, and 2 m temperature at individual stations.

Result: Incorporating profiler-derived atmospheric structure improved forecast error prediction across all three variables. Gains were largest at shorter lead times and during enhanced PBL activity. Precipitation error prediction showed a twofold increase in skill, with better capture of convectively driven error evolution.

Conclusion: Combining temporal sequence learning with vertically informed attention mechanisms provides a physically meaningful approach to improving forecast error prediction in operational NWP, offering enhanced guidance on model bias and forecast confidence.

Abstract: Forecast errors in high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems are often linked to unresolved planetary boundary layer (PBL) processes, convection, terrain-induced circulations, and other vertically structured atmospheric phenomena. Previous work demonstrated that Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can successfully predict forecast errors in the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model using mesonet observations, but we believe performance degradation is linked to periods of complex vertical atmospheric evolution. To address this limitation, we develop a hybrid LSTM-Vision Transformer (LSTM-ViT) framework that combines temporal sequence learning from surface observations with atmospheric profiles from the New York State Mesonet profiler network. The LSTM-ViT framework is trained to predict HRRR hourly precipitation, 10 m wind speed, and 2 m temperature forecast errors at individual mesonet stations. Across all three predictors, incorporation of profiler-derived atmospheric structure improves forecast error prediction skill relative to the baseline LSTM architecture, with the largest gains occurring at shorter forecast lead times and during periods of enhanced PBL activity. Improvements are particularly pronounced for precipitation forecast error, where the LSTM-ViT framework achieves approximately a twofold increase in predictive skill relative to the baseline LSTM while better capturing convectively driven error evolution and reducing degradation associated with PBL processes. These results demonstrate that combining temporal sequence learning with vertically informed attention mechanisms provides a physically meaningful pathway for improving forecast error prediction in operational NWP systems. Our research offers forecasters enhanced guidance regarding model bias and forecast confidence.

</details>


### [261] [Geometric and Stochastic Analysis of Discontinuities in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19036)
*Tho Tran Huu,Huu-Tuan Nguyen,Thien-Hai Nguyen,Nhat-Tri Ho,Viet-Hoang Tran,Tho Quan,Tan Minh Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a rigorous geometric and stochastic analysis of discontinuities in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) architectures caused by Top-k routing. The authors classify discontinuities by order, prove that lower-order discontinuities dominate in volume, and show that random input perturbations almost surely hit order-1 discontinuities first. Motivated by these findings, they propose a lightweight smoothing mechanism that improves both continuity and empirical performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Top-k expert selection in SMoE models creates inherent discontinuities in the input-output mapping, where arbitrarily close inputs can activate different expert sets and produce significantly different outputs. Understanding the geometric structure and stochastic properties of these discontinuities is essential for diagnosing and mitigating their impact on model robustness and performance.

Method: The authors (1) classify discontinuities by order based on the number of tied experts at switching events; (2) use measure-theoretic slicing arguments to derive asymptotic volume estimates for thickened discontinuity surfaces; (3) model random input perturbations as a diffusion process to analyze hitting probabilities and occupation times near discontinuities; and (4) propose a simple smoothing mechanism that softly incorporates experts near discontinuity regions with bounded computational overhead.

Result: Lower-order discontinuity sets dominate in volume, while higher-order ones occupy negligible relative volume. A random diffusion path almost surely hits an order-1 discontinuity first, with explicit finite-time probability bounds. Occupation-time bounds quantify time spent near each discontinuity order. The proposed smoothing mechanism incurs small computational overhead, enforces continuity, and improves empirical performance on both language and vision tasks.

Conclusion: The theoretical analysis reveals that lower-order discontinuities are the most practically significant in SMoEs. The proposed smoothing method effectively addresses these discontinuities with minimal overhead, yielding both theoretical continuity guarantees and improved downstream task performance across modalities.

Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) architectures are now widely deployed in state-of-the-art language and vision models, where conditional routing allows scaling to very large networks. However, this very Top-$k$ expert selection that enables conditional routing also renders the SMoE map inherently discontinuous. In the vicinity of these discontinuity surfaces, even inputs that are arbitrarily close may activate substantially different sets of experts resulting in significantly different outputs. In this work we give a rigorous geometric and stochastic analysis of these discontinuities. We first classify them by order, determined by the number of tied experts at a switching event. Using measure-theoretic slicing arguments, we establish asymptotic volume estimates for the thickened discontinuity surfaces, showing that lower-order discontinuity sets dominate, whereas higher-order ones occupy a vanishingly small relative volume. Next, modeling random perturbations in the input space via a diffusion process, we prove that the path eventually encounter a discontinuity, and moreover that the first hit almost surely occurs on an order-1 discontinuity with explicit finite-time probability bounds. We further derive occupation-time bounds that quantify the duration the random path spend in the neighborhoods of each discontinuity order. These theoretical results imply that inputs are more likely to lie near lower order discontinuities. Motivated by this insight, we propose a simple smoothing mechanism that can be directly applied to existing SMoEs, softly incorporating experts near discontinuities; our analysis guarantees that the added computational overhead remains small while providing localized smoothing near discontinuities, and experiments across language and vision tasks show that smoothing not only enforces continuity of the SMoE map but also enhances empirical performance.

</details>


### [262] [Smoothness-Based Derandomization of PAC-Bayes Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19105)
*Alexandre Lemire Paquin,Brahim Chaib-Draa,Philippe Giguère*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper develops PAC-Bayes derandomization bounds for smooth loss functions, showing that the cost of moving from a Gibbs (stochastic) predictor to a deterministic one at the posterior mean is precisely the generalization gap of the Jensen gap class. This is controlled via Rademacher complexity, yielding bounds involving Jacobians and Hessians of the score map. The theory motivates a practical regularizer tested on CIFAR-10 with BatchNorm networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PAC-Bayes bounds typically apply to randomized predictors (Gibbs classifiers), but practical deployment uses deterministic predictors. The authors aim to bridge this gap by deriving high-probability generalization bounds for deterministic predictors, exploiting smoothness properties of the loss and predictor class rather than relying on Lipschitz continuity or boundedness alone.

Method: The authors analyze the derandomization cost from Gibbs predictor to the posterior mean predictor, identifying this cost as the generalization gap of the "Jensen gap class." They bound this class's Rademacher complexity, yielding deterministic generalization bounds that depend on flatness quantities: parameter Jacobians (first-order derivatives) and Hessians (second-order derivatives) of the score map. The framework handles both bounded and unbounded smooth losses and is specialized to linear predictors and smooth neural networks. The derived flatness quantities are repurposed as a practical regularizer, particularly for BatchNorm networks where the regularizer is computed with respect to effective weights obtained by folding BatchNorm into adjacent affine layers.

Result: The authors derive generalization bounds for deterministic predictors that scale with Jacobian and Hessian-based flatness measures rather than worst-case Lipschitz constants. The practical regularizer arising from these theoretical quantities is evaluated on CIFAR-10 across different batch sizes, demonstrating its behavior in conjunction with BatchNorm networks.

Conclusion: Smoothness-based PAC-Bayes derandomization provides principled generalization bounds for deterministic predictors, with the Jensen gap class serving as the key analytical bridge. The resulting Jacobian and Hessian flatness quantities offer both theoretical insight and practical regularization value, particularly for modern architectures with BatchNorm.

Abstract: We study PAC-Bayes derandomization for smooth loss functions. Our goal is to obtain generalization bounds that hold with high probability for deterministic predictors by exploiting smoothness properties of both the loss and the predictor class. We show that passing from the Gibbs predictor to the deterministic predictor at the posterior mean has a precise cost, given by the generalization gap of the Jensen gap class. We control this class through its Rademacher complexity, leading to bounds for deterministic predictors that involve flatness quantities expressed in terms of parameter Jacobians and Hessians of the score map. The framework applies to both bounded and unbounded smooth loss functions, and we specialize the results to linear predictors and smooth neural networks. Finally, the Jacobian and Hessian quantities appearing in the theory motivate a practical regularizer. For BatchNorm networks, we compute this regularizer with respect to effective BatchNorm weights obtained by folding the BatchNorm transformation into the adjacent affine weights. Experiments on CIFAR-10 illustrate the behavior of this regularizer under different batch sizes.

</details>


### [263] [JourneyFormer: Encoding Airbnb Guest Journey with Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19108)
*Daochen Zha,Chun How Tan,Xin Liu,Bin Xu,Han Zhao,Xiaowei Liu,Tracy Yu,Hui Gao,Huiji Gao,Liwei He,Stephanie Moyerman,Sanjeev Katariya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JourneyFormer is a sequence modeling solution deployed for search ranking at Airbnb, addressing production challenges of long, exploratory guest sequences and sparse booking labels through careful design choices in event selection, ID embeddings, model architecture, label attribution, and training/inference acceleration strategies, with validated gains in both offline metrics and online A/B tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sequence models are theoretically well-suited for capturing user historical behaviors in recommendation/ranking, but practical deployment in production systems like Airbnb is difficult due to: (1) long, exploratory, and complex guest interaction sequences, and (2) sparse booking labels. These challenges necessitate careful trade-offs between model effectiveness and scalability.

Method: The authors propose JourneyFormer, a production sequence modeling framework for Airbnb's search ranking. Key design considerations include: (a) guest event selection — determining which historical events to include in the sequence; (b) ID embeddings — how to represent entity identifiers; (c) model architecture design for handling long, complex sequences; (d) label attribution — determining which historical actions to associate with sparse booking labels. Additionally, tailored strategies are introduced to accelerate both training and inference.

Result: JourneyFormer was deployed across two production surfaces at Airbnb. Offline evaluation showed improved ranking metrics. Online A/B testing demonstrated significant gains in key business metrics, confirming the practical effectiveness of the design choices and acceleration strategies.

Conclusion: Sequence modeling can be effectively deployed at scale in production ranking systems when careful attention is paid to data selection, embedding design, architecture choices, label handling, and computational efficiency. JourneyFormer serves as a case study demonstrating that thoughtful engineering and modeling trade-offs can yield measurable business impact in large-scale recommendation systems.

Abstract: Sequence modeling has become increasingly popular in recommendation and ranking algorithms, owing to its capacity to model users' historical behaviors and infer user intentions. Despite its theoretical simplicity, the practical deployment of a sequence model in production is non-trivial due to complexity of the sequence and sparse labels. For example, in Airbnb, guest sequences are often long, exploratory and complex, and we focus on booking labels, which are sparse. As such, we are often required to make various design decisions regarding data and modeling to strike a balance between effectiveness and scalability. This work delved into these production challenges and deployed JourneyFormer, a sequence modeling solution for search ranking at Airbnb.
