We detail crucial design considerations, covering aspects such as guest event selection, ID embeddings, model architecture, and label attribution. Additionally, we describe several tailored strategies to accelerate model training and inference. JourneyFormer has been successfully deployed within Airbnb's production, where its effectiveness and impact have been evidenced not only by improved offline ranking metrics but also by significant gains in key business metrics through online A/B testing across 2 production surfaces.

</details>


### [264] [Seeing Before Reasoning: Decoupling Perception and Reasoning for Shortcut-Resilient Multimodal On-Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19120)
*Sihan Wang,Xiyao Liu,Lianqing Liu,Zhi Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ViGOS extends on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) to multimodal LLMs by adding a visual description phase supervised by an image-only teacher, preventing the model from shortcutting to text-only reasoning and improving image-grounded behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directly applying OPSD to MLLMs creates a shortcut where the privileged teacher's dense token-level targets can guide generation based primarily on the text reference rather than visual input, undermining multimodal grounding. The authors aim to preserve OPSD's benefits while enforcing genuine visual reasoning.

Method: ViGOS uses a two-phase student rollout: first a visual description, then reasoning to the final answer. Three teachers are employed — (1) an image-only perception teacher that supervises the description using only visual input for valid rollouts, (2) a privileged reasoning teacher that supervises reasoning and answer conditioned on both image and reference text, and (3) a reference teacher used only for invalid rollouts to recover output format. This structurally enforces visual grounding before reasoning.

Result: ViGOS retains the main benefits of OPSD while significantly improving image-grounded behavior in shortcut-prone settings. Improvements are demonstrated across diverse benchmarks including general vision-language, expert reasoning, visual math, spatial grounding, and visual-language-prior tasks.

Conclusion: Forcing the model to generate explicit visual descriptions under image-only supervision before reasoning effectively mitigates the text-only shortcut in OPSD for MLLMs, yielding a robust visually grounded self-distillation framework for multimodal post-training.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a model on its own rollouts and uses a frozen copy to provide dense token-level targets conditioned on a reference target. This works well for LLM reasoning, but a direct extension to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can create a shortcut: the privileged target may guide tokens mainly based on the text reference target rather than the image. We propose ViGOS, a visually grounded OPSD framework for MLLM post-training. The student first writes a visual description and then reasons toward the final answer. For valid rollouts, an image-only perception teacher supervises the description, while a privileged reasoning teacher supervises the reasoning and final answer on the same student prefix. A reference teacher is used only for invalid rollouts to recover the output format. Across general vision-language, expert reasoning, visual math, spatial grounding, and visual-language-prior benchmarks, ViGOS keeps the main benefits of OPSD and improves image-grounded behavior in shortcut-prone settings.

</details>


### [265] [Pareto Q-Learning with Reward Machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19134)
*Arnaud Lequen,Clément Legrand-Lixon,Léo Saulières*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PQLRM integrates Pareto Q-Learning with Reward Machines to enable sample-efficient multi-objective RL under non-Markovian reward structures, outperforming both naive PQL on cross-product MDPs and single-objective QRM in synthesizing Pareto-optimal policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multi-objective RL struggles with non-Markovian reward signals (e.g., temporally extended tasks). Reward Machines can encode such structure, but existing RM-based methods like QRM are single-objective. PQL can approximate Pareto fronts but lacks sample efficiency when naively applied to the cross-product MDP. The authors aim to combine the strengths of both approaches.

Method: PQLRM marries Pareto Q-Learning (maintaining sets of vector-valued Q-estimates per state to track the Pareto front) with QRM's counter-based Q-value tracking that leverages the RM's automaton structure. This avoids the cross-product state explosion by exploiting factored RM states while maintaining multi-dimensional value estimates, enabling multi-policy, sample-efficient learning.

Result: Experimental trials demonstrate that PQLRM converges faster than a naive PQL baseline operating on the full cross-product MDP and can successfully synthesize Pareto-optimal policies that the single-objective QRM algorithm cannot produce.

Conclusion: PQLRM effectively bridges multi-objective RL and reward-machine-based RL, yielding a sample-efficient algorithm capable of learning Pareto fronts under non-Markovian reward specifications, with clear empirical advantages over both naive PQL and standard QRM.

Abstract: We present Pareto Q-Learning with Reward Machines (PQLRM), a multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm for tasks whose reward structure is specified by a set of reward machines (RMs). PQLRM combines Pareto Q-Learning (PQL), which maintains sets of vector-valued Q-estimates to approximate the Pareto front, with enhancements from Q-Learning with Reward Machines (QRM), which exploits the factored automaton structure of the reward signal. This yields a multi-policy algorithm that remains sample-efficient under non-Markovian, RM-encoded rewards. Experimental trials show that PQLRM converges faster than a naive PQL baseline applied to the cross-product MDP and can synthesize Pareto-optimal policies that QRM cannot.

</details>


### [266] [INDEQS: Informed Neural controlled Differential EQuationS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19138)
*Michael Detzel,Gabriel Nobis,Kristiyan Blagov,Juri Schubert,Jackie Ma,Wojciech Samek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: INDEQS is a graph-based Neural CDE framework that injects prior knowledge of a directed graph at distinct architectural positions (inner vs. outer mixing), with variants spanning lightweight constrained to expressive adaptive models. Across synthetic advection simulations and real-world hydrology/traffic tasks, outer informedness consistently improves accuracy, while inner informedness offers parameter efficiency; continuous-time decoders outperform discrete ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard graph-based NCDE extensions learn spatial structure purely from data, even when a directed graph is known a priori. The authors aim to systematically study when and how incorporating known graph structure benefits forecasting, and to design architectures that can leverage such prior knowledge effectively.

Method: INDEQS separates two distinct mixing operations: (1) inner mixing—message passing among hidden states across graph nodes within the vector field, and (2) outer mixing—interaction between the vector field and the control (input features). It offers a graph-constrained variant that strictly uses the known adjacency and a more expressive variant using adaptive graph convolutions to learn additional connections. The framework is evaluated on a novel continuous advection simulation on directed graphs (synthetic ground-truth), river discharge forecasting on a hydrological network, and traffic flow prediction on PeMS08. Both discrete convolutional and continuous-time decoders are compared.

Result: Outer informedness consistently improves MAE over uninformed NCDE baselines with comparable parameters, especially on larger graphs. Inner informedness provides a more parameter-efficient option when strict adherence to the known adjacency is needed. Continuous-time decoders yield better accuracy and greater temporal flexibility than discrete convolutional decoders on real-world tasks.

Conclusion: Injecting known directed graph structure into NCDEs is broadly beneficial, with outer informedness being the more robust strategy for accuracy and inner informedness favoring parameter efficiency. The choice of decoder (continuous vs. discrete) meaningfully impacts performance. The released codebase and advection simulation support reproducibility and further research.

Abstract: Neural Controlled Differential Equations (NCDE) provide a powerful continuous-time framework for forecasting time series, but standard graph-based extensions typically learn spatial structure purely from data, even in settings where a directed graph structure is known a priori. We introduce Informed Neural controlled Differential EQuationS (INDEQS), a graph-based NCDE forecasting method that incorporates prior knowledge of a directed graph at distinct architectural positions. INDEQS separates inner mixing of hidden states across graph nodes from outer mixing between vector field and control, and offers both a lightweight graph-constrained variant and a more expressive variant, learning additional graph connections from data via adaptive graph convolutions. To systematically study when graph informedness is beneficial in forecasting, we devise a continuous advection simulation on directed graphs, yielding synthetic spatio-temporal datasets with known ground-truth flow structure. We then evaluate INDEQS on two real-world tasks: river discharge forecasting on a hydrological network and traffic flow prediction on PeMS08. Across these synthetic and real-world benchmarks, outer informedness consistently improves mean absolute error over an uninformed NCDE with comparable parameter count, particularly on larger graphs, while inner informedness offers a more parameter-efficient alternative when strict adherence to a known adjacency is desired. A comparison of discrete convolutional and continuous-time decoders further shows that continuous decoders yield better accuracy and greater temporal flexibility on real-world tasks. An implementation of INDEQS and the advection simulation is available at https://github.com/Mitchi1/indeqs.

</details>


### [267] [ChronoSurv: A Clinical Pathway-Guided Graph Framework for Multimodal Survival Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19140)
*Hugo Miccinilli,Theo Di Piazza*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ChronoSurv is a progression-aware, heterogeneous hierarchical directed graph framework for multimodal survival analysis in head and neck cancer that models patient care as a clinical trajectory, achieving state-of-the-art discriminative performance with reliable calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep survival models for head and neck cancer rely on static fusion strategies or temporally agnostic modeling, failing to capture the structured, sequential nature of clinical workflows across heterogeneous multimodal data.

Method: ChronoSurv models patient care as a progression-aware clinical trajectory using directed graphs aligned with key diagnostic steps. It employs a hierarchical topology with fine-grained, coarse, and global representations, supports flexible adaptation to missing modalities, and uses heterogeneous message passing to model complex, asymmetric relationships across modalities and clinical steps.

Result: On two public datasets, ChronoSurv achieves state-of-the-art discriminative performance and statistically reliable calibration. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each architectural component.

Conclusion: Trajectory-aware graph modeling shows strong potential for multimodal survival prediction, with ChronoSurv's progression-aware design and hierarchical heterogeneous message passing proving effective for capturing structured clinical workflows.

Abstract: Accurate survival prediction is essential for personalized treatment planning in head and neck cancer, yet remains challenging due to the heterogeneous and high-dimensional nature of multimodal clinical data. While deep survival models have improved predictive performance over classical statistical approaches, existing methods typically rely on static fusion strategies or temporally agnostic modeling, limiting their ability to capture structured clinical workflows. In this work, we propose ChronoSurv, a heterogeneous hierarchical directed graph framework for multimodal survival analysis. ChronoSurv represents patient care as a progression-aware clinical trajectory using directed graphs aligned with key diagnostic steps. A hierarchical topology incorporates fine-grained, coarse, and global representations, further supporting flexible adaptation to missing modalities, while heterogeneous message passing models complex and asymmetric relationships across modalities and clinical steps. Experimental results on two public datasets demonstrate that ChronoSurv achieves state-of-the-art discriminative performance while maintaining statistically reliable calibration. Comprehensive ablation studies further confirm the contribution of each architectural component, highlighting the potential of trajectory-aware graph modeling for multimodal survival prediction.

</details>


### [268] [OrthoReg: Orthogonal Regularization for Hybrid Symbolic-Neural Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19145)
*Till Richter,Niki Kilbertus*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OrthoReg introduces orthogonal regularization to prevent neural components from absorbing learned symbolic structure in hybrid dynamical system models, improving interpretability and out-of-distribution generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid modeling combines interpretable symbolic/physics-based components with flexible neural networks, but the neural part often relearns what the symbolic part already captures — especially when the symbolic structure is itself discovered via sparse regression. Standard L² regularization fails here because its projection argument breaks under sparse discovery, leading to redundancy and uninterpretability.

Method: OrthoReg directly penalizes functional overlap between symbolic and neural components by enforcing orthogonality in the learned representations. This ensures a complementary decomposition: the symbolic component captures what the candidate library can express, while the neural residual captures only what remains unexplained.

Result: On benchmark dynamical systems with partial library mismatch, OrthoReg improves symbolic recovery accuracy and enhances out-of-distribution prediction performance compared to standard L²-regularized baselines.

Conclusion: OrthoReg provides a principled way to achieve truly complementary hybrid models, preventing redundancy and yielding more interpretable and robust dynamical system representations when the symbolic structure is learned from data.

Abstract: Dynamical systems are fundamental to modeling the natural world, yet modeling them involves a persistent trade-off: manually prescribed mechanistic models are interpretable by design but often overly simplistic and misspecified; in contrast, flexible data-driven neural methods lack physical insight. Hybrid modeling aims for the best of both worlds by combining a prescribed or symbolic, physics-based component with a flexible neural network. A critical challenge, however, is that the neural component may relearn mechanistic parts, yielding redundant and uninterpretable models, especially when the symbolic structure itself is discovered from data. Existing methods based on standard $L^2$ regularization rely on a projection argument that breaks when the symbolic component is learned through sparse discovery, allowing the neural augmentation to overlap with symbolic structure. We introduce \textbf{OrthoReg} (Orthogonal Regularization), which directly penalizes overlap between the symbolic and neural components, preventing symbolic structure from being absorbed by the neural residual. This yields a complementary decomposition: the symbolic part captures what the library can express, and the neural part captures what remains. On benchmark dynamical systems with partial library mismatch, OrthoReg improves symbolic recovery and out-of-distribution behavior.

</details>


### [269] [Complementary Attention Head Pruning for Efficient Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19150)
*Yaniv Livertovsky,Shahar Somin,Gonen Singer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CAHP is a post-hoc structured pruning method that frames attention head selection as a graph-theoretical problem, using clustering and information-theoretic distance to automatically retain a diverse, complementary subset of heads without manual sparsity tuning. It outperforms baselines on SST-5 and MNLI, especially under high compression, and avoids the proximity bias of gradient-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer scaling yields massive parameter counts, hindering deployment in resource-constrained settings. Existing structured pruning methods (gradient-based importance ranking, stochastic gating) suffer from instability, structural degeneration, and require extensive manual hyperparameter tuning. There is a need for a principled, automated approach that selects attention heads based on global complementarity rather than isolated importance scores.

Method: CAHP (Complementary Attention Head Pruning) formulates head selection as a global graph-theoretical problem. It applies graph-based clustering with information-theoretic distance measures to identify a topologically diverse subset of complementary attention heads across layers. The framework automatically determines the number of heads to retain by detecting a diminishing marginal performance curve — a sharp degradation threshold identified via a chosen polynomial degree — eliminating the need for predefined sparsity ratios.

Result: CAHP consistently outperforms competitive baselines on SST-5 and MNLI benchmarks across different Transformer scales, with particularly strong gains in high-compression regimes. Structural analysis reveals that CAHP avoids the "proximity bias" of gradient-based methods (which over-preserve heads near the output layer) and instead retains functionally critical heads concentrated in intermediate layers.

Conclusion: CAHP demonstrates that global, complementarity-driven head selection via graph-theoretic and information-theoretic principles yields superior structured pruning outcomes compared to isolated importance ranking. The automatic sparsity determination and avoidance of proximity bias make it a robust, tuning-free compression framework suitable for resource-constrained deployment.

Abstract: The remarkable success of Transformer-based models in natural language processing stems from architectural scaling, which leads to a large number of parameters and hinders deployment in resource-constrained environments. While structured pruning offers a pathway to compression, existing state-of-the-art methods often rely on gradient-based importance ranking or stochastic gating, which suffer from instability, structural degeneration, and the need for extensive manual hyperparameter tuning. In this paper, we introduce CAHP (Complementary Attention Head Pruning), a novel post-hoc framework that redefines head selection as a global graph-theoretical problem. Rather than evaluating heads in isolation, CAHP utilizes graph-based clustering combined with information-theoretic distance measures to identify and preserve a topologically diverse subset of complementary attention heads. Without requiring a predefined sparsity level or pruning ratio, the framework automatically determines the number of selected attention heads across layers by identifying a diminishing marginal performance curve, where pruning additional heads leads to a sharp degradation in performance, as determined by the chosen polynomial degree. Extensive evaluations on the SST-5 and MNLI benchmarks, across different Transformer model scales, demonstrate that CAHP consistently outperforms competitive baselines, particularly in high-compression regimes. Furthermore, our structural analysis shows that CAHP avoids the "proximity bias" of gradient-based pruning methods, which tend to preserve heads mainly in layers close to the output, and instead retains a functionally critical set of attention heads in the model's intermediate layers.

</details>


### [270] [The Reward Was in Your Data All Along: Correcting Flow Matching with Discriminator-Guided RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19162)
*Nicolas Beltran-Velez,Felix Friedrich,Zhang Xiaofeng,Reyhane Askari-Hemmat,Xiaochuang Han,Adriana Romero-Soriano,Michal Drozdzal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies a structural mismatch in score/flow-matching models where training with ℓ2 regression on velocity/score fields poorly aligns with the perceptual properties that determine sample quality. The authors propose Discriminator-Guided RL (DRL), which trains a discriminator in a pretrained representation space and uses its logit as a reward for KL-regularized RL, achieving substantial improvements in FID and semantic metrics without human preference data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Score- and flow-matching models exhibit a structural mismatch: ℓ2 regression on velocity/score fields under training-time marginals is a poor proxy for the visual and semantic properties that determine inference-time sample quality. While preference-based RL can bypass this mismatch by directly optimizing sample quality, obtaining rewards without expensive human annotations remains a key challenge. The authors aim to provide an automatic reward signal that targets the true data distribution without conflating data realism with annotator inclinations.

Method: Discriminator-Guided RL (DRL) trains a discriminator to distinguish data samples from base-model samples within a pretrained representation space (e.g., DINOv3). The discriminator's logit serves as an estimate of the log-likelihood ratio between data and model distributions — the theoretically optimal reward for targeting the data distribution under KL-regularized RL. The pretrained space constrains the discriminator to perceptually meaningful directions, preventing exploitation of low-level artifacts. This reward is then used in KL-regularized reinforcement learning to fine-tune the generative model on its own samples.

Result: DRL achieves substantial improvements across multiple backbones: on SiT, guidance-free FID drops from 9.38 to 2.62, and DINOv3 semantic-space FD drops from 88.2 to 19.3. Consistent gains are observed across SiT, JiT, REPA, and RAE architectures. DRL also improves human-preference rewards without training on preference data, yields a better Pareto frontier between preference reward and image fidelity under subsequent preference-based post-training, increases alignment, and reduces low-level artifacts such as oversaturation and excessive brightness.

Conclusion: The structural mismatch between matching-based training objectives and perceptual sample quality necessitates RL-based fine-tuning, but human preference data is not required. DRL provides an effective, automatic reward signal via a discriminator operating in pretrained representation space, serving as an optimal log-likelihood ratio estimator. This approach consistently improves sample quality across diverse model architectures and complements subsequent preference-based alignment.

Abstract: Score- and flow-matching models often rely on preference-based reinforcement learning for two purposes: aligning with subjective preferences and, surprisingly, recovering properties such as visual realism and coherent object structure that matching-based training is intended to learn from the data itself. We argue that this reflects a structural mismatch. Matching losses measure $\ell_2$ regression error on the velocity or score field under training-time marginals, a proxy poorly aligned with the visual and semantic properties that determine sample quality at inference. Given a reward aligned with these properties, RL sidesteps the mismatch by evaluating the model on its own samples and following the reward landscape directly. The challenge is to obtain such a reward without relying on human preferences, which are expensive and conflate data realism with annotator inclinations.
  We propose Discriminator-Guided RL (DRL). DRL trains a discriminator to separate data from base-model samples in a pretrained representation space and uses its logit as the reward in KL-regularized RL. The pretrained space restricts the discriminator to perceptually meaningful directions, and the logit estimates the log-likelihood ratio between data and model, which is the optimal reward for targeting the data distribution. Across SiT, JiT, REPA, and RAE, DRL reduces guidance-free FID (e.g., $9.38 \to 2.62$ on SiT) and semantic-space FD (e.g., $88.2 \to 19.3$ on DINOv3 for SiT), with consistent gains across all backbones, and improves human-preference rewards without training on them. It also yields a better Pareto frontier between preference reward and image fidelity under subsequent preference-based post-training, increasing alignment while reducing low-level artifacts such as oversaturation and excessive brightness.

</details>


### [271] [Essential Subspace Merging for Multi-Task Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19164)
*Longhua Li,Lei Qi,Xin Geng,Qi Tian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Essential Subspace Decomposition (ESD) for model merging, observing that task-specific output shifts concentrate in few principal directions (essential subspace) while remaining directions cause interference. Two training-free methods are introduced: ESM (static merging via orthogonalization) and ESM++ (dynamic merging with low-rank experts and prototype routing).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model merging suffers from inter-task interference when combining multiple fine-tuned models. The authors identify that task-relevant energy is concentrated in a small number of principal directions (essential subspace), while the accumulation of low-energy directions across tasks causes severe interference during merging.

Method: First, Essential Subspace Decomposition (ESD) decomposes each task update according to principal components of its activation shift. Then, Essential Subspace Merging (ESM) performs training-free static merging by orthogonalizing and fusing essential components into one compact model. ESM++ extends this to dynamic merging by decomposing task-specific residuals into low-rank experts and using prototype-based routing during inference to select the most relevant expert.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple task sets and model scales demonstrate that both ESM and ESM++ effectively preserve task knowledge while reducing inter-task interference.

Conclusion: The essential subspace framework provides an effective lens for understanding and mitigating inter-task interference in model merging. ESM and ESM++ offer practical training-free solutions — static and dynamic respectively — that successfully balance task knowledge preservation with interference reduction across diverse settings.

Abstract: Model merging aims to enable multi-task learning by integrating the capabilities of multiple models fine-tuned from the same pre-trained checkpoint into a single model. Its core challenge is inter-task interference among task-specific parameter updates. In this paper, we analyze the output shifts induced by task updates and observe that their energy is concentrated in a small number of principal directions. We call the subspace spanned by these directions the essential subspace. In contrast, most remaining directions carry little task-relevant energy, but their accumulation across multiple task updates can cause severe interference during merging. Motivated by this observation, we propose Essential Subspace Decomposition (ESD), which decomposes each task update according to the principal components of its activation shift. Based on ESD, we introduce Essential Subspace Merging (ESM), a training-free static merging method that orthogonalizes and fuses essential components into one compact multi-task model. We further extend ESM to ESM++, a training-free dynamic merging method that decomposes task-specific residuals into low-rank experts and selects the most relevant expert through prototype-based routing during forward inference. Extensive experiments across multiple task sets and model scales demonstrate that ESM and ESM++ effectively preserves task knowledge while reducing inter-task interference.

</details>


### [272] [Compute Efficiency and Serial Runtime Tradeoffs for Stochastic Momentum Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19179)
*Depen Morwani,Alexandru Meterez,Pranav Nair,Sham Kakade*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes stochastic momentum methods (HB and ASGD) for linear regression, deriving lower bounds on batch-size tradeoffs. Key findings: HB preserves SGD-level compute efficiency over a larger batch-size window (up to √κ wider than SGD's critical batch size) but doesn't improve the CE frontier. ASGD improves small-batch CE for rapidly decaying spectra but trades this advantage for serial runtime as batch size grows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stochastic momentum methods like heavy ball and accelerated SGD are widely deployed in practice, yet their stochastic benefits are poorly understood in terms of the interplay between serial runtime (iterations to target accuracy) and compute efficiency (inverse total gradient/FLOP cost). Larger batches can reduce serial runtime without harming CE only if the contraction gap scales linearly with batch size — but when and whether this holds for momentum methods remains an open question requiring rigorous theoretical characterization.

Method: The authors study stochastic HB and ASGD in the setting of consistent linear regression with Gaussian covariates. They prove finite-dimensional, discrete-time lower bounds on the batch-size tradeoffs, characterizing the contraction gap's scaling behavior with batch size. The analysis distinguishes between arbitrary spectra and power-law spectra (both rapidly and slowly decaying) to reveal spectrum-dependent regimes.

Result: (1) HB does not improve the compute efficiency (CE) frontier over SGD for arbitrary spectra; it maintains SGD-level CE over a larger batch-size window that is up to a factor √κ wider than the SGD critical batch size. (2) For ASGD with rapidly decaying power-law spectra, small-batch CE improves over HB/SGD, but as batch size increases, this CE advantage is traded for improved serial runtime. (3) For slowly decaying spectra, ASGD and HB nearly overlap. Synthetic linear-regression experiments confirm these qualitative regimes.

Conclusion: Stochastic momentum methods offer nuanced, spectrum-dependent tradeoffs between compute efficiency and serial runtime. HB provides robustness to larger batch sizes without degrading CE, while ASGD offers a tunable CE–serial runtime tradeoff for rapidly decaying spectra. These insights clarify when and why momentum helps in stochastic training beyond the deterministic acceleration regime.

Abstract: Stochastic momentum methods such as heavy ball (HB), Nesterov momentum, and variants of Accelerated SGD (ASGD) [Kidambi et al., 2018] are widely used in modern training, but their stochastic benefits depend on two distinct quantities: serial runtime, the number of iterations needed to reach a target accuracy, and compute efficiency (CE), the inverse total gradient-query or FLOP cost. Larger batches reduce serial runtime without hurting CE only when the contraction gap grows linearly with batch size.
  We study stochastic HB and ASGD for consistent linear regression with Gaussian covariates and prove finite-dimensional, discrete-time lower bounds on their batch-size tradeoffs. Our first result shows that HB does not improve the CE frontier over SGD for arbitrary spectra; rather, it preserves SGD-level CE over a larger batch-size window, allowing larger batches to reduce serial runtime until HB reaches its deterministic accelerated scale. This window can be a factor $\sqrtκ$ larger than the SGD critical batch size. For ASGD, the picture is more spectrum-dependent: for rapidly decaying power-law spectra, ASGD improves small-batch CE over HB/SGD, but as batch size grows it trades this CE advantage for improved serial runtime. Synthetic linear-regression experiments verify these qualitative regimes, including near-overlap of ASGD and HB for slowly decaying spectra and the predicted CE--serial tradeoff for rapidly decaying spectra.

</details>


### [273] [AGDN: Learning to Solve Traveling Salesman Problem with Anisotropic Graph Diffusion Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19185)
*Bolin Shen,Ziwei Huang,Zhiguang Cao,Yushun Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AGDN is a Graph Neural Network for TSP that uses a MixScore transition matrix and anisotropic graph diffusion to overcome the limitations of fully connected graphs and graph sparsification, achieving state-of-the-art performance with strong generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-based learning methods for TSP face two key challenges: (1) fully connected TSP graphs lack informative topological priors, making it hard for GNNs to extract meaningful structure; (2) common graph sparsification techniques risk discarding edges that belong to the optimal TSP tour, degrading solution quality.

Method: The authors propose the Anisotropic Graph Diffusion Network (AGDN) with two core components: a MixScore transition matrix that fuses node similarity with pairwise distance information, and an anisotropic graph diffusion mechanism that enables efficient multi-hop information propagation while preserving edge-specific characteristics rather than using isotropic smoothing.

Result: Comprehensive experiments across diverse instance sizes and node distributions demonstrate that AGDN consistently outperforms existing methods while maintaining competitive computation time. The model also exhibits strong generalization to problem sizes and distributions unseen during training.

Conclusion: AGDN effectively addresses the structural limitations of applying GNNs to TSP by enriching graph topology with the MixScore matrix and anisotropic diffusion. The approach is practical, generalizable, and the code is publicly released.

Abstract: The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is a cornerstone of combinatorial optimization and arises in many practical scenarios. Although graph-based learning approaches have been explored for TSP, the question of how to exploit graph structure more effectively remains open. We present the Anisotropic Graph Diffusion Network (AGDN), a new Graph Neural Network framework designed to solve TSP. Our method tackles two central difficulties: (1) the lack of informative topological prior in fully connected TSP graphs, and (2) losing connected nodes in the optimal solution after the commonly used graph sparsification techniques. To overcome these issues, we construct a MixScore transition matrix that merges node similarity with pairwise distance, and we develop an anisotropic graph diffusion strategy that supports efficient information exchange across multiple hops. Comprehensive experiments spanning diverse instance sizes and node distributions show that AGDN consistently outperforms existing methods while keeping computation time competitive. Furthermore, AGDN generalizes well to problem sizes and distributions beyond those seen during training. The implementation is publicly available at: https://github.com/LabRAI/AGDN.

</details>


### [274] [Forecasting what Matters: Decision-Focused RL for Controlled EV Charging with Unknown Departure Times](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19199)
*Giuseppe Gabriele,Fabio Pavirani,Seyed Soroush Karimi Madahi,Chris Develder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a decision-focused reinforcement learning (DF-RL) framework where an EV charging forecaster is trained end-to-end with feedback from the RL controller, yielding up to 14% better total reward and 55% less unsupplied energy compared to RL without departure-time forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Growing EV adoption stresses power grids via peak demand and instability. Smart RL-based charging can help, but critical features like departure time are often unavailable in practice, degrading RL performance. Standard forecasters trained for accuracy may propagate errors that harm downstream control decisions.

Method: The authors propose DF-RL, a decision-focused reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains a forecaster and an RL charging agent end-to-end. The forecaster receives feedback from the RL agent's policy actions rather than being optimized solely for prediction accuracy, aligning forecasting objectives with downstream decision quality.

Result: DF-RL achieves up to 14% improvement in total reward and a 55% reduction in unsupplied energy (missed charging due to premature EV departure) compared to RL baselines that lack departure time forecasting.

Conclusion: End-to-end, decision-focused joint training of forecaster and controller significantly mitigates the negative impact of forecast errors on sequential decision-making, resulting in more reliable and effective EV charging policies under real-world uncertainty.

Abstract: The recent growth of EV adoption poses challenges for power systems, including increased peak demand and potential grid instability. Smart control of EV charging -- e.g., based on reinforcement learning (RL) -- can alleviate these issues by learning temporal and contextual patterns from historical data. Yet, in real-world scenarios, key features, such as departure time, often are unavailable. This, in turn, makes it harder for an RL agent to learn and execute an effective charging policy. To mitigate this uncertainty, a trained forecaster can approximate the unknown features from available data. However, since these forecasting models are typically trained for accuracy (rather than their impact on a downstream agent's decision quality), their errors may propagate and hinder the overall performance of a controller that is using the forecasts. To avoid this, we propose a decision-focused RL (DF-RL) framework in which the forecaster is trained end-to-end, i.e., with feedback from the charging policy actions taken by the RL agent. Such joint training of both the forecaster and controller ultimately results in higher-quality actions: our proposed DF-RL method yields superior charging decisions compared to other baselines, achieving up to a 14% improvement in total reward and a 55% reduction of unsupplied energy (i.e., charging that failed to happen because the EV already left), relative to the RL method without departure time forecasting.

</details>


### [275] [Machine Unlearning for the XGBoost Model with Network Intrusion Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19220)
*Diana Magalhães,Eva Maia,João Vitorino,Isabel Praça*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces XGBoost-Forget, a machine unlearning approach for XGBoost models applied to tabular network intrusion detection datasets (IoT-23, GeNIS), demonstrating fast unlearning with minimal predictive performance loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine unlearning research predominantly targets deep learning and image data, leaving a gap for tabular data domains like network intrusion detection. There is a need for efficient unlearning in XGBoost models — a popular choice for tabular NI tasks — to remove specific data points without full retraining.

Method: XGBoost-Forget, an unlearning approach tailored for the XGBoost model. Evaluated on two tabular Network Intrusion datasets (IoT-23 and GeNIS) using multiple metrics covering model performance, unlearning efficiency, and forgetting quality.

Result: XGBoost-Forget maintains predictive performance close to the original (fully retrained) model while achieving significantly faster unlearning, demonstrating practical feasibility for MU in tabular NI settings.

Conclusion: XGBoost-Forget is a viable and efficient MU solution for XGBoost in tabular network intrusion detection, bridging the gap left by image- and deep-learning-focused MU research.

Abstract: Machine Unlearning (MU) has emerged as an important technique for removing specific data points from trained models without requiring full retraining. However, most existing MU research focuses on deep learning and image data, leaving a gap in the domain of network intrusion detection, which relies heavily on tabular data. This work introduces XGBoost-Forget, an unlearning approach for the XGBoost model, to address this gap. The approach is evaluated on two tabular Network Intrusion (NI) datasets, IoT-23 and GeNIS, using multiple metrics to assess model performance, unlearning efficiency, and forgetting quality. The results show that XGBoost-Forget maintains predictive performance close to the original model while providing significantly faster unlearning, demonstrating its potential for MU in tabular NI settings.

</details>


### [276] [Mechanism-Guided Selective Unlearning for RLVR-Induced Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19222)
*Chenyu Zhou,Qiliang Jiang,Shuning Wu,Xu Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAST is a mechanism-aligned unlearning method that selectively updates top-ranked attention-projection tensors to forget RLVR-induced reasoning while preserving general mathematical capabilities, outperforming full-parameter gradient ascent which causes collateral damage to retain sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard full-parameter unlearning methods for removing RLVR-induced reasoning cause significant collateral damage to retained capabilities (MATH retain, GSM8K). The authors observe that the SFT-to-RLVR parameter increment is structurally distinct from the SFT update itself, motivating a targeted, mechanism-aware approach that only modifies parameters most responsible for the RLVR-specific behavior.

Method: MAST ranks attention-projection tensors using three criteria: off-principal energy, update magnitude, and forget-gradient coupling magnitude. Only the top-ranked subset of parameters is updated. The method is evaluated against full-parameter unlearning baselines (gradient ascent, NPO, SimNPO) on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Qwen3-1.7B-Base using matched SFT/RLVR checkpoint pairs, with forget performance measured on MATH forget split and retention on MATH retain and GSM8K.

Result: On the primary model (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B), MAST reduces MATH forget accuracy from 45/150 to 37/150 (McNemar p=0.0078, statistically significant) while preserving GSM8K (+0.8 pp) and MATH retain (-0.5 pp). Full-parameter unlearning damages both retain sets. Results replicate across seeds, NPO/SimNPO objectives, and on Qwen3-1.7B-Base, where MAST preserves GSM8K while full-parameter unlearning causes it to collapse.

Conclusion: Mechanism-aligned selective intervention in attention-projection tensors enables effective unlearning of RLVR-induced reasoning with minimal collateral damage, demonstrating that the RLVR increment is localized to specific parameter subspaces rather than distributed throughout the model.

Abstract: We propose MAST (Mechanism-Aligned Selective Targeting), a mechanism-guided method for unlearning RLVR-induced reasoning with substantially lower collateral damage than standard full-parameter updates. In matched SFT/RLVR checkpoints on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Qwen3-1.7B-Base, the SFT-to-RLVR increment differs sharply from the SFT update in token-level delta-log-probability, and full-parameter gradient ascent forgets only by damaging retain MATH and GSM8K. MAST ranks attention-projection tensors by off-principal energy, update magnitude, and forget-gradient coupling magnitude, then updates only the top-ranked subset. On the primary model, MAST induces statistically significant target forgetting (MATH forget 45/150 to 37/150; McNemar p=0.0078) while preserving GSM8K (+0.8 pp) and MATH retain (-0.5 pp). The advantage reproduces across seeds, NPO/SimNPO objectives, and Qwen3, where MAST preserves GSM8K while full-parameter unlearning collapses it.

</details>


### [277] [SCAN: Enhance Time Series Anomaly Detection via Multi-Scale Neighborhood-Centered Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19255)
*Xingze Zheng,Hanyin Cheng,Siyuan Wang,Yiting Hao,Peng Chen,Yuan Jun,Yang Shu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCAN enhances reconstruction-based time series anomaly detection by introducing multi-scale clustering to provide dual detection criteria (reconstruction error + cluster membership probability) and using neighborhood-centered representations for improved clustering, achieving state-of-the-art performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection methods suffer from over-generalization (anomalies reconstructed too well, leading to missed detections) and under-generalization (normal patterns poorly reconstructed, causing false alarms). These two issues are inherently difficult to balance, motivating the need for an additional mechanism to constrain and guide the reconstruction process.

Method: SCAN operates at two levels: (1) At the representation level, it integrates cluster center representations of normal patterns to constrain the model toward reconstructing representative normal patterns, mitigating the dominance of powerful model capacity. (2) At the anomaly criterion level, it derives an anomaly confidence score from cluster membership probabilities and combines it with reconstruction error for dual-criteria detection. Additionally, neighborhood-centered representations are extracted for multi-view clustering to improve clustering performance, which in turn boosts the effectiveness of both the cluster centers and the anomaly confidence score.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets from diverse application domains show that SCAN achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: Multi-scale clustering effectively addresses the over-generalization and under-generalization problems in reconstruction-based anomaly detection by providing both representational constraints and supplementary anomaly scoring, validated by SOTA results across diverse domains.

Abstract: Time series anomaly detection plays a crucial role in a wide range of real-world applications. Reconstruction-based methods have become the mainstream paradigm, but they suffer from over-generalization and under-generalization problems, which are challenging to balance. To address this, we introduce multi-scale clustering to enhance reconstruction-based methods. At the representation level, we integrate the cluster center representations of normal patterns to constrain the model to target representative normal patterns for reconstruction, preventing dominance of powerful capacity and representation capability. At the anomaly criterion level, we derive anomaly confidence score based on cluster membership probability and combine it with reconstruction error, providing dual criteria for detection. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the cluster center representations and anomaly confidence score depends on the clustering performance. Accordingly, we extract neighborhood-centered representations for multi-view clustering to improve clustering performance. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets from diverse application domains demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of SCAN.

</details>


### [278] [Detecting Hidden ML Training With Zero-Overhead Telemetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19262)
*Robi Rahman,Sabiha Tajdari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Evaluates adversarial robustness of GPU workload classification using zero-overhead NVML telemetry for AI governance. Tests 20 evasion strategies across 9 GPUs over 5 rounds, achieving 98.2% binary accuracy for training detection, with 43-87% accuracy against adversarially disguised workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI compute governance proposals rely on hardware-level GPU monitoring to detect regulated workloads (e.g., large training runs), but these schemes fail if adversaries can evade detection. The paper investigates whether content-agnostic NVML telemetry can withstand adversarial attacks designed to disguise training workloads.

Method: Uses only zero-overhead, privacy-preserving NVML (NVIDIA Management Library) telemetry signals — content-agnostic physical side-channel metrics (power, temperature, utilization) that require no access to model weights, data, or hyperparameters. Conducts 5 rounds of iterative adversarial evaluation: classifier is developed, evaders attempt to circumvent it, classifier is hardened, and the cycle repeats. Evaluates 20 evasion strategy families across 9 GPU models spanning 4 architecture generations.

Result: The developed classifier achieves 98.2% binary accuracy at distinguishing training from non-training workloads across the entire corpus. Against the most challenging adversarially disguised unexpected workloads, accuracy ranges from 43% to 87%, demonstrating partial but incomplete robustness to evasion.

Conclusion: GPU workload classification via NVML telemetry shows significant promise for AI compute governance, maintaining utility even under adversarial pressure. However, the 43-87% accuracy ceiling against sophisticated evaders indicates that monitoring alone may be insufficient and should be complemented by other governance mechanisms.

Abstract: Hardware-enabled monitoring of GPU workloads underpins many proposals for AI compute governance, but if developers can defeat monitoring mechanisms, such schemes are unworkable. We evaluate the adversarial robustness of GPU workload classification using only zero-overhead, privacy-preserving NVML telemetry: content-agnostic signals that observe physical effects of computation without accessing model weights, training data, or hyperparameters. Across 5 rounds of monitor-evader iteration, we evaluate 20 evasion strategy families on 9 GPU models spanning 4 architecture generations. We develop a classifier that achieves 98.2% binary accuracy at identifying training workloads across the whole corpus, and 43-87% accuracy against the most challenging unexpected workloads even when they are adversarially disguised.

</details>


### [279] [Risk Stratification for ICU Delirium using Pervasive Ambient Sensing Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19292)
*Jiaqing Zhang,Sabyasachi Bandyopadhyay,Miguel Contreras,Jessica Sena,Yuanfang Ren,Andrea Davidson,Ziyuan Guan,Tezcan Ozrazgat-Baslanti,Subhash Nerella,Azra Bihorac,Parisa Rashidi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Ambient sound and light data from ICUs can predict delirium onset. A convolutional neural network achieved AUC=0.80 using sound alone or combined with light. Sound was the dominant predictor, and adding light improved short-term (<1 week) predictions, offering a practical, interpretable signal for multimodal delirium risk estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Delirium in the ICU is common, serious, and difficult to predict early. While environmental factors like sound and light are plausible contributors, they are typically overlooked in risk assessments. The authors aimed to determine whether ambient sound pressure levels and light intensity can serve as independent predictors of delirium across multiple prediction horizons.

Method: Data were collected from 9 ICUs across 309 patients, measuring ambient light intensity and sound pressure levels. Four efficient sequential neural network models were evaluated for predicting delirium across 10 prediction-window sizes. Feature importance and direction of influence were assessed using SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) analysis.

Result: The convolutional model performed best, achieving AUC=0.80 on both sound-only and combined (sound+light) data. Sound features were the dominant predictors overall. Integrating sound with light improved short-term (<1 week) prediction, with the highest risk assigned immediately after the sensing period.

Conclusion: Passive ambient sensing—particularly sound—provides a clinically meaningful and interpretable signal for delirium risk estimation. This approach offers a practical pathway to enrich multimodal ICU prediction and prevention strategies.

Abstract: Delirium is a common and serious complication in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), associated with increased morbidity, prolonged hospital stays, and higher healthcare costs. Despite its prevalence, early prediction and prevention remain challenging. Environmental factors such as ambient sound and light may influence the onset of delirium, yet they are often overlooked in risk assessments. In this study, we examined whether light intensity and sound pressure levels can independently predict delirium across multiple prediction horizons. We evaluated four efficient sequential neural network models on data collected from 9 ICUs across 309 patients to predict delirium for 10 prediction-window sizes. We reported feature importance and direction of influence using Shapley Additive Explanations analysis. The convolutional model achieved the strongest discrimination, with AUC = 0.80 on sound data and on combined data. Sound features were the dominant predictors overall. Integrating sound with light improved short-term ($<1$ week) prediction, with the combined model assigning the highest risk immediately after the sensing period. These findings suggest that passive ambient sensing, especially sound, can add a clinically meaningful, interpretable signal for delirium risk estimation and offer a practical pathway to enrich multimodal ICU prediction and prevention strategies.

</details>


### [280] [Does VLA Even Know the Basics? Measuring Commonsense and World Knowledge Retention in Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19297)
*Nikita Kachaev,Andrey Moskalenko,Matvey Skripkin,Nikita Kurlaev,Daria Pugacheva,Albina Burlova,Mikhail Kolosov,Denis Shepelev,Andrey Kuznetsov,Elena Tutubalina,Aleksandr I. Panov,Alexey K. Kovalev,Vlad Shakhuro*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Act2Answer proposes a lightweight evaluation protocol that converts VLM knowledge benchmarks into embodied tabletop action episodes, using object-placement as answer selection. It reveals that VLA models retain solid knowledge on simple concepts but show larger gaps on richer semantics compared to their source VLMs, with answer-relevant signals peaking in middle layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning pretrained VLMs into embodied VLA models may cause catastrophic forgetting of commonsense and factual knowledge, but existing evaluation conflates missing knowledge with poor low-level control. A clean, action-grounded protocol is needed to isolate knowledge retention from control capability.

Method: Act2Answer converts each knowledge-probe question into a short tabletop manipulation episode where the agent places an object to select among candidate answers. Success depends on correct action selection, yielding an action-grounded success rate. The authors also introduce layerwise intent probing to localize where answer-relevant information resides across the VLM backbone and action head. Evaluation covers 7 VLA models and 9 VLM baselines across diverse commonsense and world-knowledge categories.

Result: VLAs show solid performance on simple concepts but larger gaps on richer semantic categories relative to their source VLMs. VQA co-training correlates with better knowledge retention. Layerwise probing reveals that answer-relevant signals peak in middle VLA layers and attenuate in upper layers.

Conclusion: Act2Answer provides a reliable, control-confounded evaluation of knowledge retention in embodied VLA models, revealing systematic patterns of knowledge degradation and informing better co-training strategies for future VLA development.

Abstract: Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically obtained by fine-tuning powerful pretrained VLMs on robotics data, yet it is unclear how much commonsense and factual knowledge they retain after adaptation. Failures on knowledge-sensitive tasks are ambiguous, conflating missing knowledge with poor generalization of low-level control. We introduce Act2Answer, a lightweight protocol that adapts VLM knowledge benchmarks to VLA evaluation by requiring agents to answer through action. Each question becomes a short tabletop episode where the agent performs a single object-placement action to select among candidate answers, yielding an action-grounded success rate with reduced control confounds. We curate a test suite of such environments across diverse commonsense and world-knowledge categories and introduce layerwise intent probing to localize answer-relevant information across the VLM backbone and action head. In a large-scale study of 7 VLA models and 9 VLM baselines, we systematically rank models across categories, finding that VLAs show solid performance on simple concepts while exhibiting larger gaps on richer semantic categories relative to their source VLMs, that VQA co-training is associated with better knowledge retention, and that answer-relevant signals peak in middle VLA layers but attenuate in upper layers. Act2Answer is available at https://tttonyalpha.github.io/act2answer/.

</details>


### [281] [P-K-GCN: Physics-augmented Koopman-enhanced Graph Convolutional Network for Deep Spatiotemporal Super-resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19303)
*Xizhuo,Zhang,Zekai Wang,Fei Liu,Bing Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes P-K-GCN, a Physics-augmented Koopman-enhanced Graph Convolutional Network for spatiotemporal super-resolution on irregular geometries. It combines spline-based GCN for spatial dependencies, Koopman operator theory for linearized temporal dynamics in latent space, and physics-based loss for physical consistency. Theoretical analysis shows reduced Rademacher complexity and tighter generalization bounds. The method is validated on 3D cardiac electrodynamics reconstruction, outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-fidelity spatiotemporal simulation is computationally prohibitive. Existing data-driven super-resolution methods lack physical constraints, and simple physics-informed learning fails on irregular spatial geometries and complex temporal dynamics. There is a need for a method that jointly handles irregular geometries, nonlinear dynamics, and physical consistency.

Method: P-K-GCN integrates three components: (1) a continuous spline-based Graph Convolutional Network that extracts spatial dependencies directly from coarse irregular graphs; (2) Koopman operator theory to project nonlinear dynamics into a compact latent space where temporal progression becomes linear; (3) a physics-based loss term augmenting the optimization objective to enforce adherence to governing physical laws. A rigorous theoretical analysis is provided, linking physics augmentation and Koopman regularization to reduced Rademacher complexity and tighter generalization bounds.

Result: Numerical experiments on 3D cardiac electrodynamics demonstrate that P-K-GCN achieves superior accuracy compared to baseline models when reconstructing high-resolution spatiotemporal data from sparse low-resolution measurements.

Conclusion: The proposed P-K-GCN framework effectively addresses spatiotemporal super-resolution on irregular geometries by combining spline-based GCN, Koopman operator theory, and physics-based loss. Both theoretical guarantees and empirical results on cardiac electrodynamics confirm its superior accuracy and robustness over existing methods.

Abstract: High-fidelity simulation of spatiotemporal dynamics is computationally prohibitive, necessitating efficient super-resolution techniques to reconstruct high-resolution data from coarse-grained inputs. Traditional data-driven methods often lack physical constraints, and simple physics-informed learning struggles with irregular spatial geometries and intricately evolving temporal dynamics. To tackle these challenges, we propose a Physics-augmented Koopman-enhanced Graph Convolutional Network (P-K-GCN) for spatiotemporal super-resolution on irregular geometries. Specifically, a continuous spline-based GCN is first designed to extract spatial dependencies directly from coarse graph, and Koopman operator theory is incorporated to project the nonlinear dynamics into a compact latent space where temporal progression is linearized. Second, we augment the optimization objective with a physics-based loss to force the data-driven reconstructions to adhere to physical laws for improving predictive fidelity and robustness. Finally, we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis, establishing that the physics augmentation and Koopman regularization mathematically guarantees a reduction in super-resolution error by diminishing Rademacher complexity and tightening generalization bounds. We evaluate our framework on reconstructing spatially high-resolution cardiac electrodynamics across a 3D heart geometry from sparse low-resolution measurements. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy compared to baseline models.

</details>


### [282] [Diffusion-Proof: Recipe for Formal Theorem Proving Beyond Auto-Regressive Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19315)
*Ruida Wang,Rui Pan,Pengcheng Wang,Shizhe Diao,Tong Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Diffusion-Proof is the first framework to train and apply diffusion LLMs for formal theorem proving, comprising two models — dLLM-Prover-7B for whole-proof writing and dLLM-Corrector-7B for local proof correction via bi-directional infilling. It outperforms AR LLM baselines by 1.61% on ProofNet-Test and 6.14% on MiniF2F-Test, and solves an IMO problem that DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B could not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Auto-regressive LLMs suffer from long-range coherence degradation and compounding errors over long sequences in formal theorem proving. Diffusion LLMs, which generate via iterative multi-token denoising, offer a promising alternative but remain largely unexplored for formal mathematics, where coherence is critical.

Method: The framework introduces two diffusion-based models: (1) dLLM-Prover-7B for whole-proof generation with long-range coherent tactic usage, and (2) dLLM-Corrector-7B, a block diffusion-based correction model that exploits dLLM infilling capabilities for local proof correction using bi-directional context.

Result: Diffusion-Proof achieves absolute improvements of 1.61% on ProofNet-Test and 6.14% on MiniF2F-Test over an AR LLM baseline trained on the same dataset. It also solves one IMO problem unsolved by DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B.

Conclusion: Diffusion-Proof demonstrates that diffusion LLMs offer unique advantages over auto-regressive models for formal theorem proving, particularly in maintaining long-range coherence and enabling bi-directional proof correction.

Abstract: Enhancing the formal math reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) has become a key focus in both mathematical and computer science communities in recent years. While significant progress has been made in using state-of-the-art Auto-Regressive (AR) LLMs for formal theorem proving, these models suffer from inherent limitations. Their next-token prediction generation methods may yield suboptimal performance due to the challenges of long-range coherence and the compounding of errors over long sequences. Recent advancements in diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), which generate text through iterative denoising of a multi-token block, offer a promising alternative. However, the application of dLLMs to formal mathematics, where maintaining long-range coherence is critical, remains largely understudied. To address the challenges above, we propose **Diffusion-Proof**, to the best of our knowledge, the first framework to train and apply dLLMs for formal theorem proving. Our frameworks contain training and inference methods for two models. The first one is *dLLM-Prover-7B*, which performs whole-proof writing with long-range coherent tactic usage. The second one is *dLLM-Corrector-7B*, which is a novel large block diffusion-based correction model. It leverages the in-filling capabilities of dLLMs to perform local proof correction using bi-directional information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that **Diffusion-Proof** relatively significantly outperforms the AR LLM baseline trained under the same dataset. **Diffusion-Proof** achieves an absolute improvement of **1.61%** on ProofNet-Test and **6.14%** on MiniF2F-Test benchmarks compare to the baseline. Notably, **Diffusion-Proof** successfully resolves one IMO problem that more advanced thinking model DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B could not solve, showcasing the unique advantage of dLLMs in formal theorem proving.

</details>


### [283] [Explaining Attention with Program Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19317)
*Amiri Hayes,Belinda Li,Jacob Andreas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a method to approximate transformer attention heads with human-readable Python programs. By prompting a language model with attention matrix summaries, generating candidate programs, and re-ranking them based on held-out performance, the authors show that <1,000 programs can reproduce attention patterns at >75% IoU similarity, and replacing 25% of heads with programmatic surrogates incurs only a 16% perplexity increase across GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Llama-3B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interpretable deep learning has long sought to replace opaque neural computations with symbolic, human-meaningful descriptions. Existing interpretability methods often produce explanations that are not executable or fail to capture functional behavior precisely. The paper is motivated by the need for a scalable pipeline that reverse-engineers neural components—specifically attention heads—into executable code, enabling genuine symbolic transparency rather than post-hoc approximations.

Method: The proposed pipeline has three stages: (1) For a target attention head, compute attention matrices over a random sample of training sentences. (2) Prompt a pre-trained language model with a textual summary of these attention patterns, asking it to generate Python programs that reproduce the attention behavior from input text alone. (3) Re-rank the generated programs by evaluating how accurately they predict attention patterns on held-out inputs (measured via Intersection-over-Union). The top-ranked programs serve as programmatic surrogates that can functionally replace the original attention heads.

Result: On GPT-2, TinyLlama-1.1B, and Llama-3B using the TinyStories dataset: fewer than 1,000 generated programs achieve average IoU similarity above 75% with original attention patterns. Replacing 25% of attention heads with programmatic surrogates across the three models results in only a 16% average increase in perplexity, while downstream QA benchmark performance is largely maintained.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates a scalable, effective pipeline for reverse-engineering transformer attention heads into executable, human-readable Python programs. This advances the goal of symbolic transparency in neural models by showing that programmatic surrogates can faithfully approximate and functionally replace neural components with minimal performance degradation.

Abstract: A longstanding goal of research on interpretable deep learning is to replace opaque neural computations with human-meaningful symbolic descriptions. In this paper, we propose an approach for approximating the behavior of components of deep networks with executable programs. We focus on attention heads in transformer language models. For a given head, we first compute its associated attention matrices on a collection of randomly selected training examples. Next, we prompt a pre-trained language model with a summary of these matrices, and instruct it to generate a set of Python programs that can reproduce the associated attention patterns given only text from the input sentence. Finally, we re-rank programs according to how well our final set of programs predict behavior on held-out inputs. We demonstrate that a set of fewer than 1,000 such generated programs can reproduce the attention patterns of heads in GPT-2, TinyLlama-1.1B, and Llama-3B, achieving an average Intersection-over-Union similarity above 75% on TinyStories. Moreover, the best-fit programs can replace neural attention heads without substantially affecting model behavior: replacing 25% of attention heads with programmatic surrogates across the three models incurs only a 16% average perplexity increase, while maintaining performance on a variety of downstream question answering benchmarks. This work contributes a scalable pipeline for reverse-engineering attention heads in transformer models using human-readable, executable code, advancing a path toward symbolic transparency in neural models.

</details>


### [284] [UBP2: Uncertainty-Balanced Preference Planning for Efficient Preference-based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19328)
*Mohamed Nabail,Leo Cheng,Jingmin Wang,Nicholas Rhinehart*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UBP2 is a model-based preference-based RL method that actively explores by jointly reasoning over uncertainties in reward, dynamics, and value functions, achieving superior sample efficiency with sublinear regret guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing preference-based RL methods rely on passive data collection, suffering from poor sample efficiency, especially early in learning. There is a need for an active exploration strategy that is principled rather than relying on ad hoc heuristics.

Method: UBP2 uses ensembles of reward, dynamics, and value function models. It evaluates candidate trajectories via a unified score combining expected reward, terminal value, and epistemic uncertainty. Planning under this objective naturally balances exploitation and information acquisition. Regret analysis is provided for both finite-horizon and infinite-horizon settings.

Result: Experiments on Meta-World demonstrate that UBP2 achieves substantially higher sample efficiency compared to model-free preference-based methods and non-optimistic model-based baselines.

Conclusion: Joint reasoning over uncertainties in reward, dynamics, and value functions enables principled active exploration in preference-based RL, leading to strong empirical performance and formal regret guarantees.

Abstract: Preference-based RL provides an approach to learning reward models from pairwise comparisons of behaviors, bypassing the need for explicit reward design. However, existing methods typically rely on passive data collection and suffer from poor sample efficiency, especially during the early stages of learning. We introduce a model-based approach that actively directs exploration by jointly reasoning over uncertainties in the reward, dynamics, and value functions. Our method, Uncertainty-Balanced Preference Planning (UBP2), uses ensembles of reward, dynamics, and value function models to evaluate candidate trajectories according to a unified score that combines expected reward, terminal value, and epistemic uncertainty. Planning under this objective yields an explicit tradeoff between exploitation and information acquisition without requiring ad hoc exploration heuristics. Under standard regularity assumptions, we establish sublinear regret guarantees for both finite-horizon and infinite-horizon settings. Empirically, experiments on the Meta-World benchmark show UBP2 achieves substantially higher sample efficiency than model-free preference-based methods and non-optimistic model-based baselines.

</details>
